Itaque per oves hoc loco, innocentes et mites notantur; qui septem millia referuntur, quia septenario designatur perfectio in septemplici dono Spiritus Sancti, quo isti ad numerum quemdam perfectum assurgunt, quem Mille insinuat.
paras.en: [[1:3|And his possession was seven thousand sheep|Et fuit possessio ejus septem millia ovium]]. Although all things are Christ's according to his Godhead by right of creation, and all things are also subject to his humanity, above all by reason of its hypostatic union with the Word, yet certain men are said to be Christ's in a special way, by predestination and grace. Of these he declares: [[John 6:37|All that the Father giveth to me shall come to me|Omne quod dat mihi Pater, ad me veniet]]. And the Apostle to the Ephesians: God [[Eph 1:4|chose us in him before the foundation of the world|elegit nos in Christo ante mundi constitutionem]]. And again: [[Eph 1:5|hath predestinated us unto the adoption of children through Jesus Christ|Prædestinavit nos in adoptionem filiorum per Jesum Christum]] [[Eph 1:5|according to the purpose of his will|secundum propositum voluntatis suæ]]. These, according to their different properties and virtues, are designated by the names of different animals, at times even in the letter of Scripture, as in Isaias, where we have: [[Is 11:6|The wolf shall dwell with the lamb: and the leopard shall lie down with the kid: the calf and the lion, and the sheep shall abide together|Habitabit lupus cum agno, et pardus cum hœdo accubabit; vitulus, ovis et leo simul morabuntur]]. So by the sheep in this place the innocent and meek are meant; and they are numbered at seven thousand because by the number seven is signified the perfection in the sevenfold gift of the Holy Ghost, by which these rise to a certain perfect number, which a thousand indicates.

paras.t: Et tria millia camelorum. Per camelos, gentiles vitiis torti instar cameli expressi sunt: qui per tres virtutes theologicas fidemque supergloriosæ Trinitatis ad virtutum æqualitatem venerunt: et Christi possessio facti sunt, qui olim idolis servientes, a dæmonibus possidebantur. Quingenta quoque juga boum. Per boves terram arantes, intelliguntur prædicatores, audientium corda ad pœnitentiæ dolorem divinique seminis susceptionem scindentes: quod et Paulus insinuat, illud legis allegando præceptum, Non obturabis os bovi trituranti. Isti ad millenarium perducuntur: quingenta enim juga, quingenta sunt paria, scilicet mille; quoniam vitæ perfectio per mille signata, ad aliorum doctores, pastores et prædicatores præcipue pertinet. Et quingentæ asinæ. Per asinas onerum ac hominum portatrices, rudes plebes audientium ac obedientium exprimuntur: quæ quingentæ feruntur, quia si mediam prædicatorum sanctorum ac magistrorum suorum perfectionem attingant, magnum est eis. Ac familia multa nimis, id est reliqua fidelium turba horum animalium proprietatibus non expressa: tot namque sunt gradus, status et ordines, virtutes ac proprietates credentium, quod paucis nominibus nequeunt explicari.
paras.en: [[1:3|and three thousand camels|Et tria millia camelorum]]. By the camels are expressed the Gentiles, twisted by vices like a camel, who through the three theological virtues and the faith of the most glorious Trinity have come to an evenness of virtues [as if the camel's crooked back were made level], and have become Christ's possession, they who once, serving idols, were possessed by demons. [[1:3|five hundred yoke of oxen|Quingenta quoque juga boum]]. By the oxen that plough the earth are understood the preachers, who cleave the hearts of their hearers to the sorrow of penance and to the receiving of the divine seed: which Paul too indicates, citing that precept of the law, [[1 Cor 9:9|Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn|Non obturabis os bovi trituranti]][[Deut 25:4||]]. These are brought up to a thousand: for five hundred yoke are five hundred pairs, that is, a thousand; since the perfection of life, signified by a thousand, belongs chiefly to the teachers of others, to pastors and preachers. [[1:3|and five hundred she asses|Et quingentæ asinæ]]. By the she asses, bearers of burdens and of men, are expressed the simple common folk who hear and obey: they are put at five hundred because, if they attain to half the perfection of their holy preachers and masters, it is a great thing for them. [[1:3|and a family exceedingly great|Ac familia multa nimis]], that is, the remaining crowd of the faithful, not expressed by the properties of these animals: for so many are the degrees, states and orders, the virtues and properties of believers, that they cannot be set forth in a few names.

paras.t: Eratque vir ille magnus inter omnes orientales, id est præ cunctis electis, in splendore lucis æternæ degentibus, et fervore Solis justitiæ inflammatis. Denique ipse Christus a Zacharia Oriens appellatur, Domino prædicente: Ecce ego adducam servum meum Orientem. De quo legitur et in Luca: Visitavit nos Oriens ex alto. Christus autem ut Deus, magnitudinis, id est perfectionis, est simpliciter infinitæ; secundum assumptam quoque naturam, major, dignior sive perfectior est omnibus creaturis simul acceptis.
paras.en: [[1:3|and this man was great among all the people of the east|Eratque vir ille magnus inter omnes orientales]], that is, above all the elect, who dwell in the splendour of the eternal light and are set on fire by the heat of the Sun of justice [orientales, the people of the east, are taken as those of the sunrise]. Indeed Christ himself is called the Orient by Zacharias, the Lord foretelling: [[Zach 3:8|behold, I WILL BRING MY SERVANT THE ORIENT|Ecce ego adducam servum meum Orientem]]. And of him we read in Luke too: [[Luke 1:78|the Orient from on high hath visited us|Visitavit nos Oriens ex alto]]. Christ as God is of a greatness, that is, of a perfection, simply infinite; and according to the nature he assumed, he is greater, worthier or more perfect than all creatures taken together.

paras.t: Et ibant filii ejus et filiæ, et faciebant convivia, id est, spirituales epulas cœlestis prædicationis præbebant, per domos, id est in diversis hominum locis, terris ac mansionibus, unusquisque in die suo, id est tempore sibi divinitus præordinato; vel, In die suo, id est in mentis suæ illustratione desuper sibi facta. Sicut enim ignorantia nox cordis vocatur, ita illuminatio dies est ejus, dicente Apostolo: Nos qui diei sumus, sobrii simus. Christus vero, ut in Evangelio patet, Apostolos misit ad prædicandum solis Judæis ante passionem; postea misit eos ad omnes gentes, dicens: Euntes in mundum universum, prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ. Præterea in Actis docemur, quemadmodum filii Christi in primitiva Ecclesia erant simul omnia habentes communia. Quotidie quoque perdurantes unanimiter in templo, et frangentes circa domos panem, sumebant cibum cum exsultatione et simplicitate cordis, collaudantes Deum et habentes gratiam ad omnem plebem. Septem autem diaconis ad mensas providentibus, Apostoli ministerio verbi, id est prædicationi, instabant, quilibet utique die et hora competenti, quamvis sæpe plures die eodem. De hoc Psalmista prædixit: Justi epulentur et exsultent in conspectu Dei. De spirituali quoque convivio, quod in refectione veritatis consistit, loquitur Plato in primo Timæi: Ergone, inquiens, magnifice invitatus sum hodie!
paras.en: [[1:4|And his sons went|Et ibant filii ejus]], and his daughters, [[1:4|and made a feast|et faciebant convivia]], that is, they set out the spiritual banquets of heavenly preaching, [[1:4|by houses|per domos]], that is, in the different places, lands and dwellings of men, [[1:4|every one in his day|unusquisque in die suo]], that is, at the time divinely foreordained for him; or, [[1:4|in his day|In die suo]], that is, in the enlightening of his mind given him from above. For as ignorance is called the night of the heart, so enlightenment is its day, as the Apostle says: [[1 Thess 5:8|let us, who are of the day, be sober|Nos qui diei sumus, sobrii simus]]. Christ, as is plain in the Gospel, sent the Apostles to preach to the Jews alone before the passion[[Matt 10:5||]]; afterwards he sent them to all nations[[Matt 28:19||]], saying: [[Mark 16:15|Go ye into the whole world and preach the gospel to every creature|Euntes in mundum universum, prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ]]. Moreover we are taught in the Acts how the sons of Christ in the primitive Church were together, having all things in common[[Acts 2:44||]] [one margin reference here is illegible; it may be Acts 4:32, where the same is said]. [[Acts 2:46|And continuing daily with one accord in the temple and breaking bread from house to house, they took their meat with gladness and simplicity of heart|Quotidie quoque perdurantes unanimiter in templo, et frangentes circa domos panem, sumebant cibum cum exsultatione et simplicitate cordis]], [[Acts 2:47|Praising God and having favour with all the people|collaudantes Deum et habentes gratiam ad omnem plebem]]. And while seven deacons provided for the tables, the Apostles were instant in the ministry of the word, that is, in preaching, each at the day and hour that suited, though often several on the same day. Of this the Psalmist foretold: [[Ps 67:4|let the just feast, and rejoice before God|Justi epulentur et exsultent in conspectu Dei]]. Of the spiritual banquet too, which consists in the refreshment of truth, Plato speaks in the first book of the Timaeus, saying: So I am splendidly entertained today! [the first word is hard to read in the print]

paras.t: Et mittentes vocabant tres sorores suas, ut comederent et biberent cum eis, id est, inferiores fidelium status, seu congregationes devotas, ad refectionem et consolationem invitabant internam, implentes quod ait Salvator: Gratis accepistis, gratis date. Secundum Gregorium bene dicitur, Ut comederent et biberent cum eis: quia Scriptura aliquando nobis cibus est, aliquando potus. Cibus, in obscurioribus locis, quia quasi exponendo frangitur, spiritualiterque glutitur: potus, in locis apertioribus, quia ita sorbetur ut invenitur.
paras.en: [[1:4|And sending, they called their three sisters|Et mittentes vocabant tres sorores suas]], [[1:4|to eat and drink with them|ut comederent et biberent cum eis]], that is, they invited the lower states of the faithful, or the devout congregations, to inward refreshment and consolation, fulfilling what the Saviour says: [[Matt 10:8|freely have you received, freely give|Gratis accepistis, gratis date]]. According to Gregory it is well said, [[1:4|to eat and drink with them|Ut comederent et biberent cum eis]], because Scripture is sometimes food to us, sometimes drink: food in the more obscure places, because it is, as it were, broken by expounding and swallowed spiritually; drink in the plainer places, because it is drunk down just as it is found.

paras.t: Quumque in orbem transissent dies convivii, id est, prædicationes in locis diversis hinc inde peragerentur. Scribitur quippe in Luca: Designavit Dominus Jesus et alios septuaginta duos discipulos, et misit illos binos et binos ante faciem suam in omnem civitatem et locum, quo ipse erat venturus. Quibus et prædicare præcepit: specialiter autem direxit ad prædicandum Apostolos. Mittebat ad eos Job: id est, Christus Spiritus Sancti instinctum ac gratias cordibus illorum infudit, suos ubique custodiens et gubernans. Et sanctificabat illos, id est a venialibus quæ quotidie incurrebant, præsertim ante Domini passionem, eos purgavit, virtutibusque ornavit.
paras.en: [[1:5|And when the days of their feasting were gone about|Quumque in orbem transissent dies convivii]], that is, when preachings were carried on here and there in different places. For it is written in Luke: [[Luke 10:1|the Lord appointed also other seventy-two. And he sent them two and two before his face into every city and place whither he himself was to come|Designavit Dominus Jesus et alios septuaginta duos discipulos, et misit illos binos et binos ante faciem suam in omnem civitatem et locum, quo ipse erat venturus]]. These too he commanded to preach; but in particular he directed the Apostles to preaching. [[1:5|Job sent to them|Mittebat ad eos Job]]: that is, Christ poured into their hearts the prompting and the graces of the Holy Ghost, guarding and governing his own everywhere. [[1:5|and sanctified them|Et sanctificabat illos]], that is, he cleansed them from the venial sins into which they fell daily, especially before the Lord's passion, and adorned them with virtues.

paras.t: Consurgensque diluculo. Certum est, Christum somno diuturno non indulsisse. Consurrexit quoque diluculo, id est, mentem erexit, vel potius erectam incessabiliter tenuit ad Patrem, exsistens in lumine creato gratiæ sibi infusæ, quod ad lumen gloriæ comparatur sicut aurora ad diem seu lucem meridianam; vel in lumine gloriæ sibi infuso, quod ad increatum Deitatis lumen se habet ut diluculum ad lucem clarissimam, atque ut imperfectum ad perfectum. Offerebat holocausta per singulos, id est fervida orationis sacrificia pro cunctis, ut decuit. Unde et scriptum est: Dirigatur oratio mea sicut incensum in conspectu tuo. Et in Luca inducitur: Exiit Jesus in montem orare, et erat pernoctans in oratione Dei.
paras.en: [[1:5|and rising up early|Consurgensque diluculo]] It is certain that Christ did not indulge in long sleep. He also rose early, that is, he lifted up his mind, or rather kept it unceasingly lifted up to the Father, abiding in the created light of the grace infused into him, which compares with the light of glory as the dawn with the day or the light of noon; or in the light of glory infused into him, which stands to the uncreated light of the Godhead as early dawn to the brightest light, and as the imperfect to the perfect. [[1:5|offered holocausts for every one of them|Offerebat holocausta per singulos]], that is, fervent sacrifices of prayer for all, as was fitting. Hence it is also written: [[Ps 140:2|Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight|Dirigatur oratio mea sicut incensum in conspectu tuo]]. And in Luke we are told: [[Luke 6:12|he went out into a mountain to pray: and he passed the whole night in the prayer of God|Exiit Jesus in montem orare, et erat pernoctans in oratione Dei]].

paras.t: Dicebat enim: Ne forte. Sobrie loquitur, ad insinuandum arbitrii libertatem, sicut in Evangelio ait pater: Forsitan verebuntur filium meum. Peccaverint filii mei spirituales, quos non ignoravit esse infirmos et fragiles ante suam passionem; et benedixerint Deo, per sensum (ut dictum est) contrarium, in cordibus suis, id est, inhonoraverint Deum de donis sibi divinitus datis, laudem appetendo humanam, vel cogitando illicite. Sic faciebat Job cunctis diebus. Non dubium quin Christus quotidie oravit pro suis, quum et de ipso jam in cœlis regnante dicat Apostolus: Qui etiam interpellat pro nobis. Et Joannes in prima sua Canonica: Advocatum habemus apud Patrem Jesum Christum justum; et ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris.
paras.en: [[1:5|For he said: Lest perhaps|Dicebat enim: Ne forte]]. He speaks with restraint, to indicate the freedom of the will, as the father says in the Gospel: [[Luke 20:13|It may be, when they see him, they will reverence him|Forsitan verebuntur filium meum]] [Denis's wording, they will reverence my son, is closer to Matt 21:37; the margin gives Luke]. [[1:5|my sons have sinned|Peccaverint filii mei]], his spiritual sons, whom he knew to be weak and frail before his passion; [[1:5|and have blessed God|et benedixerint Deo]], in the contrary sense (as was said) [that is, have cursed God: bless stands here for its opposite], [[1:5|in their hearts|in cordibus suis]], that is, have dishonoured God in the gifts divinely given them, by seeking human praise, or by thinking unlawfully. [[1:5|So did Job all days|Sic faciebat Job cunctis diebus]]. There is no doubt that Christ prayed daily for his own, since the Apostle says of him even now that he reigns in heaven: [[Rom 8:34|who also maketh intercession for us|Qui etiam interpellat pro nobis]]. And John in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 John 2:1|we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the just|Advocatum habemus apud Patrem Jesum Christum justum]]; [[1 John 2:2|and he is the propitiation for our sins|et ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris]].

paras.t: Quadam autem die, quum venissent filii Dei ut adsisterent coram Domino, adfuit inter eos etiam Satan. Juxta sensum præcedenti articulo positum, istud, sicut sequentia, applicatur ad Christum. Hic tamen per quamdam diem, intelligitur tempus dominicæ incarnationis seu primi adventus Christi, quo cœpit evangelica lex proponi ac prædicari: quod quum sit tempus gratiæ, merito dies vocatur. De quo ait Apostolus: Nox præcessit, dies autem appropinquavit. Et Isaias: In die illa erit germen Domini, scilicet Filius Dei, in magnificentia et gloria, et fructus terræ sublimis, videlicet Christus proles virginei ventris Mariæ. Unde prædixit Psalmista: Terra nostra dabit fructum suum. Hoc autem tempore cœperunt angeli sancti de hominum insolita conversione præcipue gratulari, atque eorum profectus Domino majestatis offerre: quo viso, Satan acerrime cœpit furere ac sævire.
paras.en: [[1:6|Now on a certain day, when the sons of God came to stand before the Lord, Satan also was present among them|Quadam autem die, quum venissent filii Dei ut adsisterent coram Domino, adfuit inter eos etiam Satan]]. In the sense set out in the preceding article, this, like what follows, is applied to Christ. Here, however, by *a certain day* is understood the time of the Lord's incarnation, or of Christ's first coming, in which the law of the Gospel began to be set forth and preached: and since this is the time of grace, it is rightly called a *day*. Of it the Apostle says: [[Rom 13:12|The night is passed And the day is at hand|Nox præcessit, dies autem appropinquavit]]. And Isaias: [[Is 4:2|In that day the bud of the Lord|In die illa erit germen Domini]], namely the Son of God, [[Is 4:2|shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth shall be high|in magnificentia et gloria, et fructus terræ sublimis]], namely Christ, the offspring of the virginal womb of Mary. Hence the Psalmist foretold: [[Ps 84:13|our earth shall yield her fruit|Terra nostra dabit fructum suum]]. And at this time the holy angels began to rejoice especially at the unwonted conversion of men, and to offer up their progress to the Lord of majesty; and at the sight of this Satan began to rage and storm most fiercely.

paras.t: Cui dixit Dominus, per Christi adventum nequitias ejus refrenans, eumque increpans: Unde venis? Ait: Circuivi terram, et perambulavi eam. Constat totum pene mundum idololatriæ fuisse deditum, dempta Judæa, usque ad Christi et Apostolorum prædicationem: imo Christus gentilibus paucis et raro legitur prædicasse. Apostolis autem post Spiritus Sancti missionem ad gentes pergentibus, prædicantibusque eisdem, innumerabiles convertebantur gentiles. Itaque Satan usque ad Christi et Apostolorum prædicationem pene ubique ad libitum circuivit, ambulavit et conculcavit.
paras.en: [[1:7|And the Lord said to him|Cui dixit Dominus]], restraining his wickedness by the coming of Christ, and rebuking him: [[1:7|Whence comest thou?|Unde venis?]] He said: [[1:7|I have gone round about the earth, and walked through it|Circuivi terram, et perambulavi eam]]. It is certain that almost the whole world, Judea excepted, was given over to idolatry until the preaching of Christ and the Apostles: indeed Christ is read to have preached to the Gentiles only to a few, and seldom. But when the Apostles, after the sending of the Holy Ghost, went to the Gentiles and preached to them, countless Gentiles were converted. So until the preaching of Christ and the Apostles Satan went round almost everywhere at his pleasure, walked about it and trampled it underfoot.

paras.t: Dixitque Dominus ad eum: Numquid considerasti servum meum Job, id est Christum: qui secundum naturam assumptam servus Dei Patris, sed et totius superadorandæ Trinitatis, imo et sui ipsius, secundum quod Deus est, appellatur. Exinanivit enim semetipsum, formam servi accipiens, juxta Apostolum. De quo per Isaiam loquitur Deus Pater: Ecce servus meus, suscipiam eum; electus meus, complacuit sibi in illo anima mea. Quomodo autem Deus interroget Satan, an electos suos in terra degentes consideravit, præcedenti articulo patuit. Gregorius quoque hic dicit: Dei ad Satan dicere, Numquid considerasti servum meum, hunc Job, scilicet Christum, est unigenitum Filium contra Satan in forma servi admirabilem demonstrare: eo enim quo illum tantæ virtutis in carne ostendit, superbienti adversario, quid dolens consideraret, indicavit.
paras.en: [[1:8|And the Lord said to him: Hast thou considered my servant, Job|Dixitque Dominus ad eum: Numquid considerasti servum meum Job]], that is, Christ: who according to the nature he assumed is called the servant of God the Father, and indeed of the whole Trinity, to be adored above all, and even of himself, according as he is God. For he [[Phil 2:7|emptied himself, taking the form of a servant|Exinanivit enim semetipsum, formam servi accipiens]], according to the Apostle. Of him God the Father speaks through Isaias: [[Is 42:1|Behold my servant, I will uphold him: my elect, my soul delighteth in him|Ecce servus meus, suscipiam eum; electus meus, complacuit sibi in illo anima mea]]. How God asks Satan whether he has considered his elect who dwell on earth was made clear in the preceding article. Gregory too says here: For God to say to Satan, [[1:8|Hast thou considered my servant|Numquid considerasti servum meum]], this Job, namely Christ, is to show forth his only-begotten Son against Satan as wonderful in the form of a servant: for in showing him to be of such great virtue in the flesh, he pointed out to the proud adversary what he should consider with grief.

paras.t: Quod non sit ei similis in terra, similitudine æqualitatis. Christus enim Deus et homo, in quantum Deus, infinite cunctis est altior; sed ut homo, habuit gratiam, virtutes et dona, secundum plenitudinem tantam, quantum capere potest natura mentis creatæ, ita quod tota capacitas fuit in eo impleta. Homo simplex, etc., sicut expositum est.
paras.en: [[1:8|that there is none like him in the earth|Quod non sit ei similis in terra]]: with a likeness of equality. For Christ, God and man, inasmuch as he is God, is infinitely higher than all; but as man he had grace, virtues and gifts in a fullness as great as the nature of a created mind can hold, so that its whole capacity was filled in him. [[1:8|a simple|Homo simplex]] man, etc., as has been explained.

paras.t: Cui respondit Satan: Numquid frustra timet Job, id est Christus ut homo, Deum? id est, timet te non propter te ex puro tui amore, sed propter dona a te sibi donata, et ne illis privetur. Satan, qui Christum tentavit, interdum suspicabatur quod Dei Filius esset homo ille, quem tantæ sanctitatis perpendit: unde tentando dicebat, Si Filius Dei es. Postea aliter sensit; timere tamen et colere Deum, illum non denegavit.
paras.en: [[1:9|And Satan answering, said|Cui respondit Satan]]: [[1:9|Doth Job|Numquid frustra timet Job]], that is, Christ as man, [[1:9|fear God in vain?|Deum?]] That is, does he fear thee not for thy own sake, out of pure love of thee, but for the gifts thou hast given him, and lest he be deprived of them? Satan, who tempted Christ, sometimes suspected that that man, whom he perceived to be of such great holiness, was the Son of God: hence in tempting him he said, [[Matt 4:3|If thou be the Son of God|Si Filius Dei es]] [the margin note here cannot be read; the words stand in Matt 4:3 and 4:6]. Afterwards he thought otherwise; yet he did not deny that he feared and worshipped God.

paras.t: Nonne tu vallasti eum, ita quod nec Herodes potuit eum infantem occidere, nec tentator unquam ad culpam inflectere, nec Judæi ante tempus præfixum perimere; ac domum ejus, id est conscientiæ suæ consistorium, quam tentatio penetrare nequivit; universamque substantiam ejus? id est totum corpus et animam, vel spirituales ipsius opes, gratias et virtutes, quas ei nullus tollere valuit. Operibus manuum ejus, id est actionibus suarum virtutum ac virium activarum, benedixisti, ita quod in omnibus prospere et sine difficultate agit promptissime cuncta quæ cupit; et possessio ejus, id est spiritualium bonorum exuberantia, crevit in terra, ita quod prævenisti eum in benedictionibus dulcedinis copiose. Præterea substantia Christi intelligi potest electorum collectio, quam, Deo vallante, Satan non potest dejicere, prout loquitur Christus: Oves meæ vocem meam audiunt, et non peribunt in æternum, et non rapiet eas quisquam de manu mea. Et nemo potest rapere de manu Patris mei.
paras.en: [[1:10|Hast thou not made a fence for him|Nonne tu vallasti eum]], so that neither could Herod kill him as an infant, nor the tempter ever bend him to sin, nor the Jews put him to death before the appointed time; [[1:10|and his house|ac domum ejus]], that is, the council-chamber of his conscience, which temptation could not enter; [[1:10|and all his substance|universamque substantiam ejus?]] that is, his whole body and soul, or his spiritual riches, the graces and virtues, which no one could take from him. [[1:10|the works of his hands|Operibus manuum ejus]], that is, the acts of his virtues and of his active powers, thou hast [[1:10|blessed|benedixisti]], so that in all things he does all that he wishes prosperously, without difficulty and most readily; [[1:10|and his possession|et possessio ejus]], that is, the abundance of spiritual goods, [[1:10|hath increased on the earth|crevit in terra]], so that [[Ps 20:4|thou hast prevented him with blessings of sweetness|prævenisti eum in benedictionibus dulcedinis]] [that is, gone before him with them] abundantly. Moreover, the substance of Christ can be understood as the gathering of the elect, which, while God fences it about, Satan cannot cast down, as Christ says: [[John 10:27|My sheep hear my voice|Oves meæ vocem meam audiunt]], [[John 10:28|and they shall not perish for ever. And no man shall pluck them out of my hand|et non peribunt in æternum, et non rapiet eas quisquam de manu mea]]. And [[John 10:29|no one can snatch them out of the hand of my Father|nemo potest rapere de manu Patris mei]].

paras.t: Sed extende paululum manum tuam, et tange cuncta quæ possidet, id est populos pertinentes ad ipsum, qui animalium nominibus exprimuntur, ut dictum est; nisi in facie benedixerit tibi. Dum Jesum Satan putavit non esse Filium Dei, seu Christum in lege promissum, sola Dei custoditum gratia æstimavit, et posse peccare putavit: ideo petiit licentiam hunc tentandi. Ac si aperte pronuntiet: Pulsatus afflictionibus, homo et peccator agnoscetur, qui in miraculis Dei Filius creditur.
paras.en: [[1:11|But stretch forth thy hand a little, and touch all that he hath|Sed extende paululum manum tuam, et tange cuncta quæ possidet]], that is, the peoples belonging to him, who are expressed by the names of animals, as has been said; [[1:11|and see if he bless thee not to thy face|nisi in facie benedixerit tibi]]. While Satan thought that Jesus was not the Son of God, or the Christ promised in the law, he judged him to be kept by the grace of God alone, and thought he could sin: therefore he asked leave to tempt him. As if he were saying openly: Struck with afflictions, he will be known for a man and a sinner, who in his miracles is believed to be the Son of God.

paras.t: Dixit ergo Dominus ad Satan: Ecce universa quæ habet, in manu tua sunt, id est, tentationis tuæ exercitio conceduntur. Universa ista quæ habuit Christus, agmina fuerunt populi olim electi, videlicet Judæorum, præsertim adhærentium Christo: quos tamen Satan tentavit, plurimosque eorum a Christo avertit, ut Evangelistæ testantur. Tantum in eum ne extendas manum tuam. Refrenavit quippe Dominus malignitatem Satanæ ac Judæorum rebellium a Christi occisione, quousque ipsemet Christus sciens tempus divinitus præstitutum adesse, sponte obtulit se ad mortem, quemadmodum fassus est: Nemo tollit animam meam a me, sed ego pono eam.
paras.en: [[1:12|Then the Lord said to Satan: Behold, all that he hath is in thy hand|Dixit ergo Dominus ad Satan: Ecce universa quæ habet, in manu tua sunt]], that is, they are granted to the exercise of thy temptation. All these things that Christ had were the hosts of the people once chosen, namely of the Jews, especially of those who clung to Christ: whom Satan nevertheless tempted, and turned very many of them away from Christ, as the Evangelists bear witness. [[1:12|only put not forth thy hand upon his person|Tantum in eum ne extendas manum tuam]]. For the Lord held back the malice of Satan and of the rebellious Jews from putting Christ to death, until Christ himself, knowing that the time divinely appointed was at hand, offered himself freely to death, as he declared: [[John 10:18|No man taketh it away from me: but I lay it down|Nemo tollit animam meam a me, sed ego pono eam]] [Denis has ‘my life’ (animam meam) where the Vulgate has ‘it’; the margin note here cannot be read].

paras.t: Quum autem quadam die filii et filiæ ejus comederent, et biberent vinum in domo fratris sui primogeniti, id est, quum Apostoli Christi, et ceteræ inferiorum sibi adhærentium congregationes, adhuc ante Christi passionem spiritualiter reficerentur prædicando soli populo Judæorum, dicente ad eos Christo, In viam gentium ne abieritis: qui Judaicus populus respectu populi gentilis postea conversi, quasi prior, major ac primogenitus fuit; nuntius venit ad Job, qui diceret: Boves arabant, et asinæ pascebantur juxta eos. Per boves (ut dictum est) doctores et prædicatores signantur. Habuerunt autem Judæi doctores, Scribas et Pharisæos, corda audientium seu simplices, qui per asinas intelliguntur, verbis legis ac Prophetarum serentes, juxta quos simpliciores quique verbo Dei utcumque reficiebantur.
paras.en: [[1:13|Now upon a certain day, when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine, in the house of their eldest brother|Quum autem quadam die filii et filiæ ejus comederent, et biberent vinum in domo fratris sui primogeniti]]: that is, when the Apostles of Christ, and the other companies of lesser folk who clung to him, were still, before Christ's passion, being refreshed spiritually by preaching to the people of the Jews alone, Christ saying to them, [[Matt 10:5|Go ye not into the way of the Gentiles|In viam gentium ne abieritis]]: and this Jewish people, in respect of the Gentile people converted afterwards, was as it were the earlier, the elder and the first-born; [[1:14|There came a messenger to Job, and said: The oxen were ploughing, and the asses feeding beside them|nuntius venit ad Job, qui diceret: Boves arabant, et asinæ pascebantur juxta eos]]. By the oxen (as has been said) the doctors and preachers are signified. And the Jews had doctors, the Scribes and Pharisees, who sowed with the words of the law and of the Prophets the hearts of their hearers, that is, of the simple, who are understood by the she-asses; and beside them all the simpler sort were refreshed in some fashion by the word of God.

paras.t: Et irruerunt Sabæi, id est dæmones tentatores. Sabæi enim, captivantes interpretantur; dæmones vero, animarum captores sunt, dicente ad Timotheum Apostolo: Resipiscant, scilicet homines mali, a laqueis diaboli, a quo captivi tenentur ad ipsius voluntatem. Tuleruntque omnia, id est, prædictorum Judæorum animas tenebris infidelitatis ceperunt et involverunt, ita quod Christum negabant; et pueros percusserunt gladio, eos videlicet qui juveniles affectiones, mores et sensus per sapientiam et virtutes non transcenderunt. Unde ad Timotheum dicit Apostolus: Juvenilia desideria fuge, sectare autem justitiam, caritatem et pacem. Per gladium vero acuta signatur tentatio, seu fraudulenta persuasio: de cujusmodi gladio scribitur, Gladius in labiis eorum.
paras.en: [[1:15|And the Sabeans rushed in|Et irruerunt Sabæi]], that is, the tempting demons. For *Sabeans* is interpreted ‘those who take captive’; and the demons are takers of souls, as the Apostle says to Timothy: [[2 Tim 2:26|they may recover themselves|Resipiscant]], namely evil men, [[2 Tim 2:26|from the snares of the devil by whom they are held captive at his will|a laqueis diaboli, a quo captivi tenentur ad ipsius voluntatem]]. [[1:15|and took all away|Tuleruntque omnia]], that is, they seized the souls of the said Jews and wrapped them in the darkness of unbelief, so that they denied Christ; [[1:15|and slew the servants with the sword|et pueros percusserunt gladio]] [pueri, ‘servants’, also means ‘boys’, hence what follows], namely those who had not risen above youthful affections, ways and feelings by wisdom and virtues. Hence the Apostle says to Timothy: [[2 Tim 2:22|flee thou youthful desires, and pursue justice, faith, charity and peace|Juvenilia desideria fuge, sectare autem justitiam, caritatem et pacem]]. And by the sword is signified sharp temptation, or deceitful persuasion: of such a sword it is written, [[Ps 58:8|a sword is in their lips|Gladius in labiis eorum]].

paras.t: Et evasi ego solus, ut nuntiarem tibi: quia non absolute omnes Scribæ et Pharisæi ac auditores eorum a Christo se averterunt, sed quidam eorum, quamvis pauci, sibi hæserunt. Hi per unum evadentem, ob paucitatem, notantur. Hinc per Jeremiam Deus prædixit, Salvabo vos unum de civitate, et duos de populo: insinuans paucitatem Judæorum credentium Christo, comparatione eorum qui credere contempserunt. Nuntiabatur autem quid Christo, non quasi ignoranti: nam et de Joannis Baptistæ discipulis scriptum est, quod decollato Joanne venerunt et nuntiaverunt Jesu. Gregorius autem per unum evadentem, intelligit sermonem propheticum, qui pereuntibus Judæis, sicut prædixit, ostenditur verax.
paras.en: [[1:15|and I alone have escaped to tell thee|Et evasi ego solus, ut nuntiarem tibi]]: for not all the Scribes and Pharisees and their hearers without exception turned away from Christ, but some of them, though few, clung to him. These are marked by the one who escapes, because they were few. Hence God foretold through Jeremias, [[Jer 3:14|I will take you, one of a city, and two of a kindred|Salvabo vos unum de civitate, et duos de populo]] [Denis has ‘I will save you … two of the people’, where the Vulgate has ‘I will take you … two of a kindred’], hinting at how few were the Jews who believed in Christ, compared with those who scorned to believe. And things were told to Christ, not as to one who did not know them: for of the disciples of John the Baptist too it is written that when John had been beheaded they [[Matt 14:12|came and told Jesus|venerunt et nuntiaverunt Jesu]]. Gregory, however, understands by the one who escapes the word of prophecy, which, as the Jews perish, is shown to be true, as it foretold.

paras.t: Quumque adhuc ille loqueretur, venit alter, et dixit: Ignis Dei cecidit de cœlo, et tactas oves puerosque consumpsit. Ignis iste de cœlo ruens, est flamma invidiæ, indignationis et iræ, de superiori parte populi Judæorum, puta de sacerdotum principibus ac magistratibus, qui cœlesti dignitate atque officio videbantur fulgere, ad simplices innocentesque cadens, qui per superiores præfatos decepti atque succensi sunt contra Christum. Quidam tamen pauci illorum fallacias evaserunt, qui per unum evadentem signantur. Vel ignis iste est ignis tentationis aeriarum potestatum, quæ Judæos contra Christum concitaverunt.
paras.en: [[1:16|And while he was yet speaking, another came, and said: The fire of God fell from heaven, and striking the sheep and the servants, hath consumed them|Quumque adhuc ille loqueretur, venit alter, et dixit: Ignis Dei cecidit de cœlo, et tactas oves puerosque consumpsit]]. This fire falling from heaven is the flame of envy, indignation and wrath, falling from the upper part of the people of the Jews, that is, from the chief priests and magistrates, who seemed to shine with a heavenly dignity and office, upon the simple and innocent, who were deceived and inflamed against Christ by those superiors. Some few, however, escaped their deceits, and these are signified by the one who escapes. Or this fire is the fire of temptation of the powers of the air, which stirred up the Jews against Christ.

paras.t: Sed et illo adhuc loquente, venit alius, et dixit: Chaldæi fecerunt tres turmas, et invaserunt camelos. Chaldæi interpretantur feroces seu dirigentes: quibus signantur atrocissimi atque fictissimi illi persecutionis Christi auctores, ejusque tentatores, qui aliorum directores in bono videri volebant, quum fuerint directores ad malum. Isti fecerunt tres turmas, dum Pharisæi et Sadducæi ac Herodiani inter se divisi, Christum tentare aggressi sunt. Et camelos, id est non solum Judæos vitiis tortos, sed et multos gentilium, qui ad diem festum confluxerant, Christumque videre cupiebant, atque ad fidei susceptionem se disponebant, prout in Joanne plenius fertur, averterunt a Christo, et traxerunt eosdem post se, præsertim in die Parasceves, omnibus persuadentes quod Jesus esset seductor: quanquam nonnulli illorum divinitus præservati, evaserint, qui per unum qui evasit, sunt figurati. Nec dubium quin more humano quidam adhærentium Christo, sæpe venerunt ad eum nuntiantes sibi quæ perceperunt aut conspexerunt de concernentibus ipsum.
paras.en: [[1:17|And while he also was yet speaking, there came another, and said: The Chaldeans made three troops, and have fallen upon the camels|Sed et illo adhuc loquente, venit alius, et dixit: Chaldæi fecerunt tres turmas, et invaserunt camelos]]. *Chaldeans* is interpreted ‘fierce’ or ‘directing’: by them are signified those most savage and most false authors of the persecution of Christ, and his tempters, who wished to seem the directors of others in good, though they were directors to evil. These [[1:17|made three troops|fecerunt tres turmas]] when the Pharisees and Sadducees and Herodians, divided among themselves, set about tempting Christ. And [[1:17|the camels|camelos]], that is, not only the Jews, twisted by vices, but also many of the Gentiles who had flocked together for the festival day[[John 12:20||]] and desired to see Christ[[John 12:21||]], and were disposing themselves to receive the faith, as is told more fully in John: these they turned away from Christ and drew after them, especially on the day of the Parasceve [that is, the day of preparation, the day of Christ's death], persuading everyone that Jesus was a seducer; although some of them, preserved by God, escaped, and these are figured by the one who escaped. Nor is there any doubt that, in human fashion, some of those who clung to Christ often came to him, telling him what they had perceived or seen concerning him.

paras.t: Adhuc loquebatur, et alius dicit: Filiis tuis et filiabus, id est Apostolis et collectionibus credentium eis subjectis, vescentibus et bibentibus vinum in domo fratris sui primogeniti, id est in habitatione Judaicæ plebis, sanctæ prædicationis deliciis amorose utentibus, repente ventus vehemens, id est grandis et impetuosa tentatio, irruit a regione deserti, id est, de infidelium cordibus, seu dæmonum a Deo relictorum suggestionibus prodiit contra fideles, et concussit quatuor angulos domus, id est, Synagogam ad infidelitatem commovit: quæ Synagoga seu domus quatuor angulis stabat, id est, in sacerdotibus et Scribis, Pharisæis quoque et senioribus populi seu judicibus ordinariis sustentabatur; quæ corruens, oppressit liberos tuos, et mortui sunt: quia Judæis taliter victis et prostratis a dæmonum tentamentis, ipsi Apostoli, quum Christus a Judæis comprehenderetur, carnali timore fugerunt, vitamque fidei perdiderunt. Unus tamen animus de numero credentium stetit invictus, quoniam Virgo beata nunquam in fide nutavit.
paras.en: [[1:18|He was yet speaking|Adhuc loquebatur]], and another says: [[1:18|Thy sons and daughters|Filiis tuis et filiabus]], that is, the Apostles and the gatherings of believers subject to them, [[1:18|were eating and drinking wine in the house of their eldest brother|vescentibus et bibentibus vinum in domo fratris sui primogeniti]], that is, in the dwelling of the Jewish people, lovingly enjoying the delights of holy preaching, [[1:19|A violent wind|repente ventus vehemens]], that is, a great and impetuous temptation, [[1:19|came on a sudden from the side of the desert|irruit a regione deserti]], that is, came forth against the faithful from the hearts of unbelievers, or from the suggestions of demons forsaken by God, [[1:19|and shook the four corners of the house|et concussit quatuor angulos domus]], that is, moved the Synagogue to unbelief: for this Synagogue or house stood on four corners, that is, it was upheld by the priests and Scribes, the Pharisees too[[Matt 27:62||]], and the ancients of the people[[Matt 26:3||]][[Matt 26:57||]] or ordinary judges; [[1:19|and it fell upon thy children, and they are dead|quæ corruens, oppressit liberos tuos, et mortui sunt]]: for when the Jews had been thus overcome and laid low by the temptations of the demons, the Apostles themselves, when Christ was seized by the Jews, fled in carnal fear[[Matt 26:56||]], and lost the life of faith. Yet one soul of the number of believers stood unconquered, since the Blessed Virgin never wavered in faith.

paras.t: Tunc surrexit Job: id est, his factis et cognitis, Christus justo judicio utens, contra reprobos mentem erexit. Hic dicit Gregorius: Surgit, dum contra reprobos judicium justitiæ exserit. Et scidit vestimenta sua, id est, populos Judæorum, qui Deo quasi vestis aliquando adhæserunt, in duo divisit, discernens reprobos ab electis, et præscitos usque in finem relinquens, electos vero ex Synagoga gratiosius sibi nectens. Unde per Jeremiam Dominus protestatur: Sicut adhæret lumbare ad lumbos viri, sic agglutinavi mihi omnem domum Israel. Et sicut nunc Ecclesia vestis est Christi, ita tunc vestis Dei fuerat Synagoga, sicut per Isaiam prædictum est: His omnibus quasi vestimento ornaberis.
paras.en: [[1:20|Then Job rose up|Tunc surrexit Job]]: that is, when these things had been done and made known, Christ, using just judgment, raised up his mind against the reprobate. Here Gregory says: He rises, when he puts forth the judgment of justice against the reprobate. [[1:20|and rent his garments|Et scidit vestimenta sua]], that is, he divided in two the peoples of the Jews, who once clung to God like a garment, separating the reprobate from the elect, and leaving to the end the foreknown [that is, those whom God foreknows will be lost], but binding the elect of the Synagogue to himself the more graciously. Hence the Lord declares through Jeremias: [[Jer 13:11|as the girdle sticketh close to the loins of a man, so have I brought close to me all the house of Israel|Sicut adhæret lumbare ad lumbos viri, sic agglutinavi mihi omnem domum Israel]]. And as the Church is now the garment of Christ, so then the Synagogue was the garment of God, as was foretold through Isaias: [[Is 49:18|thou shalt be clothed with all these as with an ornament|His omnibus quasi vestimento ornaberis]] [Denis's wording means ‘thou shalt be adorned with all these as with a garment’, where the Vulgate has ‘clothed … as with an ornament’; the margin note here cannot be read].

paras.t: Et tonso capite, corruens in terram, adoravit. Per pilos capitis, cogitationes affectionesque cordis solent signari. Quoniam ergo Salvator relictis juste reprobis illis Judæis, pro illorum salvatione cogitationes et affectiones assumptas abjecit (aliquo enim modo ante pro eis oravit, juxta illud in Psalmo, Pro eo ut me diligerent, detrahebant mihi, ego autem orabam), quasi caput totondit, corruitque in terram: quia et pereuntibus naturali condolebat affectu, et usque ad infima se humiliavit. Patrem quoque adoravit, secundum quod homo, et pro gentilitate rogavit, atque pro electis Judæis, apud Joannem loquens, Non pro his, puta Apostolis et electis Judæis, rogo tantum, sed et pro eis qui credituri sunt per verbum eorum in me, ut omnes sint unum.
paras.en: [[1:20|and having shaven his head, fell down upon the ground, and worshipped|Et tonso capite, corruens in terram, adoravit]]. By the hairs of the head the thoughts and affections of the heart are commonly signified. Since, then, the Saviour, having justly left those reprobate Jews, cast off the thoughts and affections he had taken up for their salvation (for in some manner he had prayed for them before, according to that in the Psalm, [[Ps 108:4|Instead of making me a return of love, they detracted me: but I gave myself to prayer|Pro eo ut me diligerent, detrahebant mihi, ego autem orabam]]), he as it were shaved his head, and fell to the ground: because he both grieved with natural affection for those who were perishing, and humbled himself to the lowest. He also worshipped the Father, according as he is man, and prayed for the Gentiles, and for the elect Jews, speaking in John: [[John 17:20|And not for them|Non pro his]], namely the Apostles and the elect Jews, [[John 17:20|only do I pray, but for them also who through their word shall believe in me|rogo tantum, sed et pro eis qui credituri sunt per verbum eorum in me]], [[John 17:21|That they all may be one|ut omnes sint unum]].

paras.t: Et dixit: Nudus egressus sum de utero matris meæ, et nudus revertar illuc. Compassionis dolorem, quo de pereuntibus Judæis Christus naturali amore affligebatur, ipse sapientissime temperavit, conformans dispositioni æternæ naturalem humanitatis affectum, et pensans quod ipse secundum quod homo, nihil habuit ex se ipso, et nisi ea quæ Deus sibi dedit ex tempore, ita quod corpore natus est nudus, pauperque rebus vixit in sæculo: ideo de illorum salvatione debuit contentari quos Deus prædestinavit salvandos per ipsum, nec de aliorum reprobatione, ablationeve immoderanter affligi.
paras.en: [[1:21|And said: Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither|Et dixit: Nudus egressus sum de utero matris meæ, et nudus revertar illuc]]. The sorrow of compassion with which Christ, out of natural love, was afflicted over the Jews who were perishing, he himself tempered most wisely, conforming the natural affection of his humanity to the eternal disposition, and weighing that he himself, as man, had nothing of himself, nothing but what God gave him in time, so that in body he was born naked, and lived in the world poor in goods: and so he ought to be content with the salvation of those whom God predestined to be saved through him, and not be afflicted beyond measure over the reprobation, or the taking away, of the others.

paras.t: Ideo subdit: Dominus Pater seu Trinitas, dedit eos qui salvarentur, scilicet prædestinatos: de quibus ait Christus, Omne quod dat mihi Pater, ad me veniet. Hos enim sua pietate et merito Christi gratiose convertit ad ipsum, quemadmodum ait: Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit eum. Dominus abstulit, id est, reprobos juste relinquit, et ab electis discernit. Sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est. Omnia enim quæcumque voluit Dominus, fecit in cœlo et in terra. De quo ad Ephesios ait Apostolus: Omnia operatur secundum propositum voluntatis suæ. Dei quippe voluntas, est prima entium causa, quæ nec irrationabilis esse potest, neque injusta, quum essentialiter sit ipsa divinæ mentis sapientia atque justitia. Sic et in Matthæo loquitur Christus: Confiteor tibi, Pater, Domine cœli et terræ, quia abscondisti hæc a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revelasti ea parvulis. Ita, Pater, quia sic placitum fuit ante te.
paras.en: And so he adds: [[1:21|The Lord|Dominus]], the Father or the Trinity, [[1:21|gave|dedit]] those who were to be saved, namely the predestined: of whom Christ says, [[John 6:37|All that the Father giveth to me shall come to me|Omne quod dat mihi Pater, ad me veniet]]. For these he converts to him graciously by his own goodness and the merit of Christ, as he says: [[John 6:44|No man can come to me, except the Father|Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater meus]] [[John 6:44|draw him|traxerit eum]]. [[1:21|the Lord hath taken away|Dominus abstulit]], that is, he justly leaves the reprobate, and separates them from the elect. [[1:21|as it hath pleased the Lord, so is it done|Sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est]]. For [[Ps 134:6|Whatsoever the Lord pleased he hath done, in heaven, in earth|quæcumque voluit Dominus, fecit in cœlo et in terra]]. Of this the Apostle says to the Ephesians: He [[Eph 1:11|worketh all things according to the counsel of his will|Omnia operatur secundum propositum voluntatis suæ]] [Denis has ‘purpose’ (propositum) where the Vulgate has ‘counsel’]. For the will of God is the first cause of beings, and it can be neither unreasonable nor unjust, since in its essence it is the very wisdom and justice of the divine mind. So too in Matthew Christ says: [[Matt 11:25|I confess to thee, O Father, Lord of Heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones|Confiteor tibi, Pater, Domine cœli et terræ, quia abscondisti hæc a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revelasti ea parvulis]]. [[Matt 11:26|Yea, Father: for so hath it seemed good in thy sight|Ita, Pater, quia sic placitum fuit ante te]].

paras.t: Sit nomen Domini benedictum. Christus secundum naturam assumptam gratias egit Deo de omni dono ejus ac dispensatione mysteriorum ipsius. Propter quod ait: Ego non quæro gloriam meam: et: Claritatem ab hominibus non accipio. Rursusque scriptum est: Jesus elevatis sursum oculis, dixit: Pater, gratias ago tibi quoniam audisti me.
paras.en: [[1:21|blessed be the name of the Lord|Sit nomen Domini benedictum]]. Christ, according to the nature he assumed, gave thanks to God for his every gift and for the dispensation of his mysteries. Therefore he says: [[John 8:50|I seek not my own glory|Ego non quæro gloriam meam]]; and: [[John 5:41|I receive not glory from men|Claritatem ab hominibus non accipio]]. And again it is written: [[John 11:41|Jesus lifting up his eyes, said: Father, I give thee thanks that thou hast heard me|Jesus elevatis sursum oculis, dixit: Pater, gratias ago tibi quoniam audisti me]].

paras.t: In omnibus his non peccavit Job, etc. Christus namque ut Deus, impeccabilitatem habuit per naturam, sed secundum humanitatem assumptam habuit eam per gratiam consummatam et plenam: quia ab incarnationis instanti fuit confirmatus in bono sublimius quam Beati in patria, præsertim quum fuerit comprehensor, quantum ad vires suæ animæ superiores. Unde et per beatificam divinitatis fruitionem fuit immobilitatus in Deo. Ideo dixit Judæis: Quis ex vobis arguet me de peccato? Et Isaias ait: Iniquitatem non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore ejus. Porro dolus in ore quanto apud homines prudentius callet, tanto apud Deum stultius desipit. Neque stultum quid contra Deum locutus est, quamvis dixerint infideles Judæi, Blasphemavit. Quum enim in forma Dei esset, non rapinam arbitratus est esse se æqualem Deo, secundum Apostolum ad Philippenses.
paras.en: [[1:22|In all these things Job sinned not|In omnibus his non peccavit Job]], etc. For Christ as God had sinlessness by nature, but according to the humanity he assumed he had it by grace, consummate and full: because from the instant of the incarnation he was confirmed in good more loftily than the blessed in the homeland, above all since he was a comprehensor [that is, one who already enjoys the vision of God, as the blessed do, and not only a wayfarer on the way to it] as to the higher powers of his soul. Hence through the beatific enjoyment of the Godhead he was also made immovable in God. Therefore he said to the Jews: [[John 8:46|Which of you shall convince me of sin?|Quis ex vobis arguet me de peccato?]] And Isaias says: [[Is 53:9|he hath done no iniquity, neither was there deceit in his mouth|Iniquitatem non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore ejus]] [Denis gives it in the words of 1 Pet 2:22, which quotes this verse]. Now the more shrewdly guile in the mouth is cunning before men, the more foolishly it plays the fool before God. [[1:22|nor spoke he any foolish thing against God|Neque stultum quid contra Deum locutus est]], although the unbelieving Jews said, [[Matt 26:65|He hath blasphemed|Blasphemavit]][[John 10:36||]]. For he, [[Phil 2:6|being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God|Quum enim in forma Dei esset, non rapinam arbitratus est esse se æqualem Deo]], according to the Apostle to the Philippians.

1.title: Expositio tropologica seu moralis ejusdem capituli primi.
1.title_en: Tropological or moral exposition of the same first chapter

paras.t: Moralitas seu tropologia instruit quid agendum, estque tropologicus sacræ sensus Scripturæ, dum ea quæ de Christo aut Sanctis scribuntur, ad nostram informationem moralem aptantur, trahuntur seu exponuntur.
paras.en: The moral sense, or tropology, teaches what is to be done; and it is the tropological sense of sacred Scripture when the things written of Christ or of the Saints are fitted, drawn, or expounded to our moral instruction.

paras.t: Porro, ut dictum est, Job interpretatur dolens; Hus, consiliator vel sapientia. Itaque, Vir erat in terra Hus, nomine Job. Per quem virum moraliter designatur quicumque fidelis, salubriter dolens, sua vel proximorum peccata deplangens, cœlestis desiderio patriæ incolatum hujus exsilii deflens, pro gratia proficiendi cum lacrimis orans, Christo propter se passo cordialiter condolens: et quod omnibus majus est istis, ex pura et fervida ad Deum affectione et complacentia ejus et ex congratulatione suæ beatitudinis prorsus immensæ, pias lacrimas fundit, ac intime dolet quod Deus a suis creaturis sic inhonoratur. Qui talis est, homo consilii est, et in terra sapientis, id est Ecclesia militante, veraciter habitat tanquam vividum Christi membrum. Sed, ut ait Gregorius, sunt quidam qui vitam suam negligunt; dumque transitoria appetunt, et æterna vel non intelligunt, vel intellecta parvipendunt, salubrem dolorem non sentiunt, nec sanum habere consilium curant, et esse se in bonis miseri putant. Simplex et rectus. Quicumque enim in statu salutis est, caritatem scilicet et gratiam gratum facientem habens, simplex est intentione, et rectus in opere. Ac timens Deum, filiali vel saltem initiali timore. Qui timores realiter idem dicuntur, si timor habitum nominet: non enim differunt, nisi secundum majus et minus perfectum. Qui autem solum servilem habet timorem, non est in caritate et gratia.
paras.en: Now, as has been said, Job is interpreted “grieving”; Hus, “counsellor” or “wisdom”. So: [[1:1|There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job|Vir erat in terra Hus, nomine Job]]. By this man is designated, in the moral sense, every faithful soul that grieves to its salvation: bewailing its own sins or those of its neighbours, lamenting the sojourn of this exile out of desire for the heavenly fatherland, praying with tears for the grace to advance, condoling from the heart with Christ who suffered for it; and, what is greater than all these, it sheds holy tears out of a pure and fervent affection towards God, out of delight in Him and rejoicing with Him in His wholly boundless beatitude, and it grieves inwardly that God is so dishonoured by His creatures. Whoever is such is a man of counsel, and truly dwells in the land of the wise, that is, in the Church militant, as a living member of Christ. But, as Gregory says, there are some who neglect their life: while they seek after passing things, and either do not understand eternal things or, understanding them, think little of them, they feel no wholesome grief, nor do they care to have sound counsel, and, wretches that they are, they think themselves well off. [[1:1|simple and upright|Simplex et rectus]]. For whoever is in the state of salvation, having charity, that is, and sanctifying grace [gratia gratum faciens: the grace that makes a man pleasing to God], is simple in intention and upright in deed. [[1:1|and fearing God|Ac timens Deum]], with a filial or at least an initial fear [initial fear: the fear of a beginner in charity, which still dreads punishment but already fears offending God]. These fears are said to be really the same, if fear names the habit; for they differ only as more and less perfect. But one who has only servile fear is not in charity and grace.

paras.t: Natique sunt ei septem filii, id est septem dona Spiritus Sancti, secundum Gregorium, et tres filiæ, id est tres virtutes theologicæ, secundum eumdem. Sed quum dona et virtutes theologicæ non habeantur nisi per creationem et infusionem a Spiritu Sancto, non videntur convenienter dici filii et filiæ hominis virtuosi: filii namque et filiæ oriuntur ab eo, cujus sunt filii ac filiæ. Ad quod dicendum videtur, quod virtutes et dona frequenter sumuntur ut nominant actum; actus autem eorum a nobis causantur, qui spiritualiter filii et filiæ appellantur. Rursus, virtutes et dona ut nominant habitum, aliquo modo filii vocantur et filiæ, in quantum homo dispositive cooperatur ad infusionem eorum.
paras.en: [[1:2|And there were born to him seven sons|Natique sunt ei septem filii]], that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost, according to Gregory, [[1:2|and three daughters|et tres filiæ]], that is, the three theological virtues, according to the same. But since the gifts and the theological virtues are had only by creation and infusion from the Holy Ghost, they do not seem fittingly called the sons and daughters of the virtuous man; for sons and daughters spring from him whose sons and daughters they are. To this it seems we must answer that the virtues and gifts are often taken as they name the act; and their acts are caused by us, and these are spiritually called sons and daughters. Again, the virtues and gifts, as they name the habit, are in some way called sons and daughters inasmuch as man cooperates dispositively towards their infusion [that is, by disposing himself to receive them].

paras.t: Et fuit possessio ejus septem millia ovium. Per oves intelliguntur cogitationes et affectiones piæ, innocentes et simplices, quibus anima locupletatur super aurum et topazion. Qui enim sic cogitat atque afficitur, Deum habet se alloquentem, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Cum simplicibus sermocinatio ejus. Et tria millia camelorum. Per camelos dantur intelligi cogitationes et affectiones compassivæ, quibus nos invicem caritative supportamus, implentes illud Apostoli: Alter alterius onera portate. Iterum per camelos intelligi possunt cogitationes rudes atque distortæ, quas possidemus quum per rationis censuram eas ad spiritualem subtilitatem in meditando, et ad justitiæ æqualitatem in appetendo ac operando convertimus. Quingenta quoque juga boum. Per boves exprimuntur considerationes judiciales ac sapientiales, quibus per rationem regimus nosmetipsos, cordisque duritiam confringentes, cordis agrum sanctis operibus fecundamus: quod totum quia agendum est per caritatis imperium et rationis judicium, boves per paria explicantur. Et quingentæ asinæ. Per quas curæ et occupationes circa corporis necessitudines denotantur, quæ ceteris viliores ac tardiores exsistunt. Cur autem oves septem millia, cameli tria millia, boves mille et asinæ quingentæ esse dicantur, ex præcedenti est trahendum articulo, ubi de horum mysterio numerorum prætactum est. Ac familia multa nimis: id est, cogitationes affectionesque nostræ sine numero multiplicantur, quas dum per rationem sub divinæ legis obedientia coarctamus, multam valde familiam possidemus. Qui item prædictis bonis ditatus est, magnus est plane inter omnes orientales, hoc est inter omnes qui divinæ gratiæ perfunduntur splendore, ac radio sapientiæ illustrantur.
paras.en: [[1:3|And his possession was seven thousand sheep|Et fuit possessio ejus septem millia ovium]]. By the sheep are understood loving thoughts and affections, innocent and simple, by which the soul is enriched above gold and the topaz. For whoever thinks and is moved in this way has God speaking with him, according to that saying of Proverbs: [[Prov 3:32|his communication is with the simple|Cum simplicibus sermocinatio ejus]]. [[1:3|and three thousand camels|Et tria millia camelorum]]. By the camels are given to be understood thoughts and affections of compassion, by which we bear with one another in charity, fulfilling that saying of the Apostle: [[Gal 6:2|Bear ye one another's burdens|Alter alterius onera portate]]. Again, by the camels may be understood rough and crooked thoughts, which we possess when, by the judgment of reason, we turn them to spiritual fineness in meditating, and to the evenness of justice in desiring and doing. [[1:3|five hundred yoke of oxen|Quingenta quoque juga boum]]. By the oxen are expressed the considerations of judgment and of wisdom by which we rule ourselves through reason, and, breaking the hardness of the heart, make the field of the heart fruitful with holy works; and because all this is to be done under the command of charity and the judgment of reason, the oxen are set out in pairs. [[1:3|and five hundred she asses|Et quingentæ asinæ]]. By these are denoted the cares and occupations concerning the needs of the body, which are baser and slower than the rest. Why the sheep are said to be seven thousand, the camels three thousand, the oxen a thousand and the she asses five hundred is to be taken from the preceding article, where the mystery of these numbers was touched on. [[1:3|and a family exceedingly great|Ac familia multa nimis]]: that is, our thoughts and affections are multiplied without number, and while we hold them in by reason under obedience to the divine law, we possess a very great household. Whoever, again, is enriched with the goods named is plainly [[1:3|great among all the people of the east|magnus est plane inter omnes orientales]], that is, among all who are flooded with the splendour of divine grace and enlightened by the ray of wisdom.

paras.t: Et ibant filii ejus, et faciebant convivia per domos, unusquisque in die suo. Filii et filiæ eunt, dum dona et virtutes præfatæ in actus suos procedunt; faciuntque convivia in cubilibus mentis, dum bona operatione mentem delectant, reficiunt et confortant: operatio equidem virtuosa, cibus est animæ, et delectatio operationi bonæ annexa refectiva est potio. Quælibet autem virtus et quodlibet donum propriam habet delectationem actui suo conjunctam: et quoniam virtutes se invicem fulciunt, juvant et roborant, imo et sibi invicem cedunt, quia nunc hujus, nunc illius virtutis insistendum est actui, prout causa, locus, tempus seu alia exigunt; una virtus et donum unum aliis facit convivium, et quælibet die suo. Denique secundum Gregorium, donum sapientiæ in die suo convivium facit, quoniam mentem de æternorum spe et certitudine reficit. Intellectus in die suo convivium parat, quia audita et credita penetrando cor reficit, et tenebras ejus illustrat. Consilium die suo convivium exhibet, quia dum esse præcipitem prohibet, ratione animum replet. Fortitudo in suo, quia dum adversa non trepidat, trepidanti menti confidentiæ cibos apponit. Scientia in suo, quia in ventre mentis ignorantiæ jejunium superat. Pietas in suo, quoniam cordis viscera misericordiæ operibus implet. Timor in suo, quia dum premit mentem ne de præsentibus superbiat, de futuris eam spei cibo confortat. De hoc autem septem donorum spirituali convivio plenius dixi in tractatu de donis Spiritus Sancti, ubi et verba hæc clarius fuerunt exposita.
paras.en: [[1:4|And his sons went|Et ibant filii ejus]], [[1:4|and made a feast by houses, every one in his day|et faciebant convivia per domos, unusquisque in die suo]]. The sons and daughters go when the gifts and virtues named go forth into their acts; and they make feasts in the chambers of the mind when they delight, refresh and strengthen the mind by good working: for virtuous working is the food of the soul, and the delight joined to good working is a refreshing drink. Now each virtue and each gift has its own delight joined to its act; and since the virtues prop up, help and strengthen one another, and indeed give way to one another (for now the act of this virtue, now that of another, must be attended to, as the cause, place, time or other things require), one virtue and one gift makes a feast for the others, and each in its own day. Then, according to Gregory, the gift of wisdom makes a feast in its day, because it refreshes the mind with the hope and certainty of eternal things. Understanding prepares a feast in its day, because by penetrating what is heard and believed it refreshes the heart and lights up its darkness. Counsel holds a feast in its day, because, while it keeps the mind from being headlong, it fills it with reason. Fortitude in its day, because, while it does not tremble at adversity, it sets the food of confidence before the trembling mind. Knowledge in its day, because in the belly of the mind it overcomes the fast of ignorance. Piety in its day, because it fills the bowels of the heart with works of mercy. Fear in its day, because, while it presses down the mind lest it grow proud of present things, it strengthens it with the food of hope for the things to come. Of this spiritual feast of the seven gifts I have spoken more fully in the treatise On the Gifts of the Holy Ghost, where these words too were more clearly expounded.

paras.t: Et mittentes vocabant tres sorores suas, ut comederent et biberent cum eis. Septem dona theologicas tres virtutes ad epulandum secum invitant, quia eisdem connexa sunt, nec sine eis operari aliquid meritorie possunt. Quum enim sit caritas animæ vita spiritualis, certum est, nullam actionem sine caritate coram Deo vivam aut meritoriam esse: ideo omnis operatio meritoria ex caritate procedit imperative. Oportet autem in actibus meritoriis debitum ac ultimum finem intendi: quem fides menti ostendit. Ideo scriptum est, Justus ex fide vivit; et, Sine fide impossibile est placere Deo. Insuper, in cunctis quæ meritorie agimus, æternæ felicitatis exspectationem vel spem habere docemur; æternamque beatitudinem, ad quam fides nostram dirigit intentionem, spes facit esse præstolabilem ac reputari nobis possibilem. Quemadmodum autem theologicæ istæ virtutes dona actuant, dirigunt atque perficiunt, sic et perficiuntur ab eis: dona quippe ad agendum expeditas reddunt ipsas virtutes et perficiunt eas, sicut virtutes perficiunt animæ vires ad operandum.
paras.en: [[1:4|And sending, they called their three sisters, to eat and drink with them|Et mittentes vocabant tres sorores suas, ut comederent et biberent cum eis]]. The seven gifts invite the three theological virtues to feast with them, because they are bound up with them and can do nothing meritoriously without them. For since charity is the spiritual life of the soul, it is certain that no action without charity is living or meritorious before God; and so every meritorious work proceeds from charity by its command. Again, in meritorious acts the due and last end must be intended, and faith shows it to the mind. Therefore it is written: The [[Heb 10:38|just man liveth by faith|Justus ex fide vivit]]; and: [[Heb 11:6|without faith it is impossible to please God|Sine fide impossibile est placere Deo]]. Moreover, we are taught to have the expectation or hope of eternal happiness in all that we do meritoriously; and hope makes the eternal beatitude, to which faith directs our intention, something to be waited for and reckoned possible for us. And as these theological virtues bring the gifts into act, direct and perfect them, so they are also perfected by them: for the gifts make the virtues themselves ready for action and perfect them, as the virtues perfect the powers of the soul for working.

paras.t: Quumque in orbem transissent dies convivii, id est, quum virtutes et dona multas operationes laudabiles, delectationesque mundas et confortationes produxissent in thalamo cordis, mittebat ad eos Job: id est, vir virtuosus salubriter dolens, rationis intuitum destinavit ad considerandum actus præfatos, an essent vere virtuosi, non solum ex genere et quoad substantiam actus, sed et proprie, et quantum ad circumstantias ad actus veraciter virtuosos exactas. Non enim sufficit facere bonum, nisi fiat et bene. Propter quod dicit Apostolus: Rationabile obsequium vestrum. Et Christus: Habete, inquit, in vobis sal, id est discretionem, in omnibus. Et sanctificabat illos, id est, a defectuositatibus et culpis annexis purgavit, separando pretiosum a vili, verum a falso, bonum a malo. Nempe ob imperfectiones, defectuositates et culpas, quæ bonis actibus nostris jugiter admiscentur, loquitur Isaias: Facti sumus ut immundi omnes nos; quasi pannus menstruatæ universæ justitiæ nostræ. Quidquid enim boni est, Deo cum gratiarum actione attribuamus; quidquid imperfectionis et culpæ miscetur, nostrum noscamus, et pœnitendo purgemus.
paras.en: [[1:5|And when the days of their feasting were gone about|Quumque in orbem transissent dies convivii]], that is, when the virtues and gifts had brought forth many praiseworthy works, and pure delights and strengthenings, in the bridal chamber of the heart, [[1:5|Job sent to them|mittebat ad eos Job]]: that is, the virtuous man, grieving to his salvation, turned the gaze of reason to consider those acts, whether they were truly virtuous, not only by their kind and as to the substance of the act, but also properly, and as to the circumstances required for acts truly virtuous. For it is not enough to do good unless it is also done well. Therefore the Apostle says: [[Rom 12:1|your reasonable service|Rationabile obsequium vestrum]]. And Christ: [[Mark 9:49|Have|Habete]], he says, [[Mark 9:49|salt in you|in vobis sal]], that is, discretion, in all things. [[1:5|and sanctified them|Et sanctificabat illos]], that is, he purged them of the defects and faults joined to them, separating the precious from the vile, the true from the false, the good from the evil. For it is because of the imperfections, defects and faults that are continually mingled with our good acts that Isaias says: [[Is 64:6|we are all become as one unclean|Facti sumus ut immundi omnes nos]], [[Is 64:6|and all our justices as the rag of a menstruous woman|quasi pannus menstruatæ universæ justitiæ nostræ]]. Whatever good there is, let us ascribe to God with thanksgiving; whatever imperfection and fault is mingled with it, let us know to be our own and purge it by doing penance.

paras.t: Consurgensque diluculo, id est mane alacriter luce compunctionis perfusus, et spiritualem diem mentis a pœnitentia inchoans. Justorum enim semita quasi lux splendens procedit, et crescit usque ad perfectam diem. Diluculo quippe præteritæ noctis debemus culpas abluere, atque ad fructuose deducendum diem instantem, nosmetipsos spiritualibus armis accingere, sicut de sero elapsi diei debemus peccata corrigere, et ad noctem virtuose expendendam cor nostrum disponere. Somnolentis autem et acediosis Salomon clamat: Usquequo, piger, dormies? quando consurges de somno tuo? Offerebat holocausta, id est orationes ferventes, per singulos, id est pro remissione culparum, cujuslibet virtutis ac doni actibus commixtarum. Itaque super custodiam nostram stemus, nec de bonis quæ agimus, inaniter gloriemur, aut stultissime tumescamus, neque vana securitate laxemur aut ignaviter torpeamus. Sed de eo quod bonum est, Deo humiliter regratiemur; de eo autem quod nostra fragilitate ac cæcitate mali admixtum est, cordialiter doleamus; timoratique simus, ne Deo reddamur ingrati, atque quotidie digne proficere ac coram Deo sollicitius ambulare nitamur.
paras.en: [[1:5|and rising up early|Consurgensque diluculo]], that is, flooded in the morning, eagerly, with the light of compunction, and beginning the spiritual day of the mind with penance. For [[Prov 4:18|the path of the just, as a shining light, goeth forwards, and increaseth even to perfect day|Justorum enim semita quasi lux splendens procedit, et crescit usque ad perfectam diem]]. At daybreak, indeed, we ought to wash away the faults of the night gone by, and gird ourselves with spiritual arms to spend the coming day fruitfully; just as in the evening we ought to correct the sins of the day that has passed, and dispose our heart to spend the night virtuously. To the drowsy and slothful Solomon cries: [[Prov 6:9|How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep?|Usquequo, piger, dormies? quando consurges de somno tuo?]] He [[1:5|offered holocausts|Offerebat holocausta]], that is, fervent prayers, [[1:5|for every one of them|per singulos]], that is, for the remission of the faults mingled with the acts of each virtue and gift. Let us therefore stand upon our watch[[Hab 2:1||]], and not glory vainly in the good we do, nor swell up most foolishly, nor slacken in a vain security, nor grow sluggish and idle. But for what is good let us humbly give thanks to God in return; for the evil that is mingled with it through our frailty and blindness let us grieve from the heart; and let us be God-fearing, lest we become ungrateful to God, and strive daily to advance worthily and to walk more solicitously before God[[Mich 6:8||]].

paras.t: Dicebat enim in corde suo, æquitatis zelator ac suæ salutis sollicitus operator: Ne forte peccaverint filii mei, et benedixerint, id est maledixerint, Deo, etc. Secundum Augustinum, virtus est bonus habitus animi, quo bene vivitur, quo nullus male utitur: quomodo igitur timet vir justus, ne virtutes et dona egerint mala? Et respondendum, quod donis et virtutibus nullus male utitur directe ac immediate, sed indirecte et occasionaliter. Actus namque a virtute elicitus, semper est virtuosus; sed virtus et donum fieri possunt occasio delinquendi, non ex se, sed ex rationis et voluntatis imperfectione, utpote ratione erronee subsumente, et eo quod bonum est occasionaliter male utente, quemadmodum aliqui dicuntur se ex caritatis fervore ac nimia devotione destruere: quod non vere directe et elicitive venit ex caritatis fervore et devotione, sed rationis indiscretione atque errore. Itaque metuendum est justo, ne virtutes et dona sibi concessa peccaverint occasionaliter, id est, mala habeant sibi adjuncta, et vel magis vel minus quam debuit factum sit. Maledicunt insuper Deo, dum erigunt hominem in spiritualem superbiam, vanitatem, jactantiam, dumque operans suis viribus tribuit aut meritis, quod ex Dei pura pietate sortitus est. Præterea hostis antiquus bona nostra tribus modis insequitur. Interdum enim in principio maculat intentionem; interdum quum illam polluere nequit, inficit actionem per admixtionem passionum et negligentiarum nostrarum; quod quum facere nequit, insidiatur operi jam completo, ut inde aliquid proprii commodi, favoris aut laudis insipienter quæramus.
paras.en: [[1:5|For he said|Dicebat enim]] in his heart, a zealot for justice and a careful worker of his own salvation: [[1:5|Lest perhaps my sons have sinned, and have blessed|Ne forte peccaverint filii mei, et benedixerint]], that is, cursed, [[1:5|God|Deo]], etc. According to Augustine, virtue is a good habit of the mind, by which one lives rightly and which no one uses ill: how then does the just man fear lest the virtues and gifts have done evil? We must answer that no one uses the gifts and virtues ill directly and immediately, but indirectly and by occasion. For an act elicited by a virtue is always virtuous; but a virtue and a gift can become an occasion of sinning, not of themselves, but from the imperfection of the reason and will: as when the reason subsumes wrongly [that is, applies a sound principle wrongly to the case in hand], and uses ill, by occasion, what is good; as some are said to destroy themselves out of the fervour of charity and excessive devotion, which does not truly come, directly and as its elicited act, from the fervour of charity and devotion, but from the indiscretion and error of reason. So the just man must fear lest the virtues and gifts granted him have sinned by occasion, that is, have evils joined to them, and more or less has been done than ought. Moreover, they curse God when they lift a man up into spiritual pride, vanity and boasting, and when the doer ascribes to his own strength or merits what he has received from the pure goodness of God. Besides, the old enemy pursues our good works in three ways. Sometimes he stains the intention at the beginning; sometimes, when he cannot defile that, he infects the action by mingling with it our passions and negligences; and when he cannot do that, he lies in wait for the work already finished, so that we foolishly seek from it some profit, favour or praise of our own.

paras.t: Sic faciebat Job cunctis diebus. Ideo monet Apostolus: Benefacientes nolite deficere; tempore enim suo metemus non deficientes. Sola nempe perseverantia dicitur coronari, quia videlicet sine ea nulla virtus feliciter præmiatur. Itaque non solum in bono perseveremus, sed et opus Dei quotidie diligentius, perfectius atque ardentius exsequi studeamus, et quo illud exstat frequentius, eo purius vigilantiusque solvatur: alioqui torpore et damno mentis multiplici percutiemur.
paras.en: [[1:5|So did Job all days|Sic faciebat Job cunctis diebus]]. Therefore the Apostle warns: [[Gal 6:9|in doing good, let us not fail. For in due time we shall reap, not failing|Benefacientes nolite deficere; tempore enim suo metemus non deficientes]]. For perseverance alone is said to be crowned[[Matt 10:22||]], because without it no virtue is happily rewarded. So let us not only persevere in good, but also strive daily to carry out the work of God [opus Dei: the Divine Office, the daily round of the Church's prayer] more diligently, more perfectly and more ardently; and the more often it comes round, the more purely and watchfully let it be paid: otherwise we shall be struck with sluggishness and with manifold loss of mind.

paras.t: Quadam autem die, quum venissent filii Dei ut adsisterent coram Domino, adfuit inter eos etiam Satan. Certum omnino est, singulorum justorum in hoc mundo recte dolentium per Job significatorum, angelos singulos certis vicibus de cœlo ad terras descendere, hincque illuc redire, vota, preces et merita sibi commissorum Deo offerre, opem impendere. Dæmones quoque non cessant pariter in contrarium niti, culpas objicere, ad accusandum adstare, tentandi licentiam postulare: et si Deus quemquam electorum suorum ipsi Satan laudaverit, adversarius ille non metuit bona ipsius interpretari ad malum, atque præsumere quod si a Deo permittatur laudatum tentare, cito dejiciet eum adversis, qui Deum in prosperis colere videbatur. Deus autem vallat electos in sæculo isto variis bonis, donis naturæ et gratiæ ac fortunæ, generalibus ac specialibus beneficiis multis ac meritis copiosis: quæ dæmon molitur auferre, ac per hoc tentatum ad impatientiam murmurationemque contra Deum succendere. Deus insuper electos suos permittit variis modis tentari, paulatimque gravius infestari; nunquam tamen permittit eos finaliter vinci aut prorsus perire. Itaque juxta hunc modum, perfacile est textum sequentem ad quemcumque justum per sanctum Job designatum tropologice applicare proportionabiliter secundum expositiones præhabitas. Quæ ergo ex præinductis clarissime patent, transilio, ne nimia prolixitas tædium gignat.
paras.en: [[1:6|Now on a certain day, when the sons of God came to stand before the Lord, Satan also was present among them|Quadam autem die, quum venissent filii Dei ut adsisterent coram Domino, adfuit inter eos etiam Satan]].
