It is altogether certain that the angels of each of the just in this world who grieve rightly, signified by Job, come down from heaven to earth at fixed turns, one angel for each, and go back thither again, offering to God the vows, prayers and merits of those committed to them, and bringing them help. The demons likewise do not cease to strive in the contrary direction: to cast up faults, to stand by to accuse, to ask leave to tempt; and if God has praised any of His elect to Satan himself, that adversary does not fear to interpret his good deeds as evil, and to presume that, if God allows him to tempt the man praised, he will soon cast down by adversity one who seemed to worship God in prosperity. But God fences in His elect in this world with various goods: with gifts of nature, of grace and of fortune, with many general and special benefits and with abundant merits; and these the demon labours to take away, and so to kindle the one tempted to impatience and murmuring against God. God moreover permits His elect to be tempted in various ways, and little by little to be more grievously assailed; yet He never permits them to be finally overcome or to perish utterly. So, after this manner, it is very easy to apply the text that follows tropologically, in due proportion, to any just man designated by holy Job, according to the expositions already given. What is therefore quite plain from what has been set out before, I pass over, lest too much length breed weariness.

paras.t: Quum autem quadam die filii et filiæ ejus comederent, et biberent vinum in domo fratris sui primogeniti: id est, quum actus donorum atque virtutum in thalamo sapientiæ, quæ in apice intellectus consistit, ipso usu ac delectatione sapientis roborarentur, ac perfunderentur luce contemplationis ipsius: sapientia quippe est primum atque dignissimum septem donorum ordine perfectionis; nuntius venit ad Job, qui diceret: Boves arabant: id est, considerationes judiciales atque sapientiales quibus ratio regit hominem, cordisque duritiam ad pœnitentiam frangendo emollit, mentem ad condignos pœnitentiæ fructus parabant: et asinæ, id est occupationes et curæ circa necessitudines corporales, pascebantur juxta eos, id est, per rationem ordinabantur secundum exigentiam spiritualis profectus, ita quod superfluæ non fuerunt, sed implebatur illud Apostoli: Habentes victum et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus: et irruerunt Sabæi, id est dæmones animarum latrocinatores, tuleruntque omnia, id est, suis tentationibus animam præfatis bonis cogitationibus spoliaverunt, vel eis vana ac frivola miscuerunt, quemadmodum ait Salvator in Evangelio: Semen est verbum Dei, et volucres cœli, id est dæmones, auferunt illud; et pueros percusserunt gladio: imperfectas enim boni conceptiones et affectiones gladio suæ suggestionis de facili perimunt; pueros quoque, id est circumspectores et quasi custodes cogitationum bonarum, multoties obruunt. Et evasi ego solus, ut nuntiarem tibi. Iste qui solus evadit, et homini damnum quod passus est indicat, est considerativus rationis discursus, qui naturalis est rationi: quem nec peccata, nec tentatio totaliter auferunt; per quem homo tentatus et victus pristina devotione ac opibus animæ se deprehendit privatum.
paras.en: [[1:13|Now upon a certain day, when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine, in the house of their eldest brother|Quum autem quadam die filii et filiæ ejus comederent, et biberent vinum in domo fratris sui primogeniti]]: that is, when the acts of the gifts and virtues, in the bridal chamber of wisdom, which stands at the summit of the understanding, were being strengthened by the very use and delight of the wise man, and flooded with the light of his contemplation (for wisdom is the first and worthiest of the seven gifts in the order of perfection), [[1:14|There came a messenger to Job, and said|nuntius venit ad Job, qui diceret]]: [[1:14|The oxen were ploughing|Boves arabant]]: that is, the considerations of judgment and wisdom by which reason rules a man, and softens the hardness of the heart by breaking it to penance, were preparing the mind for fruits worthy of penance[[Matt 3:8||]]; [[1:14|and the asses|et asinæ]], that is, the occupations and cares concerning the needs of the body, [[1:14|feeding beside them|pascebantur juxta eos]], that is, were set in order by reason according to what spiritual progress requires, so that they were not superfluous, but that saying of the Apostle was fulfilled: [[1 Tim 6:8|having food and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content|Habentes victum et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus]]; [[1:15|And the Sabeans rushed in|et irruerunt Sabæi]], that is, the demons, robbers of souls, [[1:15|and took all away|tuleruntque omnia]], that is, by their temptations stripped the soul of those good thoughts, or mingled vain and frivolous things with them, as the Saviour says in the Gospel: [[Luke 8:11|The seed is the word of God|Semen est verbum Dei]], and [[Luke 8:5|the fowls of the air|volucres cœli]], that is, the demons, take it away[[Luke 8:12||]] [the margin gives Luc. viii]; [[1:15|and slew the servants with the sword|et pueros percusserunt gladio]]: for with the sword of their suggestion they easily kill imperfect conceptions and affections of good; and the servants [pueri: literally “boys”], that is, those who look about and keep guard, as it were, over good thoughts, they often overwhelm. [[1:15|and I alone have escaped to tell thee|Et evasi ego solus, ut nuntiarem tibi]]. He who alone escapes and tells the man the loss he has suffered is the considering discourse of reason, which is natural to reason: neither sins nor temptation take it away entirely; and by it the man tempted and overcome finds himself deprived of his former devotion and of the riches of the soul.

paras.t: Ignis Dei cecidit de cœlo, id est, tentatio æstus carnalis, iræ, indignationis seu impatientiæ a Deo permissa, ab aeriis potestatibus est immissa: de quibus ait Apostolus, quod colluctatio nobis est contra spiritualia nequitiæ in cœlestibus; et tactas oves, id est cogitationes affectionesque pias, innocentes ac simplices, puerosque, id est circumspectores illarum custodes, consumpsit. Unum enim contrariorum, aliud corrumpit ac tollit. Et effugi ego solus: quia per considerativum rationis discursum istud homini innotescit.
paras.en: [[1:16|The fire of God fell from heaven|Ignis Dei cecidit de cœlo]], that is, the temptation of the heat of the flesh, of anger, indignation or impatience, permitted by God, is sent in by the powers of the air, of whom the Apostle says that [[Eph 6:12|our wrestling|colluctatio nobis est]] is [[Eph 6:12|against the spirits of wickedness in the high places|contra spiritualia nequitiæ in cœlestibus]]; and, [[1:16|striking the sheep|tactas oves]], that is, the loving thoughts and affections, innocent and simple, [[1:16|and the servants|puerosque]], that is, those who look about and guard them, [[1:16|hath consumed them|consumpsit]]. For of two contraries, one corrupts and takes away the other. [[1:16|and I alone have escaped|Et effugi ego solus]]: because by the considering discourse of reason this becomes known to the man.

paras.t: Illo adhuc loquente. Frequenter enim, procurante diabolo, tentatio super tentationem advenit homini, ut dum deliberationis non intervenit mora, subitis ac inundantibus frangatur adversis. Venit alius et dixit: Chaldæi, id est dæmones ferocissimi, ad omne vitium dirigentes, fecerunt tres turmas: quia per se ipsos, per mundum et carnem impugnant electos. Sed et quidam illorum inducunt ad diversa peccata; et quidam eorum occulte impugnant, quidam apertius tentant, quidam apertissime, etiam sensibiliter apparendo, interdum usque ad verbera seu terrores prosiliunt. Et invaserunt camelos, id est, cogitatus atque affectus compassionis ac motus olim rudes ac tortos, nunc reformatos, suis tentationibus abstulerunt.
paras.en: While he [[1:17|was yet speaking|Illo adhuc loquente]]. For often, by the devil's contriving, temptation comes upon a man on top of temptation, so that, with no pause for deliberation coming between, he may be broken by sudden and overflowing adversities. [[1:17|there came another, and said|Venit alius et dixit]]: [[1:17|The Chaldeans|Chaldæi]], that is, the fiercest demons, who steer towards every vice, [[1:17|made three troops|fecerunt tres turmas]]: because they attack the elect through themselves, through the world and through the flesh. And also some of them lead into divers sins; and some of them attack in secret, some tempt more openly, some most openly, even appearing to the senses, and at times they go so far as blows or terrors. [[1:17|and have fallen upon the camels|Et invaserunt camelos]], that is, by their temptations they carried off the thoughts and affections of compassion, and the movements once rough and crooked but now reformed.

paras.t: Filiis tuis et filiabus vescentibus et bibentibus vinum in domo fratris sui primogeniti: quod modo expositum est; ventus vehemens, id est impetuosa et grandis tentatio, irruit a regione deserti, id est a dæmonum divinitus derelictorum collegio; et concussit quatuor angulos domus, id est virtutes cardinales, quæ quatuor sunt, quibus interior fabrica animi virtuosi stabilitur ac sustentatur. Quæ corruens, oppressit liberos tuos, et mortui sunt, id est, dona Spiritus Sancti exstinxit. Virtutes namque et dona connexa sunt, potissime quantum ad esse formatum, et quocumque peccato mortali tolluntur. Istud autem percipit victus discursu rationis sibi id nuntiante, et facit quod subditur.
paras.en: [[1:18|Thy sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their eldest brother|Filiis tuis et filiabus vescentibus et bibentibus vinum in domo fratris sui primogeniti]]: this has just been expounded. [[1:19|A violent wind|ventus vehemens]], that is, a vehement and great temptation, [[1:19|came on a sudden from the side of the desert|irruit a regione deserti]], that is, from the company of the demons forsaken by God, [[1:19|and shook the four corners of the house|et concussit quatuor angulos domus]], that is, the cardinal virtues, which are four, by which the inner building of the virtuous soul is made firm and upheld; [[1:19|and it fell upon thy children, and they are dead|Quæ corruens, oppressit liberos tuos, et mortui sunt]], that is, it extinguished the gifts of the Holy Ghost. For the virtues and gifts are bound up together, above all as to their formed being [that is, as they are informed by charity], and are taken away by any mortal sin. This the man overcome perceives by the discourse of reason, which tells it to him, and he does what follows.

paras.t: Tunc surrexit Job, id est, justus sic tentatione dejectus, casum suum intelligens, de ruina peccati, qua fuit jacuitque prostratus, caducis, vanis ac infimis inhærendo, per pœnitentiam consurrexit, contra hostes suæ salutis mentem erexit, ad recuperandum deperdita se armavit; et scidit vestimenta sua, id est, carnes suas seu corporis membra, quibus quasi vestitur ac tegitur anima, flagellis attrivit et graviter castigavit. Debemus nempe Dei injuriam in nobismetipsis ulcisci, corpusque jejuniis, disciplinis atque laboribus virtuosis usque ad lassitudinem rationabiliter exercere. Per vestimenta quoque possunt intelligi opera, juxta quod in Apocalypsi loquitur Christus: Qui non inquinaverunt vestimenta sua, ambulabunt mecum in albis, quia digni sunt. Vestimenta hæc pœnitens scindit, quia opera quibus deliquit, destruit et abhorret. Et tonso capite, id est, cogitationibus cordis, quibus inaniter gloriabatur, seque ornari putabat, avulsis, sentire incipit humiliter de se ipso. Ideo subditur, corruens in terram, Deo humillime se prosternens, pulverem quoque et cinerem se esse cognoscens, juxta id Psalmi: Humiliata est in pulvere anima nostra, conglutinatus est in terra venter noster; adoravit, Deum pro venia flagitans, majestatem Dei et vilitatem sui perpendens. Multis enim ad recognoscendum ac revolvendum indesinenter propriam insufficientiam, defectuositatem et vilitatem atque ad omne vitium pronitatem, aliquando occasionaliter expedit tentationibus vinci, ut cautiores resurgant, ac de cetero custoditius vivant. Ideo dicit Gregorius: Mira nobiscum dispensatione agitur, ut mens nostra culpæ nonnunquam pulsatione feriatur: nam esse se magnarum virium homo crederet, si nullum unquam earumdem virium defectum intra mentis arcana sentiret. Sed dum tentatione irruente quatitur, et quasi ultra quam sufficit fatigatur, ei contra hostis sui insidias munimen ostenditur; et unde se timet enormiter cadere, inde accipit stare.
paras.en: [[1:20|Then Job rose up|Tunc surrexit Job]], that is, the just man thus cast down by temptation, understanding his fall, rose up by penance from the ruin of sin, in which he had been and had lain prostrate, clinging to things perishable, vain and lowly; he lifted up his mind against the enemies of his salvation and armed himself to win back what he had lost; [[1:20|and rent his garments|et scidit vestimenta sua]], that is, he wore down with scourges and sharply chastised his flesh, or the members of his body, with which the soul is clothed and covered as with a garment. For we ought to avenge on ourselves the wrong done to God, and to exercise the body, within reason, with fasts, disciplines [that is, the scourge used in penance] and virtuous labours to the point of weariness. By the garments, too, works may be understood, according to what Christ says in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:4|which have not defiled their garments: and they shall walk with me in white, because they are worthy|Qui non inquinaverunt vestimenta sua, ambulabunt mecum in albis, quia digni sunt]]. These garments the penitent rends, because he destroys and abhors the works by which he sinned. [[1:20|and having shaven his head|Et tonso capite]], that is, the thoughts of the heart in which he vainly gloried and thought himself adorned being plucked away, he begins to think humbly of himself. Therefore it is added: [[1:20|fell down upon the ground|corruens in terram]], prostrating himself most humbly before God, knowing himself to be dust and ashes[[Gen 3:19||]] [the margin gives Gen. iii, 19; “dust and ashes” is Abraham's phrase at Gen 18:27], according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 43:25|our soul is humbled down to the dust: our belly cleaveth to the earth|Humiliata est in pulvere anima nostra, conglutinatus est in terra venter noster]]; [[1:20|and worshipped|adoravit]], begging God for pardon, weighing the majesty of God and his own baseness. For it is sometimes expedient for many to be overcome by temptations, by occasion, so that they may ceaselessly recognize and turn over in mind their own insufficiency, defectiveness and baseness and their proneness to every vice, and may rise again more wary and live more guardedly thereafter. Therefore Gregory says: It is by a wonderful dispensation that we are dealt with, so that our mind is sometimes struck by the blow of a fault: for man would believe himself to be of great strength if he never felt any failing of that strength within the secret places of the mind. But while he is shaken by the onrush of temptation, and wearied, as it were, beyond what he can bear, a defence against the snares of his enemy is shown him; and from the very thing by which he fears to fall grievously, he receives the power to stand.

paras.t: Et dixit: Nudus egressus sum de utero matris meæ, et nudus revertar illuc. Ad vitandum absorbentem superfluumque mœrorem sive de exterioribus, sive de interioribus damnis, atque ad refocillandam spem, potest et debet quicumque fidelis per Job significatus graviterque tentatus, et damna vel temporalium rerum vel spiritualium passus bonorum, verba hæc dicere, secundum sensum quo ad litteram exposita sunt de Job, articulo tertio. Spiritualius autem loquendo, per matrem intelligitur Ecclesia; per uterum matris, Baptismus, in quo intus renascimur, et de quo nudi egredimur, non quantum ad habitus gratiæ et virtutum atque donorum, quippe quum hi in Baptismate infundantur, sed quantum ad actus eorum ac propria merita. Unde infantes baptizati ante discretionem decedentes, non suo, sed merito Christi salvantur. Denique propriam infirmitatem pensantes, fatemur quod nudi revertemur illuc, id est, sine propriis meritis decedemus, vel quia propriis viribus non habebimus ea, vel quia si habuerimus, non nobis ea, sed divinæ adscribemus clementiæ.
paras.en: [[1:21|And said|Et dixit]]: [[1:21|Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither|Nudus egressus sum de utero matris meæ, et nudus revertar illuc]]. To avoid a sorrow that is excessive and swallows a man up, whether over outward or inward losses, and to revive hope, every faithful soul signified by Job, grievously tempted, and having suffered losses whether of temporal things or of spiritual goods, can and ought to say these words, in the sense in which they were expounded literally of Job in the third article. Speaking more spiritually, however, by the mother is understood the Church; by the mother's womb, Baptism, in which we are inwardly born again[[John 3:5||]], and from which we come out naked: not as to the habits of grace, of the virtues and of the gifts, since these are infused in Baptism, but as to their acts and our own merits. Hence baptized infants who die before the age of discretion are saved not by their own merit but by Christ's. Lastly, weighing our own weakness, we confess that we shall return thither naked, that is, we shall depart without merits of our own: either because we shall not have them by our own strength, or because, if we have them, we shall ascribe them not to ourselves but to the divine clemency.

paras.t: Dominus dedit quidquid boni in nobis exstiterit, quum et merita nostra ejus sint dona, dicente Apostolo: Quid habes quod non accepisti? Et Jacobus: Omne, inquit, donum optimum et omne datum perfectum, desursum est descendens. Dominus abstulit. Dona gratiæ et virtutum Deus non aufert nisi ob nostra demerita, utpote permissive; exteriora vero quandoque aufert et effective. Sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est: non quod nostra ruina, et tentationi succumbere directe placeat Deo: sed quod tentamur, ejus venit licentia ac permissu. Itemque in quantum electis vicissim expedit cadere, aliquo modo placet Deo eorum ruina, non ut est culpa, sed ut est ad majorem cautelam, humiliationem ac fervorem proficua. Sit nomen Domini benedictum. Quidquid enim mali acciderit nobis, Deo gratias referre debemus, non de ipso malo culpæ secundum se, sed de justo Dei judicio, quo derelinqui ac labi meruimus: maxime quoque de hoc, quod post culpam nos ex sua infinita misericordia ad pœnitentiam illustravit; quod peccantes nos non statim occidit, ad inferosque projecit, sed pro malo reddidit bonum.
paras.en: [[1:21|the Lord gave|Dominus dedit]] whatever good there may be in us, since even our merits are His gifts, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 4:7|what hast thou that thou hast not received|Quid habes quod non accepisti]]? And James: [[Jas 1:17|Every|Omne]], he says, [[Jas 1:17|best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down|donum optimum et omne datum perfectum, desursum est descendens]]. [[1:21|and the Lord hath taken away|Dominus abstulit]]. The gifts of grace and of the virtues God does not take away except for our demerits, that is, by permitting it; but outward things He sometimes takes away also by His own working. [[1:21|as it hath pleased the Lord, so is it done|Sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est]]: not that our ruin and our yielding to temptation directly please God; but that we are tempted comes by His leave and permission. And again, inasmuch as it is expedient for the elect to fall at times, their ruin in some way pleases God, not as it is a fault, but as it is profitable for greater wariness, humility and fervour. [[1:21|blessed be the name of the Lord|Sit nomen Domini benedictum]]. For whatever evil befalls us, we ought to give thanks to God: not for the evil of the fault itself in itself, but for the just judgment of God by which we deserved to be forsaken and to slip; and above all for this, that after the fault He has enlightened us to penance out of His infinite mercy; that when we sinned He did not slay us at once and cast us down to hell, but returned good for evil.

paras.t: In omnibus his non peccavit Job labiis suis. Quia vir bonus quidquid ei contingat, qualitercumque tentetur ac superetur, Deo nequaquam debet culpam imponere, nec causam suæ ruinæ in ipsum impie retorquere, sicut de impiis scribitur: Quoniam declinaverunt in te mala. Neque stultum quid contra Deum locutus est, sed totam suæ perversæ voluntati culpam sapienter imposuit.
paras.en: [[1:22|In all these things Job sinned not by his lips|In omnibus his non peccavit Job labiis suis]]. For the good man, whatever befalls him, however he is tempted and overcome, ought by no means to lay the blame on God, nor wickedly to turn back on Him the cause of his own ruin, as is written of the wicked: [[Ps 20:12|For they have intended evils against thee|Quoniam declinaverunt in te mala]] [the Latin, declinaverunt in te mala, can be read “they turned aside evils upon thee”, which is the sense Denis takes]. [[1:22|nor spoke he any foolish thing against God|Neque stultum quid contra Deum locutus est]], but wisely laid the whole blame on his own perverse will.

paras.t: Postremo, quæ de donis gratiæ gratum facientis exposita sunt quoad viros fideles per Job designatos, possunt exponi et de donis gratiæ gratis datæ, ut sunt sermo sapientiæ, sermo scientiæ, gratia sanitatum, linguarum ac prophetiæ, etc., quæ hominibus quandoque dispensative utiliterque tolluntur, sive ad tempus, sive jugiter: sed et de exterioribus bonis, quoad aliquos opulentos. Quidam enim in evangelica lege tentati sunt et perpessi singulariter similiter sancto Job, præsertim B. Eustachius, secundum quod Christus ei in sua conversione prædixit, ut in ejus Legenda habetur.
paras.en: Lastly, what has been expounded of the gifts of sanctifying grace with regard to the faithful designated by Job can also be expounded of the gifts of grace freely given [gratia gratis data: graces such as prophecy or healing, given for the good of others rather than for the holiness of the one who has them], such as the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, the grace of healings, of tongues and of prophecy, etc., which are sometimes taken from men by God's dispensation and for their profit, whether for a time or for good; and also of outward goods, with regard to certain rich men. For some under the law of the Gospel have been tempted and have suffered in a singular way like holy Job, above all Bl. Eustachius, as Christ foretold to him at his conversion, as is found in his Legend.

2.title: Expositio litteralis capituli secundi: Factum est autem quum quadam die venissent filii Dei et starent coram Domino.
2.title_en: Literal exposition of the second chapter: And it came to pass, when on a certain day the sons of God came, and stood before the Lord

paras.t: Ulterius ad declarandum patientiam atque constantiam sancti Job, tentatio ejus succrescit et gravior fit. Contingit nempe sæpe, virum constantem temporalium opum ablationem æquanimiter ferre, tamen prolis suæ orbationem dolorosius quam oportet deflere. Alium autem constantiorem contingit utrumque istorum patienter perferre, qui nihilo minus propter proprii corporis amarissimam afflictionem ad impatientiam concitatur. Ut ergo beatus Job perfecte constans ac patiens comprobetur, inducitur præsens capitulum, recitans quomodo propriæ personæ tribulationem dirissimam tulerit patienter. Unde et Stoici asserebant, quod in sapientem non cadit perturbatio mentis, ut propter quodcumque perturbans in eventu rerum vel filiorum aut propriæ personæ, quidpiam indecens meditetur, dicat aut faciat. Hinc decuit Job probari in periculis propriæ personæ suæque famæ atque honoris: nam et fama præponenda est opibus, diffamiaque vitanda, in quantum est aliorum scandalizativa et Dei inhonorativa.
paras.en: Further, to make plain the patience and constancy of holy Job, his temptation grows and becomes heavier. For it often happens that a constant man bears the taking away of his temporal wealth with an even mind, yet bewails the loss of his children more grievously than he ought. Another, more constant still, happens to bear both of these patiently, and is nevertheless driven to impatience by a most bitter affliction of his own body. So, that blessed Job may be proved perfectly constant and patient, the present chapter is brought in, relating how he patiently bore a most cruel tribulation in his own person. Hence the Stoics too asserted that no perturbation of mind befalls the wise man such that, on account of anything disturbing that happens to his goods, his children or his own person, he should think, say or do anything unbecoming. Hence it was fitting that Job should be tried in perils to his own person and to his good name and honour: for a good name is to be preferred to riches, and disrepute is to be avoided, in so far as it gives scandal to others and dishonours God.

paras.t: Factum est autem quum quadam die venissent filii Dei, et starent coram Domino, venissetque Satan inter eos, et staret in conspectu ejus, ut diceret Dominus ad Satan. Verba hæc præcedenti capitulo scripta sunt, tribusque præinductis articulis diffuse exposita; nec facilibus et præexpositis arbitror immorandum. Unde venis? Per hoc quod Dominus ait nunc ad Satan, Unde venis? implicite superbiam ejus præsumptionemque percutit, secundum Gregorium. Quasi Dominus dicat: Ecce nunc ab uno mortali homine vinceris, qui te contra Creatorem tuum erigere niteris. Qui respondens, ait: Circuivi terram, et perambulavi eam.
paras.en: [[2:1|And it came to pass, when on a certain day the sons of God came, and stood before the Lord, and Satan came amongst them, and stood in his sight,|Factum est autem quum quadam die venissent filii Dei, et starent coram Domino, venissetque Satan inter eos, et staret in conspectu ejus]] [[2:2|That the Lord said to Satan|ut diceret Dominus ad Satan]]. These words are written in the preceding chapter and were expounded at length in the three articles before this; and I think there is no need to dwell on things that are easy and already explained. [[2:2|Whence comest thou?|Unde venis?]] By the Lord's saying now to Satan, [[2:2|Whence comest thou?|Unde venis?]] he implicitly strikes at his pride and presumption, according to Gregory. As if the Lord said: See, thou who strivest to raise thyself against thy Creator art now overcome by one mortal man. [[2:2|And he answered, and said: I have gone round about the earth, and walked through it|Qui respondens, ait: Circuivi terram, et perambulavi eam]].

paras.t: Et dixit Dominus ad Satan: Numquid considerasti servum meum Job, quod non sit ei similis in terra, vir simplex et rectus, ac timens Deum, et recedens a malo? Totum ut supra, usque ibi. Et adhuc retinens innocentiam, id est cordis a culpa immunitatem, ita quod peccando nec sibi nec alteri intulit nocumentum sive injuriam, etiam inter tot flagella, et post tantam tribulationem. Nam et aliqui adversa, dum inferuntur, æquanimiter tolerant; sed eis finitis, ex sola eorum recordatione ad impatientiam inflammantur: quod ex superbia solet accidere. Talis autem non fuit Job. Unde nunc ultra præfatas ejus virtutes de innocentia quoque constanti commendatur, quam utique in prosperis gloriose servavit, gloriosius autem in adversis.
paras.en: [[2:3|And the Lord said to Satan: Hast thou considered my servant, Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a man simple and upright, and fearing God, and avoiding evil|Et dixit Dominus ad Satan: Numquid considerasti servum meum Job, quod non sit ei similis in terra, vir simplex et rectus, ac timens Deum, et recedens a malo?]]? All as above, as far as this: [[2:3|and still keeping his innocence|Et adhuc retinens innocentiam]], that is, the freedom of his heart from guilt, so that by sinning he brought neither harm nor injury to himself or to another, even amid so many scourges and after so great a tribulation. For some bear adversities with an even mind while they are being inflicted; but when they are over, they are inflamed to impatience by the mere remembering of them: which commonly comes of pride. But Job was not such. Hence now, beyond his virtues already named, he is commended also for a constant innocence, which he kept gloriously in prosperity, but more gloriously in adversity.

paras.t: Tu autem commovisti me adversus eum. Æternus et invariabilis Deus, æternaliter uno modo se habens, in quo idem sunt, esse, posse et agere, seu essentia, potentia, actio, nihil de novo concipit aut vult, nec per quemquam ad aliquid agendum provocatur, accenditur aut movetur; sed ipse ex sua pietate loquitur in Scripturis more humano, nostræ condescendens capacitati, ut melius capiamus divina. Sicut ergo fertur irasci aut pœnitere, dum per modum irati aut pœnitentis se habet, ita nunc dicitur commoveri, quoniam instar commoti se habuit, dum ad instantiam Satan virum justum tradidit impio tribulandum. Unde secundum Albertum, quum dicitur, Commovisti me, anthropospathos est: ut sit sensus, Movisti, ut tuæ eum tentationi exponerem. Homines quippe ab aliquo commoveri dicuntur, dum propter illum quidpiam agunt. Invariabilitatem autem suam Deus fatetur, dicens: Ego Dominus, et non mutor.
paras.en: [[2:3|But thou hast moved me against him|Tu autem commovisti me adversus eum]]. The eternal and unchangeable God, who from eternity is ever in one way of being, in whom to be, to be able and to act, or essence, power and action, are the same, conceives or wills nothing anew, nor is he provoked, kindled or moved by anyone to do anything; but of his goodness he speaks in the Scriptures in human fashion, condescending to our capacity, so that we may better grasp divine things. As, then, he is said to be angry or to repent when he behaves in the manner of one angry or repenting, so now he is said to be moved, since he behaved like one moved when, at Satan's urging, he gave up a just man to the wicked one to be afflicted. Hence, according to Albert, when it is said, [[2:3|thou hast moved me|Commovisti me]], it is *anthropospathos* [that is, a figure of speech that ascribes human feelings to God]: so that the sense is, Thou hast moved me to expose him to thy temptation. For men are said to be moved by someone when they do something on his account. But God confesses his unchangeableness, saying: [[Mal 3:6|I am the Lord, and I change not|Ego Dominus, et non mutor]].

paras.t: Ut affligerem, id est, a te affligi permitterem, eum frustra. Secundum Albertum et Thomam, quod ait, Frustra, non ad Dei, sed Satanæ intentionem refertur. Nam et Philosophus dicit: Deus et natura nil faciunt frustra. Deus etenim permisit Job tentari ad suæ patientiæ demonstrationem, gratiæ incrementum, meriti cumulum, atque ad nostram ædificationem: quod totum sic accidit, sicut Deus intendit. Satan vero tentavit, ut virum sanctum ad murmurationem blasphemiamque induceret: quod sortitus non est, imo oppositum accidit. Ideo ejus intentio est frustrata, id est fine intento privata: quia, ut dicitur secundo Physicorum, Frustra fit, quod finem intentum non obtinet, quemadmodum medicina ad quam non sequitur sanitas. Et in hoc differt a vano, quoniam vanum nec est ad finem, nec finem consequitur, ut motus digiti, quando propter nihil sine advertentia movetur.
paras.en: [[2:3|that I should afflict|Ut affligerem]], that is, that I should permit him to be afflicted by thee, [[2:3|him without cause|eum frustra]]. According to Albert and Thomas, the words *without cause* [Latin *frustra*, that is, in vain, to no purpose] refer not to God's intention but to Satan's. For the Philosopher too says: God and nature do nothing in vain. For God permitted Job to be tempted for the showing forth of his patience, the increase of grace, the heaping up of merit, and for our edification: and all this came about just as God intended. But Satan tempted him in order to lead the holy man into murmuring and blasphemy: which he did not achieve; rather the opposite came about. Therefore his intention was frustrated, that is, deprived of the end intended: because, as is said in the second book of the Physics, that is done in vain which does not attain the end intended, like a medicine that is not followed by health. And in this it differs from what is idle [Latin *vanum*], since what is idle is neither directed to an end nor attains an end, like the movement of a finger when it is moved for nothing, without attention.

paras.t: Porro opera hominis propter aliquid fiunt quinque modis, ut dicit Rabbi Moyses in tertia Collatione Ducis neutrorum. Aut enim fiunt propter bonum honestum, aut propter bonum delectabile, aut propter utile, aut propter ludum, et tunc consequuntur finem. Aut fiunt propter aliquid, et non consequuntur illud, et tunc fiunt frustra, ut quis vadit ad forum ut sumat pecuniam, quam si non acceperit, frustra ivit. Vana vero sunt, in quibus nihil intendit. In operibus autem Dei est honestum et delectabile ac utile, lusivum nihil: quia lusivus est mollis, ut dicitur septimo Ethicorum. Frustra non est, quia omnia refert ad se ipsum; nihilque vanum, quia in omnibus intendit se ipsum. Verba hæc sunt partim intricata et resolutionis egentia, quum et in Proverbiis increata Sapientia Unigenitus Patris dicat: Delectabar per singulos dies, ludens coram eo omni tempore, ludens in orbe terrarum. Verumtamen Gregorius tangit, quomodo quod dicitur, Frustra, possit referri ad Deum, ut dicatur afflixisse sanctum Job frustra, quia sine ejus demerito, scilicet sine culpa, quæ solet esse communis causa percussionis humanæ.
paras.en: Now the works of man are done for the sake of something in five ways, as Rabbi Moses says in the third Collation of the *Dux neutrorum* [that is, Part III of Maimonides' *Guide of the Perplexed*, ch. 25]. For either they are done for the sake of a virtuous good, or of a pleasant good, or of the useful, or for play, and then they attain their end. Or they are done for the sake of something and do not attain it, and then they are done in vain, as when someone goes to the market to get money, and if he does not receive it, he has gone in vain. But those are idle in which nothing is intended. Now in the works of God there is the virtuous, the pleasant and the useful, but nothing of play: because one given to play is soft, as is said in the seventh book of the Ethics. Nothing is in vain, because he refers all things to himself; and nothing idle, because in all things he intends himself. These words are partly intricate and need resolving, since in the Proverbs too the uncreated Wisdom, the Only-begotten of the Father, says of himself that he [[Prov 8:30|was delighted every day, playing before him at all times|Delectabar per singulos dies, ludens coram eo omni tempore]], [[Prov 8:31|Playing in the world|ludens in orbe terrarum]]. Yet Gregory touches on how the words *without cause* can be referred to God, so that he is said to have afflicted holy Job without cause, because it was without any demerit of his, that is, without guilt, which is commonly the cause of men's being struck.

paras.t: Cui respondit Satan, et ait. Improbus et impudens calumniator semel repulsus ac victus, non cessat insidiari, volens adhuc probare quod Job patientiam non servavit ex Dei amore, sed amore privato, timens sibimetipsi, ne scilicet si murmuraret contra Deum, contingeret sibi sicut contigit filiis suis; sicque non propter Dei honorem, sed ob corporis sui vitam ac sanitatem servandam, fecit quæ bona apparuerunt, ita quod intentio ejus fuit semper obliqua et ad commodum corporale. Ideo Satan ait: Pellem pro pelle, id est, pellem seu corporis partem duriorem, exponit homo periculo pro pelle seu corporis sui parte teneriori ac cariori, ut manum pro oculi defensione. Vel sic: Pellem pro pelle, id est, corpus alterius permittet homo æquanimiter percuti, ut proprium corpus possit a cæde eruere: per hoc insinuans, quod Job filiorum suorum mortem patienter tulit, ne propria sua caro divinitus plagaretur. Et cuncta quæ habet homo, omnes videlicet opes, dabit pro anima sua, id est pro vita sua tuenda et conservanda. Libentius etenim exteriora amittit, quam propriam vitam, quum illa ordinentur ad corporalis vitæ sustentationem; quamvis quidam ex pertinacia malint occidi, quam sua alicui dare, dum per violentiam impetuntur, et sciunt se non posse resistere: quod (secundum Thomam) est vitiosum, quoniam minus bonum pro conservatione majoris boni est exponendum.
paras.en: [[2:4|And Satan answered, and said|Cui respondit Satan, et ait]]. The shameless and brazen slanderer, once repulsed and beaten, does not cease to lie in wait, wishing still to prove that Job had kept his patience not out of love of God but out of love of self, fearing for himself, lest, that is, if he murmured against God, it should befall him as it had befallen his sons; and so it was not for God's honour but to keep his body's life and health that he did the things that appeared good, so that his intention was always crooked and turned to bodily advantage. Therefore Satan says: [[2:4|Skin for skin|Pellem pro pelle]], that is, a man exposes to danger his skin, or the harder part of his body, for the skin, or the more tender and dearer part of his body, as he puts out his hand to defend his eye. Or thus: [[2:4|Skin for skin|Pellem pro pelle]], that is, a man will let another's body be struck with an even mind, so that he may save his own body from slaughter: hinting by this that Job bore the death of his sons patiently so that his own flesh might not be smitten by God. [[2:4|and all that a man hath|Et cuncta quæ habet homo]], all his riches, namely, [[2:4|he will give for his life|dabit pro anima sua]], that is, for guarding and keeping his life. For a man more willingly loses outward things than his own life, since they are ordered to the sustaining of bodily life; though some out of obstinacy would rather be killed than give their goods to anyone, when they are attacked with violence and know they cannot resist: which (according to Thomas) is a fault, since a lesser good is to be risked to keep a greater one.

paras.t: Alioqui, id est, si ut dico, non est, nec creditur mihi, mitte manum tuam, id est, potestatem exerce, et tange, id est, a me tangi desine, os ejus et carnem, id est, non solum circa superficiem corporis sui, sed usque ad interiora corporis distemperetur et torqueatur, et tunc videbis, in ipso effectu, quod nunc vides in te ipso. Deus enim quamvis a rebus notitiam nusquam accipiat, sed omnia in sua æternæ sapientiæ conspiciat luce, sic tamen cognoscit res in se ipso, ut nihilo minus cognoscat eas in suis naturis atque effectibus, id est, in se ipso cognoscit, quando et quomodo res sunt in propriis exsistentiis ac naturis, et quando ita non sunt. Vel, Videbis, id est, alios scire videreque facies: juxta illud Dei ad Abraham, Nunc cognovi quod timeas Deum, et non peperceris filio tuo. Quod in faciem benedicat tibi, id est, palam maledicet. De istis, quia jam ante prolixe exposita sunt, transeo. Quod autem in Scripturis benedictio Dei hoc modo pro suo accipiatur contrario, constat ex eo quod tertio Regum Jezabel impiissima scripsit civibus Naboth, ut producerent contra eum testes, dicentes: Benedixit Naboth Deo et regi.
paras.en: [[2:5|But|Alioqui]], that is, if it is not as I say, and I am not believed, [[2:5|put forth thy hand|mitte manum tuam]], that is, exercise thy power, [[2:5|and touch|et tange]], that is, let him be touched by me [the print reads *desine*, “cease”, which seems a slip for *sine*, “let”], [[2:5|his bone and his flesh|os ejus et carnem]], that is, so that he be not only troubled on the surface of his body but disordered and tormented even to the inward parts of his body, [[2:5|and then thou shalt see|et tunc videbis]] in the effect itself what thou now seest in thyself. For God, though he never takes knowledge from things, but beholds all things in the light of his eternal wisdom, yet so knows things in himself that he none the less knows them in their natures and effects; that is, he knows in himself when and how things are in their own existences and natures, and when they are not so. Or, [[2:5|thou shalt see|Videbis]], that is, thou shalt make others know and see: according to that word of God to Abraham, [[Gen 22:12|now I know that thou fearest God, and hast not spared thy only begotten son|Nunc cognovi quod timeas Deum, et non peperceris filio tuo]]. [[2:5|that he will bless thee to thy face|Quod in faciem benedicat tibi]], that is, he will openly curse. These I pass over, since they have already been explained at length. But that in the Scriptures *blessing* God is in this way taken for its contrary is clear from the fact that, in the third book of Kings, the most wicked Jezabel wrote to the citizens of Naboth that they should bring forth witnesses against him, saying: [[3 Kings 21:13|Naboth hath blasphemed God and the king|Benedixit Naboth Deo et regi]] [the Latin is *benedixit*, “blessed”; Jezabel's letter is at v. 10, but Denis's words, with Naboth's name, are those of v. 13].

paras.t: Dixit ergo Dominus ad Satan, ut ejus falsitatem ostenderet, et sancti Job declararet virtutes, præmiumque augeret: Ecce in manu tua est, id est, potestati tuæ eum trado tentandum et affligendum in corpore infra mortem. Non enim servos suos Dominus omnino tradit satanæ voluntati ac potestati tentandos, sed secundum mensuram decentem ac complacentem sibi. Verumtamen animam illius serva, id est, animalem seu corporalem ipsius vitam non præsumas exstinguere: quod utique, visa patientia Job, Satan fecisset, si permissus fuisset.
paras.en: [[2:6|And the Lord said to Satan|Dixit ergo Dominus ad Satan]], to show his falsehood, to declare the virtues of holy Job, and to increase his reward: [[2:6|Behold, he is in thy hand|Ecce in manu tua est]], that is, I give him up to thy power to be tempted and afflicted in the body, short of death. For the Lord does not give his servants up altogether to the will and power of Satan to be tempted, but according to a measure that is fitting and pleasing to him. [[2:6|but yet save his life|Verumtamen animam illius serva]] [Latin *animam*, which means both “soul” and “life”], that is, do not presume to put out his animal or bodily life: which Satan would certainly have done, seeing Job's patience, had he been allowed.

paras.t: Rabbi Moyses autem, quod dicitur, Animam illius serva, exponit de eo quod manet post mortem. Sed quia id immortificabile est, prior expositio aptior judicatur: nisi forte intelligatur de morte peccati, ut sit sensus, Animam illius serva, id est, ad peccatum eam non induces. Unde Gregorius ait: Servare Satan dicitur, irrumpere non audere. Sicut enim Deus inducere nos in tentationem dicitur, si nos induci ab adversario patiatur; sic Satan servare animam dicitur, quum hanc tentando superare prohibetur. Itaque, sicut Deus asseritur reprobos indurare et excæcare, non quod indurationis directe sit causa, sed quia non removet eam, faciendo ejus oppositum; sic Satan animam a morte peccati servare nunc fertur, non quod conservationem in bono efficiat, sed quia ejus oppositum inferre nequibit. Sicque expositio Rabbi Moysis erit subtilis, intelligendo per animam usum rationis, ut scilicet Dominus innuat afflictionem non esse tantam debere, quod rationis tolleret usum. Sic quoque, ut recitat Lyra, Rabbi Salomon interpretatur.
paras.en: But Rabbi Moses explains the words [[2:6|save his life|Animam illius serva]] of that which remains after death [that is, of the soul]. But since that cannot be put to death, the former explanation is judged more fitting: unless perhaps it is understood of the death of sin, so that the sense is, [[2:6|save his life|Animam illius serva]], that is, thou shalt not lead it into sin. Hence Gregory says: Satan's saving it means his not daring to break in upon it. For as God is said to lead us into temptation if he suffers us to be led into it by the adversary, so Satan is said to save the soul when he is prevented from overcoming it by tempting. And so, as God is said to harden and blind the reprobate[[John 12:40||]][[2 Cor 4:4||]] [the margin is partly unreadable here; it seems to give John xii, 40 and 2 Cor. iv, 4], not that he is directly the cause of the hardening, but because he does not remove it by doing its opposite, so Satan is now said to keep the soul from the death of sin, not that he brings about its keeping in good, but because he will be unable to bring in its opposite. And so the explanation of Rabbi Moses will be subtle, if by *soul* is understood the use of reason: that is, that the Lord intimates that the affliction must not be so great as to take away the use of reason. So also, as Lyra relates, Rabbi Salomon interprets it.

paras.t: Egressus igitur Satan a facie Domini: quod supra expositum est; percussit Job ulcere pessimo, id est pœnalissimo et (ut quidam dicunt) incurabili: quod non apparet, si paulo ante per animam vita corporalis ac animalis intelligatur. Sic enim hoc ulcus mortem naturaliter intulisset, quod Dominus prohibuit Satan: nisi quis dicat, quod Dominus prohibuit ne eum subito vel in brevi necaret. Aliqui enim incurabiles morbi satis diu stant simul cum vita. A planta pedis usque ad verticem ejus, scilicet capitis, ita quod toto fuit corpore ulcerosus. Potuit dici de Job illud Isaiæ: A planta pedis usque ad verticem capitis, non est in eo sanitas; vulnus, et livor, et plaga tumens. Unde hoc loco singulare ponitur pro plurali, scilicet ulcus pro innumerabilibus pene ulceribus, sicut in Psalmo, Dixit, et venit locusta; in Exodo quoque scribitur, Venit musca gravissima. Dicit autem Albertus: Ulcus calido interiori et humido putrescente, in fontes membrorum ebulliens, lepra est, ut dicit Galenus: quod pessimum dicitur, quia ex corruptione omnium generatur humorum. Puto tamen, inquit, quod fuit herpestiomenus. Ille namque corrodit carnem et ossa, secundum Galenum. Gregorius quoque ait: Duobus modis flagella pensanda sunt, scilicet qualia sint et quanta, id est quam multa et quam gravia. Sæpe enim si multa sunt, levigantur, si non sint gravia; et rursus levigantur, si quum sint gravia, non sint multa. Ad insinuandum ergo acerbissimam sancti Job afflictionem, dicitur percussus ulcere pessimo, quoad qualitatem; et a calcaneo usque ad verticem, quoad quantitatem, ita quod flagella ejus fuerunt multitudine et magnitudine præacerba.
paras.en: [[2:7|So Satan went forth from the presence of the Lord|Egressus igitur Satan a facie Domini]]: which was explained above; [[2:7|and struck Job with a very grievous ulcer|percussit Job ulcere pessimo]], that is, most painful and (as some say) incurable: which does not seem so, if a little before by *soul* the bodily and animal life is understood. For so this ulcer would naturally have brought death, which the Lord forbade Satan: unless someone says that the Lord forbade him to kill him suddenly or in a short time. For some incurable diseases last quite a long time together with life. [[2:7|from the sole of the foot even to the top of his head|A planta pedis usque ad verticem ejus]], namely of the head, so that he was ulcerous in his whole body. That saying of Isaias could have been said of Job: [[Is 1:6|From the sole of the foot unto the top of the head, there is no soundness therein: wounds and bruises and swelling sores|A planta pedis usque ad verticem capitis, non est in eo sanitas; vulnus, et livor, et plaga tumens]]. Hence in this place the singular is put for the plural, namely *ulcer* for almost countless ulcers, as in the Psalm, [[Ps 104:34|He spoke, and the locust came|Dixit, et venit locusta]]; and in Exodus too it is written, [[Ex 8:24|there came a very grievous swarm of flies|Venit musca gravissima]] [Latin *musca*, “fly”, in the singular]. And Albert says: An ulcer from an inward heat and a rotting moisture, boiling out into the sources of the limbs, is leprosy, as Galen says: and it is called *very grievous* because it is generated from the corruption of all the humours. Yet I think, he says, that it was *herpestiomenus* [that is, *herpes esthiomenus*, an “eating” sore that devours the flesh]. For this eats away flesh and bones, according to Galen. Gregory too says: Scourges are to be weighed in two ways, namely of what kind and how great they are, that is, how many and how heavy. For often if they are many they are lightened, if they are not heavy; and again they are lightened if, though heavy, they are not many. So, to convey the most bitter affliction of holy Job, he is said to be struck [[2:7|with a very grievous ulcer|ulcere pessimo]], as to its quality; and [[2:7|from the sole of the foot even to the top of his head|a calcaneo usque ad verticem]] [Latin *a calcaneo*, “from the heel”], as to its quantity, so that his scourges were exceedingly bitter in number and in greatness.

paras.t: Qui testa, id est fragmento fictilis vasis, saniem radebat, id est, scatentes ex vulneribus humores dure deposuit, ita quod magis abrasit quam tersit; sedens in sterquilinio. Solent ægrotantibus remedia lenitiva exterius adhiberi, molliaque stramenta supponi, et loca amœna ac suaves odores his provideri: quorum nullo, sed eorum contrariis usus est Job, scilicet testa et fœtido loco. Quod secundum Thomam et alios, dupliciter contingere potuit. Vel quia Job fuit omnino depauperatus, cunctis suis exterioribus bonis ei ablatis. Illa enim Dominus dedit Satanæ potestati. Vel quia Job sponte auxit sibi dolorem, seque ultra necessitatem humiliavit ad patientiæ demonstrationem, et ut misericordiam Dei citius impetraret: sicut et David fugiens Absalonem, nudis pedibus flens incessit, et maledictiones atque injurias Semei patientissime tulit, ut secundo Regum libro legitur. Et apparet quibusdam, quod primum istorum sit satis probabile. Potius autem reor secundum verius esse, tum quoniam scriptum non est quod utensilia domus Job fuerunt ablata, aut domus ejus combusta; nec potuit tanta ei esse paupertas, quin alium locum faciliter invenisset quam sterquiliniosum, aptius quoque instrumentum mundandi quam testam; nec verisimile, quod vir tantæ bonitatis fuerit a suis cognatis ac vicinis, in quorum medio habitavit, ita contemptus, quin ei in mutuatione lecti et similium necessariorum libenter succurrissent. Ex maxima ergo sui ipsius humiliatione, contemptu, patientia, devotione hæc fecit. Et secundum Albertum, manum percutientis adjuvit, ne mollibus utens, levius ferret, et sub manu disciplinantis sedit immobilis in loco fœtido et immundo.
paras.en: [[2:8|And he took a potsherd|Qui testa]], that is, a fragment of an earthen vessel, [[2:8|and scraped the corrupt matter|saniem radebat]], that is, roughly cleared away the humours oozing from his wounds, so that he scraped rather than wiped them; [[2:8|sitting on a dunghill|sedens in sterquilinio]]. To the sick, soothing remedies are commonly applied outwardly, soft bedding is laid under them, and pleasant places and sweet scents are provided for them: none of which Job used, but their contraries, namely a potsherd and a stinking place. Which, according to Thomas and others, could have come about in two ways. Either because Job had been made utterly poor, all his outward goods having been taken from him; for the Lord had given these into Satan's power. Or because Job of his own will increased his pain, and humbled himself beyond necessity, to show forth his patience and to obtain God's mercy the sooner: as David too, fleeing Absalom, went weeping and barefoot[[2 Kings 15:30||]], and most patiently bore the curses and insults of Semei[[2 Kings 16:9||]] [the margin seems to give II Reg. xvi, 9–13], as is read in the second book of Kings. And to some it seems that the first of these is quite probable. But I rather think the second the truer, since it is not written that the furnishings of Job's house were taken away or his house burnt; nor could his poverty have been so great that he would not easily have found some other place than a dunghill, and a fitter instrument for cleansing than a potsherd; nor is it likely that a man of such goodness was so despised by his kinsmen and neighbours, in whose midst he lived, that they would not gladly have helped him by lending a bed and like necessaries. So it was out of the greatest humbling of himself, contempt of self, patience and devotion that he did these things. And according to Albert, he helped the hand of the one striking him, lest by using soft things he should bear it more lightly, and he sat unmoved under the hand of the one chastising him, in a stinking and unclean place.

paras.t: Hinc dicit Gregorius: Hoc facto patenter ostenditur, corpus suum quomodo sibi sanum Job subdidit, quod et percussum sic despiciens curavit; quam ille mollitiem suæ sanæ carni concessit, qui non vestem, non digitos, sed testam etiam vulneribus admovit.
paras.en: Hence Gregory says: By this deed it is plainly shown how Job kept his body subject to himself when it was sound, since even when it was struck he tended it with such contempt; how little softness he granted his flesh when it was sound, who put to his wounds not a cloth, not his fingers, but even a potsherd.

paras.t: Iterum ait: Intueri libet quid est quod omnipotens Deus, quos sibi tam caros in æternum conspicit, tam vehementer quasi despiciens affligit. Ecce dum beati Job vulnera cruciatusque considero, repente mentis oculos ad Joannem Baptistam reduco; et non sine gravissima admiratione perpendo, quod ille in utero matris Spiritu Sancto impletus, sponsi amicus, quo inter natos mulierum major nemo surrexit, propheta et plus quam propheta, ab iniquis in carcerem mittitur, et pro puellæ saltatu capite truncatur, ac tantæ virtutis vir pro risu turpium moritur, et pro temulenti verbis in præmium saltationis occiditur. Quid est quod omnipotens Deus sic vehementer in hoc sæculo despicit, quos sic sublimiter ante sæcula elegit, nisi hoc quod pietati fidelium patet, quoniam sic eos premit in infimis, quia videt quomodo remuneret in summis, et foras usque ad despecta dejicit, quia intus usque ad incomprehensibilia perducit? Quid ergo illic passuri sunt, quos reprobat, si hic sic cruciat quos amat?
paras.en: Again he says: It is worth looking into why almighty God so vehemently afflicts, as though despising them, those whom he sees to be so dear to him for eternity. See, while I consider the wounds and torments of blessed Job, I suddenly turn the eyes of my mind to John the Baptist; and not without the deepest wonder I ponder that he who was filled with the Holy Ghost in his mother's womb[[Luke 1:15||]], the friend of the Bridegroom[[John 3:29||]], than whom none greater has risen among those born of women[[Matt 11:11||]], a prophet and [[Matt 11:9|more than a prophet|plus quam propheta]], is cast into prison by wicked men and beheaded for a girl's dancing, and a man of such virtue dies for the laughter of the base, and is slain at the word of a drunken man as the reward of a dance. Why is it that almighty God so vehemently despises in this world those whom he so sublimely chose before the ages, unless it be this, which is plain to the devotion of the faithful: that he so presses them down in the lowest things because he sees how he will reward them in the highest, and casts them outwardly down even to what is despised because inwardly he leads them on even to things beyond comprehension? What then will they suffer there whom he rejects, if here he so torments those whom he loves?

paras.t: Dixit autem illi uxor sua: quam Satan vivam reliquit, ut per eam sanctum virum tentaret, sciens quomodo viri soleant uxoribus decipi: non enim videtur quin licentiam habuit auferendi uxorem, quemadmodum filios. Adhuc permanes in simplicitate tua? quasi dicat: Mirum est quod tot adversitatibus pressus, nondum intelligis quod simplicitas tua fuit inanis, et quod infructuosum fuit tibi simpliciter vivere. Mulier ista fuit de numero hominum imperfectorum, qui quum cernunt bonis in sæculo isto evenire adversa, malisque prospera, scandalizantur et putant inutile esse servire Deo, quasi in præsenti vita esset retributio ultimata. Contra quos Dominus ait per Malachiam: Invaluerunt super me verba vestra: et dixistis, Vanus est qui servit Domino. Et quod emolumentum quia custodivimus præcepta ejus, et ambulavimus tristes coram Domino? Ergo nunc beatos dicimus arrogantes, siquidem ædificati sunt.
paras.en: [[2:9|And his wife said to him|Dixit autem illi uxor sua]]: she whom Satan left alive, so that through her he might tempt the holy man, knowing how men are wont to be deceived by their wives: for it seems that he had leave to take away the wife as well as the sons. [[2:9|Dost thou still continue in thy simplicity?|Adhuc permanes in simplicitate tua?]] as if she said: It is a wonder that, pressed by so many adversities, thou dost not yet understand that thy simplicity was empty, and that it was fruitless for thee to live simply. This woman was of the number of imperfect men, who, when they see adversity befall the good in this world and prosperity the wicked, are scandalized and think it useless to serve God, as though the final retribution were in the present life. Against them the Lord says through Malachias: [[Mal 3:13|Your words have been unsufferable to me|Invaluerunt super me verba vestra]]: [[Mal 3:14|And you have said|et dixistis]], [[Mal 3:14|He laboureth in vain that serveth God, and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinances, and that we have walked sorrowful before the Lord|Vanus est qui servit Domino. Et quod emolumentum quia custodivimus præcepta ejus, et ambulavimus tristes coram Domino?]]? [[Mal 3:15|Wherefore now we call the proud people happy, for they that work wickedness are built up|Ergo nunc beatos dicimus arrogantes, siquidem ædificati sunt]].

paras.t: Benedic Deo, et morere. Non consulendo, sed deridendo hoc dicit. Quasi pronuntiet: Si amplius benedixeris et gratias egeris Deo post istam adversitatem, sicut jam ante benedixisti ei post filiorum tuorum mortem, nil restat nisi ut tua augeatur afflictio, et discedas: quasi diceret, Si per oppositum malediceres Deo, viveres, et bene tibi succederet, sicut et aliis fraudulentis. Vel ex impatientia dicit hoc, ut sit sensus: Quia benedicente te Deo, tot tibi contigerunt adversa, maledic ei, et morere, quia in tanta miseria melior tibi est mors quam vita. Sicque ad desperationem ac blasphemiam provocavit.
paras.en: [[2:9|bless God and die|Benedic Deo, et morere]]. She says this not in counsel but in mockery. As if she declared: If thou blessest God further and givest him thanks after this adversity, as thou didst bless him before, after the death of thy sons, nothing remains but that thy affliction be increased and thou depart; as if she said, If on the contrary thou wouldst curse God, thou wouldst live and it would go well with thee, as with other deceitful men. Or she says this out of impatience, so that the sense is: Since, while thou blessest God, so many adversities have befallen thee, curse him, and die, for in such misery death is better for thee than life. And so she provoked him to despair and blasphemy.

paras.t: Qui ait ad illam, instructive, quoniam vir tenetur uxori correctionem et instructionem: Quasi una de stultis mulieribus locuta es, quia contra veram sapientiam sunt quæ dicis: et, Quasi, dicit hic veritatem, non similitudinem tantum. Nec ait absolute, Quasi una de mulieribus, ne vitium sexui imputetur. Nec etiam dicit, Quasi una de malis mulieribus, sed, Quasi una de stultis, ut iniquitas ejus per stultitiam quodammodo allevietur: nam et mulier hæc ex subita tentatione, animi instabilitate, feminea commotione ac rationis debilitate magis quam ex malitia videtur peccasse. Et quoniam uxor hæc non tam viro, quam divinæ providentiæ derogavit, sanctus Job Dei injuriam dissimulare non quivit, nec debuit: quoniam teste Chrysostomo, quamvis pium sit propriam injuriam æquanimiter ferre, tamen Dei injuriam impium est sustinere.
paras.en: [[2:10|And he said to her|Qui ait ad illam]], by way of instruction, since a husband owes his wife correction and instruction: [[2:10|Thou hast spoken like one of the foolish women|Quasi una de stultis mulieribus locuta es]], for what thou sayest is against true wisdom: and *like* [Latin *quasi*, “as it were”] here expresses the truth, not a likeness only. Nor does he say absolutely, *Like one of the women*, lest the fault be imputed to the sex. Nor again does he say, *Like one of the wicked women*, but, *Like one of the foolish*, so that her wickedness might in some way be lightened by foolishness: for this woman too seems to have sinned from sudden temptation, instability of mind, a woman's agitation and weakness of reason rather than from malice. And since this wife disparaged not so much her husband as divine providence, holy Job could not, and ought not, pass over the injury done to God: since, as Chrysostom witnesses, though it is godly to bear an injury to oneself with an even mind, yet it is ungodly to endure an injury to God.

paras.t: Deinde contra stultitiam instruit eam. Si, pro Quia, bona suscepimus de manu Domini, id est opulentiam rerum, prolis fecunditatem, corporis sanitatem, et quidquid habemus ac sumus, et præsertim dona gratiæ in exhibitione, donaque gloriæ in promissione; mala pœnalia, id est adversa, quare non sustineamus? id est, cur ea patienter ferre non debemus? tanquam dicat: Imo debemus ea cum patientia tolerare, eo quod omnia nostra bona sint Dei dona, qui sicut sponte ac misericorditer dedit, sic libere ac juste tollere sua potest; nec nostrum est murmurare, sed in omnibus regia via incedere, ut nec prosperis inaniter erigamur, neque adversis enerviter deprimamur: quemadmodum ad Philippenses scribit Apostolus, Scio humiliari, scio et abundare. Propter quod dicit Gregorius: Magna consolatio tribulationis est, si quum adversa patimur, Dei dona ad memoriam revocemus. Hinc namque in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: In die bonorum ne immemor sis malorum, et in die malorum ne immemor sis bonorum.
paras.en: Then he instructs her against foolishness. [[2:10|If|Si]], put for *since*, [[2:10|we have received good things at the hand of God|bona suscepimus de manu Domini]], that is, abundance of goods, fruitfulness in children, health of body, and whatever we have and are, and above all the gifts of grace bestowed and the gifts of glory promised; [[2:10|evil|mala]], that is, the evils of punishment, adversities: [[2:10|why should we not receive|quare non sustineamus]] them? that is, why ought we not to bear them patiently? as if he said: Nay, we ought to bear them with patience, because all our goods are the gifts of God, who, as he freely and mercifully gave, so can freely and justly take away what is his; nor is it for us to murmur, but in all things to walk the king's way, so that we be neither vainly lifted up by prosperity nor feebly cast down by adversity: as the Apostle writes to the Philippians, [[Phil 4:12|I know both how to be brought low, and I know how to abound|Scio humiliari, scio et abundare]]. For which reason Gregory says: It is a great consolation in tribulation if, when we suffer adversity, we call to mind the gifts of God. For hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 11:27|In the day of good things be not unmindful of evils: and in the day of evils be not unmindful of good things|In die bonorum ne immemor sis malorum, et in die malorum ne immemor sis bonorum]].

paras.t: In omnibus his non peccavit Job labiis suis; quia nec loquenda tacuit, nec tacenda expressit. Nos autem duobus modis labiis nostris peccamus, videlicet vel injusta dicendo, aut justa tacendo.
paras.en: [[2:10|In all these things Job did not sin with his lips|In omnibus his non peccavit Job labiis suis]]; for he neither kept silent what should be spoken nor uttered what should be kept silent. But we sin with our lips in two ways, namely either by saying unjust things or by keeping silent about just ones.

paras.t: Patet itaque ex inductis, quod undique tribulatio Job augetur. Nam ægris atque afflictis solent verba consolatoria pro relevamine dici: pro quo ipsi Job verba derisoria, invectiva et increpatoria sunt prolata, non solum a conjuge, sed a tribus quoque præcipuis suis amicis, et deinceps a quarto: per quos Satan tentat eum per derogationem honoris. Imponebant etenim sancto Job multiplicem culpam, sicut patebit.
paras.en: It is clear, then, from what has been brought forward, that Job's tribulation is increased on every side. For to the sick and afflicted, words of consolation are commonly spoken for their relief: instead of which, to Job himself words of mockery, invective and rebuke were uttered, not only by his wife but also by his three chief friends, and afterwards by a fourth: through whom Satan tempts him by the disparaging of his honour. For they laid manifold guilt upon holy Job, as will appear.

paras.t: Igitur audientes tres amici Job omne malum pœnæ, quod accidisset ei: tanta namque tanti viri adversitas, tam inaudita atque insolita, velociter undique vulgabatur; venerunt singuli de loco suo. Multos autem habuit Job amicos, sed isti ampliori, imo et specialissima amicitia fuerant ei conjuncti, sicut ex facto ostensum est. Eliphas Themanites, et Baldad Suhites, et Sophar Naamathites. Isti tres viri, reges vocantur in libro Tobiæ, quo legitur: Sicut beato Job insultabant reges, ita Tobiæ parentes et cognati ejus. Ambrosius quoque in libro de Officiis, nominat eos reges. Illis quippe temporibus reges quidem non erant tot urbibus, locis seu villis præsidentes, ut modo communiter, prout ex libro Josue constat. Siquidem filii Israel in terra Chanaan occiderunt triginta unum reges. Unde et viri hi tres a suis urbibus seu terris cognomina sortiuntur.
paras.en: [[2:11|Now when Job's three friends heard all the evil|Igitur audientes tres amici Job omne malum]] of punishment [[2:11|that had befallen him|quod accidisset ei]]: for so great an adversity of so great a man, so unheard-of and unusual, was quickly spread abroad on every side; [[2:11|they came every one from his own place|venerunt singuli de loco suo]]. Job had many friends, but these had been joined to him by a fuller, nay a most special, friendship, as the deed showed. [[2:11|Eliphaz, the Themanite, and Baldad, the Suhite, and Sophar, the Naamathite|Eliphas Themanites, et Baldad Suhites, et Sophar Naamathites]]. These three men are called kings in the book of Tobias, where we read: [[Tob 2:15|as the kings insulted over holy Job|Sicut beato Job insultabant reges]], so did the relations and kinsmen of Tobias. Ambrose too, in his book On Duties, names them kings. For in those times kings did not rule over as many cities, places or towns as is commonly the case now, as appears from the book of Josue: for the children of Israel slew one and thirty kings in the land of Chanaan[[Jos 12:24||]] [the margin gives Josue xii, 9–24, the list of those kings]. Hence these three men too take their surnames from their cities or lands.

paras.t: Condixerant enim sibi, ut pariter venientes, visitarent eum et consolarentur. Et puto, quod non sine magna et condecenti familia advenerunt. In hoc autem condictu et visitatione hac ostenderunt se veros amicos, quia amicum suum in necessitate, afflictione, inopia non reliquerunt: unde et simul venerunt, ut gravissime afflictum abundantius pariter consolarentur. Hinc in Ecclesiastico habetur: Si possides amicum, in tentatione posside eum, et ne facile credas ei te ipsum: est enim amicus secundum tempus suum, et non permanet in die tribulationis. Et alibi: In tristitia viri amicus agnitus est. Denique amici præsentia et adspectus consolatorii sunt, et amicorum compassio consolativa est: quia per hanc adversitas, quæ est velut onus grave, levius fertur. Et quoniam delectabilissimum est sumere experimentum de amicitia alicujus, quod potissime accipitur ex compassione in adversis; idcirco compassio in quantum de consolatione adducit, tantum de afflictione dirimit: tristitia namque ex admixtione delectationis alleviatur. Propter quod Ecclesiasticus ait: Amicus fidelis, protectio fortis; qui invenit illum, invenit thesaurum. Amicus fidelis, medicamentum vitæ et immortalitatis.
paras.en: [[2:11|For they had made an appointment to come together and visit him, and comfort him|Condixerant enim sibi, ut pariter venientes, visitarent eum et consolarentur]]. And I think they came not without a large and fitting retinue. In this agreement and visit they showed themselves true friends, because they did not forsake their friend in need, affliction and want: hence too they came together, so that together they might more abundantly comfort one so grievously afflicted. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 6:7|If thou wouldst get a friend, try him before thou takest him, and do not credit him easily|Si possides amicum, in tentatione posside eum, et ne facile credas ei te ipsum]] [Denis adds *te ipsum*: “do not easily trust thyself to him”]: [[Ecclus 6:8|For there is a friend for his own occasion, and he will not abide in the day of thy trouble|est enim amicus secundum tempus suum, et non permanet in die tribulationis]]. And elsewhere: [[Ecclus 12:9|a friend is known in his adversity|In tristitia viri amicus agnitus est]] [Denis has *in tristitia viri*, “in a man's sadness”]. Lastly, the presence and sight of a friend are consoling, and the compassion of friends brings consolation: because through it adversity, which is like a heavy burden, is borne more lightly. And since it is most delightful to make trial of someone's friendship, which is had above all from compassion in adversity, therefore compassion takes away as much from affliction as it brings of consolation: for sadness is lightened by the admixture of delight. For which reason Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 6:14|A faithful friend is a strong defence: and he that hath found him, hath found a treasure|Amicus fidelis, protectio fortis; qui invenit illum, invenit thesaurum]]. [[Ecclus 6:16|A faithful friend is the medicine of life and immortality|Amicus fidelis, medicamentum vitæ et immortalitatis]].

paras.t: Quumque elevassent oculos procul, id est a tanta distantia, qua homo potest determinate per visum cognosci, non cognoverunt eum, per visum, propter maximam sui corporis ac vestitus et pristinæ dispositionis immutationem. Verumtamen aliunde, scilicet ex relatu, sciverunt quod ipse esset qui ita sedebat: aliter non fecissent quod subditur. Et exclamantes, præ compassionis vehementia, ploraverunt, scissisque vestibus, ad mœroris indicium, et ut nudato congruerent, sparserunt pulverem super caput suum in cœlum, id est, pulverem in aerem projiciebant, et capitibus superposuerunt, a Deo cœli consolationem poscentes, et suum affectum atque effectum affectui effectuique amici afflicti fideliter conformantes, cum humiliato et dejecto se humiliantes ac dejicientes, et malum ipsius quasi proprium æstimantes, ut amicitia vera requirit, quia et hoc præsertim lenit afflicti dolorem, dicente Gregorio: Ordo consolationis est, ut quum volumus quempiam afflictum a mœrore suspendere, studeamus prius mœrendo ejus luctui concordare. Dolentem namque non potest consolari, qui non concordat dolori: quia eo ipso quo a mœrentis dolore discrepat, minus ab illo recipitur, a quo mentis qualitate separatur. Neque enim ferrum ferro conjungitur, si non utrumque exustione ignis liquetur.
paras.en: [[2:12|And when they had lifted up their eyes afar off|Quumque elevassent oculos procul]], that is, from such a distance as a man can be clearly recognized by sight, [[2:12|they knew him not|non cognoverunt eum]] by sight, because of the very great change in his body, his clothing and his former condition. Yet they knew from elsewhere, namely by report, that it was he who sat there: otherwise they would not have done what follows. [[2:12|and crying out|Et exclamantes]], from the vehemence of their compassion, [[2:12|they wept, and rending their garments|ploraverunt, scissisque vestibus]], as a sign of grief, and to be like him who was stripped bare, [[2:12|they sprinkled dust upon their heads toward heaven|sparserunt pulverem super caput suum in cœlum]], that is, they threw dust into the air and put it upon their heads, asking consolation from the God of heaven, and faithfully conforming their own feeling and state to the feeling and state of their afflicted friend, humbling and casting themselves down with him who was humbled and cast down, and counting his evil as their own, as true friendship requires; for this especially soothes the pain of one afflicted, as Gregory says: The order of consolation is that, when we wish to raise someone afflicted out of his grief, we first strive by grieving to be in accord with his mourning. For he who is not in accord with the pain cannot console one in pain: because by the very fact that he is at variance with the mourner's grief, he is the less received by him from whom he is separated in disposition of mind. For iron is not joined to iron unless both are melted by the burning of fire.

paras.t: Et sederunt cum eo in terra: quod magnæ exstitit humilitatis; septem diebus et septem noctibus: quod magnæ fuit longanimitatis. Porro Gregorius relinquit sub dubio, an toto tempore hoc continue manserint secum, an frequenter visitaverint eum infra hos dies. Thomas vero aliique communiter dicunt, quod non continue ibi secum fuerunt, sed congruentibus horis. Verumtamen considerata magnitudine dilectionis eorum ad Job, et quomodo in aliis conformaverunt se ei, potius arbitror cum Gregorio dubitandum, quam incaute quid proferendum.
paras.en: [[2:13|And they sat with him on the ground|Et sederunt cum eo in terra]]: which showed great humility; [[2:13|seven day and seven nights|septem diebus et septem noctibus]]: which showed great long-suffering. Now Gregory leaves it in doubt whether they stayed with him continually all this time, or visited him often during these days. But Thomas and others commonly say that they were not with him there continually, but at fitting hours. Yet, considering the greatness of their love for Job, and how in other things they conformed themselves to him, I think it better to doubt with Gregory than to assert anything rashly.

paras.t: Et nemo ex illis loquebatur, infra hoc tempus, verbum quodcumque: quum tamen amicis aspera passis soleant ab amicis eorum blanda et consolatoria dici pro relevamine pœnæ suæ. Videbant enim dolorem esse vehementem: unde putabant quod Job tristitia victus esset, et adversitatibus sic dejectus quod eorum consolationem non attenderet nec curaret. Vehementes equidem passiones rationem absorbere consueverunt. Unde quidam de morte suorum sic contristantur, quod consolationem nullam admittunt, sicut de Jacob in Genesi scribitur. Idcirco dixit Poeta: Quis matrem, nisi mentis inops, in funere nati Flere vetat? Verumtamen in Job ita non fuit, cujus perfectionem amici præfati non plene noverunt. Itaque viri isti manserunt sancto Job in principio veri amici. Hocque (ut tactum est) unum exstat remedium desolationis et pœnæ afflictorum, dum vident sibi mansisse amicos fideles: qui inter exteriora hominis bona computantur majora, juxta illud Ecclesiastici, Non est digna ponderatio auri vel argenti contra bonitatem fidei amici fidelis.
paras.en: [[2:13|and no man spoke to him|Et nemo ex illis loquebatur]] in all this time [[2:13|a word|verbum]] of any kind: though to friends who have suffered harsh things, gentle and consoling words are commonly spoken by their friends to relieve their pain. [[2:13|for they saw that his grief was very great|Videbant enim dolorem esse vehementem]]: hence they thought that Job was overcome by sadness and so cast down by adversities that he would neither heed nor care for their consolation. For vehement passions are wont to swallow up reason. Hence some are so saddened by the death of their own that they admit no consolation, as is written of Jacob in Genesis[[Gen 37:35||]]. Therefore the Poet said: Who but one out of his wits would forbid a mother to weep at her son's funeral? [Ovid, *Remedia amoris* 127–128] But in Job it was not so, whose perfection these friends did not fully know. So these men remained, at the beginning, true friends to holy Job. And this (as was touched on) is the one remedy for the desolation and pain of the afflicted, when they see that faithful friends have remained to them: who are counted among the greater outward goods of man, according to that saying of Ecclesiasticus, [[Ecclus 6:15|no weight of gold and silver is able to countervail the goodness of his fidelity|Non est digna ponderatio auri vel argenti contra bonitatem fidei amici fidelis]].

2.title: De spirituali seu mystico ejusdem capituli secundi intellectu.
2.title_en: On the spiritual or mystical sense of the same second chapter

paras.t: Mysticus seu spiritualis sacræ Scripturæ sensus triplex consistit, videlicet allegoricus, tropologicus, anagogicus. Allegorice autem interpretando præsens capitulum, hoc est de Christo, expositio ex præcedentis capituli allegorica expositione, pro maxima parte dependet ac patet. Quemadmodum enim Satan non tentavit Job sine Dei licentia ac permissu, ita nec Christum in carne mortali. Et sicut expetiit Job tentandum in propria persona, quum aliarum rerum sublationem patienter tulisset: ita quum Christum nec in tentatione in deserto incepta, nec postea vincere potuisset, nec eum esse Dei Filium ac Messiam pro certo novisset, tandem sanctissimam ac fructuosissimam ejus in hoc sæculo conversationem non ferens, expetiit ut eum in proprio corpore suo per iniquos homines vulnerare ac persequi sineretur: quod et concessum est. Nam Evangelista ait, quod diabolus misit in cor Judæ Iscariotis, ut traderet eum. Christus quoque passione instante, Venit, inquit, ad me princeps mundi, et in me non habet quidquam. Sed et iterum ait Judæis: Vos ex patre diabolo estis, et desideria patris vestri vultis perficere me occidendo. Rursusque trina Christi tentatione descripta, in deserto inchoata, Lucas adjecit: Consummata omni tentatione, diabolus recessit ab eo usque ad tempus: quo innuit quod postea rediit, non utique sine licentia permissioneque Dei. Ex his magna ex parte patescit, quomodo præsens capitulum competat Christo. Aliqua tamen difficiliora tangenda sunt.
paras.en: The mystical or spiritual sense of sacred Scripture is threefold: namely, allegorical, tropological and anagogical [that is, the sense concerning Christ and the Church, the moral sense, and the sense concerning the things of heaven]. Now when the present chapter is interpreted allegorically, that is, of Christ, its exposition depends for the most part on the allegorical exposition of the preceding chapter, and is plain from it. For just as Satan did not tempt Job without God’s leave and permission, so neither did he tempt Christ in his mortal flesh. And as he asked that Job be tempted in his own person, when Job had borne patiently the taking away of his other things: so, since he had been unable to overcome Christ either in the temptation begun in the desert[[Matt 4:1||]] [the margin reference here is misread; the temptation in the desert is told in Matt 4:1] or afterwards, and did not know for certain that he was the Son of God and the Messias, at length, unable to bear his most holy and most fruitful way of life in this world, he asked to be allowed to wound and persecute him in his own body through wicked men: and this too was granted. For the Evangelist says that the devil put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot to betray him[[John 13:2||]].
