Electi quippe, dum mentis suæ oculis judicia divina proponunt, et de occulta super se summi Judicis sententia trepidant; dum se ad Deum pervenire posse confidunt, et tamen ne non perveniant metuunt; dum peccata sua præterita recolunt quæ deplorant, et quæ sibi adhuc futura sunt nesciunt: quasi quædam volumina, id est abundantiæ cogitationum, curarum et affectionum instar aquarum nascuntur, quæ in mœroris rugitus quasi in subjectiora littora defluunt.
paras.en: [[3:24|Before I eat I sigh|Antequam comedam, suspiro]]. For the soul to eat is to be fed on the contemplation of the light above. It sighs, then, before it eats, because it is first afflicted with the groaning of tribulation, and afterwards filled with the refreshment of contemplation. For unless it sighs, it does not eat: since he who does not humble himself in this exile by laments of heavenly longing does not taste the joys of the eternal fatherland; and those who are glad in the poverty of this pilgrimage are fasting from the food of truth. [[3:24|and as overflowing waters, so is my roaring|Et quasi inundantis aquæ, sic rugitus meus]]: that is, the voice of my grief and lamentation, which I have sent forth out of inward sorrow, is great and violent, as overflowing waters come on with force and swell. For the elect, while they set the divine judgments before the eyes of their mind, and tremble at the hidden sentence of the supreme Judge upon them; while they trust that they can come to God, and yet fear that they may not come; while they recall their past sins, which they lament, and do not know what is still to come upon them: there arise, as it were, certain billows [*volumina*, literally "rollings", as of waves], that is, floods of thoughts, cares and affections, like waters, which flow down into roarings of grief as on to lower shores.

paras.t: Quia timor quem timebam, id est formidatus effectus, evenit mihi; et quod verebar, accidit mihi. Justus nil amplius quam displicere Deo aut relinqui ab eo formidat. Unde in ipsis flagellis justi timore turbantur, ne forte malum quod patiuntur, non piæ disciplinæ correctio sit, sed animadversio justæ vindictæ. Ideo dicit Psalmista: Quis novit potestatem iræ tuæ, etc.?
paras.en: [[3:25|For the fear which I feared|Quia timor quem timebam]], that is, the outcome I dreaded, [[3:25|hath come upon me|evenit mihi]]; [[3:25|and that which I was afraid of, hath befallen me|et quod verebar, accidit mihi]]. The just man dreads nothing more than to displease God or to be abandoned by him. Hence in their very scourges the just are troubled with fear, lest perhaps the evil they suffer be not the correction of a loving discipline but the chastisement of just vengeance. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 89:11|Who knoweth the power of thy anger|Quis novit potestatem iræ tuæ]], etc.?

paras.t: Qualis vero sanctus Job fuit in potestate, subjungitur. Nonne dissimulavi? id est, per potestatem et auctoritatem me ipsum non extuli, nec iracundiæ locum dedi, sed dissimulavi injuriam, patiens fui. Nonne silui a verbis inordinatis, superbis, irrefrenatis, in quæ præsidentes labi consueverunt? Nonne quievi ab opere malo? Quamvis autem ubique peccemus cogitando, loquendo, agendo, magis tamen quum mundi prosperitate levamur. Nam quum se alios præire potestate animus conspicit, alta de se elate cogitans sentit; et quum auctoritati vocis a nullo resistitur, lingua licentius per abrupta ac impia defrenatur; quumque quod libet facere licet, juste sibi omnia licere quæ libent, existimat. Talis vero Job non fuisse describitur. Nihilo minus subdit, et venit super me indignatio, id est dira hæc flagellatio.
paras.en: What manner of man holy Job was in power is added next. [[3:26|Have I not dissembled?|Nonne dissimulavi?]] that is, I did not exalt myself through my power and authority, nor give place to anger, but I let the injury pass as if unseen [*dissimulavi*, the word of the verse]: I was patient. [[3:26|have I not kept silence|Nonne silui]] from disordered, proud, unbridled words, into which those in authority are wont to slip? [[3:26|have I not been quiet|Nonne quievi]] from evil work? Now though we sin everywhere in thought, word and deed, we do so the more when we are lifted up by the prosperity of the world. For when the mind sees itself ahead of others in power, it thinks proudly of itself and feels itself lofty; and when no one resists the authority of its voice, the tongue runs unbridled the more freely over steep and impious places; and when it may do what it pleases, it reckons that all things that please it are rightly lawful for it. But Job is described as not having been such. Nevertheless he adds: [[3:26|and indignation is come upon me|et venit super me indignatio]], that is, this dreadful scourging.

paras.t: Hæc ex verbis B. Gregorii breviter sumpta sunt: de cujus expositione quid judicare, parvitatis meæ non est. Præterea quædam hujus capituli verba moraliter interpretatur, dicendo:
paras.en: These things have been taken briefly from the words of blessed Gregory: it is not for my littleness to pass judgment on his exposition. He also interprets certain words of this chapter morally, saying:

paras.t: Pereat dies, id est mundana prosperitas, seu peccati delectatio, in qua natus sum, non Deo, sed mundo ac dæmoni, inficiendo esse naturæ per mala culpæ, per quæ carni, mundo ac dæmoni vivitur; et nox in qua dictum est, Conceptus est homo. Nox ista est cæcitas mentis, ex qua culpa originatur. Idcirco in nocte dicitur homo conceptus, et natus in die, quia nequaquam ad peccati delectationem raperetur, nisi prius per voluntarias mentis tenebras infirmaretur. Denique sacra Scriptura de homine tripliciter loquitur. Primo, quantum ad id quod est per naturam, sicut quum dicitur: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram. Secundo, quoad id quod est per culpam, ut quum loquitur Paulus: Quum sit inter vos zelus et contentio, nonne carnales estis, et secundum hominem ambulatis? Tertio, quantum ad id quod est per infirmitatem, ut quum ait Propheta: Maledictus qui spem suam ponit in homine, id est in infirmitate.
paras.en: [[3:3|Let the day perish|Pereat dies]], that is, worldly prosperity, or the delight of sin, [[3:3|wherein I was born|in qua natus sum]], not to God but to the world and the devil, by infecting the being of nature through the evils of guilt, by which one lives to the flesh, the world and the devil; [[3:3|and the night in which it was said: A man child is conceived|et nox in qua dictum est, Conceptus est homo]]. This night is the blindness of the mind, from which guilt takes its origin. Therefore man is said to be conceived in the night and born in the day, because he would never be carried off to the delight of sin unless he were first weakened by wilful darkness of mind. Moreover, Holy Scripture speaks of man in three ways. First, as to what he is by nature, as when it is said: [[Gen 1:26|Let us make man to our image and likeness|Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram]]. Secondly, as to what he is by guilt, as when Paul says: [[1 Cor 3:3|whereas there is among you envying and contention, are you not carnal and walk you not according to man?|Quum sit inter vos zelus et contentio, nonne carnales estis, et secundum hominem ambulatis?]] Thirdly, as to what he is by weakness, as when the Prophet says: [[Jer 17:5|Cursed be the man that trusteth in man|Maledictus qui spem suam ponit in homine]], that is, in weakness [the margin's reference is garbled; the words are Jer 17:5, which Denis gives freely: "who putteth his hope in man"].

paras.t: Dies illa vertatur in tenebras, id est, quæ dies falso putatur, vitiosa noscatur: et quod delectatione mala patratum est, dolore pœnitentiæ emendetur. Non requirat eum Deus desuper, ad vindicandum, id est, det nobis gratiam pœnitendi et satisfaciendi pro eo. Tunc enim Deus eum non vindicabit, dicente Apostolo: Si nosmetipsos dijudicaverimus, non utique dijudicaremur. Non illustretur lumine, id est, Deus lumine suæ justitiæ eum non manifestet in hora judicii, sed interim ignoscendo tegat et deleat eum. Beati enim quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates, et quorum tecta sunt peccata.
paras.en: [[3:4|Let that day be turned into darkness|Dies illa vertatur in tenebras]], that is, let what is falsely thought to be day be known as vicious, and let what was done by evil delight be amended by the sorrow of penance. [[3:4|let not God regard it from above|Non requirat eum Deus desuper]], to avenge it [*requirere*, to seek out, to call to account], that is, let him give us the grace to repent and make satisfaction for it. For then God will not avenge it, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 11:31|if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged|Si nosmetipsos dijudicaverimus, non utique dijudicaremur]] [the margin's chapter number is misread]. [[3:4|and let not the light shine upon it|Non illustretur lumine]], that is, let not God show it forth with the light of his justice in the hour of judgment, but in the meantime, by forgiving, let him cover it and blot it out. For [[Ps 31:1|Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered|Beati enim quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates, et quorum tecta sunt peccata]].

paras.t: Obscurent eum tenebræ, id est pœnitentiæ lamenta, ne amplius pateat, et umbra mortis, id est, oblivione Deus eum quasi non recordando abjiciat; occupet eum caligo, id est dolor pœnitentialis interior, qui bene contristat, confundit et turbat: est enim confusio adducens gratiam et gloriam; et involvatur amaritudine, ut quo major fuit delectatio in peccando, eo major sit afflictio in satisfaciendo.
paras.en: [[3:5|Let darkness|Obscurent eum tenebræ]] cover it, that is, the laments of penance, so that it may lie open no longer, [[3:5|and the shadow of death|et umbra mortis]]: that is, let God cast it away in forgetfulness, as though not remembering it; [[3:5|let a mist overspread it|occupet eum caligo]], that is, the inward sorrow of penance, which saddens, confounds and troubles to good purpose: for there is [[Ecclus 4:25|a shame that bringeth glory and grace|confusio adducens gratiam et gloriam]] [*confusio*, "shame", is the word behind "confounds" just before]; [[3:5|and let it be wrapped up in bitterness|et involvatur amaritudine]], so that the greater the delight in sinning, the greater the affliction in making satisfaction.

paras.t: Noctem illam tenebrosus turbo possideat, id est mœror mentem virtuose obnubilans, ut instar tempestatis tota concutiatur vehementi horrore, quoniam Deum offendit; non computetur in diebus anni, id est inter virtutes anni gratiæ seu gloriæ, per quas scilicet anima clarificatur, et ad durationem gloriosam patriæ Beatorum perducitur. Virtus enim est quasi spiritualis animæ dies. Nec numeretur in mensibus. Menses sunt multiplicata facta virtutum.
paras.en: [[3:6|Let a darksome whirlwind seize upon that night|Noctem illam tenebrosus turbo possideat]], that is, a grief that clouds the mind to virtuous purpose, so that, like a storm, it is wholly shaken with violent horror because it has offended God; [[3:6|let it not be counted in the days of the year|non computetur in diebus anni]], that is, among the virtues of the year of grace or of glory, by which the soul is made bright and led to the glorious duration of the fatherland of the blessed. For virtue is, as it were, the spiritual day of the soul. [[3:6|nor numbered in the months|Nec numeretur in mensibus]]. The months are the multiplied deeds of the virtues.

paras.t: Sit nox illa solitaria, id est, cæcitati impietatique nostræ non aliam adjiciamus, gloriando in malis, vel excusando, aut defendendo peccata; nec laude digna: imo confiteamur quod omni exprobratione, confusione et pœna digna sit nostra culpa.
paras.en: [[3:7|Let that night be solitary|Sit nox illa solitaria]], that is, let us not add another to our blindness and impiety by glorying in evil, or by excusing or defending our sins; [[3:7|and not worthy of praise|nec laude digna]]: nay rather, let us confess that our guilt is worthy of every reproach, confusion and punishment.

paras.t: Maledicant ei qui maledicunt diei, id est prosperitati mundanæ inani, quæ lux et dies ab impiis æstimatur. Qui enim illam despiciunt, merito nocti peccati maledicere possunt, quia veraciter eam abhorrent atque vituperant. Qui parati sunt suscitare Leviathan, id est contra se provocare diabolum. Nempe per hoc, quod ea quæ mundi ac dæmonis sunt, aspernantur, atque in Deo inflammantur, diabolum ad sui impugnationem mox concitant: qui contra electos tanto plus furit, quanto ad Deum se fortius erigunt.
paras.en: [[3:8|Let them curse it who curse the day|Maledicant ei qui maledicunt diei]], that is, the empty prosperity of the world, which the wicked take for light and day. For those who despise it can rightly curse the night of sin, because they truly abhor and reprove it. [[3:8|who are ready to raise up a leviathan|Qui parati sunt suscitare Leviathan]], that is, to provoke the devil against themselves. For by this, that they spurn what belongs to the world and the devil, and are set on fire in God, they at once stir up the devil to attack them; and he rages the more against the elect, the more strongly they lift themselves up to God.

paras.t: Obscurentur stellæ caligine ejus. Non optando, sed prænuntiando id dicitur, quoniam stellæ, id est sublimiter virtuosi, gratia, vita, exemplo, fama lucentes, aliquid culpæ incurrunt, quo eorum puritas obscuratur seu minus clara efficitur. Exspectet lucem, et non videat: id est, cæcitas nostræ mentis, quantumlibet lumen gloriæ præstoletur, seu Deum qui æterna lux est, hanc tamen in præsenti clare et sicuti est, videre non poterit. Nec ortum surgentis auroræ, id est resuscitationem Ecclesiæ in die judicii, quando et corpore glorificabuntur electi, quorum gloria tanta erit, quod nunc comprehendi non valet.
paras.en: [[3:9|Let the stars be darkened with the mist thereof|Obscurentur stellæ caligine ejus]]. This is said not as a wish but as a foretelling: for the stars, that is, those of lofty virtue, shining with grace, life, example and good name, incur some fault, by which their purity is darkened or made less bright. [[3:9|let it expect light, and not see it|Exspectet lucem, et non videat]]: that is, however much the blindness of our mind awaits the light of glory, or God, who is the eternal light, it will not be able to see that light clearly and as it is in this present life. [[3:9|nor the rising of the dawning of the day|Nec ortum surgentis auroræ]], that is, the resurrection of the Church on the day of judgment, when the elect will be glorified in body too, and their glory will be so great that it cannot now be comprehended.

paras.t: Quia non conclusit, sed aperuit, ostia ventris qui portavit me, id est carnalia desideria, quæ ostia sunt quibus itur ad mortem culpæ exterioris atque gehennæ: istaque ostia aperit intima mentis infectio. Venter autem est obliqua seu infecta nostra voluntas, in qua ad peccandum concipimur, dum ruinæ nostræ origo efficimur. Nec abstulit, sed irrogavit seu intulit, mala pœnæ et culpæ, oculis meis, ita quod ea experior, per experientiamque intueor.
paras.en: [[3:10|Because it shut not up|Quia non conclusit]], but opened, [[3:10|the doors of the womb that bore me|ostia ventris qui portavit me]], that is, carnal desires, which are the doors through which one goes to the death of outward sin and of hell; and these doors are opened by the inward infection of the mind. The womb is our crooked or infected will, in which we are conceived for sinning, when we become the origin of our own ruin. [[3:10|nor took away|Nec abstulit]], but laid or brought [[3:10|evils|mala]] of punishment and of guilt upon [[3:10|my eyes|oculis meis]], so that I experience them, and by experience behold them.

paras.t: Ista ex Gregorio sumpta sunt, secundum propriam mentem nil asserendo, sed ejus expositionem fideliter ac breviter recitando, ut scripturæ hujus capituli difficillimi veritas, ex his atque sequentibus evidentius elucescat: et lector, quod rationabilius sibi visum fuerit, eligat.
paras.en: These things have been taken from Gregory, asserting nothing according to my own mind, but reciting his exposition faithfully and briefly, so that the truth of the text of this most difficult chapter may shine out more clearly from these things and from what follows; and let the reader choose what seems to him more reasonable.

3.title: De verbis Alberti Magni circa expositionem præsentis capituli.
3.title_en: On the words of Albert the Great concerning the exposition of the present chapter

paras.t: Disputatio hujus libri, quæ est inter quinque, videlicet inter Job et tres ejus amicos et Eliu, secundum Albertum, tota est de providentia seu cura, qua Creator res regit humanas: et omnes conveniunt in hoc, quod apud Deum creatorem et gubernatorem, perfecta notitia est omnium humanorum; item, quod in cura et gubernatione rerum a Deo nulla est iniquitas; rursus in hoc, quod actus humanos magis intus inspicit Deus, quam homo qui agit, et ideo defectum in eis aliquando deprehendit, qui etiam ipsum hominem latet. Differunt autem in hoc, quod Job primo conqueritur, quod actus sui secundum seu ad humanam rationem et providentiam, id est secundum processum vel modum seu ordinem humanæ justitiæ, non judicantur. Unde dicit infra: Si judicatus fuero, justus inveniar; et illud: Utinam appenderentur peccata mea quibus iram merui, et calamitas quam patior, in statera, etc. Propter quod sermones suos ostendendo et prosequendo, in omnibus justitias suas conclusit: et sequitur, quod tres viri disputationes suas omiserunt, eo quod sibi justus videretur. Quod enim præfato modo, scilicet secundum ordinem humanæ justitiæ, gubernari et judicari deberet, videtur: quia justitia gubernationis humanæ, exemplata et derivata est ab ordine justitiæ divinæ, ex quo videtur, quod cum illa concordari deberet, et quod nihil esset in una, puta in ista exemplata, quod non esset in alia, scilicet justitia exemplari divina.
paras.en: The disputation of this book [the first word is damaged in the scan; read as Disputatio], which is among five, namely between Job, his three friends and Eliu, is, according to Albert [Albert the Great, in his commentary on Job], wholly about the providence or care by which the Creator rules human affairs: and all agree in this, that with God, the creator and governor, there is perfect knowledge of all human things; likewise, that in God’s care and government of things there is no iniquity; and again in this, that God sees into human acts more inwardly than the man who does them, and therefore sometimes detects a defect in them which is hidden even from the man himself. But they differ in this, that Job first complains that his acts are not judged according to, or by the measure of, human reason and providence, that is, according to the procedure, manner or order of human justice. Hence he says below: [[Job 13:18|If I shall be judged|Si judicatus fuero]], [[Job 13:18|I shall be found just|justus inveniar]]; and that: [[Job 6:2|O that my sins, whereby I have deserved wrath, and the calamity that I suffer, were weighed in a balance|Utinam appenderentur peccata mea quibus iram merui, et calamitas quam patior, in statera]], etc. For which reason, in setting forth and pursuing his discourses, he concluded his justices [that is, his claims to be just] in all of them: and it follows that the three men left off their disputations, [[Job 32:1|because he seemed just to himself|eo quod sibi justus videretur]]. For it seems that he ought to be governed and judged in the aforesaid way, namely according to the order of human justice: since the justice of human government is copied and derived from the order of divine justice; from which it seems that it should agree with it, and that there should be nothing in the one, namely in this copy, that is not in the other, namely in divine justice, the exemplar.

paras.t: Sed quoniam postea ex determinatione Dei cognovit Job, quod ordo justitiæ divinæ penitus dissimilis est justitiæ humanæ (homo enim ex luto factus, vilior est, quam quod Deus respiciat eum secundum ordinem humanæ justitiæ); ideo in verum rediens intellectum, dicit in fine: Auditu auris audivi te, quasi prædicatum ex humana justitia, quod scilicet secundum illam procederes in judicando. Nunc autem oculus meus videt te. Quasi dicat: Ex tua determinatione rediens ad intellectum, cognovi gubernationem tuam dissimilem esse humanæ: idcirco ipse me reprehendo, et ago pœnitentiam. Et de quo agat pœnitentiam, aperit dicens, Unum locutus sum, quod utinam non dixissem: Innocentem et impium ipse condemnat. Quod injustum esset, si sua gubernatio ordine justitiæ humanæ procederet. Itaque in hoc capitulo, ut materiam det disputationi, ipse Job querelam proponit de die quia principium vitæ est, quam Satan in suam accepit potestatem convertendi in tristitiam, in facultatibus, prole, persona, conjuge et amicis.
paras.en: But since Job afterwards learned from God’s decision that the order of divine justice is wholly unlike human justice (for man, made of clay, is too vile for God to regard him according to the order of human justice), therefore, coming back to the true understanding, he says at the end: [[Job 42:5|With the hearing of the ear, I have heard thee|Auditu auris audivi te]], as it were what is preached from human justice, namely that thou wouldst proceed according to it in judging; [[Job 42:5|but now my eye seeth thee|Nunc autem oculus meus videt te]]. As if to say: Coming back to understanding from thy decision, I have learned that thy government is unlike human government: [[Job 42:6|Therefore I reprehend myself, and do penance|idcirco ipse me reprehendo, et ago pœnitentiam]]. And what he does penance for, he discloses, saying: [[Job 39:35|One thing I have spoken, which I wish I had not said|Unum locutus sum, quod utinam non dixissem]]: [[Job 9:22|both the innocent and the wicked he consumeth|Innocentem et impium ipse condemnat]] [the Vulgate has consumit, consumeth; Albert reads condemnat, condemneth]. And this would be unjust, if his government proceeded by the order of human justice. And so in this chapter, to give matter for the disputation, Job himself puts forward a complaint about the day, because it is the beginning of the life which Satan took into his power to turn into sorrow, in goods, children, person, wife and friends.

paras.t: His præmissis, Albertus textum hoc modo exponit. Post hæc aperuit Job os suum, ut locum daret disputationi, et aperte loqueretur. Ideo dicit, Aperuit os suum: in hoc enim notatur, quod patens fuit locutio, et quod de rebus magnis fuerat locuturus. Maledixit diei suo, judicio justitiæ, non livore vindictæ: et hoc secundum omnem expositionem tam litteralem quam mysticam. Et dixit: Pereat dies in qua natus sum. Dies naturaliter est principium vitæ nascentis ex utero ad lucem; et hæc dies secundum totam periodum, in quam Satan accepit potestatem, ut malitiam suæ voluntatis in ea exerceat, in rebus et liberis, persona atque amicis, quos adversarios vertit, non potest optari, nisi ut pereat. Si enim peribit, tristitias et infelicitates non ingeret; si autem procedet de mane in meridiem, et de meridie in vesperam, multis afflictionibus vitam consumet: et ideo optandum non est, nisi ut pereat. Nec maledicitur dies, in quantum est singularis, sed in quantum principium est totius vitæ decursus in afflictionibus Satanæ.
paras.en: With this said first, Albert expounds the text in this way. [[3:1|After this, Job opened his mouth|Post hæc aperuit Job os suum]], to give room to the disputation and to speak openly. That is why he says, [[3:1|opened his mouth|Aperuit os suum]]: for by this it is noted that his speech was open, and that he was about to speak of great things. [[3:1|and cursed his day|Maledixit diei suo]], by a judgment of justice, not out of the spite of revenge: and this according to every exposition, literal as well as mystical. [[3:2|And he said|Et dixit]]: [[3:3|Let the day perish wherein I was born|Pereat dies in qua natus sum]]. The day is by nature the beginning of the life of one born from the womb into the light; and this day, taken for the whole period over which Satan received power to exercise in it the malice of his will, in goods and children, person and friends, whom he turned into adversaries, cannot be wished anything but to perish. For if it perishes, it will not bring on sorrows and misfortunes; but if it goes on from morning to noon, and from noon to evening, it will consume life with many afflictions: and therefore nothing is to be wished for it but that it perish. Nor is the day cursed inasmuch as it is a single day, but inasmuch as it is the beginning of the whole course of life in the afflictions of Satan.

paras.t: Et nox in qua dictum est, Conceptus est homo. Sicut dies exterior, ut est principium exterioris vitæ, in luce hac optatur perire; ita nox quæ per conceptum principium est conceptionis talis hominis, in quem potestatem accepit Satan atque in omnia ejus secundum totam vitæ periodum, non potest optari, nisi ut pereat: non enim aliud facit, nisi quod vitam in amaritudinem vertit. Et dicit, Dies nativitatis, et nox conceptus: quia nox frigiditate subrepente, poros corporis claudit, ut spiritu et calore ad interius redundantibus, semina concepta intrinsecus magis coalescant; redeunte autem luce diei, calore perfusa corpora laxantur in poris et spongiositate corporis, et disponuntur ad emittendum quod conceptum est. Ideo dies partui, nox conceptui debetur, secundum congruentiam. His verbis jungit Albertus: Expositio Gregorii ab hac non differt, nisi quod ille processum dicit in peccatis, nos autem in afflictionibus Satanæ.
paras.en: [[3:3|and the night in which it was said: A man child is conceived|Et nox in qua dictum est, Conceptus est homo]]. Just as the outward day, being the beginning of outward life in this light, is wished to perish, so the night which by conception is the beginning of the conceiving of such a man, over whom Satan received power, and over all that is his, for the whole period of his life, cannot be wished anything but to perish: for it does nothing else but turn life into bitterness. And he says the day of birth and the night of conception, because the night, as the cold creeps on, closes the pores of the body, so that, the breath and heat flowing back within, the seed conceived may grow together the more inwardly; but when the light of day returns, bodies suffused with heat are loosened in their pores and in the spongy texture of the body, and are disposed to bring forth what has been conceived. So by fittingness the day belongs to birth, the night to conception. To these words Albert adds: The exposition of Gregory does not differ from this, except that he speaks of a course in sins, and we of one in the afflictions of Satan.

paras.t: Insuper ait: Dies illa, data in potestatem Satanæ in hac vita, vertatur in tenebras, ut effectus Satanæ nusquam videatur, nusquam appareat. Hæc est enim de qua dicitur, Ab altitudine diei timebo: quia quo altius ascenderit, plures calamitates ingeret: a quibus homo absconditur, si coram hominibus infausta, id est infelix, dies non oriatur. Faustus, secundum Britonem, est idem quod felix: inde infaustus, id est infelix, et cui fortuna non favet. Non requirat eum Deus desuper. Deus per sublimia inferiora gubernans, mensuras et terminos ponit vitæ humanæ, numerumque dierum; et si deest dies, a Deo ordinatore vitæ requiritur. Petit ergo, quod dies potestatis Satanæ non requiratur ad numerum dierum suorum. Et non sit in recordatione viventis. Si enim non est in recordatione, tunc nunquam fuit in præterita vita. Recordatio enim mali, male et ad tristitiam afficit animam, juxta illud in Isaia: Recogitabo omnes annos meos in amaritudine animæ meæ. Nec illustretur lumine, ad hoc scilicet ut abundantiori lumine infausta, id est infortunata seu infelicia vitæ, monstrentur, quum magis sit utile talia occumbere, quam illustrari.
paras.en: He says further: [[3:4|Let that day|Dies illa]], given into the power of Satan in this life, [[3:4|be turned into darkness|vertatur in tenebras]], so that the working of Satan may nowhere be seen, nowhere appear. For this is the day of which it is said: [[Ps 55:4|From the height of the day I shall fear|Ab altitudine diei timebo]]: because the higher it climbs, the more calamities it will bring; and from these a man is hidden if the ill-starred, that is, unhappy, day does not rise before men. Faustus, according to Brito [William Brito, author of a dictionary of the words of the Bible], is the same as felix, happy: hence infaustus, that is, unhappy, one whom fortune does not favour. [[3:4|let not God regard it from above|Non requirat eum Deus desuper]] [requirere is also “to require”, and Albert takes it so]. God, governing lower things through higher ones, sets measures and bounds to human life, and the number of its days; and if a day is lacking, it is required by God, who orders life. He asks, then, that the day of Satan’s power be not required for the number of his days. And let it not be in the remembrance of the living [these words are not in the Vulgate text of this verse]. For if it is not in remembrance, then it never was in his past life. For the remembrance of evil affects the soul with evil and sorrow, according to that in Isaias: [[Is 38:15|I will recount to thee all my years in the bitterness of my soul|Recogitabo omnes annos meos in amaritudine animæ meæ]]. [[3:4|and let not the light shine upon it|Nec illustretur lumine]], that is, so that the ill-starred, that is, the unfortunate or unhappy things of life, may not be shown by a more abundant light, since it is more useful that such things should set than be lit up.

paras.t: Obscurent eum tenebræ. Tenebræ ab inferioribus oriuntur, et significant dispositiones quibus privatur lumen infaustum tam in corpore quam in anima: et talia privantia lumen infaustum, dicuntur tenebræ per effectum. Et umbra mortis. Umbra mortis dicitur recordatio mentis, vel aversiones lucis infaustæ hanc perimentes. Occupet eum caligo, id est fortissima et inspissata ad contrarium dispositio. Caligo enim, est caliginoso vapore inspissata tenebra, lucem impediens: et significat spissam dispositionem sapientis, vel meritum boni contra lucem Satanæ. Dispositio autem sapientis, ut dicit Philo, vel pœnitentis, ut dicit Gregorius, non dicitur caligo, ita quod omnem lucem privet, sed tantum propter hoc, quia obstat illi infaustæ, scilicet luci Satanæ: sicut in Exodo legitur Moyses ingressus in caliginem, ut scilicet omnia quæ lux mundi hujus illustrat, ei occumberent, et ipse solus in lumine Dei mirabilis esset. Et involvatur amaritudine dispositionis contrariæ vel in corpore, vel in anima, vel pariter in utroque. Sic involvatur lux ista infausta, ut se diffundere per vitam non possit.
paras.en: [[3:5|Let darkness|Obscurent eum tenebræ]] cover it. Darkness rises from lower things, and signifies the dispositions by which the ill-starred light is taken away, in the body as well as in the soul: and such things as take away the ill-starred light are called darkness by their effect. [[3:5|and the shadow of death|Et umbra mortis]]. The shadow of death is the name given to the remembrance of the mind [perhaps for recordatio mortis, the remembrance of death], or to the turnings away from the ill-starred light that destroy it. [[3:5|let a mist overspread it|Occupet eum caligo]], that is, a very strong and thickened disposition to the contrary. For mist is darkness thickened by a misty vapour, hindering the light: and it signifies the thick disposition of the wise man, or the merit of the good man, against the light of Satan. But the disposition of the wise man, as Philo says, or of the penitent, as Gregory says, is not called mist as though it took away all light, but only because it stands in the way of that ill-starred light, namely the light of Satan: as we read in Exodus that Moses entered into the mist[[Ex 20:21||]][[Ex 24:18||]] [caligo, here “mist”, is the dark cloud of Ex 20:21], so that all things which the light of this world lights up might set for him, and he alone might be wonderful in the light of God. [[3:5|and let it be wrapped up in bitterness|Et involvatur amaritudine]] of a contrary disposition, either in the body, or in the soul, or in both alike. So let this ill-starred light be wrapped up, that it may not be able to spread itself through life.

paras.t: Et subdit de nocte conceptus, quæ initium fuit formationis vitæ quæ data est in potestatem Satanæ. Noctem illam, in qua semina formandi infaustam vitam coaluerunt, tenebrosus turbo possideat. Turbo ventus est, involutum habens flatum: et significat dispositiones cordis et corporis ex multis compositas, effectum Satanæ corrumpentes et reprimentes. Nec computetur in diebus anni, id est circuli vitæ, ita quod in tota vita desit ad computum, quia vitæ mala inducit; nec numeretur in mensibus. Luna propter vicinitatem in humanis majorem habet potestatem; et singulis mensibus facit ver, æstatem, autumnum et hiemem: quod in anno facit sol. Petit ergo quod effectus Satanæ in particularibus immutationibus se non possit diffundere. Sit nox illa solitaria, nec laude digna. Quia enim laude digna non est, petendum est ut sit solitaria, ne se multiplicando per vitam diffundat.
paras.en: And he adds of the night of conception, which was the beginning of the forming of the life that was given into Satan’s power: [[3:6|Let a darksome whirlwind seize upon|tenebrosus turbo possideat]] [[3:6|that night|Noctem illam]], in which the seeds for forming the ill-starred life grew together. A whirlwind is a wind that has a coiled blast: and it signifies dispositions of heart and body made up of many things, which spoil and hold back the working of Satan. [[3:6|let it not be counted in the days of the year|Nec computetur in diebus anni]], that is, of the circle of life, so that in the whole of life it be missing from the count, since it brings evils on life; [[3:6|nor numbered in the months|nec numeretur in mensibus]]. The moon, because of its nearness, has greater power over human things; and in each month it makes spring, summer, autumn and winter, which the sun does in the year. He asks, then, that the working of Satan may not be able to spread itself in particular changes. [[3:7|Let that night be solitary, and not worthy of praise|Sit nox illa solitaria, nec laude digna]]. For since it is not worthy of praise, one must ask that it be solitary, lest by multiplying itself it spread through life.

paras.t: Et quod divisim dixit de die et nocte, dicit conjunctim: Maledicant ei, scilicet tali diei et nocti, qui maledicunt diei, id est, maledicere sciunt et consueverunt tali diei, quæ infecta est nequitiis Satanæ; qui parati sunt suscitare Leviathan. Secundum Abraham Judæum philosophum et Rabbi Moysen, diabolus, secundum quod a principio diei vitæ, per omnes dies, menses et annos venenum diffundens, malum malo addit, et totam rotam nativitatis nostræ sic inficit, Leviathan est: sic enim ut serpens serpit, et ut vectis rigide nobis obsistit. Unde de lingua hujus serpentis sic venenum immittentis, dicit Jacobus: Lingua maculat et inflammat totam rotam nativitatis nostræ, inflammata a gehenna. Qui autem in contrarium nituntur, serpenti obsistunt, et ideo suscitant eum, ut omnes vires suas examinet, sicut et Dominus dixit in Genesi: Inimicitias ponam inter te et mulierem. Ipsa conteret caput tuum, et tu insidiaberis calcaneo ejus.
paras.en: And what he said separately of the day and the night, he says together: [[3:8|Let them curse it|Maledicant ei]], namely such a day and night, [[3:8|who curse the day|qui maledicunt diei]], that is, who know how and are wont to curse such a day, which is infected with the wickedness of Satan; [[3:8|who are ready to raise up a leviathan|qui parati sunt suscitare Leviathan]]. According to Abraham the Jewish philosopher [probably Abraham ibn Ezra] and Rabbi Moyses [Moses Maimonides], the devil, inasmuch as from the beginning of the day of life, through all its days, months and years, he pours out his venom, adds evil to evil, and so infects the whole wheel of our nativity, is Leviathan: for so he creeps like a serpent, and like a bar stiffly withstands us [Isaias calls Leviathan the bar serpent, serpentem vectem, Is 27:1]. Hence of the tongue of this serpent, that thus pours in its venom, James says: The tongue [[Jas 3:6|defileth|maculat]] and [[Jas 3:6|inflameth the wheel of our nativity, being set on fire by hell|inflammat totam rotam nativitatis nostræ, inflammata a gehenna]]. But those who strive against him withstand the serpent, and so they rouse him to try all his strength; as the Lord too said in Genesis: [[Gen 3:15|I will put enmities between thee and the woman|Inimicitias ponam inter te et mulierem]]. [[Gen 3:15|she shall crush thy head, and thou shalt lie in wait for her heel|Ipsa conteret caput tuum, et tu insidiaberis calcaneo ejus]].

paras.t: Obtenebrentur stellæ caligine ejus. Stellas vocat, novas ad infausta scintillationes, quas petit obscurari caligine dispositionis contrariæ. Exspectet ipse Satan lucem, id est infaustæ suæ lucis ortum, et non videat eam, quam peto in ortu suo occumbere, ne diem humanæ nativitatis illustret; nec ortum surgentis auroræ, supple, videat. Aurora est, quando radii solis immiscent se tenebris noctis; et sic aurora infaustæ lucis est, quando primum immiscet se diebus vitæ humanæ: quam postulat non oriri. Et subdit causam tantæ maledictionis. Quia non conclusit ostia ventris qui portavit me, ut scilicet clausis ostiis, intra ventrem mortuus essem, ne ad hanc infaustam lucem peperisset me mater mea, juxta illud, Beatæ steriles quæ non pepererunt; nec abstulit mala ab oculis meis, id est a sensu experientiæ: quæ mala Satan in totam rotam nativitatis infudit. Idem in Jeremia: Maledictus qui me non interfecit ab utero, etc.
paras.en: [[3:9|Let the stars be darkened with the mist thereof|Obtenebrentur stellæ caligine ejus]]. He calls stars the new sparklings towards ill fortune, which he asks may be darkened by the mist of a contrary disposition. [[3:9|let it expect light|Exspectet ipse Satan lucem]]: let Satan himself expect it, that is, the rising of his ill-starred light, [[3:9|and not see it|et non videat eam]], which I ask may set at its rising, lest it light up the day of man’s birth; [[3:9|nor the rising of the dawning of the day|nec ortum surgentis auroræ]], supply: let him see. Dawn is when the rays of the sun mingle with the darkness of night; and so there is a dawn of the ill-starred light when it first mingles with the days of human life: and this he asks may not rise. And he adds the cause of so great a curse: [[3:10|Because it shut not up the doors of the womb that bore me|Quia non conclusit ostia ventris qui portavit me]], that is, so that, the doors being shut, I should have died within the womb, lest my mother should have borne me to this ill-starred light; according to that saying, [[Luke 23:29|Blessed are the barren|Beatæ steriles]] that have not borne; [[3:10|nor took away evils from my eyes|nec abstulit mala ab oculis meis]], that is, from the sense of experience: the evils which Satan poured into the whole wheel of our nativity. So too in Jeremias: Cursed be he[[Jer 20:15||]] [[Jer 20:17|Who slew me not from the womb|qui me non interfecit ab utero]], etc. [the margin gives Jer. xx, 15; Denis joins the curse of v. 15 to the words of v. 17].

paras.t: Quare non in vulva mortuus sum? ut mala Satanæ nec vidissem, nec sensissem, sed in principio ortus, subtractus fuissem venenis ejus: secundum illud in Matthæo, Melius illi erat si natus non fuisset; egressus ex utero, non statim perii? id est, quare non statim tunc perii? quia etsi tunc Satanæ mala sensissem, tamen per rationem non discrevissem. Cur exceptus genibus, id est a matris genibus ab obstetrice, et ploratu prodidi mala Satanæ? Cur lactatus uberibus? id est, cur me aluit mater ad mala Satanæ experienda? Sic enim nutrire parvulum, crudele est.
paras.en: [[3:11|Why did I not die in the womb?|Quare non in vulva mortuus sum?]] so that I should neither have seen nor felt the evils of Satan, but at the beginning of my birth should have been withdrawn from his venom: according to that in Matthew, [[Matt 26:24|It were better for him, if that man had not been born|Melius illi erat si natus non fuisset]]. [[3:11|why did I not perish when I came out of the belly?|egressus ex utero, non statim perii?]] that is, why did I not perish at once then? for even if I had then felt the evils of Satan, I should not have discerned them by reason. [[3:12|why received upon the knees|Cur exceptus genibus]], that is, by the midwife on my mother’s knees, and with my weeping betrayed the evils of Satan? [[3:12|why suckled at the breasts?|Cur lactatus uberibus?]] that is, why did my mother nourish me to experience the evils of Satan? For to nourish a little child so is cruel.

paras.t: Nunc enim, id est, in diem infaustæ lucis non progressus, dormiens, per mortem ligatus sensibus, silerem, id est, querulas voces de malo Satanæ non emitterem, cum regibus. Reges vocat, qui secundum perfectionem justitiæ homines regebant. Et consulibus terræ. Consules vocantur, qui prudentia agendorum suo consilio in dubiis valent dirigere. Quæ ædificant sibi solitudines. Ad litteram, in solitudine ædificant, ut studio sapientiæ veritatisque dediti, inquietudini Satanæ quam in mundo concitat, se subducant: sicut libro de Contemplatione dicit Philo, quod fecerunt Bragmani philosophi et primi monachi in Ægypto, facile præsentia contemnentes, ne inquietudinibus Satanæ rotarentur. Aut cum principibus, principalibus scilicet inter illos, qui possident aurum, id est, multum aurum habuerunt et contempserunt, ne inquietudine Satanæ bona perderent animæ. In idem redit quod sequitur, et replent domos suas argento (nisi quod aurum, thesaurum contentum in pretiosissimis significat; argentum, in minus pretiosis), ut bona animæ adipiscerentur. Sicut Plato dicitur projecisse aurum de sinu, dicens, Melius est perdere aurum quam animum. Et vult dicere: Quæcumque lucra sapientes contempserunt, ne molestiis Satanæ rotarentur, vellem me non habuisse, quia tunc me rota Satanæ non calcaret.
paras.en: [[3:13|For now|Nunc enim]], that is, not having gone forth into the day of the ill-starred light, [[3:13|I should have been asleep|dormiens]], bound in my senses by death, [[3:13|and still|silerem]], that is, I should not utter plaintive cries about the evil of Satan, [[3:14|With kings|cum regibus]]. He calls kings those who ruled men according to the perfection of justice. [[3:14|and consuls of the earth|Et consulibus terræ]]. Those are called consuls who by prudence in action are able by their counsel to give direction in doubtful matters. [[3:14|who build themselves solitudes|Quæ ædificant sibi solitudines]]. To the letter, they build in solitude, so that, given to the pursuit of wisdom and truth, they may withdraw from the disquiet that Satan stirs up in the world: as Philo says in the book On Contemplation that the Bragmani philosophers [the Brahmins] did, and the first monks in Egypt, readily despising present things, lest they be whirled about by the disquiet of Satan [rotari, to be turned on a wheel, plays on the wheel of our nativity]. [[3:15|Or with princes|Aut cum principibus]], that is, with the chief among them, [[3:15|that possess gold|qui possident aurum]], that is, who had much gold and despised it, lest through the disquiet of Satan they should lose the goods of the soul. What follows comes to the same, [[3:15|and fill their houses with silver|et replent domos suas argento]] (except that gold signifies treasure held in the most precious things, silver in less precious ones), so that they might gain the goods of the soul. So Plato is said to have thrown gold out of his lap, saying: It is better to lose gold than the soul. And he means: Whatever gains the wise despised, lest they be whirled about by the troubles of Satan, I would I had not had them; for then the wheel of Satan would not tread me down.

paras.t: Aut sicut abortivum absconditum non subsisterem. Sensus est: Aut non subsisterem sicut abortivum non subsistit, quod bona et mala hujus sæculi non gustavit. Abortivum est, quod a primo ortu et conceptu seminum, corruptum est antequam formaretur in partum per animæ adeptionem et vitæ. Vel qui concepti, formati in partum, morte præventi, non viderunt lucem infaustam vitæ præsentis. Antequam enim oculos aperirent ad eam, mortui sunt: quibus melius erat sic non esse, quam malis Satanæ rotari. Ibi impii, inquiete viventes, se et alios inquietantes, cessaverunt a tumultu, quo se et alios inquietaverunt. Mortuus enim nec tumultum facit, nec sentit ut prius. Et ibi requieverunt fessi robore. Robore dicitur, propter hoc quod viribus suis confidentes, alios oppresserunt: a quo robore mortui, fessi cessaverunt. Et quondam vincti, id est capti et afflicti a robustis et tumultuosis, pariter cum illis requieverunt, sine molestia, ita quod molestiam ultra non senserunt. In hoc ergo mors utilis est, quod liberat a sensu malorum: et in hoc affectu dixit David, Heu mihi! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est; et Dominus, O generatio incredula, quamdiu apud vos ero? quamdiu vos patiar? Quare autem vincti sint, subdit, et suppletur: quia non exaudierunt vocem exactoris, id est tyranni opprimentis. Et differentias sic quiescentium subdit. Parvus et magnus ibi sunt, supple, æquales et pariter quiescentes; et servus, et liber a domino suo, id est, qui dominum non habet. Et ideo mors desiderabilis est, quia a tantis malis liberat.
paras.en: [[3:16|Or as a hidden untimely birth, I should not be|Aut sicut abortivum absconditum non subsisterem]]. The sense is: Or I should not be, as an untimely birth is not, which has not tasted the goods and evils of this world. An untimely birth is that which, from the first rising and conception of the seed, is spoiled before it is formed for birth by the gaining of a soul and of life. [[3:16|or as they that, being conceived|Vel qui concepti]], formed for birth but overtaken by death, [[3:16|have not seen the light|non viderunt lucem]], the ill-starred light of the present life. For they died before they opened their eyes upon it: and for them it was better so not to be, than to be whirled about by the evils of Satan. [[3:17|There the wicked|Ibi impii]], who live in disquiet, disquieting themselves and others, [[3:17|cease from tumult|cessaverunt a tumultu]], with which they disquieted themselves and others. For a dead man neither makes tumult nor feels as before. [[3:17|and there the wearied in strength are at rest|Et ibi requieverunt fessi robore]]. He says in strength because, trusting in their own powers, they oppressed others: and from this strength, being dead, they have ceased, wearied. [[3:18|And they sometime bound together|Et quondam vincti]], that is, taken and afflicted by the strong and tumultuous, have rested together with them, [[3:18|without disquiet|sine molestia]], so that they felt disquiet no longer. In this then death is useful, that it frees from the feeling of evils: and in this feeling David said, [[Ps 119:5|Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged!|Heu mihi! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est]] and the Lord, [[Mark 9:18|O incredulous generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I suffer you?|O generatio incredula, quamdiu apud vos ero? quamdiu vos patiar?]] And why they were bound he adds, and it is to be supplied: because they [[3:18|have not heard the voice of the oppressor|non exaudierunt vocem exactoris]], that is, of the tyrant who oppresses them. And he adds the differences of those who rest thus: [[3:19|The small and great are there|Parvus et magnus ibi sunt]], supply: equal, and resting alike; [[3:19|and the servant is free from his master|et servus, et liber a domino suo]] [Albert reads and the servant, and he that is free from his master], that is, he who has no master. And therefore death is to be desired, because it frees from such great evils.

paras.t: Quare. Ostendit hic lucem vitæ datam in potestatem Satanæ, inutilem esse misero. Quare, id est qua utilitate, misero, infelicitatibus Satanæ subjecto, data est lux? Ex luce enim nihil habet, nisi quod videt miseriam suam et plus dolet: ideo lux sibi nocet. Et vita, in exteriori luce quare data est, his qui in amaritudine animæ sunt, id est in amaritudine pertingente usque ad animam et animæ subversionem? Qui exspectant mortem, quæ sit finis miseriæ, et non venit, ut amplius miseri sint; quasi effodientes thesaurum, quoniam mortem thesaurum et lucrum reputant, in quantum est finis miseriæ. In Ecclesiastico enim dicitur: O mors, bonum est judicium tuum homini indigenti, et qui minoratur viribus, defecto ætate, et cui cura est de omnibus. Sic et Tobias dixit ad Dominum: Fac mecum misericordiam, et præcipe in pace recipi spiritum meum; expedit enim mihi mori magis quam vivere. Sic Elias petivit animæ suæ ut moreretur, et ait: Sufficit mihi, Domine, tolle animam meam. Et hoc exaggerans, subdit, viro cujus abscondita est via. Nescit enim homo utrum bonum vel malum exitum habeat. Sunt justi atque sapientes, et opera eorum in manu Dei sunt; et tamen nescit homo, utrum amore dignus sit vel odio. Et circumdedit eum Deus tenebris, quod scilicet ignorat finem suum, et finis qualitatem et tempus.
paras.en: Why. Here he shows that the light of life, given into the power of Satan, is useless to the wretched man. Why, that is, to what use, [[3:20|is light given to him that is in misery|data est lux]], subject as he is to the misfortunes of Satan? For from the light he has nothing but that he sees his misery and grieves the more: and so the light harms him. [[3:20|and life|Et vita]], in the outward light, why is it given [[3:20|to them that are in bitterness of soul|his qui in amaritudine animæ sunt]], that is, in a bitterness that reaches even to the soul and to the overthrow of the soul? [[3:21|That look for death|Qui exspectant mortem]], which is the end of misery, [[3:21|and it cometh not|et non venit]], so that they are the more wretched; [[3:21|as they that dig for a treasure|quasi effodientes thesaurum]], since they reckon death a treasure and a gain, inasmuch as it is the end of misery. For it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 41:3|O death thy sentence is welcome to the man that is in need, and to him whose strength faileth|O mors, bonum est judicium tuum homini indigenti, et qui minoratur viribus]], [[Ecclus 41:4|Who is in a decrepit age, and that is in care about all things|defecto ætate, et cui cura est de omnibus]]. So too Tobias said to the Lord: Deal mercifully with me, and [[Tob 3:6|command my spirit to be received in peace: for it is better for me to die, than to live|præcipe in pace recipi spiritum meum; expedit enim mihi mori magis quam vivere]]. So Elias [[3 Kings 19:4|requested for his soul that he might die, and said: It is enough for me, Lord; take away my soul|petivit animæ suæ ut moreretur, et ait: Sufficit mihi, Domine, tolle animam meam]]. And making more of this, he adds, [[3:23|To a man whose way is hidden|viro cujus abscondita est via]]. For man does not know whether he will have a good end or a bad one: [[Eccles 9:1|there are just men and wise men, and their works are in the hand of God: and yet man knoweth not whether he be worthy of love, or hatred|Sunt justi atque sapientes, et opera eorum in manu Dei sunt; et tamen nescit homo, utrum amore dignus sit vel odio]]. [[3:23|and God hath surrounded him with darkness|Et circumdedit eum Deus tenebris]], that is, in that he does not know his end, nor the manner and time of his end.

paras.t: Deinde ostendit hoc taliter evenisse in se. Antequam comedam, non ad delicias, sed ad refectionem, suspiro, ad pondus miseriæ prementis. In hoc multi reprehenduntur, qui ante suspirium cibum accipiunt. Et quasi inundantis aquæ, quæ sonat, sic rugitus meus in planctum: secundum illud Isaiæ, Rugiemus quasi ursi omnes, et quasi columbas meditantes gememus. Quia timor, id est causa timoris, quem timebam, evenit mihi, in bonis et liberis ac persona; et quod verebar, in amicis et uxore, accidit. Et subdit de innocentia: Nonne dissimulavi mala mihi illata, patientia volens vincere? juxta illud ad Romanos, Noli vinci a malo, sed vince in bono malum. Nonne quievi, nulli inquietudinem faciens? Nonne silui in tumultu et contradictione peccatorum: secundum illud in Psalmo, Obmutui et humiliatus sum et silui a bonis. Et, supple, tamen, venit super me indignatio, id est plaga ex indignatione, prout dicitur in Threnis: Effudit quasi ignem indignationem suam; factus est Dominus velut inimicus. Hæc dixit Job, ut materiam daret disputantibus.
paras.en: Then he shows that this has so befallen him. [[3:24|Before I eat|Antequam comedam]], not for delights but for refreshment, [[3:24|I sigh|suspiro]], under the weight of the misery that presses on me. In this many are blamed, who take food before they sigh. [[3:24|and as overflowing waters|Et quasi inundantis aquæ]], which resound, [[3:24|so is my roaring|sic rugitus meus]] in lament: according to that of Isaias, [[Is 59:11|We shall roar all of us like bears, and shall lament as mournful doves|Rugiemus quasi ursi omnes, et quasi columbas meditantes gememus]]. [[3:25|For the fear|Quia timor]], that is, the cause of fear, [[3:25|which I feared, hath come upon me|quem timebam, evenit mihi]], in goods and children and person; [[3:25|and that which I was afraid of|et quod verebar]], in friends and wife, [[3:25|hath befallen me|accidit]]. And he adds of his innocence: [[3:26|Have I not dissembled|Nonne dissimulavi]] the evils brought upon me, wishing to conquer by patience? according to that to the Romans, [[Rom 12:21|Be not overcome by evil: but overcome evil by good.|Noli vinci a malo, sed vince in bono malum]] Again: [[3:26|have I not been quiet|Nonne quievi]], causing disquiet to no one? [[3:26|have I not kept silence|Nonne silui]] in the tumult and contradiction of sinners? according to that in the Psalm, [[Ps 38:3|I was dumb, and was humbled, and kept silence from good things|Obmutui et humiliatus sum et silui a bonis]]. And yet (this is to be supplied) [[3:26|indignation is come upon me|venit super me indignatio]], that is, a blow out of indignation, as it is said in Lamentations: [[Lam 2:4|he hath poured out his indignation like fire|Effudit quasi ignem indignationem suam]]; [[Lam 2:5|The Lord is become as an enemy|factus est Dominus velut inimicus]]. Job said these things to give matter to the disputants.

paras.t: Hucusque verba Alberti. Circa quæ multa occurrunt, quæ dubitationem et difficultatem inducunt: videntur enim pro magna parte stare non posse ut sonant. Unde quæ menti vel circa vel contra ea occurrunt, breviter tangam, non ut tanto doctori in aliquo irreverentialiter contradicam, sed ut per inquisitionem scholasticam veritas sacræ Scripturæ clarius innotescat.
paras.en: Thus far the words of Albert. Concerning them many things come to mind that raise doubt and difficulty: for in great part they seem unable to stand as they sound. Hence I will touch briefly on what occurs to my mind about them or against them, not so as to contradict so great a doctor irreverently in anything, but so that by scholastic inquiry the truth of sacred Scripture may become more clearly known.

3.title: Introductio dubiorum et difficultatum circa præscripta verba.
3.title_en: Setting out the doubts and difficulties concerning the words given above

paras.t: Primo præterea oritur difficultas circa verbum Alberti, quo ait, quod Job conqueritur de hoc, quod actus sui non judicantur a Deo secundum formam, modum seu ordinem humanæ justitiæ. Querimonia enim videtur impatientiæ esse. Job autem de patientia specialissime commendatur, nec ab ea cecidisse asseritur, sicut jam patuit. Verum aliquis dicere potest, quod etiam sit quædam pia querela ex caritate et humilitate procedens, ut quum quis fratrem peccantem, de ejus excessibus conquerendo spirituali patri, caritative accusat, vel humilis de humili conqueritur, quod omnia ad humilitatem spectantia opera sibi præripiat, nec se aliquid talium agere sinat. Sed propter pœnas a Deo directe vel permissive inflictas, conqueri, reprehensibile esse videtur, et potissime de divino judicio conqueri.
paras.en: First, then, a difficulty arises about the saying of Albert in which he says that Job complains of this, that his acts are not judged by God according to the form, manner or order of human justice. For complaint seems to belong to impatience. But Job is commended most especially for patience, and is said not to have fallen from it[[Job 1:22||]] [the margin reference is unclear: perhaps Job i, 22], as has already been made plain. Someone may say, indeed, that there is also a devout kind of complaint that proceeds from charity and humility: as when someone, complaining of a brother’s excesses to his spiritual father, accuses the sinning brother out of charity; or a humble man complains of a humble man that he snatches for himself all the works that belong to humility, and does not let him do any of them. But to complain because of pains inflicted by God, directly or by his permission, seems to be blameworthy, and most of all to complain of the divine judgment.

paras.t: Insuper oritur difficultas circa verbum Alberti, quo ait, quod Job postea, scilicet sanitate adepta vel circiter, rediens ad verum intellectum, Deo docente cognovit, quod ordo divinæ justitiæ penitus dissimilis est ordini justitiæ humanæ; et ideo homo non debeat judicari a Deo secundum humanæ æquitatis processum: cujus oppositum in principio suæ plagationis putavit Job, ut ex verbis inductis Alberti consequitur. Istud non videtur firmiter dictum, quod scilicet vir tantæ perfectionis ac sapientiæ antequam præfato modo affligeretur, nescierit ordinem, processum et modum divinæ justitiæ dissimilem esse modo et ordini justitiæ humanæ, atque humanam justitiam in infinitum deficere a divina. Præterea, processus et ordo humanæ justitiæ est, ut nulli infligatur pœna nisi pro culpa. Si ergo Job primo putavit se judicari debere a Deo secundum humanam justitiam, fuisset ejusdem opinionis, imo erroris, cujus et sui amici id æstimantes, secundum Thomam, vel saltem cujus et Eliphaz, id æstimans, secundum Albertum hunc ipsum. Hoc enim vel omnes tres, vel Eliphaz sensit, quod homines judicarentur a Deo secundum processum humanæ justitiæ, ita videlicet, quod Deus nulli infligeret pœnam nisi pro culpa: quod erroneum fuit: nec Job illius fuit erroris, sicut patet ex his quæ in expositione primi capituli dicta sunt circa verba Job.
paras.en: Further, a difficulty arises about the saying of Albert in which he says that Job afterwards, namely when he had recovered his health or about that time, coming back to the true understanding, learned by God’s teaching that the order of divine justice is wholly unlike the order of human justice, and that therefore man ought not to be judged by God according to the procedure of human equity: the opposite of which Job thought at the beginning of his scourging, as follows from the words of Albert quoted above. This does not seem to be soundly said: namely that a man of such perfection and wisdom, before he was afflicted in the aforesaid way, did not know that the order, procedure and manner of divine justice is unlike the manner and order of human justice, and that human justice falls infinitely short of the divine. Moreover, the procedure and order of human justice is that no pain be inflicted on anyone except for a fault. If then Job at first thought that he ought to be judged by God according to human justice, he would have been of the same opinion, nay the same error, as his friends, who thought so according to Thomas, or at least as Eliphaz, who thought so according to this same Albert. For either all three, or Eliphaz, held that men are judged by God according to the procedure of human justice, namely in such a way that God inflicts pain on no one except for a fault: which was erroneous; and Job was not of that error, as is plain from what was said on Job’s words in the exposition of the first chapter.

paras.t: Amplius oritur difficultas circa verbum Alberti, dicentis, quod in fine se ipsum reprehendit atque pœnituit, eo quod taliter sensit, et quoniam dixit: Innocentem et impium ipse, scilicet Deus, condemnat. Ex quo sequi videtur, quod Job loquendo quæ isto scribuntur libro, peccavit: cujus oppositum S. Gregorius in principio primi libri Moralium multipliciter probat et asserit, inter cetera dicens: Quædam verba responsionum ipsius Job, imperitis lectoribus aspera resonant, quia Sanctorum dicta pie intelligere, sicut dicuntur, ignorant. Et quoniam animum dolentis et justi in semetipsis assumere nesciunt, ideo doloris verba bene interpretari non possunt. Credunt ergo beatum Job in suis sermonibus deliquisse, minus intuentes, quia si beati Job responsa redarguunt, falsam de eo et Dei sententiam fuisse testantur. Diabolo namque a Domino dicitur: Considerasti servum meum Job, quod non sit ei similis super terram, etc.? Cui mox a diabolo respondetur: Numquid Job gratis timet Deum? mitte manum tuam, etc. Hostis itaque in beato Job vires suas exercuit, sed certamen contra Deum assumpsit. Inter Deum itaque et diabolum, Job in medio, materia certaminis fuit. Quisquis ergo sanctum virum inter flagella positum, dictis suis peccasse asserit, quid aliud quam Deum qui pro illo proposuerat, perdidisse reprehendit? Idem probat Gregorius per hoc, quod in fine tentationis omnia ipsi Job in duplo sunt restituta; et quod per intercessionem ipsius, Deus amicis ejus ignovit. Verumtamen istam difficultatem specialiter differo, et infra congruis locis tangendam solvendamque confido.
paras.en: Again, a difficulty arises about the saying of Albert, who says that at the end Job reproved himself and repented because he had thought thus, and because he had said: [[Job 9:22|both the innocent and the wicked|Innocentem et impium]] he, that is, God, condemneth. From which it seems to follow that Job sinned in speaking the things written in this book: the opposite of which St. Gregory, at the beginning of the first book of the Morals, proves and asserts in many ways, saying among other things: Some words of the answers of Job himself sound harsh to unskilled readers, because they do not know how to understand the sayings of the Saints devoutly, in the sense in which they are spoken. And since they cannot take into themselves the mind of one who grieves and is just, they cannot interpret aright the words of grief. They believe therefore that blessed Job sinned in his discourses, not considering that if they find fault with blessed Job’s answers, they bear witness that God’s own judgment of him was false. For it is said to the devil by the Lord: [[Job 1:8|Hast thou considered my servant, Job, that there is none like him in the earth|Considerasti servum meum Job, quod non sit ei similis super terram]], etc.? And the devil at once answers him: [[Job 1:9|Doth Job fear God in vain?|Numquid Job gratis timet Deum?]] [[Job 1:11|stretch forth thy hand|mitte manum tuam]], etc. So the enemy exercised his strength on blessed Job, but took up the contest against God. So between God and the devil, Job in the middle was the matter of the contest. Whoever then asserts that the holy man, set among the scourges, sinned by his words, what else does he do but charge God, who had put him forward, with having lost? Gregory proves the same by this, that at the end of the temptation everything was restored to Job twofold[[Job 42:10||]], and that through his intercession God pardoned his friends. However, I put off this difficulty in particular, and trust to touch on it and resolve it below, in the fitting places.

paras.t: Rursus oritur difficultas, quum ait Albertus, sanctum Job verba hujus dixisse capituli, ut amicis suis disputandi præberet materiam. Quum enim fuerit in tot ac tantis afflictionibus constitutus, videtur quod occasionem disputandi non exquisierit, nec disputare optaverit, quum talis actus debilibus et infirmis in maximis doloribus positis sit onerosus: nisi forte quis dicat, quod voluit sibi tribulationem augere. Et tamen infra reprehendit amicos, quod disputando ipsum afflixerint: Consolatores, inquiens, onerosi vos omnes. Et iterum: En decies confunditis me, et non erubescitis me affligentes sermonibus.
paras.en: Once more, a difficulty arises when Albert says that holy Job spoke the words of this chapter to give his friends matter for disputing. For since he was set in so many and such great afflictions, it seems that he did not seek an occasion for disputing, nor wish to dispute, since such an act is burdensome to the weak and sick who are in the greatest pains: unless perhaps someone should say that he wished to increase his tribulation. And yet below he reproves his friends for having afflicted him by disputing, saying: [[Job 16:2|you are all troublesome comforters|onerosi vos omnes]]. And again: [[Job 19:3|Behold, these ten times you confound me|En decies confunditis me]], [[Job 19:3|and are not ashamed|et non erubescitis]] to afflict me with words.

paras.t: Adhuc autem oritur difficultas, quum ait Albertus: Dies naturaliter est principium vitæ nascentis ex utero ad lucem; et hæc dies secundum totam periodum, in quam Satan accepit potestatem, ut malitiam suæ voluntatis in ea exerceat, in rebus et liberis, persona atque amicis, non potest optari nisi ut pereat. Si enim peribit, tristitias et infelicitates non ingeret; si autem procedet de mane in meridiem, et de meridie in vesperam, multis afflictionibus vitam consumet: et ideo optandum non est, nisi ut pereat.
paras.en: A further difficulty arises when Albert says: The day is by nature the beginning of the life of one born from the womb into the light; and this day, taken for the whole period over which Satan received power to exercise in it the malice of his will, in goods and children, person and friends, cannot be wished anything but to perish. For if it perishes, it will not bring on sorrows and misfortunes; but if it goes on from morning to noon, and from noon to evening, it will consume life with many afflictions: and therefore nothing is to be wished for it but that it perish.

paras.t: Ex quibus Alberti verbis sequi videtur, quod tempus et vita hæc temporalis quæ sine illo esse non potest in sæculo isto corporeque mortali, sint optanda non esse propter mala pœnalia quæ occurrunt: quod stare non posse censetur, quia hoc impatientiæ, non patientiæ atque constantiæ seu fortitudinis animi, esset. Patientia quippe, perfecta præsertim, omnem adversitatem, pœnam et persecutionem fortiter sustinet; nec ob talia succumbit, cupiens mortem secundum se, vel solum ut est finis adversitatis, sed bene ut est janua felicitatis. Itaque dies cujuscumque tribulationis potest optari, non ut pereat, sed ut maneat, in quantum in ipso die maxime per patientiam promeremur, aliis exemplum patientiæ ædificationemque impendimus, Christo propter nos passo conformamur, in gratia atque virtutibus crescimus, futura tormenta præsentibus pœnis brevioribus minoribusque redimimus. Sic quoque martyres sancti fecerunt. Denique, teste Apostolo, pro Christo pati, donum est Dei. Et Christus testatur: Beati eritis quum maledixerint vobis homines, et persecuti vos fuerint. Gaudete in illa hora, quoniam merces vestra copiosa est in cælo. Sic et Jacobus: Omne (inquit) gaudium existimate, fratres, quum in diversas tentationes incideritis. Absolute ergo et secundum rectam rationem loquendo, dies non est optanda perire, nec vita optanda statim finiri seu nunquam fuisse, propter mala pœnalia: imo quo illa sunt graviora, patientiusque ex Dei amore feruntur, eo dies hujusmodi beatior perhibetur.
paras.en: From these words of Albert it seems to follow that time, and this temporal life, which cannot be without time in this world and in the mortal body, are to be wished not to be, because of the penal evils [evils of pain, that is, of punishment or suffering, as against evils of fault, that is, sins] that befall: which is judged unable to stand, since this would belong to impatience, not to patience and constancy or fortitude of soul. For patience, above all perfect patience, bravely bears every adversity, pain and persecution; nor does it give way because of such things, desiring death for its own sake, or only as the end of adversity, but rather as the gate of happiness. So the day of any tribulation may be wished, not to perish, but to remain, inasmuch as on that very day we merit most through patience, give others an example of patience and edification, are conformed to Christ who suffered for us, grow in grace and the virtues, and redeem future torments by present pains that are shorter and lesser. So too the holy martyrs did. Lastly, on the witness of the Apostle, to suffer for Christ is the gift of God[[Phil 1:29||]]. And Christ bears witness: [[Matt 5:11|Blessed are ye when they shall revile you|Beati eritis quum maledixerint vobis homines]][[Luke 6:22||]], [[Matt 5:11|and persecute you|et persecuti vos fuerint]]. [[Luke 6:23|Be glad in that day|Gaudete in illa hora]] [Denis has in that hour], [[Matt 5:12|for your reward is very great in heaven|quoniam merces vestra copiosa est in cælo]]. So too James: [[Jas 1:2|My brethren, count it all joy, when you shall fall into divers temptations|Omne (inquit) gaudium existimate, fratres, quum in diversas tentationes incideritis]]. Speaking absolutely, then, and according to right reason, a day is not to be wished to perish, nor life to be ended at once or never to have been, because of penal evils: nay, the heavier these are, and the more patiently they are borne out of the love of God, the more blessed such a day is held to be.

paras.t: Iterum ex verbis his sequitur, quod Albertus ista exponit de die exteriori vere temporali, consueto, sensibili. Talis autem dies dudum præteriit, quando Job verba hæc protulit: sicque impossibile fuit, diem illam repeti, esse, perire, obscurari, et cetera pati seu suscipere, quæ ei in isto capitulo imprecatur. Unde Gregorius satis probat, quod de illo die ista exponi non queant, secundum quod verba jacent et sonant. Unde et Thomas, qui de hujusmodi die ista exponit, aliter mutat ac ordinat verba, et aliqua interponit ac addit: quod non facit Albertus. Ex quibus id quoque elicitur, quod expositio inducta Alberti, non solum differat ab expositione Gregorii, in hoc quod Gregorius processum dicit in peccatis, Albertus, in pœnis seu afflictionibus Satanæ (quamvis Albertus quo nescio sensu hoc dicat): imo in aliis valde multis ab invicem differunt, quemadmodum intuenti amborum præscriptas expositiones patescit. Imo et expositio Gregorii in hoc puncto rationabilior rite ostenditur, quoniam tempus et vita præsens magis optanda essent non esse nec fuisse ac perire, propter mala culpæ, quam propter mala pœnæ. Et tamen Gregorius non exponit hæc de exteriori, sensibili, temporali ac solito die, nec de persona beati Job. Sed nec propter mala culpæ quæ fecimus, debemus penitus velle nunquam fuisse aut esse: quia ad veniam licet venire, et in culparum remissione divina misericordia declaratur, Deusque præclare laudatur. Sed et malum culpæ non totaliter perimit bonum naturæ.
paras.en: Again, it follows from these words that Albert expounds these things of the outward day, truly temporal, ordinary and perceptible to the senses. But such a day had long gone by when Job uttered these words; and so it was impossible for that day to be repeated, to be, to perish, to be darkened, and to suffer or undergo the other things that he calls down upon it in this chapter. Hence Gregory proves well enough that these things cannot be expounded of that day according as the words lie and sound. Hence too Thomas, who expounds them of such a day, changes and rearranges the words, and inserts and adds some things: which Albert does not do. From which this too is drawn, that the exposition of Albert quoted above differs from the exposition of Gregory not only in this, that Gregory speaks of a course in sins, Albert of one in the pains or afflictions of Satan (though in what sense Albert says this I do not know): nay, they differ from each other in very many other things, as is plain to anyone who looks at the expositions of both given above. Nay, the exposition of Gregory is rightly shown to be the more reasonable on this point, since time and the present life would sooner be wished not to be, nor to have been, and to perish, because of the evils of fault than because of the evils of pain. And yet Gregory does not expound these things of the outward, sensible, temporal and ordinary day, nor of the person of blessed Job. But not even because of the evils of fault that we have committed ought we to wish altogether never to have been or to be: since it is open to us to come to pardon, and in the remission of faults the divine mercy is shown, and God is gloriously praised. And besides, the evil of fault does not wholly destroy the good of nature.

paras.t: Juxta hunc modum possent et multa similia objici verbis Alberti, sicut quum ait: Dies Satanæ, in quo scilicet Satan afflixit Job, non requiratur ad numerum dierum beati Job: ita quod Job orat pro hoc. Certum est autem, quod dies illa præterita non potuit non pertinere ad dies vitæ Job. Rursus, quum ait: Recordatio mali, male et ad tristitiam afficit animam. Certum est autem, quod recordatio tam mali pœnalis, quam mali culpabilis, frequenter bene ac delectabiliter afficit animam, ut quum aliquis gaudet se propter Deum pertulisse adversa, vel de pristinæ infirmitatis curatione lætatur, vel pœnitens de suis peccatis salubriter per pœnitentiam recordatur, vel quod Deus sibi pepercit, atque ad emendationem pervenit. Hinc nempe ait Psalmista: Lætati sumus pro diebus quibus nos humiliasti; annis quibus vidimus mala. Iterum, quando ait, Utilius est talia infausta, id est infortunata, infelicia seu adversa occumbere, quam illustrari, et non apparere quam manifestari. Certum est autem, quod frequenter utilius est, talia manifestari ad Dei honorem et fidei confirmationem, hominumque ædificationem, ut patet de Sanctorum martyriis: imo et ipsum Job voluit seu permisit Deus sic flagellari, ut per hoc ejus perfectio ac patientia nobis ad nostram instructionem pateret, ut ex verbis Gregorii patuit. Item, quum ait et subdit Job causam tantæ maledictionis: Quia non conclusit dies hæc ostia ventris qui portavit me, ut scilicet clausis ostiis, intra ventrem mortuus essem, ne ad hanc infaustam lucem peperisset me mater mea. Ex isto sequi videtur, quod propter pœnalia sua mala Job optavit se natum non fuisse, aut in matris ventre obiisse: quod, sicut ex præhabitis claret, irrationabile exstitisset, prout etiam tangit Gregorius. Simili argumento sequentium verborum Job, expositio hujus doctoris impugnaretur.
paras.en: In the same way many similar objections could be made to the words of Albert; as when he says: Let the day of Satan, namely the day on which Satan afflicted Job, not be required for the number of the days of blessed Job; so that Job prays for this. But it is certain that that past day could not but belong to the days of Job’s life. Again, when he says: The remembrance of evil affects the soul with evil and sorrow. But it is certain that the remembrance of penal evil, as well as of culpable evil, often affects the soul well and delightfully: as when someone rejoices to have borne adversity for God’s sake, or is glad of being cured of a former sickness, or a penitent remembers his sins to his salvation through penance, or remembers that God spared him, and that he came to amendment. For hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 89:15|We have rejoiced for the days in which thou hast humbled us: for the years in which we have seen evils.|Lætati sumus pro diebus quibus nos humiliasti; annis quibus vidimus mala]] Again, when he says: It is more useful that such ill-starred, that is, unfortunate, unhappy or adverse things should set than be lit up, and not appear rather than be made manifest. But it is certain that it is often more useful for such things to be made manifest, for the honour of God, the strengthening of faith and the edification of men, as is plain from the martyrdoms of the Saints: nay, God willed or allowed Job himself to be scourged so, that by this his perfection and patience might be made plain to us for our instruction, as was plain from the words of Gregory. Likewise when he says, and Job adds the cause of so great a curse: [[3:10|Because it shut not up|Quia non conclusit]], namely this day, [[3:10|the doors of the womb that bore me|ostia ventris qui portavit me]]: that is, so that, the doors being shut, I should have died within the womb, lest my mother should have borne me to this ill-starred light. From this it seems to follow that because of his penal evils Job wished not to have been born, or to have died in his mother’s womb: which, as is clear from what has gone before, would have been unreasonable, as Gregory also touches on. By a like argument from the words of Job that follow, the exposition of this doctor could be attacked.

paras.t: Denique subdit, Nunc enim dormiens silerem cum regibus terræ, qui secundum perfectionem justitiæ homines regebant. Sed, ut tangit Gregorius, si intra matris alvum obiisset, nullum habuisset remedium contra originale peccatum: idcirco in silentio et quiete justorum non fuisset cum hujusmodi regibus justis, qui ante Christi passionem in sinu Abrahæ quieverunt, in ascensione vero ad cælos deducti noscuntur. Postea addit Albertus: In hoc ergo mors utilis est, quod liberat a sensu malorum: et in hoc affectu dixit David, Heu mihi! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est: et Christus, O generatio incredula, quamdiu apud vos ero? Contra istud objicitur, quoniam licet mors in hoc utilis asseratur, quod liberat a sensu malorum, id est pœnali perceptione seu sensatione pœnarum, in quantum sunt quædam mala, non tamen in quantum sunt materia patientiæ, et magni profectus beatitudinisque occasio. Ideo propter mala pœnalia, absolute loquendo, mors non est simpliciter appetenda, in quantum est mors, seu terminus vitæ seu etiam pœnæ præsentis. Nec in tali affectu dixit Psalmista, Heu mihi! sed desiderio vitæ beatæ seu melioris quietis ex caritate, secundum Augustinum aliosque expositores concorditer, sicut et Paulus profatur: Infelix ego homo, quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus? Christus quoque inducta protulit verba potius propter mala culpæ, utpote incredulitatem quorumdam, ut patet in Marco et Matthæo, quam tædio malorum pœnalium: itemque desiderio redeundi ad Patrem, et glorificationis suæ in corpore.
paras.en: Lastly he adds: [[3:13|For now I should have been asleep and still|Nunc enim dormiens silerem]] [[3:14|With kings|cum regibus terræ]] of the earth, who ruled men according to the perfection of justice. But, as Gregory touches on, if he had died within his mother’s womb, he would have had no remedy against original sin: and therefore he would not have been, in the silence and quiet of the just, with such just kings, who before Christ’s passion rested in Abraham’s bosom, and at the ascension are known to have been led into heaven.
