Afterwards Albert adds: In this then death is useful, that it frees from the feeling of evils: and in this feeling David said, [[Ps 119:5|Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged!|Heu mihi! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est]] and Christ, [[Mark 9:18|O incredulous generation, how long shall I be with you?|O generatio incredula, quamdiu apud vos ero?]] Against this it is objected that, though death is said to be useful in this, that it frees from the feeling of evils, that is, from the penal perception or sensation of pains, inasmuch as they are evils of a kind, yet it is not so inasmuch as they are matter for patience, and the occasion of great progress and of beatitude. Therefore, because of penal evils, speaking absolutely, death is not simply to be sought, inasmuch as it is death, or the end of life, or even of present pain. Nor did the Psalmist say Woe is me! in such a feeling, but out of desire for the blessed life, or for a better rest, out of charity, according to Augustine and the other expositors with one accord; as Paul too declares: [[Rom 7:24|Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?|Infelix ego homo, quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus?]] Christ too uttered the words quoted rather because of the evils of fault, namely the unbelief of certain men, as is plain in Mark and Matthew[[Mark 9:18||]][[Matt 17:16||]], than out of weariness of penal evils; and also out of desire to return to the Father, and for his glorification in the body.

paras.t: Deinde subdit Albertus: Quare misero data est lux? Ex luce enim nihil habet, nisi quod videt miseriam suam: et ita lux nocet ei. Istud rursus instantiam patitur. Afflictus enim, luce sensibili ad multa commoda adjuvatur, ut si pergat ad consolatorem, et ad Christi imaginem et crucem adspiciat, ac qua adspecta, memor sit passionis dominicæ, discat atque proficiat.
paras.en: Then Albert adds: [[3:20|Why is light given to him that is in misery|Quare misero data est lux?]]? For from the light he has nothing but that he sees his misery: and so the light harms him. This too is open to an objection [instantia, in the schools a counter-instance]. For the afflicted man is helped by the light of the senses to many advantages: as when he goes to one who consoles him, and looks upon the image and the cross of Christ, and, having looked on it, is mindful of the Lord’s passion, and learns and profits.

paras.t: Porro super illud quod subditur, Exspectant mortem quasi effodientes thesaurum, dicit, Quoniam mortem thesaurum et lucrum reputant, in quantum est finis miseriæ, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: O mors, bonum est judicium tuum homini indigenti, etc., sicut est allegatum; sicut Tobias dixit ad Dominum: Fac mecum misericordiam, et præcipe in pace recipi spiritum meum; atque Elias: Tolle animam meam. Ex his potissime expositio Alberti fulciri videtur, quod scilicet propter vitæ adversitates pœnales optanda sit mors, et ut pereat dies.
paras.en: Further, on what follows, [[3:21|That look for death|Exspectant mortem]] [[3:21|as they that dig for a treasure|quasi effodientes thesaurum]], he says: Because they reckon death a treasure and a gain, inasmuch as it is the end of misery; according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 41:3|O death thy sentence is welcome to the man that is in need|O mors, bonum est judicium tuum homini indigenti]], etc., as was alleged; as Tobias said to the Lord: Deal mercifully with me, and [[Tob 3:6|command my spirit to be received in peace|præcipe in pace recipi spiritum meum]]; and Elias: [[3 Kings 19:4|take away my soul|Tolle animam meam]]. By these things above all the exposition of Albert seems to be supported: namely that because of the penal adversities of life death is to be wished for, and that the day should perish.

paras.t: Ad quod respondendum, quod auctoritas illa Ecclesiastici nil amplius obtinet, nisi quod mors tolerabilior est egenis, infirmis, senibus atque sollicitis, in quantum pœnalibus sunt pleniores defectibus, et in quantum mors illis finem imponens, est janua ad vitam meliorem sequentem. Sicque excæcatus Tobias, et persecutionem ferens Elias, locuti sunt verba præallegata, quamvis nonnulli dicant Tobiam in verbis illis, præsertim quum dixit, Expedit mihi mori magis quam vivere, ex humana infirmitate locutum, venialiterque peccasse. Vel forsitan dixit hoc, timens ex abundantia adversitatum sibi occurrentium ad culpam corruere, sicut et Moyses in libro Numerorum ait ad Dominum: Obsecro ut interficias me, ne tantis malis afficiar. Unde omnes hi sancti, videlicet Moyses, Elias, Tobias, verba hæc locuti creduntur magis ad vitandum mala culpæ, et ne cernerent talia, quæ videre eis gravissimum fuit, ex amore Dei et zelo justitiæ, itemque desiderio quietis sequentis, quam ad vitanda mala pœnæ simpliciter. Afflictio tamen pœnosa, potest absque culpa esse alicui occasio cupiendi mortem, secundum quod mors est quidam ingressus ad vitam meliorem sequentem, in qua non peccatur ut hic, et præsupposita divina circa hoc voluntate.
paras.en: To this the answer is that that authority of Ecclesiasticus establishes no more than that death is more bearable to the needy, the sick, the old and the careworn, inasmuch as they are fuller of penal defects, and inasmuch as death, putting an end to these for them, is the gate to the better life that follows. And so Tobias, when he was blinded, and Elias, when he suffered persecution, spoke the words alleged above; though some say that Tobias in those words, especially when he said, [[Tob 3:6|it is better for me to die, than to live|Expedit mihi mori magis quam vivere]], spoke out of human weakness, and sinned venially. Or perhaps he said this fearing that from the abundance of adversities befalling him he might fall into sin: as Moses too says to the Lord in the book of Numbers: [[Num 11:15|I beseech thee to kill me|Obsecro ut interficias me]], [[Num 11:15|that I be not afflicted with so great evils|ne tantis malis afficiar]]. Hence all these saints, namely Moses, Elias and Tobias, are believed to have spoken these words rather to avoid the evils of fault, and so as not to see such things as it was most grievous for them to see, out of the love of God and zeal for justice, and also out of desire for the rest that follows, than simply to avoid the evils of pain. Painful affliction, however, can without fault be to someone an occasion of desiring death, in so far as death is a kind of entry into the better life that follows, in which there is no sinning as there is here; the divine will in this matter being presupposed.

paras.t: Hic autem desiderio veritatis meliorisque informationis, salvo per omnia honore Magni Alberti, sint inquisitive, non reprobative aut pertinaciter, dicta. Forte enim verba Alberti possunt salvari, quamvis pro magna parte eorum non videam quomodo faciliter possint salvari. Cui itaque placet tam studiosum doctorem defendere, verba ipsius elucidet ac resolvat, et quæ objecta sunt solvat.
paras.en: Let these things be said here out of desire for the truth and for better instruction, saving in all things the honour of Albert the Great: by way of inquiry, not of condemnation, nor obstinately. For perhaps the words of Albert can be saved, though for the most part I do not see how they can easily be saved. Whoever then is pleased to defend so studious a doctor, let him explain and resolve his words, and answer what has been objected.

3.title: De expositione S. Thomæ circa idem capitulum.
3.title_en: On St Thomas's exposition of the same chapter

paras.t: Quoniam expositio S. Gregorii in isto capitulo videtur ad spiritualitatem non modice tendere, Thomas conatus est præsens capitulum litteraliter explanare: cujus expositio in hac parte planior est et resolutior quam Alberti. Itaque ait: Sicut dictum est, circa passiones animi duplex fuit antiquorum opinio. Stoici enim dixerunt tristitiam in sapientem non cadere. Peripatetici vero dixerunt sapientem tristari moderate secundum rationem: quod veritati concordat. Ratio enim conditionem naturæ auferre non potest. Est autem naturale sensitivæ naturæ, convenientibus delectari, et de nocivis dolere atque tristari: quod ratio nequit auferre; sed moderatur ita, quod ratio per tristitias a sua rectitudine non divertat. Concordatque hæc opinio sacræ Scripturæ, quæ tristitiam ponit in Christo, in quo est omnis virtutis ac sapientiæ plenitudo.
paras.en: Since St Gregory's exposition of this chapter seems to tend not a little towards the spiritual sense, Thomas set out to explain the present chapter literally; and his exposition in this part is plainer and more fully worked out than Albert's. He says, then: As has been said, the ancients held two opinions about the passions of the soul. The Stoics said that sorrow does not befall the wise man; the Peripatetics, on the other hand, said that the wise man is sorrowful in moderation, according to reason, and this agrees with the truth. For reason cannot take away the condition of nature; and it is natural to the sensitive nature [that is, the part of the soul that perceives by the senses and feels the passions] to take delight in things agreeable to it, and to grieve and be sorrowful over things harmful. This reason cannot take away; but it moderates it so that reason is not turned aside from its rightness by sorrows. And this opinion agrees with Holy Scripture, which places sorrow in Christ, in whom is the fullness of all virtue and wisdom.

paras.t: Sic ergo Job ex prænarratis adversitatibus tristitiam sensit: alias patientia in eo locum non habuisset; sed propter tristitiam ratio ejus a rectitudine non recessit. Ad quod ostendendum, dicitur: Post hæc, id est post septem dies taciturnitatis præfatæ. Unde constat, quod ex ratione, non ex turbante tristitia sit locutus: alias ante protulisset hæc verba, quando tristitia vehementior fuit. Tristitia namque temporis longitudine mitigatur, et in principio magis sentitur. Ideo tam diu tacuisse videtur, ne ex perturbata mente loqui judicaretur. Solent autem sapientes ex ratione exprimere motus passionum quos sentiunt, moderate, sicut et Christus dixit: Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem. Et Boetius primo de Consolatione, tristitiam suam aperuit, ut ostenderet quomodo eam ratione mitigaret.
paras.en: So Job felt sorrow at the adversities told above (otherwise patience would have had no place in him); but his reason did not depart from its rightness because of the sorrow. To show this it is said: [[3:1|After this|Post hæc]], that is, after the seven days of silence spoken of before. From this it is clear that he spoke from reason, not from a sorrow that disturbed him; otherwise he would have uttered these words earlier, when his sorrow was more vehement. For sorrow is softened by length of time, and is felt more at the beginning. That is why he seems to have kept silence so long: lest he be judged to speak from a troubled mind. Now the wise are wont to express from reason, in moderation, the movements of the passions they feel, as Christ too said: [[Matt 26:38|My soul is sorrowful even unto death|Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem]]. And Boethius, in the first book of the Consolation, laid open his sorrow, to show how he softened it by reason.

paras.t: Et maledixit diei suo. Maledicere, multipliciter sumitur. Quum enim maledicere nihil aliud sit quam mala dicere, tot modis maledicitur, quot modis malum dicitur. Itaque tripliciter maledicitur. Primo, maledictione causante malum, quemadmodum dicere Dei, est causa eorum quæ dicit; et sententia judicis, causa est pœnæ ejus quem damnat: sicque in Genesi dicitur, Maledictus Chanaan. Et Josue maledixit Achan. Secundo fit istud, imprecando vel optando malum alicui: et sic Apostolus prohibet maledicere, dicens ad Romanos, Benedicite, et nolite maledicere; non autem primo modo. Tertio fit hoc, malum simpliciter enuntiando per modum præsentis, præteriti vel futuri. Sic Job maledixit diei suo, eum malum esse dicendo secundum morem Scripturæ, quo tempus dicitur bonum seu malum propter ea quæ fiunt in tempore.
paras.en: [[3:1|And cursed his day|Et maledixit diei suo]]. To curse is taken in several ways. For since to curse is nothing else than to speak evil [in Latin *maledicere*, to curse, is literally *mala dicere*, to speak evil things], there are as many ways of cursing as there are ways in which evil is spoken. So one curses in three ways. First, by a curse that causes the evil: as the speaking of God is the cause of what He speaks, and the sentence of a judge is the cause of the punishment of him whom he condemns. So it is said in Genesis: [[Gen 9:25|Cursed be Chanaan|Maledictus Chanaan]]. And Josue cursed Achan[[Jos 7:25||]]. Secondly, this is done by calling down or wishing evil on someone; and in this way the Apostle forbids cursing, saying to the Romans: [[Rom 12:14|bless, and curse not|Benedicite, et nolite maledicere]]; but not in the first way. Thirdly, it is done by simply stating an evil, as present, past or future. In this way Job cursed his day, saying that it was evil, after the manner of Scripture, by which a time is called good or evil because of the things that happen in it.

paras.t: Denique, licet esse et vivere sit secundum se appetibile; tamen esse et vivere in miseria est fugiendum, secundum quod hujusmodi: quamvis interdum esse in miseria, aliqui libenter ferant ob aliquem finem. Hinc misera vita quæ non ordinatur ad aliquem finem bonum, nullo modo est eligenda, prout Christus ait de Juda: Melius ei erat si natus non esset. Bonum autem quod ex miseria exspectatur, non apprehendit vis sensitiva, sed ratio tantum, sicut amaritudinem medicinæ percipit gustus, solaque ratio in fine sanitatis delectatur. Si quis ergo secundum passionem sui gustus judicaret de medicina amara, diceret eam malam; ratio tamen diceret bonam propter finem intentum. Similiter miseria quam Job patiebatur, rationi utilis videbatur, sed inferior pars animæ eam repudiabat. Unde et vivere sub tali miseria, secundum quod tale, fuerat odiosum, et etiam ea per quæ deveniebatur ad illud. Ideo Job secundum inferiorem animæ partem, cujus passionem et dispositionem exprimere intendebat, odio habuit nativitatem suam et diem suæ nativitatis, conceptionem quoque et noctem qua fuit conceptus. Et hoc est quod dicit: Pereat dies in qua natus sum: ac si diceret, Utinam nunquam natus fuissem; et nox in qua dictum est, id est, vere dici potuit, Conceptus est homo: id est, utinam nunquam conceptus fuissem. Congrue autem nativitatem adscribit diei, et conceptionem nocti: quia secundum astrologos, nativitas diurna est melior, principali sidere, scilicet sole, exsistente super terram; conceptio autem nocturna frequentior.
paras.en: Further, though being and living are in themselves desirable, yet being and living in misery is to be shunned, insofar as it is such; although some at times willingly bear being in misery for the sake of some end. Hence a wretched life which is not ordered to some good end is in no way to be chosen, as Christ says of Judas: [[Matt 26:24|It were better for him, if that man had not been born|Melius ei erat si natus non esset]] [no margin reference; the same words stand in Mark 14:21]. Now the good that is looked for from misery is not grasped by the sensitive power, but by reason alone: so the taste perceives the bitterness of a medicine, and reason alone takes delight in its end, which is health. If someone, then, judged of a bitter medicine by what his taste feels, he would call it bad; yet reason would call it good, for the sake of the end intended. In the same way the misery that Job suffered seemed useful to his reason, but the lower part of his soul rejected it. Hence living under such misery, insofar as it was such, had become hateful to him, and so too the things through which one came to it. Therefore Job, according to the lower part of the soul, whose passion and disposition he meant to express, held in hatred his birth and the day of his birth, and also his conception and the night in which he was conceived. And this is what he says: [[3:3|Let the day perish wherein I was born|Pereat dies in qua natus sum]]: as if he said, Would that I had never been born; [[3:3|and the night in which it was said|et nox in qua dictum est]], that is, could truly be said, [[3:3|A man child is conceived|Conceptus est homo]]: that is, would that I had never been conceived. And he fittingly ascribes the birth to the day and the conception to the night: because, according to the astrologers, a birth by day is better, the chief star, namely the sun, being above the earth; while conception is more frequent by night.

paras.t: Deinde Job ad maledicendum diei suæ ea inducit, per quæ dies fit odiosa. Dignitas vero diei, est claritas, qua a nocte discernitur; quam excludit, dicens: Dies illa vertatur in tenebras. Ac si dicat: Dies nativitatis meæ debuisset esse tenebrosus, ut congrueret tenebris miseriarum quas patior. Quædam enim per modum optandi dicuntur, ad exprimendum judicium quod de aliqua re habetur: et nisi sic intelligeretur verbum istud atque sequentia, frivola viderentur, quoniam dies et nox, de quibus loquebatur, præterierunt, nec poterant immutari.
paras.en: Next, in order to curse his day, Job brings in the things by which a day becomes hateful. The dignity of a day is its brightness, by which it is distinguished from the night; and this he excludes, saying: [[3:4|Let that day be turned into darkness|Dies illa vertatur in tenebras]]. As if he said: The day of my birth ought to have been dark, to suit the darkness of the miseries I suffer. For some things are said by way of wishing in order to express the judgment one holds about a thing; and unless this saying and those that follow were understood so, they would seem frivolous, since the day and the night of which he was speaking had passed and could not be changed.

paras.t: Præterea dies multipliciter clarus est. Primo, ex sanctificatione Dei, qui eum celebrem fecit: quam claritatem removens, subdit: Non requirat eum Deus desuper, id est, non exigat ut ab hominibus celebretur. Dies quippe aliqui exigebantur a Deo per homines celebrari, propter aliqua insignia beneficia in eis collata hominibus, sicut sabbatum in veteri lege propter beneficium creationis. Vult ergo Job insinuare, quod sua nativitas non sit computanda inter insignia beneficia Dei, quum ad miseriam magis quam ad lætitiam natus videatur. Secundo, dies est clarus ex hominum recordatione, secundum quod homines dies aliquos celebres ducunt, in quibus eis aliqua magna et læta acciderunt; quemadmodum Pharao et Herodes diem sui celebrabant natalis. Hanc claritatem removet, dicens: Non sit in recordatione hominum. Tertio, dies est clarus ex lumine corporali: quæ claritas quandoque aufertur per subtractionem radiorum solis. Ideo subditur: Non illustretur lumine. Quandoque autem aufertur per interpositionem nubium seu aliorum occultantium radios solis: et quantum ad hoc, dicit: Obscurent eum tenebræ. Quandoque ex defectu visus, ut dum quis moritur vel excæcatur, tunc claritas diei, quantum ad eum, aufertur: et quoad hoc, ait, et umbra mortis. Occupet eum caligo. Tunc dies caligine occupatur, dum ei primo splendenti, subito atque ex insperato tenebræ inducuntur, sicut beato Job inductæ sunt tenebræ adversitatis. Et involvatur amaritudine tristitiæ. Per quæ omnia aliud nihil intendit, quam quod dies suæ nativitatis non debeat judicari dies gaudii, sed mœroris.
paras.en: Moreover, a day is bright in several ways. First, from God's hallowing of it, who made it a solemn day; removing this brightness, he adds: [[3:4|let not God regard it from above|Non requirat eum Deus desuper]], that is, let Him not require that it be kept solemn by men. For some days were required by God to be kept by men because of some signal benefits bestowed on men in them, as the sabbath in the old law because of the benefit of creation. Job means to suggest, then, that his birth is not to be counted among the signal benefits of God, since he seems to have been born to misery rather than to gladness. Secondly, a day is bright from men's remembrance, in that men keep as solemn certain days on which great and glad things befell them; as Pharao[[Gen 40:20||]] [the margin reads Gen. xvi, 20, evidently for xl, 20] and Herod[[Mark 6:21||]] kept the day of their birth. This brightness he removes, saying: Let it not be in the remembrance of men [these words are not in the Vulgate as now printed, nor in the Douay-Rheims; they belong to the text of Job that Thomas expounded]. Thirdly, a day is bright from bodily light; and this brightness is sometimes taken away by the withdrawing of the sun's rays. So it is added: [[3:4|let not the light shine upon it|Non illustretur lumine]]. And sometimes it is taken away by clouds or other things coming between and hiding the sun's rays; and as to this he says: [[3:5|Let darkness|Obscurent eum tenebræ]] cover it. Sometimes it is taken away by a failure of sight, as when someone dies or is blinded: then the brightness of the day is taken away as far as he is concerned; and as to this he says, [[3:5|and the shadow of death|et umbra mortis]]. [[3:5|let a mist overspread it|Occupet eum caligo]]: a day is overspread with mist when, after it first shone bright, darkness is brought upon it suddenly and unexpectedly, as the darkness of adversity was brought upon blessed Job. [[3:5|and let it be wrapped up in bitterness|Et involvatur amaritudine]] of sorrow. By all these things he means nothing else than that the day of his birth ought not to be judged a day of joy, but of mourning.

paras.t: Consequenter maledicit nocti suæ conceptionis: primo, ei attribuens unde nox horribilior redditur. Quum enim sit nox horribilis propter tenebras, quo fuerit tenebrosior, eo fit horribilior. Quod fit magna tempestate oriente in nocte: et quoad hoc, subdit: Noctem illam tenebrosus turbo possideat. Quasi dicat: Congruisset noctem illam tenebroso turbine possideri, ut vitæ meæ congrueret, quæ tanto turbine adversitatis involvitur. Non computetur in diebus anni, nec numeretur in mensibus. Tanquam diceret: Nox illa non est memoria digna, quum nihil insigne, quoad me, in ea acciderit, sed potius aliquid dolorosum. Porro inter noctes quædam sunt celebres, quibus homines ad festa agenda concurrunt: quod ab ea removet, dicens: Sit nox illa solitaria, nec laude digna. Nox namque laude fit digna, propter aliquod magnum factum in ea contingens: quod in ista non accidit.
paras.en: Next he curses the night of his conception: first by giving it what makes a night more dreadful. For since night is dreadful because of its darkness, the darker it is, the more dreadful it becomes. This happens when a great storm arises in the night; and as to this he adds: [[3:6|Let a darksome whirlwind seize upon that night|Noctem illam tenebrosus turbo possideat]]. As if he said: It would have been fitting for that night to be seized by a darksome whirlwind, to suit my life, which is wrapped in so great a whirlwind of adversity. [[3:6|let it not be counted in the days of the year, nor numbered in the months|Non computetur in diebus anni, nec numeretur in mensibus]]. As though he said: That night is not worthy of remembrance, since nothing notable befell me in it, but rather something grievous. Again, among nights some are solemn, on which men gather to keep feasts; and this he removes from it, saying: [[3:7|Let that night be solitary, and not worthy of praise|Sit nox illa solitaria, nec laude digna]]. For a night becomes worthy of praise because of some great deed that comes to pass in it, which did not happen in this one.

paras.t: Maledicant ei qui maledicunt diei: et qui illi sint, subdit, qui parati sunt suscitare Leviathan, id est piscatores grandem piscem, qui secundum unam acceptionem vocatur Leviathan, in noctis tenebris moventes ac capere cupientes: qui apparente die tristantur, maledicuntque ei, in quantum per lucem diei opus eorum impeditur. Vel, Qui parati sunt suscitare Leviathan, id est homines vitiosi, qui diabolum, dictum Leviathan, suscitant, ejus voluntatem implendo: per hoc enim suscitant eum ad dominandum eis, et ad puniendum eos in posterum. Tales maledicunt diei, dum in eo peccare vetantur. Ideo dicitur apud Joannem: Omnis qui male agit, odit lucem. Diabolus autem vocatur Leviathan in Isaia, quo scribitur: Visitabit Dominus super Leviathan serpentem tortuosum, etc.
paras.en: [[3:8|Let them curse it who curse the day|Maledicant ei qui maledicunt diei]]; and who these are, he adds: [[3:8|who are ready to raise up a leviathan|qui parati sunt suscitare Leviathan]], that is, fishermen who in the darkness of the night stir up a great fish, which in one sense of the word is called leviathan, and long to catch it: they are saddened when the day appears, and curse it, inasmuch as their work is hindered by the light of day. Or, [[3:8|who are ready to raise up a leviathan|Qui parati sunt suscitare Leviathan]], that is, vicious men, who raise up the devil, called leviathan, by doing his will: for by this they raise him up to rule over them and to punish them hereafter. Such men curse the day, because in it they are kept from sinning. So it is said in John: [[John 3:20|every one that doth evil hateth the light|Omnis qui male agit, odit lucem]]. And the devil is called leviathan in Isaias, where it is written: The Lord [[Is 27:1|shall visit leviathan|Visitabit Dominus super Leviathan]] [[Is 27:1|the crooked serpent|serpentem tortuosum]], etc.

paras.t: Deinde excludit a nocte hæc pertinentia ad bonum ejus. Quorum unum est, quod decoratur adspectu et luce stellarum: unde subdit: Obscurentur stellæ caligine ejus, ut scilicet non appareant. Aliud est, quod nox decoratur spe diei: quod removens, addit: Exspectet lucem, et non videat. Nec ortum surgentis auroræ, quatenus tenebræ ejus nec finiantur per diem, nec minuantur per auroram: quod intelligendum est, sicut de die prædictum est. Quia non conclusit ostia ventris qui portavit me, id est, quia in ea non sunt ostia ista conclusa: quod dicit, ad innuendum quod desideraverit suum conceptum non venisse ad partum, neque ad pueritiam, quæ intelligitur per auroram, neque ad juventutem, quæ per plenam lucem signatur. Nec abstulit malum ab oculis meis. Quasi dicat: Ipsam vitam non propter se ipsam abhorreo, sed ob mala pœnalia quibus affligor. Unde omnia quæ supra figurative locutus est, hac clausula exposuisse videtur.
paras.en: Then he excludes from the night these things that belong to its good. One of them is that it is adorned with the sight and light of the stars; so he adds: [[3:9|Let the stars be darkened with the mist thereof|Obscurentur stellæ caligine ejus]], that is, so that they do not appear. Another is that the night is adorned with the hope of the day; removing this, he adds: [[3:9|let it expect light, and not see it|Exspectet lucem, et non videat]], [[3:9|nor the rising of the dawning of the day|Nec ortum surgentis auroræ]]: so that its darkness neither ends in the day nor lessens at the dawn. This is to be understood as was said above of the day. [[3:10|Because it shut not up the doors of the womb that bore me|Quia non conclusit ostia ventris qui portavit me]], that is, because in it those doors were not shut up. He says this to hint that he wished his conception had not come to birth, nor to boyhood, which is meant by the dawn, nor to youth, which is signified by the full light. [[3:10|nor took away evils from my eyes|Nec abstulit malum ab oculis meis]]. As if he said: I do not abhor life itself for its own sake, but because of the penal evils [that is, evils of punishment, sufferings, as distinct from the evil of sin] with which I am afflicted. And so by this clause he seems to have explained all that he said figuratively above.

paras.t: Quare non in vulva mortuus sum? Hoc dicit quantum ad statum vitæ, quo concepti primo vivunt in utero. Quantum vero ad statum vitæ, quo vivunt post nativitatem ex utero, subdit, egressus ex utero non statim perii? Et quia quum aliquis dicit, Quare hoc factum est? dat intelligere, saltem aliquando, quod inutiliter factum sit, hinc ostendit inutile, imo et nocivum sibi esse, quod conservatus est in vita.
paras.en: [[3:11|Why did I not die in the womb?|Quare non in vulva mortuus sum?]] He says this with regard to the state of life in which those conceived first live in the womb. With regard to the state of life in which they live after their birth from the womb, he adds: [[3:11|why did I not perish when I came out of the belly?|egressus ex utero non statim perii?]] And since, when someone says, Why was this done? he gives to understand, at least sometimes, that it was done to no purpose, he next shows that it was useless, and even harmful, to him that he was kept in life.

paras.t: Nunc enim dormiens silerem. Mortem nominat somnum, propter spem resurrectionis. Per silentium vero intelligit quietem ab adversitatibus quas patiebatur. Quasi diceret: Si statim post ortum mortuus fuissem, his adversis non inquietarer. Et somno meo, id est morte, requiescerem, ab inquietationibus vitæ istius, cum regibus et consulibus terræ: qui vel deliciis vel divitiis vacant. Ideo subditur: Qui ædificant sibi solitudinem, causa venationis et aliarum voluptatum, solitarii esse volentes. Aut cum principibus qui possident aurum. Quasi dicat: Si statim mortuus essem, nihil nunc minus haberem quam habent illi, qui hic in multis prosperabantur. Ex his verbis dat intelligere, hominem secundum animam post mortem subsistere. Porro si objiciatur, quod hujusmodi reges et principes non quiescunt, sed in inferno torquentur, et quod utile fuit beato Job conservari in vita ob meritum acquirendum: dicendum, quod loquitur ista ex parte sensualis partis, exprimens ejus affectum, quæ non respicit nisi ad corporalia atque præsentia bona vel mala.
paras.en: [[3:13|For now I should have been asleep and still|Nunc enim dormiens silerem]]. He calls death sleep because of the hope of the resurrection; and by stillness he means rest from the adversities he was suffering. As if he said: Had I died straight after my birth, I should not be disquieted by these adversities. [[3:13|and should have rest|requiescerem]] [[3:13|in my sleep|Et somno meo]], that is, in death, from the disquiets of this life, [[3:14|With kings and consuls of the earth|cum regibus et consulibus terræ]], who give themselves to pleasures or to riches. So it is added: [[3:14|who build themselves solitudes|Qui ædificant sibi solitudinem]], for the sake of hunting and other pleasures, wishing to be alone. [[3:15|Or with princes, that possess gold|Aut cum principibus qui possident aurum]]. As if he said: Had I died at once, I should now have nothing less than they have who prospered here in many things. By these words he gives to understand that man subsists after death according to the soul. But if it be objected that such kings and princes are not at rest, but are tormented in hell, and that it was useful for blessed Job to be kept in life in order to gain merit, the answer is that he says these things on the part of the sensual part [that is, the lower part of the soul, bound to the senses], expressing its affection, which looks only to bodily and present goods or evils.

paras.t: Aut sicut abortivum absconditum non subsistere. Hoc dicit, quoad eos qui moriuntur ante infusionem animæ rationalis: a fetibus quippe abortivis ante rationalis animæ infusionem morientibus, nil manet perpetuum. Aut qui concepti non viderunt lucem: qui moriuntur in utero post animæ rationalis infusionem. Ibi, scilicet in statu quem habent qui concepti non viderunt lucem, impii cessaverunt a tumultu, quem aliis inferebant, quos afflixerunt: quod in statu illo nondum facere potuerunt, nec in simili facere possunt; et ibi, videlicet in statu mortuorum, requieverunt fessi robore, id est, qui pugnando aut laborando sunt fatigati: non autem loquitur nisi de quiete a malis vitæ præsentis.
paras.en: [[3:16|Or as a hidden untimely birth, I should not be|Aut sicut abortivum absconditum non subsistere]]. He says this of those who die before the infusion of the rational soul [Thomas, after Aristotle, held that the rational soul is infused some time after conception]: for of miscarried fetuses that die before the infusion of the rational soul nothing remains for ever. [[3:16|or as they that, being conceived, have not seen the light|Aut qui concepti non viderunt lucem]]: those who die in the womb after the infusion of the rational soul. [[3:17|There|Ibi]], namely in the state that they have who, being conceived, have not seen the light, [[3:17|the wicked cease from tumult|impii cessaverunt a tumultu]], the tumult they brought upon others whom they afflicted: which in that state they could not yet do, nor can they do it in a like state; and there, namely in the state of the dead, [[3:17|the wearied in strength are at rest|requieverunt fessi robore]], that is, those who are wearied with fighting or toiling. But he speaks only of rest from the evils of the present life.

paras.t: Et illi qui fuerunt quondam pariter vincti, erunt ibi sine molestia, id est priori angustia, cum eis qui vinctos eos tenebant; et ibi homines oppressi angariis, non audierunt vocem exactoris, secundum illud Isaiæ: Quomodo cessavit exactor, quievit tributum? Parvus et magnus ibi est: id est, qui hic differebant per inæqualitatem prosperitatis terrenæ, sunt pariter ibi; nec parvitas et magnitudo, quoad terrena, pensata, facit ibi distantiam. Verumtamen differentia magnitudinis et parvitatis, secundum spiritualia bona, remanet ibi; sed de his modo non loquor. Et ibi servus erit liber a domino suo: ideo non habebit ibi locum exactio aut aliquid tale.
paras.en: And they who were [[3:18|sometime bound together|quondam pariter vincti]] will be there [[3:18|without disquiet|sine molestia]], that is, without their former distress, with those who held them bound; and there men oppressed with forced services [*angariæ*, compulsory labour exacted by those in power] [[3:18|have not heard the voice of the oppressor|non audierunt vocem exactoris]], according to that of Isaias: [[Is 14:4|How is the oppressor come to nothing, the tribute hath ceased?|Quomodo cessavit exactor, quievit tributum?]] [[3:19|The small and great are there|Parvus et magnus ibi est]]: that is, those who differed here by an inequality of earthly prosperity are there alike; and smallness and greatness, weighed as to earthly things, make no distance there. Yet the difference of greatness and smallness according to spiritual goods remains there; but of these I do not speak now [here Thomas speaks in his own person]. And there [[3:19|the servant is free from his master|servus erit liber a domino suo]]: so exaction or anything of the kind will have no place there.

paras.t: Postquam detestatus est Job propriam vitam, nunc detestatur totius generis humani vitam, tam quoad eos qui prosperantur, quam quoad eos qui adversitatibus exercentur: a quibus jam incipit. Quare, id est qua utilitate, data est misero, id est pœnis subjecto, lux cognitionis, quum per eam consideret mala quibus affligitur, et vita his qui in amaritudine animæ sunt? quia per amaritudinem vitæ admixtam, ipsum vivere tædiosum efficitur. Qui exspectant mortem, et non venit, tam cito ut cupiunt, quasi effodientes thesaurum, nempe qui cum grandi desiderio quæritur. Et quoniam desiderium dum completur, gaudium parit, subjungit, gaudentque vehementer quum invenerint sepulcrum, id est, quum viderint supervenire mortem, per quam inveniant monumentum. Et quoniam dici possit, quod vita detur utiliter his qui prosperantur, hoc removens, dicit: Viro cujus abscondita est via, id est, cur tali data est vita et lux? Dicitur autem via viri abscondita, quia nescitur quo præsentis prosperitatis status perveniat, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Risus dolore miscebitur, et extrema gaudii luctus occupat. Et in Jeremia: Non est in homine via ejus. In Ecclesiaste etiam: Quid necesse est homini majora se quærere, quum ignoret quid conducat ei in vita sua? Quomodo autem via abscondita sit, subdit, et circumdedit eum Deus tenebris ignorantiæ, quia rerum omnium cognitionem ei non tribuit.
paras.en: Having detested his own life, Job now detests the life of the whole human race, both as regards those who prosper and as regards those who are tried by adversities; and with these he now begins. [[3:20|Why|Quare]], that is, to what profit, [[3:20|is light given to him that is in misery|data est misero]], that is, to one subject to pains: the light, namely, of knowledge, since by it he considers the evils with which he is afflicted; [[3:20|and life to them that are in bitterness of soul?|et vita his qui in amaritudine animæ sunt?]] For by the bitterness mingled with life, living itself is made wearisome. [[3:21|That look for death, and it cometh not|Qui exspectant mortem, et non venit]] as soon as they wish, [[3:21|as they that dig for a treasure|quasi effodientes thesaurum]], which is sought, of course, with great desire. And since desire, when it is fulfilled, brings forth joy, he adds: [[3:22|And they rejoice exceedingly when they have found the grave|gaudentque vehementer quum invenerint sepulcrum]], that is, when they see death coming upon them, through which they find the tomb. And since it might be said that life is given to profit to those who prosper, removing this he says: [[3:23|To a man whose way is hidden|Viro cujus abscondita est via]], that is, why is life and light given to such a one? The way of a man is said to be hidden because it is not known where the state of present prosperity will end, according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 14:13|Laughter shall be mingled with sorrow, and mourning taketh hold of the ends of joy|Risus dolore miscebitur, et extrema gaudii luctus occupat]]. And in Jeremias: [[Jer 10:23|the way of a man is not his|Non est in homine via ejus]] [the margin reads Jer. x, 33, for x, 23; Denis's wording, the way of a man is not in him, differs a little from the Vulgate's]. And in Ecclesiastes too: [[Eccles 7:1|What needeth a man to seek things that are above him, whereas he knoweth not what is profitable for him in his life|Quid necesse est homini majora se quærere, quum ignoret quid conducat ei in vita sua?]] How the way is hidden he adds: [[3:23|and God hath surrounded him with darkness|et circumdedit eum Deus tenebris]] of ignorance, because He did not give him knowledge of all things.

paras.t: Deinde ista adversa sibi adaptat. Antequam comedam, suspiro. Suspirium, est signum moderatæ tristitiæ; rugitus vero, signum est tristitiæ vehementis: ideo subdit, et quasi inundantis aquæ sic rugitus meus. Aqua enim de facili movetur, et murmuris efficit sonum. Sic homo in magna positus afflictione, ex levi suæ calamitatis memoria ad rugitum mox provocatur. Additque, Inundantis aquæ, ut amaritudinis suæ continuitatem ostendat. Aqua namque inundans movetur continue et sonum producit.
paras.en: Then he applies these adversities to himself: [[3:24|Before I eat I sigh|Antequam comedam, suspiro]]. A sigh is the sign of moderate sorrow, but roaring is the sign of vehement sorrow: so he adds, [[3:24|and as overflowing waters, so is my roaring|et quasi inundantis aquæ sic rugitus meus]]. For water is easily moved and makes a murmuring sound; so a man set in great affliction is soon provoked to roaring by a slight remembrance of his calamity. And he adds [[3:24|overflowing waters|Inundantis aquæ]], to show the continuance of his bitterness; for overflowing water moves continually and gives forth sound.

paras.t: Porro miseria hominis ad amaritudinem provocans, in duobus consistit, videlicet, in damnis rerum vel personæ, et in dehonoratione. Quantum ad primum, ait, quia timor quem timebam, evenit mihi, id est, quæ timebam, mihi jam acciderunt. Quo enim persona exstat prudentior, tanto tempore prosperitatis magis præcogitat, quæ tempore adversitatis sibi accidere queunt, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: In die bonorum ne immemor sis malorum. Quoad secundum, subjungit, et quod verebar, accidit: est enim verecundia (secundum Philosophum) timor inhonorationis. Per quod ostendit, quod post gloriam magnam opprobria et dehonorationes sustinuit.
paras.en: Now the misery of man that provokes him to bitterness consists in two things: in losses of goods or of person, and in dishonour. As to the first he says: [[3:25|For the fear which I feared, hath come upon me|quia timor quem timebam, evenit mihi]], that is, the things I feared have now befallen me. For the more prudent a person is, the more he thinks beforehand, in time of prosperity, of what may befall him in time of adversity, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 11:27|In the day of good things be not unmindful of evils|In die bonorum ne immemor sis malorum]]. As to the second he adds: [[3:25|and that which I was afraid of, hath befallen me|et quod verebar, accidit]]; for shame (according to the Philosopher) is fear of dishonour [the Latin *verebar*, I was afraid of, is of one root with *verecundia*, shame; the Philosopher is Aristotle]. By this he shows that after great glory he suffered reproaches and dishonours.

paras.t: Et quod hoc non meruit, subdit: Nonne dissimulavi injuriam mihi illatam? Denique pœnam mereri quis potest dupliciter. Primo, dum ex illatis injuriis ultra modum provocatur ad ultionem: quod removet, dicens, Nonne dissimulavi? Alio modo, dum primitus alium ipse offendit, aut verbis: quod removet, dicens, Nonne silui, a verbis contumeliosis et impiis? aut factis: quod a se removens, subdit, Nonne quievi, ab opere malo? Quod mali non implent, quum in Isaia scriptum sit: Cor impii quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest. Et quamvis innocens fui, tamen venit super me indignatio, id est pœna a Deo, in quo ira non ponitur commotio animi, sed punitio.
paras.en: And that he did not deserve this, he adds: [[3:26|Have I not dissembled|Nonne dissimulavi]] the injury done to me? Now a man can deserve punishment in two ways. First, when he is provoked beyond measure to vengeance by injuries done to him; and this he removes, saying: [[3:26|Have I not dissembled?|Nonne dissimulavi?]] In another way, when he himself first offends another, either by words, which he removes, saying: [[3:26|have I not kept silence|Nonne silui]] from contumelious and impious words? or by deeds, which he removes from himself, adding: [[3:26|have I not been quiet|Nonne quievi]] from evil work? This the wicked do not fulfil, since it is written in Isaias: The heart of the wicked is [[Is 57:20|like the raging sea, which cannot rest|quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest]] [the margin reads Is. vii, 20, for lvii, 20; where Denis has *Cor impii*, the heart of the wicked, the Vulgate has *Impii autem*, but the wicked]. And although I was innocent, yet [[3:26|indignation is come upon me|venit super me indignatio]], that is, punishment from God, in whom anger does not mean a disturbance of the mind, but punishing.

3.title: Quid de intellectu hujus capituli rationabilius dictum videatur.
3.title_en: What seems the more reasonable thing to say about the understanding of this chapter

paras.t: Quantum capere queo, inter Gregorium asserentem præsens capitulum non posse ad litteram exponi, et Thomam asserentem ac facientem oppositum, non est tanta dissonantia in re, sicut in verbis apparet. Gregorius namque intendit probare, quod capitulum hoc non possit litteraliter exponi, secundum quod verba jacent et sonant, et ut sumantur dicta a sancto Job secundum rationem deliberatam: sic nempe (ut arguit) impossibilitatem et irrationabilitatem, maximamque impatientiam continerent. Nec Thomas sic capitulum istud exponit, quemadmodum consideranti verba ejus, præcedenti articulo introducta, evidentissime constat. Expositio quoque Alberti satis faciliter videtur posse ad expositionem Thomæ reduci, et concordari cum ea, paucis hinc inde verbis subintellectis, quæ subintelligit Thomas, et præmisso notabili, quod Thomas præmittit.
paras.en: As far as I can grasp, between Gregory, who asserts that the present chapter cannot be expounded according to the letter, and Thomas, who asserts and does the opposite, there is not so great a disagreement in fact as appears in the words. For Gregory means to prove that this chapter cannot be expounded literally according as the words lie and sound, so that the things said by holy Job would be taken as spoken from deliberate reason: for so (as he argues) they would contain impossibility and unreasonableness, and the greatest impatience. Nor does Thomas expound this chapter in that way, as is most evidently plain to anyone who considers his words, brought in in the preceding article. The exposition of Albert too seems able, easily enough, to be brought back to that of Thomas and made to agree with it, if a few words are understood here and there which Thomas understands, and if the point to be noted which Thomas sets first is set first [notabile: a preliminary remark that Thomas puts before his exposition].

paras.t: Porro Lyra, quamvis expositionem Thomæ dicat subtilem et gratiosam, objicit tamen sobrie contra eam, quoad secundum dictum Thomæ, quo asserit beatum Job loqui verba hujus capituli ad insinuandum dispositionem ac passionem sensitivæ partis suæ, miserias quas patiebatur abhorrentis, quamvis ipse secundum rationem per patientiam eas acceptaret intuitu Dei ac præmii ejus. Itaque contra istud sic arguit: Amici Job quum fuerint sapientes ac litterati, non contradixissent ipsi Job hoc modo loquenti, scientes passiones esse tristabiles secundum sensitivam animæ partem. Et ideo secundum hoc dictum, tota disputatio eorum contra Job procederet æquivoce, quum nitantur ostendere, sanctum Job ex impatientia factum maledicum ac blasphemum, tanquam ex erronea ratione loquentem: quæ tamen disputatio protrahitur usque tricesimum secundum capitulum. Nec videtur quod Job tam diu tenuisset eos in verbis æquivocis, ad propositum non spectantibus, quin aperuisset eis intentionem suam.
paras.en: Lyra, moreover, though he calls Thomas's exposition subtle and graceful, nevertheless objects soberly against it, as regards Thomas's second statement, in which he asserts that blessed Job speaks the words of this chapter to show the disposition and passion of his sensitive part [that is, the lower part of the soul, which senses and feels, the seat of the passions], which shrank from the miseries he was suffering, although he himself, according to reason, accepted them through patience with an eye to God and to his reward. So he argues against this as follows: Since Job's friends were wise and learned men, they would not have contradicted Job when he spoke in this way, knowing that the passions are painful in the sensitive part of the soul. And therefore, on this account, their whole disputation against Job would proceed equivocally [that is, at cross purposes, taking his words in another sense than he meant them], since they strive to show that holy Job had become through impatience a curser and a blasphemer, as one speaking from erring reason: and yet this disputation is drawn out as far as the thirty-second chapter. Nor does it seem that Job would have held them so long in equivocal words, not bearing on the matter, without opening his meaning to them.

paras.t: Ob hanc rationem videtur huic expositori aliter esse dicendum, videlicet quod disputans contra aliquem, frequenter dicit vel arguit procedendo ex concessis ab eo, ad concludendum aliquid contra eum, quemadmodum Apostolus ad Corinthios, ex errore negantium resurrectionem sic arguit: Si resurrectio mortuorum non est, ergo nec Christus resurrexit. Si autem Christus non resurrexit, inanis est prædicatio nostra, inanis est et fides vestra. Amici autem Job, licet convenirent cum eo in hoc, quod actus humani reguntur divina providentia, tamen dissentiebant ab eo in hoc, quod punitionem peccatorum et remunerationem bonorum in futura vita negabant. Ad quod dictum eorum sequitur, quod vita hominis in magna miseria exsistentis, a qua non apparet liberatio via humana possibilis, sit ei onerosa atque odibilis, si scilicet nulla est remuneratio in futuro seu alia vita; et per consequens, ea per quæ venit ad tantam miseriam, scilicet conceptio, nativitas, educatio, sint ei odiosa. In tali autem statu erat Job, et ideo ex sententia amicorum suorum erronea, quam agnovit, conclusit vitam suam sibi odibilem, et ea per quæ venit ad eam, ducendo eos ad inconveniens, quia istud pro inconvenienti habebant. Et secundum hunc modum Job non potest de impatientia vel blasphemia reprehendi. Nam ea quæ in isto capitulo et similia quæ in sequentibus ait, non profert ex sua sententia, sed magis tanquam ex errore amicorum deducta.
paras.en: For this reason this expositor thinks it must be put otherwise: namely, that one who disputes against another often speaks or argues by proceeding from what the other grants, so as to conclude something against him; as the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, argues thus from the error of those who denied the resurrection: [[1 Cor 15:13|if there be no resurrection of the dead, then Christ is not risen again|Si resurrectio mortuorum non est, ergo nec Christus resurrexit]]. [[1 Cor 15:14|if Christ be not risen again, then is our preaching vain: and your faith is also vain|Si autem Christus non resurrexit, inanis est prædicatio nostra, inanis est et fides vestra]]. Now Job's friends, although they agreed with him in this, that human acts are ruled by divine providence, yet disagreed with him in this, that they denied the punishment of sinners and the reward of the good in the life to come. From this statement of theirs it follows that the life of a man who is in great misery, from which no deliverance appears possible by human means, is burdensome and hateful to him, if, that is, there is no reward in the future or other life; and consequently that the things through which he came to such misery, namely conception, birth and upbringing, are hateful to him. Now Job was in such a state; and therefore, from the erroneous opinion of his friends, which he recognized, he concluded that his life was hateful to him, and the things through which he came to it, so leading them to an absurdity [ducendo ad inconveniens: arguing from an opponent's own premise to a conclusion he must reject], since they held this to be an absurdity. And in this way Job cannot be blamed for impatience or blasphemy. For what he says in this chapter, and the like things he says in those that follow, he does not utter as his own opinion, but rather as drawn from the error of his friends.

paras.t: Præterea, quantum intelligo, si textus hujus capituli litteraliter debeat explanari, videtur expositio S. Thomæ conveniens, nec facta objectio quidquam concludit. Concedendum est equidem, quod amici Job prima facie putaverunt eum verba hujus capituli ex impatientia et turbata atque erronea ratione locutum, quemadmodum ex verbis Baldad clarissime liquet. Et hoc ipsum, secundum quod tangit Gregorius, fuit in eis culpabile: quia ex pristina conversatione beati Job, quam noverunt, debuerunt advertere quod non ex impatientia loqueretur, sed mystica ratione talia promeret. Deinde addendum, quod disputatio inter Job et ejus amicos, in æquivocis non laborat; nec Job in æquivocis eos tenet, quoniam statim in prima responsione, quæ respondet primæ objectioni de Eliphaz, quæ responsio incipit sexto capitulo, orsus est insinuare ac demonstrare, quod non impatienter aut vitiose hæc protulit, sed ad exprimendum gravissimum corporalis naturæ sensitivæque partis dolorem, quem pertulit; et quod quantum ad hujuscemodi afflictionem, vita sua esset sibi odibilis ac molesta, secundum inferiorem animæ partem, non autem quod ratio passioni succumberet vel vinceretur dolore.
paras.en: Further, so far as I understand, if the text of this chapter is to be explained literally, the exposition of St. Thomas seems fitting, and the objection raised concludes nothing. It must indeed be granted that Job's friends at first sight thought he had spoken the words of this chapter from impatience and from troubled and erring reason, as is most clearly plain from the words of Baldad[[Job 8:1||]]. And this very thing, as Gregory touches on, was blameworthy in them: for from blessed Job's former manner of life, which they knew, they ought to have perceived that he was not speaking from impatience, but was bringing out such things for a mystical reason. Next it must be added that the disputation between Job and his friends does not labour in equivocations, nor does Job hold them in equivocations; for straightway in his first response, which answers the first objection of Eliphaz (that response begins in the sixth chapter), he set about showing and demonstrating that he had not uttered these things impatiently or viciously, but to express the most grievous pain of his bodily nature and of his sensitive part, which he endured; and that, as regards affliction of this kind, his life was hateful and irksome to him according to the lower part of the soul, not that his reason gave way to passion or was overcome by pain.

paras.t: Hinc nempe infra ait: Respondete, obsecro, absque contentione, et loquentes id quod justum est judicate, et non invenietis in lingua mea iniquitatem, nec in faucibus meis stultitia personabit. Statimque sequenti capitulo subdit, Militia est vita hominis super terram: quo verbo ostendit, quod homini habendum sit bellum continuum contra passiones et vitia. Quod vero præfata verba atque similia secundum sensualitatis afflictionem protulerit, pandit, dicendo: Sicut consumitur nubes et pertransit, sic qui descenderit in infernum, non ascendet nec revertetur. Quapropter et ego non parcam ori meo; loquar in tribulatione spiritus mei, confabulabor cum amaritudine animæ meæ.
paras.en: Hence indeed he says below: [[Job 6:29|Answer, I beseech you, without contention: and speaking that which is just, judge ye.|Respondete, obsecro, absque contentione, et loquentes id quod justum est judicate]] [[Job 6:30|And you shall not find iniquity in my tongue, neither shall folly sound in my mouth.|et non invenietis in lingua mea iniquitatem, nec in faucibus meis stultitia personabit]] And at once, in the following chapter, he adds: [[Job 7:1|The life of man upon earth is a warfare|Militia est vita hominis super terram]]: by which word he shows that man must wage continual war against the passions and vices. And that he uttered the aforesaid words and the like according to the affliction of sensuality [that is, of the sense appetite, the lower part of the soul], he makes plain by saying: [[Job 7:9|As a cloud is consumed, and passeth away: so he that shall go down to hell shall not come up|Sicut consumitur nubes et pertransit, sic qui descenderit in infernum, non ascendet]], [[Job 7:10|nor shall he return|nec revertetur]]. [[Job 7:11|Wherefore, I will not spare my mouth, I will speak in the affliction of my spirit: I will talk with the bitterness of my soul.|Quapropter et ego non parcam ori meo; loquar in tribulatione spiritus mei, confabulabor cum amaritudine animæ meæ]]

paras.t: Insuper adjiciendum, quod tota disputatio amicorum Job contra eum, non est ad ostendendum eum factum maledicum et blasphemum propter hæc verba: imo de hoc diu non disputant. Sed principale intentum eorum est, disputare de providentia Dei, qualiter scilicet res humanæ gubernentur a Deo, secundum Albertum et Thomam concorditer. Et quia timebant hominem non puniri, nisi pro prævia ejus culpa, consequenter conati sunt demonstrare quod Job pro suis peccatis punitus sit, quodque occulte injustus atque hypocrita fuit, non quidem ob verba hæc, ante quorum prolationem fuit plagatus, sed aliunde. Contra quos Job zelo justitiæ veritatem tuetur, suamque in omnibus æquitatem concludit, quemadmodum in processu lucebit.
paras.en: Moreover it must be added that the whole disputation of Job's friends against him is not meant to show that he had become a curser and a blasphemer because of these words: indeed they do not dispute about this for long. Their principal aim, rather, is to dispute about the providence of God, that is, how human affairs are governed by God, according to Albert and Thomas, who agree on this. And since they held [the text prints timebant, ‘feared’; a footnote gives tenebant, ‘held’, which is followed here] that a man is not punished except for some fault of his going before, they accordingly tried to show that Job was punished for his sins, and that he had been secretly unjust and a hypocrite: not indeed because of these words, before the utterance of which he had already been struck, but on other grounds. Against them Job, with zeal for justice, defends the truth and concludes his own uprightness in all things, as will be clear as we go on.

paras.t: Præterea apparentiam habere non reor, quod omnia verba hujus capituli atque similia dixerit, non quasi ex sua sententia, sed tanquam ex errore amicorum deducta. Non enim consuevit quis taliter disputare aut fari, videlicet ex errore aliorum inconveniens deducendo, nisi de tali errore mentio aliqua ipsam disputationem statim præcesserit, quemadmodum præallegato loco quo Apostolus sic arguit, errorem eorum, contra quos argumentatur, commemorat, moxque impugnat. Constat autem, quod ante verba hæc sancti Job, nulla præcesserit mentio de errore amicorum ejus prætacto.
paras.en: Further, I do not think it has any likelihood that he said all the words of this chapter and the like not as his own opinion but as drawn from the error of his friends. For no one is accustomed to dispute or speak in that way, that is, by deducing an absurdity from the error of others, unless some mention of that error has gone immediately before the disputation itself: as in the passage alleged above, where the Apostle argues in this way[[1 Cor 15:13||]], he first recalls the error of those against whom he argues, and at once attacks it. But it is plain that before these words of holy Job no mention had been made of the error of his friends touched on above.

paras.t: Postremo, quod amici Job illius fuerint opinionis atque erroris, imo perfidiæ, quod nulla sit remuneratio actuum humanorum post vitam hanc, utpote quod anima rationalis sit mortalis, pereatque cum corpore, nequaquam videtur, neque probabile arbitror, quanquam etiam S. Thomas hoc dicat: imo ex verbis amicorum Job ostendetur, quod posuerunt animam hominis immortalem. Nam et Eliphaz statim inter cetera de impiis loquitur: De mane usque ad vesperam succidentur; et quia nullus intelligit, in æternum peribunt. Infra quoque Sophar testatur: Luet quæ fecit omnia, nec tamen consumetur; juxta multitudinem adinventionum suarum sic et sustinebit. Revelabunt cæli iniquitatem ejus, et terra adversus eum consurget. Hæc est pars hominis impii a Deo. Multa quoque similia infra, Spiritu veritatis præstante, tangentur. Denique, qui noverunt casum angelorum, communiter cognoverunt illorum ruinam per homines instaurandam, sicque senserunt animam rationalem non esse mortalem, sed ad angelicam et cælestem beatitudinem perducendam. Unde Sadducæi dicentes animam hominis esse mortalem, dixerunt angelos non esse, nec spiritum, ut legitur in Actis. Amici autem Job noverunt quosdam ex angelis corruisse. Eliphaz enim dicit: Ecce qui serviunt ei, non sunt stabiles, et in angelis suis reperit pravitatem.
paras.en: Lastly, that Job's friends were of that opinion and error, nay, unbelief [perfidia: here not treachery but want of faith], that there is no reward for human acts after this life, inasmuch as the rational soul is mortal and perishes with the body, by no means seems to be so, nor do I think it probable, although St. Thomas too says it: indeed it will be shown from the words of Job's friends that they held the soul of man to be immortal. For Eliphaz too, straightway, among other things says of the wicked: [[Job 4:20|From morning till evening they shall be cut down: and because no one understandeth, they shall perish for ever|De mane usque ad vesperam succidentur; et quia nullus intelligit, in æternum peribunt]]. Below too Sophar testifies: [[Job 20:18|He shall be punished for all that he did, and yet shall not be consumed: according to the multitude of his devices so also shall he suffer|Luet quæ fecit omnia, nec tamen consumetur; juxta multitudinem adinventionum suarum sic et sustinebit]]. [[Job 20:27|The heavens shall reveal his iniquity, and the earth shall rise up against him.|Revelabunt cæli iniquitatem ejus, et terra adversus eum consurget]] [[Job 20:29|This is the portion of a wicked man from God|Hæc est pars hominis impii a Deo]]. Many like things too will be touched on below, the Spirit of truth granting it. Finally, those who knew of the fall of the angels commonly knew that their ruin was to be made good through men, and so they held that the rational soul is not mortal, but is to be brought to angelic and heavenly beatitude. Hence the Sadducees, who said that the soul of man is mortal, said that there are no angels, nor spirit, as we read in the Acts[[Acts 23:8||]]. But Job's friends knew that some of the angels had fallen. For Eliphaz says: [[Job 4:18|Behold, they that serve him are not steadfast, and in his angels he found wickedness:|Ecce qui serviunt ei, non sunt stabiles, et in angelis suis reperit pravitatem]]

paras.t: At vero, quum viri isti fuerint beato Job tam familiares atque carissimi diu ante hanc disputationem, probabile non apparet, quod tanto tempore reliquisset eos in tanta incredulitate atque insania, et non nisi in hac disputatione probasset eis animæ immortalitatem. Sed contra hoc aliquis dicere posset, quod pari ratione debuit eos jamdudum instruxisse de modo providentiæ Dei, ne circa illum errarent. Et respondendum, quod ille eorum error, quo putabant nullum a Deo puniri, nisi pro culpa, non fuit sic periculosus ac perfidus aut impeditivus salutis, ut ista perfidia de animæ mortalitate. Gregorius etiam et Albertus ita exponunt verba amicorum Job, quod posuerunt vitam post hanc vitam, et animam immortalem. Nec sequitur, si dixerunt, hominem non puniri a Deo, nisi pro sua culpa, justisque contingere prospera, quod senserunt animam esse mortalem. Nam illis temporibus communiter ita fiebat, quod virtuosis hominibus etiam temporalis evenit prosperitas, quemadmodum in veteri Testamento Deus ipsis quoque Judæis temporalium prosperitatem spopondit, si divinis obtemperarent præceptis.
paras.en: But again, since these men had been so familiar with blessed Job and so very dear to him long before this disputation, it does not appear probable that he would have left them for so long a time in so great unbelief and madness, and proved the immortality of the soul to them only in this disputation. Against this someone could say that by the same reasoning he ought long since to have instructed them about the manner of God's providence, so that they should not err concerning it. The answer must be that that error of theirs, by which they thought that no one is punished by God except for fault, was not so dangerous and faithless, or such a hindrance to salvation, as that unbelief about the mortality of the soul. Gregory and Albert too expound the words of Job's friends in such a way that they held a life after this life, and the soul immortal. Nor does it follow, if they said that a man is not punished by God except for his own fault, and that prosperity befalls the just, that they held the soul to be mortal. For in those times it commonly so came about that temporal prosperity too befell virtuous men; just as in the Old Testament God promised the Jews also prosperity in temporal things, if they obeyed the divine commandments.

paras.t: Præterea, quid B. Hieronymus circa hæc sentiat, mihi non constat, nisi quantum ex ejus expositione super Jeremiam elicio. Exponens etenim illud Jeremiæ, Maledicta dies in qua natus sum. Maledictus vir qui annuntiavit patri meo, dicens: Natus est tibi puer masculus. Maledictus vir qui non interfecit me a vulva, etc.; circa hæc scribit Hieronymus: Verba Job huic Jeremiæ testimonio coaptamus, quod scilicet sit melius non esse quam vivere in suppliciis, juxta illud quod scriptum est: Quare data est misero lux? Et in Evangelio: Melius ei fuerat, si natus non esset homo ille. Unde et Jacob, eo quod vixerat in labore, dies suos parvos et malos asseruit.
paras.en: Further, what blessed Jerome thinks about these things is not known to me, except so far as I gather it from his exposition on Jeremias. For, expounding that passage of Jeremias, [[Jer 20:14|Cursed be the day wherein I was born|Maledicta dies in qua natus sum]]. [[Jer 20:15|Cursed be the man that brought the tidings to my father, saying: A man child is born to thee|Maledictus vir qui annuntiavit patri meo, dicens: Natus est tibi puer masculus]]. Cursed be the man [[Jer 20:17|who slew me not from the womb|qui non interfecit me a vulva]], etc., Jerome writes on these words: We fit the words of Job to this testimony of Jeremias, namely that it is better not to be than to live in torments, according to that which is written: [[3:20|Why is light given to him that is in misery|Quare data est misero lux?]]? And in the Gospel: [[Matt 26:24|It were better for him, if that man had not been born|Melius ei fuerat, si natus non esset homo ille]]. Hence Jacob too, because he had lived in toil, declared his days [[Gen 47:9|few, and evil|parvos et malos]].

paras.t: Quomodo autem intelligenda sint verba Jeremiæ, ibidem plenius scripsi; utque ibidem sensi, sentio adhuc, quod scilicet tam verba Job quam Jeremiæ, intelligi possunt per modum hyperbolicæ locutionis, qua aliquid sine mendacio dicitur per excessum: non quod loquens sic asserat vel intendat, sicut verba ejus prima facie sonant, sed quoniam magnitudinem rei vel suæ affectionis, aliter nequit tam convenienter exprimere. Tales quippe locutiones in Scriptura sacra frequentes sunt, sicut in Genesi Pharao loquitur Joseph: Absque tui oris imperio nullus in universa terra Ægypti movebit manum aut pedem. Et in libro Judicum filii Benjamin dicuntur sic ad certum jecisse lapidem funda, ut capillum tangere possent. Joannes quoque ait: Multa alia fecit Jesus, quæ si scribantur per singula, nec ipsum mundum arbitror capere posse eos, qui scribendi sunt, libros.
paras.en: But how the words of Jeremias are to be understood I have written more fully in that place; and as I thought there, so I think still: namely, that the words of Job, as well as those of Jeremias, can be understood by way of hyperbolical speech, by which something is said without lying, by way of excess: not that the speaker so asserts or means it as his words sound at first sight, but because he cannot otherwise express so fittingly the greatness of the thing, or of his own feeling. Such ways of speaking are indeed frequent in sacred Scripture: as in Genesis Pharao says to Joseph: [[Gen 41:44|without thy commandment no man shall move hand or foot in all the land of Egypt|Absque tui oris imperio nullus in universa terra Ægypti movebit manum aut pedem]]. And in the book of Judges the sons of Benjamin are said to have cast stones with the sling so surely that they could touch a hair[[Judg 20:16||]]. John too says: [[John 21:25|many other things which Jesus did which, if they were written every one, the world itself. I think, would not be able to contain the books that should be written|Multa alia fecit Jesus, quæ si scribantur per singula, nec ipsum mundum arbitror capere posse eos, qui scribendi sunt, libros]].

paras.t: Præterea circa præhabita potest moveri, quomodo Gregorius dicat istud capitulum non posse exponi ad litteram, quum in omni loco Scripturæ ille dicatur sensus litteralis, qui primo principaliterque intentus est ab auctore Scripturæ. Et respondendum, quod doctores circa hoc duplicem habuerunt modum loquendi. Aliquando enim dicunt, quod ille sit sensus litteralis, qui primo per verba litteræ significatur: et ita multa sunt loca Scripturæ, quæ ad litteram capi non possunt, potissime in Prophetis. Sicque Apostolus protestatur: Littera occidit, spiritus autem vivificat. Interdum vero affirmant, quod ille sit sensus litteralis, qui primo ac principaliter est intentus ab auctore Scripturæ. Sicque omnis locus sacræ Scripturæ dicitur sensum litteralem habere, qui tamen non est semper ille qui per verba litteræ primo significatur, sed sæpe qui designatur per res significatas ipsis litteræ verbis: ut quum in libro Judicum scribitur, Ierunt ligna ut ungerent super se regem: et quarto Regum, Carduus Libani misit ad cedrum quæ est in Libano: sensus litteralis non est in istis de arboribus, sed de hominibus per arbores istis nominibus designatas significatis. Hæc de hujus capituli difficultatibus dicta sint.
paras.en: Further, concerning what has been said, the question can be raised how Gregory can say that this chapter cannot be expounded according to the letter, since in every place of Scripture that is called the literal sense which is first and principally intended by the author of Scripture. The answer must be that the doctors have had a twofold way of speaking about this. For sometimes they say that the literal sense is the one first signified by the words of the letter: and in this way there are many places of Scripture which cannot be taken according to the letter, above all in the Prophets. And so the Apostle declares: [[2 Cor 3:6|the letter killeth: but the spirit quickeneth|Littera occidit, spiritus autem vivificat]]. But at other times they affirm that the literal sense is the one first and principally intended by the author of Scripture. And in this way every place of sacred Scripture is said to have a literal sense, which however is not always the one first signified by the words of the letter, but often the one designated by the things that those very words of the letter signify: as when it is written in the book of Judges, [[Judg 9:8|The trees went to anoint a king over them|Ierunt ligna ut ungerent super se regem]]; and in the fourth book of Kings, [[4 Kings 14:9|A thistle of Libanus sent to a cedar tree, which is in Libanus|Carduus Libani misit ad cedrum quæ est in Libano]]: the literal sense in these is not about trees, but about men, signified by the trees designated by these names. Let this be said concerning the difficulties of this chapter.

4.title: Expositio capituli quarti: Respondens autem Eliphaz Themanites.
4.title_en: Exposition of the fourth chapter: Then Eliphaz the Themanite answered

paras.t: Amici Job, qui infra septem dies quibus cum ipso in terra sederunt, nec eum affati sunt, propter vehementiam suæ afflictionis, auditis verbis beati Job, sumpserunt loquendi fiduciam: imo ad loquendum provocati sunt valde, moti non parum et admirati propter verba Job, quæ videbantur eis divino derogare honori, et desperationem, præsumptionem impatientiamque sonare. Hinc zelo Dei ad loquendum moti videntur: sed non secundum scientiam, quoniam indiscrete: et qui ad consolandum venerunt, ad redargutionem, increpationem, atque acerrimam disputationem conversi sunt. Sed quia prudentes fuerunt, sibi invicem deferebant, ordinate loquendo, et principaliori inter eos loqui exordiente. Venit autem et Eliu cum eis, ut infra insinuatur; sed quoniam junior fuit, tacuit, quousque hi tres disputationes suas cum Job terminaverunt.
paras.en: The friends of Job, who during the seven days in which they sat with him on the ground did not speak to him, because of the vehemence of his affliction[[Job 2:13||]], took courage to speak once they had heard the words of blessed Job: indeed, they were strongly provoked to speak, being not a little moved and astonished at Job's words, which seemed to them to detract from the honour of God and to sound of despair, presumption and impatience. Hence they seem to have been moved to speak by zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, since they spoke without discretion: and they who had come to console were turned to reproof, rebuke and the sharpest disputation. But because they were prudent men, they deferred to one another, speaking in order, the chief among them beginning to speak. Eliu also came with them, as is indicated below[[Job 32:1||]]; but since he was the younger, he kept silent until these three had finished their disputations with Job.

paras.t: Itaque dicitur: Respondens autem Eliphaz. Quum Job fuerit proponens atque respondens, et alii fuerint objicientes, quomodo Eliphaz nunc respondens asseritur, præsertim quum Job nihil ab eo quæsierit, nec ad ipsum direxerit verbum? Et respondendum, quod in Scripturis respondere dicitur, non solum ad interrogata seu proposita loqui, et vicem solutionemve reddere, sed et proportionabiliter seu congrue verbum proferre ad dictum vel factum alterius. Unde (secundum Albertum) responsio vocatur hic, in contrarium disputatio. Themanites, quia de Theman fuit: fuitque Theman (ut dicitur) terra juxta Idumæam. Viguit quoque studium litterarum ac sapientiæ in Theman, juxta id Baruch, Sapientia non est inventa in terra Chanaan, neque visa in Theman: quod de vera et spirituali sapientia dicitur. Quo verbo innuitur in Theman quadam sapientia viguisse. Dixit:
paras.en: And so it is said: [[4:1|Then Eliphaz, the Themanite, answered|Respondens autem Eliphaz]]. Since Job was the one proposing and answering, and the others the ones objecting, how is Eliphaz now said to answer, especially since Job had asked him nothing and had not directed a word to him? The answer is that in the Scriptures *to answer* means not only to speak to what has been asked or proposed, and to give a reply or a solution, but also to utter a word in proportion or in keeping with what another has said or done. Hence (according to Albert) *answer* here means disputing against. [[4:1|the Themanite|Themanites]], because he was from Theman: and Theman (as is said) was a land near Idumea. The study of letters and of wisdom also flourished in Theman, according to that of Baruch: Wisdom has not been found [[Bar 3:22|in the land of Chanaan, neither hath it been seen in Theman|in terra Chanaan, neque visa in Theman]] [Denis reads *inventa*, "found", where the Vulgate has *audita*, "heard of"]: which is said of true and spiritual wisdom. By this word it is hinted that a certain wisdom flourished in Theman. [[4:1|and said|Dixit]]:

paras.t: Si cœperimus loqui tibi, forte moleste feres: vel propter acerbitatem tui doloris (graviter namque afflictis molestum est, multa audire et loqui: hinc quippe tot diebus conticuerunt), vel propter impatientiam tuam, quam nunc in tuis verbis perpendimus. Impatientis autem et irati consuetudo est, non posse audire loquentem usque ad congruum finem; sed mox in ipso verborum exordio provocatus, interrumpit verba loquentis. Quod quam vituperabile sit, in Proverbiis ostenditur, quo habetur: Qui prius respondet quam audiat, stultum se esse demonstrat, et confusione dignum. Vel propter inordinatum proprii sensus amorem. Nempe qui talis est, suæ impugnationem sententiæ ægre fert. Nam et Aristoteles in Ethicis ait, quod etiam poetæ sua poemata amant ut proprios filios, et de illorum impugnatione gravantur. Dicitque, Forte, ne de interioribus alterius videatur temerarie judicare, et ut sobrie loqui cernatur.
paras.en: [[4:2|If we begin to speak to thee|Si cœperimus loqui tibi]], [[4:2|perhaps thou wilt take it ill|forte moleste feres]] [the margin gives the Vulgate's reading *accipies* for Denis's *feres*; the sense is the same]: either because of the bitterness of thy grief (for to those gravely afflicted it is irksome to hear and to speak much: that is why they kept silent for so many days), or because of thy impatience, which we now perceive in thy words. For it is the habit of the impatient and the angry man not to be able to hear one speaking to a fitting end; but, provoked at the very beginning of the words, he at once interrupts the speaker. How blameworthy this is, is shown in Proverbs, where it is said: [[Prov 18:13|He that answereth before he heareth, sheweth himself to be a fool, and worthy of confusion.|Qui prius respondet quam audiat, stultum se esse demonstrat, et confusione dignum.]] Or because of an inordinate love of one's own opinion. For he who is such takes it ill that his opinion should be attacked. For Aristotle too says in the Ethics that even poets love their poems as their own children, and are aggrieved when they are attacked. And he says [[4:2|perhaps|Forte]], so as not to seem to judge rashly of another's inward state, and so as to be seen to speak soberly.

paras.t: Sed conceptum sermonem, id est intus ad proferendum dispositum per verba mentalia, tenere, id est frenare et a prolatione vocali reprimere, quis poterit? quasi dicat: Nemo, aut pauci. Quod si generaliter intelligatur, sonat in vitium. Passionati etenim cordis est levisque animi, esse in verbis præcipitem, non restringere linguam, non compescere inclinationem atque propositum non salubre, juxta illud in Ecclesiastico: Sagitta infixa femori canis, sic verbum in corde stulti. Eliphaz vero videtur hæc dicere de his, qui zelo æquitatis et veritatis amore ad loquendum interius instigantur, quos hujusmodi amor et zelus, et potissime fervida Dei dilectio, ad fandum quasi compellunt, atque ad veritatis defensionem impellunt, etiamsi alter quamvis amicus inde gravetur, quemadmodum in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Pro justitia agonizare, et usque ad mortem certa pro justitia, et Deus expugnabit pro te. Itemque: Ne reverearis proximum in casu suo, nec contineas verbum in tempore salutis. Denique, teste Philosopho primo Ethicorum, duobus exsistentibus amicis, sanctum est præhonorare veritatem. Chrysostomus quoque dicit, quod licet sit pium propriam æquanimiter ferre injuriam, impium tamen est dissimulare injuriam Dei. Verba autem Job præinducta, videbantur amicis Job ad divinam pertinere injuriam. Hinc ait et Thomas: Justi interdum ex zelo divino ea quæ ad Dei honorem dicenda concipiunt, tacere non possunt, secundum illud Jeremiæ: Dixi, non recordabor ejus, puta sermonis Dei, neque loquar ultra in nomine illius. Et factus est sermo Domini in corde meo quasi ignis exæstuans, claususque in ossibus meis; et defeci, ferre non sustinens.
paras.en: [[4:2|but who can withhold the words he hath conceived?|sed conceptum sermonem tenere quis poterit?]] that is, who can *withhold* (that is, rein in and restrain from being uttered aloud) the word *conceived*, that is, made ready within for utterance by mental words? As if to say: No one, or few. If this is understood generally, it sounds of a vice. For it belongs to a passionate heart and a light mind to be headlong in words, not to restrain the tongue, not to check an inclination and a purpose that is not wholesome, according to that in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 19:12|As an arrow that sticketh in a man's thigh: so is a word in the heart of a fool|Sagitta infixa femori canis, sic verbum in corde stulti]] [the text here reads *canis*, "of a dog", for the Vulgate's *carnis*, "of the flesh"]. But Eliphaz seems to say this of those who are inwardly urged to speak by zeal for equity and love of truth, whom such love and zeal, and above all a fervent love of God, as it were compel to speak and drive to the defence of the truth, even if another, though a friend, be aggrieved by it; as it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 4:33|Strive for justice|Pro justitia agonizare]], [[Ecclus 4:33|and even unto death fight for justice, and God will overthrow|et usque ad mortem certa pro justitia, et Deus expugnabit]] for thee. And again: [[Ecclus 4:27|Reverence not thy neighbour in his fall|Ne reverearis proximum in casu suo]], [[Ecclus 4:28|And refrain not to speak in the time of salvation|nec contineas verbum in tempore salutis]]. Lastly, on the witness of the Philosopher in the first book of the Ethics, when two are our friends, it is a holy thing to honour truth first.
