Chrysostom too says that although it is a dutiful thing to bear one's own injury with equanimity, it is impious to pass over an injury done to God. Now the words of Job set down above seemed to Job's friends to amount to an injury to God. Hence Thomas too says: The just at times, out of divine zeal, cannot keep silent the things they conceive must be said for God's honour, according to that of Jeremias: [[Jer 20:9|I said|Dixi]]: [[Jer 20:9|I will not make mention of him|non recordabor ejus]] (namely, of the word of God), [[Jer 20:9|nor speak any more in his name|neque loquar ultra in nomine illius]]. And the word of the Lord came [[Jer 20:9|in my heart as a burning fire, shut up in my bones, and I was wearied, not being able to bear it|in corde meo quasi ignis exæstuans, claususque in ossibus meis; et defeci, ferre non sustinens]].

paras.t: Porro, secundum Gregorium, triplex est genus hominum. Quidam enim mala loqui concipiunt, et nulla silentii gravitate frenantur. Alii quamvis ita concipiant, fortiter tamen se vincunt, et magno silentii se vigore restringunt. Alii tantæ perfectionis celsitudinem sunt adepti, quod nec ad loquendum perversa concipiunt. Boni itaque viri freno consilii retinent præcipitationem verbi; et caute considerant, ne loquendo incaute, audientium mentem lædant. Contra primos dicit Ecclesiasticus: Audisti verbum adversus proximum tuum? commoriatur in te, sciens quod te non disrumpet.
paras.en: Further, according to Gregory, there are three kinds of men. Some conceive evil things to say, and are reined in by no weight of silence. Others, though they conceive them in the same way, yet bravely overcome themselves and restrain themselves with great strength of silence. Others have reached such a height of perfection that they do not even conceive perverse things to say. Good men, therefore, hold back the headlong rush of speech with the rein of counsel, and consider carefully lest by speaking carelessly they wound the minds of their hearers. Against the first, Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 19:10|Hast thou heard a word against thy neighbour? let it die within thee|Audisti verbum adversus proximum tuum? commoriatur in te]], knowing that [[Ecclus 19:10|it will not burst thee|te non disrumpet]].

paras.t: Deinde Eliphaz nititur demonstrare sanctum Job esse turpiter impatientem. Quum enim Salomon dicat, Doctrina viri per patientiam noscitur, turpe est doctori patientiæ, ad impatientiam labi; inhonestumque est, quemquam alios edocere quod ipse non facit, imo cujus contrarium agit. Ideo subditur: Ecce: quod hic ponitur pro signo confusionis; docuisti plurimos ipsas virtutes, et quomodo in adversis patientiam conservarent; et manus lassas roborasti, id est homines, quorum vis operativa fuit in bonis operibus fatigata atque deficiens, tua ad bene agendum confirmasti doctrina: sicut Apostolus fecit, dicendo: Fratres, bene facientes nolite deficere; tempore enim suo metemus non deficientes. Vacillantes, id est homines in bono nutantes et in rationis judicio debiles, vel de divina providentia hæsitantes, confirmaverunt sermones tui, quibus induxisti eos ad animi firmitatem, ad veritatis certitudinem, ad boni constantiam: quemadmodum Paulus ad Corinthios, Stabiles, inquiens, estote, et immobiles, abundantes in opere Domini semper, scientes quod labor vester non est inanis in Domino; et genua trementia, id est eos qui in via justitiæ claudicabant, aut tribulationum magnitudine premebantur, quasi grave onus portantes, atque sub illo deficientes, quemadmodum homini magnum pondus ferenti genua tremunt, confortasti, hortando ad patientiam inconcussam. In geniculorum autem tremore ac dissolutione primo apparet debilitas. Docuit ergo Job sub lege naturæ, quod postea docuit Isaias sub lege scripta, et Paulus sub lege evangelica. Scriptum est enim in Isaia: Confortate manus dissolutas, et genua debilia roborate. Pusillanimes, confortamini, et nolite timere. Et ad Hebræos dicitur: Remissas manus et genua debilia erigite, et gressus rectos facite pedibus vestris. Præterea, secundum Gregorium, dum Eliphaz sanctum Job vituperare intendit, ipsum non parum commendat. Pensemus, ait Gregorius, cujus celsitudinis iste vir fuit, qui inter curam domus, inter multiplicium rerum custodiam, inter affectus pignorum, inter studia tot laborum, erudiendis se ceteris ita impendit.
paras.en: Next Eliphaz strives to show that holy Job is shamefully impatient. For since Solomon says, [[Prov 19:11|The learning of a man is known by patience|Doctrina viri per patientiam noscitur]], it is shameful for a teacher of patience to slip into impatience; and it is unseemly for anyone to teach others what he does not do himself, indeed when he does the contrary. Therefore it is added: [[4:3|Behold|Ecce]]: which is put here as a sign of confusion; [[4:3|thou hast taught many|docuisti plurimos]] [Denis reads *plurimos*, "very many", for the Vulgate's *multos*] the virtues themselves, and how they should keep patience in adversity; [[4:3|and thou hast strengthened the weary hands|et manus lassas roborasti]], that is, men whose power of working had grown tired and was failing in good works thou hast confirmed in doing good by thy teaching: as the Apostle did, saying: Brethren, [[Gal 6:9|in doing good, let us not fail|bene facientes nolite deficere]]. [[Gal 6:9|For in due time we shall reap, not failing|tempore enim suo metemus non deficientes]]. [[4:4|them that were staggering|Vacillantes]], that is, men wavering in good and weak in the judgement of reason, or hesitating about divine providence, [[4:4|Thy words have confirmed|confirmaverunt sermones tui]], by which thou didst lead them to firmness of mind, to certainty of the truth, to constancy in good: as Paul says to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 15:58|be ye steadfast|Stabiles]], he says, [[1 Cor 15:58|and unmoveable: always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labour is not in vain in the Lord|et immobiles, abundantes in opere Domini semper, scientes quod labor vester non est inanis in Domino]]; and [[4:4|the trembling knees|genua trementia]], that is, those who were limping in the way of justice, or were weighed down by the greatness of their tribulations, as though carrying a heavy burden and failing under it (as the knees of a man carrying a great weight tremble), [[4:4|thou hast strengthened|confortasti]], by exhorting them to unshaken patience. For weakness shows itself first in the trembling and giving way of the knees. Job therefore taught under the law of nature what Isaias afterwards taught under the written law, and Paul under the law of the Gospel. For it is written in Isaias: [[Is 35:3|Strengthen ye the feeble hands, and confirm the weak knees.|Confortate manus dissolutas, et genua debilia roborate.]] Ye fainthearted, [[Is 35:4|Take courage, and fear not|confortamini, et nolite timere]]. And to the Hebrews it is said: [[Heb 12:12|lift up the hands which hang down and the feeble knees|Remissas manus et genua debilia erigite]], [[Heb 12:13|And make straight steps with your feet|et gressus rectos facite pedibus vestris]]. Moreover, according to Gregory, while Eliphaz means to blame holy Job, he commends him not a little. Let us consider, says Gregory, of what height this man was, who amid the care of his household, amid the keeping of many things, amid his affection for his children, amid the pursuits of so many labours, gave himself so to the instruction of others.

paras.t: Consequenter Eliphaz innuit, quod Job propria dogmata non implevit. Nunc autem venit super te plaga, id est percussio ista et filiorum ac opum ablatio, et defecisti, a fortitudine ac patientia animi virtuosi; tetigit te plaga hæc usque ad intima, et conturbatus es, id est mente confusus, inquietatus, et inordinatus, a medio virtutis ruendo, quum tamen virtuosi ac sapientis sit, a mentis tranquillitate in adversis non labi.
paras.en: Then Eliphaz hints that Job did not fulfil his own teachings. [[4:5|But now the scourge is come upon thee|Nunc autem venit super te plaga]], that is, this blow and the taking away of thy children and riches, [[4:5|and thou faintest|et defecisti]], falling from the fortitude and patience of a virtuous mind; [[4:5|It hath touched thee|tetigit te]], this scourge, to the very depths, [[4:5|and thou art troubled|et conturbatus es]], that is, confused in mind, disquieted and disordered, falling from the mean of virtue; whereas it belongs to the virtuous and wise man not to fall from tranquillity of mind in adversity.

paras.t: Porro perversi duobus modis bonorum impetunt vitam, quia aut prava eos dicere asserunt, aut non servare recta quæ docent: quorum utrumque amici Job ei imponunt. Hinc verbis sequentibus Eliphaz innuit Job non fuisse veraciter virtuosum, nec egisse quæ docuit. Quum enim virtuosi profectus indicium, patientia vere dicatur, juxta quod scriptum est in Ecclesiastico, Vasa figuli probat fornax, et homines justos tentatio tribulationis; itemque, In igne probatur argentum et aurum, homines vero receptibiles, in camino tribulationis: ideo non videtur vere fuisse virtuosus in prosperis, qui confestim aut graviter per impatientiam labitur in adversis. Unde ad ostendendum quod Job sit virtutibus vacuatus, exprobratorie Eliphaz subdit: Ubi est timor tuus, id est timor quo te ante Deum vereri monstrasti, vel potius simulasti? quasi dicat: Nunc apparet, quod Deum non timeas, nec ante sincere timueris, quum tam repente atque enormiter pecces per verba maledictoria, quæ dixisti. Scriptum est namque: Timor Domini expellit peccatum. Hinc et infra ait hic Eliphaz: Quantum in te est, evacuasti timorem. Quemadmodum autem timor servilis expellit peccatum formidine pœnæ, sic timor filialis amore justitiæ, seu detestatione offensæ majestatis paternæ. Fortitudo tua, id est, ubi nunc est in te fortitudo illa virtus moralis, qua quis in præcipuis adversitatibus atque periculis constanter se habet, et ardua vigorose aggreditur? Potest quoque exponi de fortitudine ut est donum, quo fit mens bene prompteque mobilis a Spiritu Sancto, ad suscipiendum et prosequendum ejus instinctum in sustinendis adversis, quæ pro fidei et veritatis seu æquitatis defensionibus inferuntur. Et ubi est patientia tua, quam præcipue videbaris habere, et perfectio viarum tuarum, id est eminentia virtutum seu actuum virtuosorum, quam secundum communem famam putabaris habere? Virtutes autem et opera virtuosa, viæ justorum dicuntur: quia per eas ad ultimum suum finem, qui est beatitudo æterna seu Deus gloriosus et sanctus, pertingunt. Quasi dicat: Nunc prorsus imperfectus fuisse et esse per effectum ostenderis.
paras.en: Further, the perverse attack the life of the good in two ways: either they assert that they say wicked things, or that they do not keep the right things they teach; and Job's friends lay both of these upon him. Hence in the following words Eliphaz hints that Job was not truly virtuous and did not do what he taught. For since patience is truly called the sign of progress in virtue, according to what is written in Ecclesiasticus, [[Ecclus 27:6|The furnace trieth the potter's vessels, and the trial of affliction just men|Vasa figuli probat fornax, et homines justos tentatio tribulationis]]; and again, [[Ecclus 2:5|gold and silver are tried in the fire, but acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation|In igne probatur argentum et aurum, homines vero receptibiles, in camino tribulationis]] [Denis reads *tribulationis*, "of tribulation", for the Vulgate's *humiliationis*]: therefore he does not seem to have been truly virtuous in prosperity who at once, or gravely, falls through impatience in adversity. Hence, to show that Job is emptied of virtues, Eliphaz adds reproachfully: [[4:6|Where is thy fear|Ubi est timor tuus]], that is, the fear with which thou didst show, or rather didst feign, that thou didst revere God before? As if to say: Now it appears that thou dost not fear God, and didst not sincerely fear him before, since thou sinnest so suddenly and so enormously by the cursing words thou hast spoken. For it is written: [[Ecclus 1:27|The fear of the Lord driveth out sin|Timor Domini expellit peccatum]]. Hence this same Eliphaz says below as well: [[Job 15:4|As much as is in thee, thou hast made void fear|Quantum in te est, evacuasti timorem]]. And as servile fear drives out sin by dread of punishment, so filial fear drives it out by love of justice, or by abhorrence of offending the Father's majesty. [[4:6|thy fortitude|Fortitudo tua]], that is, where now in thee is that fortitude, the moral virtue by which one bears oneself steadfastly in the chief adversities and dangers, and vigorously undertakes hard things? It can also be explained of fortitude as it is a gift [that is, one of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost, as distinct from the moral virtue of the same name], by which the mind is made readily and promptly movable by the Holy Ghost, to receive and follow his prompting in bearing the adversities that are inflicted for the defence of faith and truth or of equity. And where is [[4:6|thy patience|patientia tua]], which thou didst seem above all to have, [[4:6|and the perfection of thy ways|et perfectio viarum tuarum]], that is, the eminence of virtues or of virtuous acts, which by common report thou wast thought to have? Now virtues and virtuous works are called the ways of the just, because by them they reach their last end, which is eternal beatitude, or God glorious and holy. As if to say: Now thou art shown by the effect to have been, and to be, altogether imperfect.

paras.t: Et recte ordinat Eliphaz quatuor ista, quoniam per primum eorum venitur ad secundum, per secundum ad tertium, per tertium ad quartum. Timor enim, quum sit fuga mali, retrahit a peccatis, quibus depulsis, fit mens secura et fortis in Deo; per fortitudinem quoque patientia roboratur, patientia autem opus perfectum habet.
paras.en: And Eliphaz rightly sets these four in order, since by the first of them one comes to the second, by the second to the third, by the third to the fourth. For fear, since it is the flight from evil, draws one back from sins; and when these are driven away, the mind becomes secure and strong in God; and by fortitude patience is strengthened, and [[Jas 1:4|patience hath a perfect work|patientia autem opus perfectum habet]].

paras.t: Insuper, quoniam in fine præcedentis capituli Job fassus est esse se innocentem, nec adversa hæc meruisse, Eliphaz nititur hæc improbare, æstimans quod nemo flagelletur a Deo nisi pro suo peccato. Recordare, præteritarum rerum historias memoriter revolvendo, obsecro, quis unquam innocens periit, per præsentis vitæ supplicia et adversa sibi aliunde illata? quasi dicat: Allegare non poteris, quod unquam id accidit, quod tibi asseris accidisse, quod scilicet quis sine suo demerito sit Deo agente aut permittente percussus seu interfectus. Aut quando recti deleti sunt? id est, dic, si potes, quando justi de hac vita per violentam sublati sunt mortem. His verbis Eliphaz sui ipsius errorem ignorantiamque demonstrat, quia et Abel justus a Cain occisus est, et in Isaia scribitur: Justus perit, et non est qui recogitet in corde suo: et viri misericordiæ tolluntur, et non est qui intelligat. Per Ezechielem quoque Dominus ad Jerusalem ait: Educam gladium meum de vagina sua, et occidam in te justum et impium. Denique in diluvio certum est multos infantes et innocentes periisse. Sed rursus videtur verbum Eliphaz confirmari, eo quod Abraham in Genesi loquitur Deo: Absit a te qui judicas omnem terram, ut facias hanc rem, et occidas justum cum impio, fiatque justus sicut impius. Sed et iterum in Genesi dicitur Deo: Num gentem justam et innocentem interficies? Et respondendum, quod sæpe tempore legis naturæ ac scriptæ, justi in temporalibus prosperabantur, non autem omnes, nec semper: quia et Jeremias ceterique Prophetæ dura valde perpessi sunt a perversis, sicut et fratres septem cum matre sua ab Antiocho rege. Inductæ autem auctoritates ex Genesi atque consimiles, intelliguntur pro tempore illo secundum cursum communem, et quod justi in hac vita non paterentur adversa seu occisionem a Deo inferente aut permittente, nisi pro beatitudine sua majori: quod Eliphaz non perpendit. Sed Salomon hoc pensavit, in Ecclesiaste affirmans: Sunt justi quibus mala proveniunt, quasi opera egerint impiorum.
paras.en: Moreover, since at the end of the preceding chapter Job declared that he was innocent and had not deserved these adversities, Eliphaz strives to disprove this, thinking that no one is scourged by God except for his own sin. [[4:7|Remember|Recordare]], turning over in thy memory the histories of past things, [[4:7|I pray thee|obsecro]], [[4:7|who ever perished being innocent|quis unquam innocens periit]], through the punishments of this present life and adversities brought on him from elsewhere? As if to say: Thou wilt not be able to allege that what thou sayest has happened to thee ever happened, namely that anyone was struck or slain, by God's doing or permission, without his own demerit. [[4:7|or when were the just destroyed?|Aut quando recti deleti sunt]] that is, tell, if thou canst, when the just were taken from this life by violent death. By these words Eliphaz shows his own error and ignorance, for Abel the just was slain by Cain[[Gen 4:8||]], and in Isaias it is written: [[Is 57:1|The just perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart, and men of mercy are taken away|Justus perit, et non est qui recogitet in corde suo: et viri misericordiæ tolluntur]], and [[Is 57:1|there is none that understandeth|non est qui intelligat]]. By Ezechiel too the Lord says to Jerusalem: [[Ezech 21:3|I will draw forth my sword out of its sheath, and will cut off in thee the just, and the wicked|Educam gladium meum de vagina sua, et occidam in te justum et impium]]. Lastly, it is certain that in the flood many infants and innocent people perished[[Gen 7:21||]]. But again the word of Eliphaz seems to be confirmed by what Abraham says to God in Genesis: [[Gen 18:25|Far be it from thee|Absit a te]], [[Gen 18:25|thou who judgest all the earth|qui judicas omnem terram]], [[Gen 18:25|to do this thing, and to slay the just with the wicked, and for the just to be in like case as the wicked|ut facias hanc rem, et occidas justum cum impio, fiatque justus sicut impius]]. And again in Genesis it is said to God: [[Gen 20:4|wilt thou slay a nation that is ignorant and just?|Num gentem justam et innocentem interficies?]] [Denis reads "just and innocent" where the Vulgate has "ignorant and just"] The answer is that often in the time of the law of nature and of the written law the just prospered in temporal things, yet not all, nor always: for Jeremias[[Jer 38:6||]][[Jer 37:15||]] [the margin's numbers are partly unreadable; it seems to give Jer. xxxviii, 6 and xxxvii, 15] and the other Prophets suffered very hard things from the wicked, as did the seven brothers with their mother at the hands of King Antiochus[[2 Mach 7:1||]]. But the passages brought from Genesis and the like are understood of that time, according to the common course of things, and as meaning that the just in this life would not suffer adversities or death by God's inflicting or permitting it except for their greater beatitude: which Eliphaz did not consider. But Solomon weighed this, affirming in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 8:14|There are just men to whom evils happen, as though they had done the works of the wicked|Sunt justi quibus mala proveniunt, quasi opera egerint impiorum]].

paras.t: Quin potius vidi, oculis mentis et corporis, experimentoque didici, eos qui operantur iniquitatem, peccando manifeste mortaliter: et aptius ait, Qui operantur, quam si diceret, Operati sunt, ut innuat se loqui de his qui permanent in peccatis, non de pœnitentibus; et seminant dolores, id est ea per quæ alii dolorem et afflictionem incurrunt: quod faciunt susurrationibus, detractionibus, dolis, insidiosis machinationibus impiisque consiliis. Quibus per Ezechielem Dominus loquitur: Mœrere fecistis cor justi, quem ego non contristavi. Et metunt eos, id est lucrum seu commodum temporale de eorum affectu acquirunt, sicut qui nata frumenta ex jactis in terram seminibus metunt atque in horreum congregant. In quo peccato, secundum Albertum, sunt judices, qui ex industria in commissione causarum cavillosas dant litteras, ut causa cum messione seu lucro ad eos denuo revertatur. Flante, id est judicium cum velocitate ac impetu faciente Deo, perisse, et spiritu, id est voluntate vel vento seu impetu, iræ, id est justæ vindictæ, ejus esse consumptos, ita quod in vita hac pro suis excessibus sunt plagati divinitus et perempti.
paras.en: [[4:8|On the contrary, I have seen|Quin potius vidi]], with the eyes of the mind and of the body, and have learned by experience, [[4:8|those who work iniquity|eos qui operantur iniquitatem]], by sinning manifestly and mortally: and he says more fittingly *who work* than if he had said *who have worked*, to hint that he is speaking of those who remain in their sins, not of penitents; [[4:8|and sow sorrows|et seminant dolores]], that is, the things by which others incur sorrow and affliction: which they do by whisperings, detractions, deceits, treacherous schemes and wicked counsels. To these the Lord says by Ezechiel: [[Ezech 13:22|you have made the heart of the just to mourn, whom I have not made sorrowful|Mœrere fecistis cor justi, quem ego non contristavi]]. [[4:8|and reap them|Et metunt eos]], that is, they acquire gain or temporal profit from their state, as those who reap the corn sprung from seed cast into the earth and gather it into the barn. In this sin, according to Albert, are judges who, in committing cases, deliberately issue captious letters, so that the case may come back to them again with a harvest, that is, with gain. [[4:9|Perishing|perisse]] [[4:9|by the blast|Flante]] of God, that is, God executing judgement with speed and force, [[4:9|and consumed|esse consumptos]] [[4:9|by the spirit|et spiritu]] (that is, by the will, or by the wind or blast) [[4:9|of his|ejus]] [[4:9|wrath|iræ]] (that is, of his just vengeance): so that in this life they are struck by God and slain for their excesses.

paras.t: Servat autem inchoatam de seminatione et messione parabolam, divinum judicium ad vindictam procedens, flatum venti appellans, ipsamque vindictam nominans spiritum, seu ventum, iræ judicis Dei. Segetes quippe vento urente siccari solent atque consumi: propter quod per Malachiam Dominus promittit Judæis: Increpabo pro vobis ventum devorantem et corrumpentem fructum terræ vestræ. Itaque humana similitudine loquitur. Nos enim quum flamus, aerem intra nos trahimus, impetuque pulmonis ac diaphragmatis eum expellimus. Pariformiter Eliphaz innuit, quod Deus facta hominum intra se pensando considerat, et quasi efflando quod intus decrevit, sententiam profert. Juxta quem modum etiam in Isaia legitur: Exsiccatum est fœnum, et cecidit flos, quia spiritus Domini sufflavit in eo. Rursusque: Spiritus Domini sicut torrens sulfuris succendens eam. Præterea, quum homo irascitur, ex accensione cordis et evaporatione, spiritus animalis multiplicatur, ad faciemque dirigitur. Idcirco in irascentibus vultus turget ac rubet, labia dilatantur, nares aperiuntur, et tunc proferunt ultionem.
paras.en: Now he keeps up the parable he began of sowing and reaping, calling the divine judgement as it proceeds to vengeance the blast of the wind, and naming the vengeance itself the spirit, or wind, of the wrath of God the judge. For crops are commonly dried up and consumed by a scorching wind: which is why the Lord promises the Jews by Malachias: [[Mal 3:11|I will rebuke for your sakes the devourer|Increpabo pro vobis ventum devorantem]] [Denis reads "the devouring wind, and the one that spoils the fruit of your land"; the Vulgate has "the devourer, and he shall not spoil the fruit of your land"]. So he speaks by a human likeness. For when we blow, we draw the air in, and drive it out by the force of the lungs and the diaphragm. In the same way Eliphaz hints that God considers the deeds of men by weighing them within himself, and, as it were by breathing out what he has decreed within, utters the sentence. In this manner too we read in Isaias: [[Is 40:7|The grass is withered, and the flower is fallen, because the spirit of the Lord hath blown upon it|Exsiccatum est fœnum, et cecidit flos, quia spiritus Domini sufflavit in eo]]. And again: [[Is 30:33|the breath of the Lord as a torrent of brimstone kindling it|Spiritus Domini sicut torrens sulfuris succendens eam]]. Moreover, when a man is angry, the animal spirit [that is, the subtle vapour that medieval physiology held to carry the soul's powers through the body] is multiplied by the kindling and steaming of the heart, and is driven to the face. That is why in angry men the face swells and reddens, the lips are spread, the nostrils open, and then they bring forth vengeance.

paras.t: Denique, sicut Gregorius tangit, verbum istud secundum intentionem Eliphaz universaliter stare non potest, quamvis bene intelligi et sic universaliter valeat verificari. Constat enim, quod impii sæpe in sæculo isto usque ad ultimam senectutem subsistunt, et magis quam justi in temporalibus prosperantur. Verumtamen, quia quantum ad animam pereunt in æternum, universaliter verum est, quod impii Deo flante dispereant, sicut et Isaias fatetur, dicendo: Et quidem neque satus, nec radicatus in terra truncus eorum; repente flavit in eos, et perierunt. Et Psalmista: Tanquam fœnum velociter arescent, et sicut olera herbarum cito decident. Itemque: Dejecisti eos dum allevarentur. Quomodo facti sunt in desolationem? Subito defecerunt, perierunt propter iniquitatem suam. Quantumlibet etenim diu vivant ac prosperentur in sæculo isto, tamen comparatione sequentis durationis atque futuræ æternæ damnationis, velut momentanee defluunt, ac subito pereunt. Unde in libro Sapientiæ sero pœnitentes fatentur: Transierunt omnia illa tanquam umbra præteriens. Circa prædicta ait Gregorius: Quoniam scriptum est, Dominus patiens redditor est, sæpe diu tolerat quos in æternum damnabit. Aliquando omnipotens Deus diu prævalere iniquos patitur, ut justorum mundius vita purgetur. Aliquando vero injustos celeriter perimit, eorumque interitu innocentium corda confirmat, pusillanimes roborat, humana se curare ostendit, et quod peccata ulciscatur, demonstrat.
paras.en: Lastly, as Gregory touches on, this word cannot stand universally in the sense Eliphaz intends, though it can be well understood and so be verified universally. For it is plain that the wicked often live on in this world to extreme old age, and prosper in temporal things more than the just. Yet because as regards the soul they perish for ever, it is universally true that the wicked perish by the blast of God, as Isaias too declares, saying: [[Is 40:24|And surely their stock was neither planted, nor sown, nor rooted in the earth|Et quidem neque satus, nec radicatus in terra truncus eorum]]: [[Is 40:24|suddenly he hath blown upon them|repente flavit in eos]], and they perished. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 36:2|they shall shortly wither away as grass, and as the green herbs shall quickly fall|Tanquam fœnum velociter arescent, et sicut olera herbarum cito decident]]. And again: [[Ps 72:18|when they were lifted up thou hast cast them down|Dejecisti eos dum allevarentur]]. [[Ps 72:19|How are they brought to desolation? they have suddenly ceased to be: they have perished by reason of their iniquity|Quomodo facti sunt in desolationem? Subito defecerunt, perierunt propter iniquitatem suam]]. For however long they live and prosper in this world, yet in comparison with the duration that follows, and with the eternal damnation to come, they flow away as in a moment and suddenly perish. Hence in the book of Wisdom those who repent too late confess: [[Wis 5:9|All those things are passed away like a shadow|Transierunt omnia illa tanquam umbra]] passing by. On the foregoing Gregory says: Since it is written that the Lord [[Ecclus 5:4|is a patient rewarder|patiens redditor est]] [Gregory, and Denis after him, has "the Lord" where the Vulgate has "the most High"], he often long bears with those whom he will damn for ever. Sometimes almighty God allows the wicked to prevail for a long time, so that the life of the just may be more purely cleansed. But sometimes he quickly destroys the unjust, and by their destruction strengthens the hearts of the innocent, encourages the fainthearted, shows that he cares for human affairs, and makes plain that he avenges sins.

paras.t: Rugitus leonis, et vox leænæ, et dentes catulorum leonum contriti sunt. Certum est, homines nominibus bestiarum illarum signari, quarum proprietates et actus amplius imitantur. Itaque verbis his innuit Eliphaz, cur Job cum pertinentibus ad se sit plagatus, per leonem designans Job ob crudelitatem, quam ei imponit: æquitatem enim, quam vicissim exhibuit sanctus Job, iste nunc crudelitatem fuisse interpretatur. Itaque ait: Rugitus leonis, id est animosa et sæva locutio Job, instar leonis feraliter præsidentis, juxta illud Proverbiorum, Leo rugiens et ursus esuriens, princeps impius super populum pauperem; et vox leænæ, id est sæva locutio conjugis Job, quæ viro suo in atrocitate consensit, ut Eliphaz asserit; et dentes catulorum leonum, id est filii Job epulantes, contriti sunt, id est repressi vel omnino exstincti, ita quod tyrannides Job ejusque conjugis, humiliata est juste, eorumque filii sunt occisi.
paras.en: [[4:10|The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the lioness, and the teeth of the whelps of lions, are broken|Rugitus leonis, et vox leænæ, et dentes catulorum leonum contriti sunt.]]. It is certain that men are signified by the names of those beasts whose properties and acts they most imitate. So by these words Eliphaz hints why Job was struck along with those who belonged to him, signifying Job by the lion because of the cruelty he lays to his charge: for the equity which holy Job showed in his turn, this man now interprets as having been cruelty. So he says: [[4:10|The roaring of the lion|Rugitus leonis]], that is, the fierce and savage speech of Job, like a lion ruling savagely, according to that of Proverbs, [[Prov 28:15|As a roaring lion, and a hungry bear, so is a wicked prince over the poor people|Leo rugiens et ursus esuriens, princeps impius super populum pauperem]]; [[4:10|and the voice of the lioness|et vox leænæ]], that is, the savage speech of Job's wife, who agreed with her husband in his cruelty, as Eliphaz asserts; [[4:10|and the teeth of the whelps of lions|et dentes catulorum leonum]], that is, Job's children as they feasted, [[4:10|are broken|contriti sunt]], that is, held down or utterly destroyed: so that the tyranny of Job and of his wife has been justly humbled, and their children slain.

paras.t: Tigris periit, eo quod non haberet prædam. Secundum Gregorium et Albertum, ipsum Job quem vocavit leonem, appellat nunc tigridem, propter velocitatem suam ad mala: tigris namque est animal sævum et velox ad prædam. Estque varietatem aliquam habens. Sic quoque Eliphaz notat Job de simulatione hypocrisis: quem dicit periisse, id est animo destitutum, eo quod non habeat prædam, id est, quoniam aliorum bona rapere magis non valet, nec laudes humanas acquirere, quoniam ejus hypocrisis cunctis jam patet. Et catuli leonum dissipati sunt: per quos filios Job, ut dictum est, exprimit; vel ministros atque domesticos ejus officiatos ad prædam tollendam. Porro (ut ait Gregorius) in translatione Septuaginta interpretum non dicitur Tigris, sed Myrmicoleon. Myrmicoleon quippe parvum valde est animal, formicis insidians, quod sub pulvere se abscondit, et formicas frumenta gestantes interficit, interfectasque consumit. Myrmicoleon autem Latine dicitur, formicarum leo, vel certe expressius, formica et leo, quoniam aliis animalibus ob suam parvitatem formica est, formicis autem est leo: eas namque devorat, atque ab aliis devoratur. Itaque, secundum hanc translationem, Eliphaz reprehendit Job de audacia et timore, ita quod contra majores fuerit pavidus, contra subditos audax.
paras.en: [[4:11|The tiger hath perished for want of prey|Tigris periit, eo quod non haberet prædam]]. According to Gregory and Albert, he now calls the same Job whom he called a lion a tiger, because of his swiftness to evil: for the tiger is a fierce animal and swift to its prey. And it has a certain variety [that is, a striped or spotted coat: hence the charge of doubleness that follows]. So Eliphaz also charges Job with the pretence of hypocrisy: he says he has *perished*, that is, lost heart, *because he had no prey*, that is, because he can no longer seize the goods of others, nor win human praise, since his hypocrisy is now plain to all. [[4:11|and the young lions are scattered abroad|Et catuli leonum dissipati sunt]] [Denis reads *leonum*, "of lions", for the Vulgate's *leonis*]: by these he means Job's children, as was said; or his servants and household, employed to carry off the prey. Further (as Gregory says), in the translation of the Seventy interpreters it does not say *tiger*, but *Myrmicoleon*. The Myrmicoleon is a very small animal that lies in wait for ants: it hides under the dust and kills the ants carrying grain, and having killed them, eats them. In Latin *Myrmicoleon* is called the ants' lion, or more exactly, ant and lion, since to other animals, because of its smallness, it is an ant, but to ants it is a lion: for it devours them, and is devoured by others. So according to this translation Eliphaz rebukes Job for boldness and fear, in that he was timid towards his betters and bold towards his subjects.

paras.t: Quoniam ergo probare intendit sanctum Job cum sobole sua pro eorum peccatis esse plagatos: quod prima facie apparentiam non habebat in Job, qui vita et fama celebris fuit; idcirco ex divina revelatione sibi (ut asserit) facta, format ac elicit argumentum. Ratio quippe humana in spiritualibus et divinis, in occultisque hominum actibus et variabilissime dispositionis eorum discussione, debilis esse solet atque incerta; et quo aliqua fuerint altiora, eo sunt humano sensu imperceptibiliora: auctoritas vero divina non fallitur. Ideo subdit: Porro ad me dictum est verbum absconditum, id est sermo aliis non auditus aut cognitus, et altæ sententiæ contentivus. Et in eo quod ait, Dictum est, notat quod per oraculum ista accepit: quæ revelatio certior est, quam quæ fit in somno, ut astruit Martialis super somnium Scipionis. Et quasi furtive, id est per modum furti, seu raptim et secrete, suscepit auris mea venas susurrii ejus. Secundum Thomam, revelatio ista facta insinuatur in plena vigilia, apertis videlicet exterioribus sensibus, ut statim tangetur. Sicque per aurem, exteriores aures possent intelligi: exterioribus etenim oculis vidit vultum sibi incognitum, ut Thomas exponit. Albertus tamen de interioribus auribus oculisque exponit, allegans Basilium super primum Proverbiorum dicentem: Intellectus per signum accipiens, dicitur auris, quemadmodum ipse intellectus per speciem accipiens, dicitur visus; et intellectus immediate contingens, dicitur tactus; intellectus autem interiora intelligibilis per exteriora accipiens, quasi per quemdam vaporem, dicitur olfactus; intellectus vero interiora intelligibilis immediate suscipiens, dicitur gustus. Porro, susurrium dicitur, quia secrete de ore in aurem percipitur; et animo audiente, alii qui adsunt, illud non audiunt. Venas quoque susurrii nominat vias ac modos revelationum, secundum Gregorium et Albertum, qui advehunt seu deducunt veritatem ad intellectus refectionem, sicut venæ corporeæ advehunt sanguinem ad nutrimentum membrorum. Unde in libro Proverbiorum legitur: Vena vitæ, os justi. Itaque, in eo quod ait, Suscepit auris mea venas susurrii ejus, insinuat, quod modum, viam seu medium hujus secretæ allocutionis et revelationis, simul cum ipsa allocutione secreta, quam susurrium vocat, percepit ac intellexit: ipsaque oris apertio, prolati verbi ad aures deductio, loquendi maneries, venæ quædam sunt revelationis, instructionis seu allocutionis. Eliphaz itaque innuit se ista audisse, non per modum claræ seu altisonæ vocis, sed per modum susurrii. Forte equidem et alii quidam tunc secum fuerunt, vel cum conjuge fuit in lecto, solusque ipse ista audivit.
paras.en: Since, then, he means to prove that holy Job with his offspring was struck for their sins (which at first sight had no likelihood in the case of Job, who was renowned in life and reputation), he therefore forms and draws out an argument from a divine revelation made to him (as he asserts). For human reason is commonly weak and uncertain in spiritual and divine things, and in examining the hidden acts of men and their most changeable dispositions; and the higher things are, the less perceptible they are to human sense: but divine authority is not deceived. Therefore he adds: [[4:12|Now there was a word spoken to me in private|Porro ad me dictum est verbum absconditum]], that is, a word not heard or known by others, and containing a lofty meaning. And in saying *spoken* he notes that he received these things by an oracle: which revelation is more certain than one that comes in sleep, as Martialis [that is, Macrobius, whose commentary on Cicero's *Dream of Scipio* is meant] maintains on the Dream of Scipio. [[4:12|and my ears by stealth, as it were|Et quasi furtive]], that is, in the manner of a theft, or hastily and secretly, [[4:12|received the veins of its whisper|suscepit auris mea venas susurrii ejus]] [the Latin has the singular, "my ear"]. According to Thomas, this revelation is suggested to have been made in full wakefulness, that is, with the outward senses open, as will be touched on presently. And so by *ear* the outward ears could be understood: for with his outward eyes he saw a face unknown to him, as Thomas explains. Albert, however, explains it of the inward ears and eyes, citing Basil on the first chapter of Proverbs, who says: The intellect receiving by a sign is called the ear, just as the intellect receiving by an image [*species*] is called sight; the intellect touching its object immediately is called touch; the intellect receiving the inner part of the intelligible through outward things, as it were through a kind of vapour, is called smell; and the intellect taking in the inner part of the intelligible immediately is called taste. Further, it is called a *whisper* because it is received secretly from mouth to ear, and while the mind hears it, others who are present do not hear it. And by the *veins of the whisper* he means the ways and modes of revelations, according to Gregory and Albert, which carry or lead truth to the refreshment of the intellect, as the veins of the body carry blood to nourish the members. Hence in the book of Proverbs we read: [[Prov 10:11|The mouth of the just is a vein of life|Vena vitæ, os justi]]. So in saying, my ears [[4:12|received the veins of its whisper|suscepit auris mea venas susurrii ejus]], he suggests that he perceived and understood the mode, way or means of this secret address and revelation together with the secret address itself, which he calls a whisper: and the very opening of the mouth, the bringing of the uttered word to the ears, the manner of speaking, are certain veins of revelation, instruction or address. So Eliphaz hints that he heard these things not in the manner of a clear or loud voice, but in the manner of a whisper. Perhaps indeed some others were with him then, or he was in bed with his wife, and he alone heard these things.

paras.t: Insuper, verbum divina revelatione perceptum, vocatur absconditum, quoniam communitati hominum, sensum et imaginationem sequentium, est occultum: quod quasi furtive auditur, dum veritas ejus clara mente adspicitur. Sicque, juxta Albertum, furtum appellatur, puri ac simplicis intellectus abstractio a strepitu sensuum et ludificationibus phantasiæ: quod bonum est furtum. Præterea, secundum Thomam, triplex modus occultationis in revelationibus solet contingere. Primo, quum veritas intelligibilis per visionem imaginariam demonstratur. Secundo, quum in imaginaria visione seu alia figurativa locutiones proferuntur, ut in Isaia: Egredietur virga de radice Jesse, etc. Tertio, quum quis revelationem divinam habet non frequentem ac diuturnam, sed subitam et transitoriam.
paras.en: Moreover, a word perceived by divine revelation is called [[4:12|in private|absconditum]] [literally "hidden"], because it is hidden from the common run of men, who follow sense and imagination: and it is heard [[4:12|by stealth, as it were|quasi furtive]] while its truth is beheld by a clear mind. And so, according to Albert, the withdrawal of pure and simple intellect from the din of the senses and the tricks of the imagination [*phantasia*] is called a theft: which is a good theft. Further, according to Thomas, a threefold mode of hiddenness commonly occurs in revelations. First, when an intelligible truth is shown by an imaginary vision [that is, a vision of images formed in the imagination, as distinct from bodily sight and pure understanding]. Second, when figurative words are uttered in an imaginary vision or otherwise, as in Isaias: [[Is 11:1|there shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse|Egredietur virga de radice Jesse]], etc. Third, when someone has a divine revelation that is not frequent and lasting, but sudden and passing.

paras.t: Spiritualiter demum, juxta Gregorium, verbum absconditum, allocutio intima adspirationis potest intelligi, de qua ait Joannes: Unctio ejus docet vos de omnibus. Venas autem superni susurrii auris cordis suscipit, quia subtilitatem locutionis intimæ mens desuper afflata et raptim et occulte cognoscit. Nisi enim ab exteriorum desideriis se abscondat, interna non penetrat. Venæ vero susurrii dicuntur causarum origines, quibus divina adspiratio ad mentem deducitur: quas nobis aperit Deus, dum latenter insinuat quibus modis ad nostræ intelligentiæ aurem venit. Aliquando enim nos amore, interdum terrore compungit. Iterum, qui susurrat, occulte loquitur, et vocem aperte non exprimit. Nos autem quousque carne corruptibili premimur, nullo modo claritatem majestatis divinæ, sicut in se ipsa incommutabilis manet, videmus: quoniam acies infirmitatis nostræ non sustinet hoc, quod de ejus æternitatis radio super nos intolerabiliter fulget. Quum ergo nobis omnipotens Deus per rimas contemplationis se indicat, nequaquam nobis loquitur, sed susurrat: quia etsi se plene non intimat, aliquid tamen de se menti humanæ ostendit. Tunc autem nequaquam susurrat, sed loquitur, quum ejus nobis certa species revelatur. Hinc in Evangelio Veritas dicit: Palam de Patre annuntiabo vobis. Et Joannes: Videbimus eum sicuti est. Hæc Gregorius.
paras.en: Finally, spiritually, according to Gregory, the [[4:12|word spoken to me in private|verbum absconditum]] can be understood as the inward address of inspiration, of which John says: [[1 John 2:27|his unction teacheth you of all things|Unctio ejus docet vos de omnibus]]. And the ear of the heart [[4:12|received the veins of its whisper|Venas autem superni susurrii]] from above, because the mind breathed upon from above knows the subtlety of the inward speech both swiftly and secretly. For unless it hides itself from the desires of outward things, it does not penetrate the inward ones. And the *veins of the whisper* are the beginnings of the causes by which the divine inspiration is led to the mind: these God opens to us when he secretly suggests by what ways he comes to the ear of our understanding. For sometimes he pricks our hearts with love, sometimes with terror. Again, he who whispers speaks secretly and does not utter his voice openly. But we, as long as we are weighed down by corruptible flesh, in no way see the brightness of the divine majesty as it remains unchangeable in itself: for the eye of our weakness does not bear what shines unbearably upon us from the ray of his eternity. When, therefore, almighty God shows himself to us through the chinks of contemplation, he does not speak to us but whispers: for though he does not make himself fully known, he yet shows something of himself to the human mind. But then he no longer whispers but speaks, when his sure appearance is revealed to us. Hence in the Gospel the Truth says: [[John 16:25|will shew you plainly of the Father|Palam de Patre annuntiabo vobis]]. And John: [[1 John 3:2|we shall see him as he is|Videbimus eum sicuti est]]. Thus far Gregory.

paras.t: Consequenter de tempore revelationis subjungit: In horrore visionis nocturnæ, id est in visione horribili, quæ tempore noctis monstratur. Vel, In horrore, id est tempore noctis tenebroso, quo homines citius timent, et revelationes frequentius fieri solent. Tempus namque nocturnum ob suam quietem, ad percipiendum revelationes magis est congruum, quando et exteriores sensus a suis occupationibus cessant, ipsaque vis imaginativa exstat quietior, atque ob id ad informationem desuper suscipiendam habilior: ideoque intellectus ad contemplationem est tunc magis dispositus. Itaque, in eo quod ait, In horrore, insinuat magnitudinem revelationis: horror etenim est de aliquo magno ac admirando, quod aut vix, aut non suffert natura humana. In eo autem quod ait, Visionis, innuit certitudinem veritatis: quoniam quod videmus, certum habemus. Addens vero, Nocturnæ, designat exterioris atque sensibilis luminis occultationem, dum strepitus sensuum non impedit intellectum.
paras.en: Next he adds the time of the revelation: [[4:13|In the horror of a vision by night|In horrore visionis nocturnæ]], that is, in a fearful vision shown in the night-time. Or, [[4:13|In the horror|In horrore]], that is, in the dark time of night, when men take fright more readily and revelations are wont to come more often. For the night-time, because of its quiet, is better suited to receiving revelations, when the outward senses too cease from their occupations, and the imaginative power itself is quieter, and so readier to receive its forming from above; and therefore the intellect is then better disposed to contemplation. So in saying [[4:13|In the horror|In horrore]] he hints at the greatness of the revelation: for horror is felt at something great and wonderful, which human nature can scarcely bear, or not at all. In saying [[4:13|of a vision|Visionis]] he hints at the certainty of the truth, since what we see, we hold for certain. And by adding [[4:13|by night|Nocturnæ]] he signifies the hiding of the outward, sensible light, while the din of the senses does not hinder the intellect.

paras.t: Quando sopor solet occupare homines, id est, quando solent dormire, sicut in hymno ait Ambrosius: Deus creator, vestiens diem decoro lumine, noctem soporis gratia. Quibus verbis, secundum Thomam, Eliphaz innuit se tunc non dormisse. Dicitque hoc loco Albertus: Sopor est profundus somnus, ligans sensus et imaginationes, sed ad intellectum non perveniens, quia intellectus non est virtus in corpore: propter quod in sopore magis operatur, quia nec operatione sensuum, nec imaginatione evocatur vel impeditur. Somnus autem commune est ligamentum sensuum, non phantasiæ nec imaginationis. Unde dicit Aristoteles primo de Somno et vigilia, quod phantasia in vigilia movetur, et magis in somno. Hujus signum est, quod dicitur in Genesi, quia quum Dominus vellet revelare intellectuali revelatione, qualiter de latere Christi fabricanda esset Ecclesia, immisit soporem in Adam, ut scilicet, non impedito intellectu, limpide perciperet revelationem. Hinc scriptum est in Canticis: Ego dormio, et cor meum vigilat. In Numerorum quoque libro, ubi commendatur visio Balaam, et dicitur quod visiones Omnipotentis intuitus est, præmittitur: Dixit homo cujus obturatus est oculus, qui cadit, et sic aperiuntur oculi ejus. Et intendit, quod quanto obturatus est oculus exterior, tanto limpidius videt interior, et quanto cadit exterior profundiori destitutus sopore, tanto apertiores habet oculos interiores ad veritatis contemplationem.
paras.en: [[4:13|when deep sleep is wont to hold men|Quando sopor solet occupare homines]], that is, when they are wont to sleep; as Ambrose says in the hymn: O God, Creator, who clothest the day with comely light, the night with the grace of sleep. By these words, according to Thomas, Eliphaz hints that he was not asleep at the time. And Albert says on this place: Deep sleep [sopor, the word of the text, as distinct from somnus, ordinary sleep] is a profound sleep that binds the senses and the imaginings but does not reach the intellect, because the intellect is not a power in a body; for which reason the intellect works the more in deep sleep, since it is neither called away nor hindered by the working of the senses or by the imagination. Sleep, on the other hand, is a common binding of the senses, not of the phantasy nor of the imagination. Hence Aristotle says in the first book On Sleep and Waking that the phantasy is moved in waking, and more so in sleep. A sign of this is what is said in Genesis: when the Lord willed to reveal by an intellectual revelation how the Church was to be fashioned from the side of Christ, he [[Gen 2:21|cast a deep sleep upon Adam|immisit soporem in Adam]], so that, with his intellect unhindered, he might perceive the revelation clearly. Hence it is written in the Canticles: [[Cant 5:2|I sleep, and my heart watcheth|Ego dormio, et cor meum vigilat]]. In the book of Numbers too, where the vision of Balaam is commended and it is said that he beheld the visions of the Almighty[[Num 24:4||]], there is put first: [[Num 24:3|The man hath said, whose eye is stopped up|Dixit homo cujus obturatus est oculus]], [[Num 24:4|he that falleth, and so his eyes are opened|qui cadit, et sic aperiuntur oculi ejus]]. And he means that the more the outward eye is stopped up, the more clearly the inward eye sees; and the more the outward man falls, left senseless by a deeper sleep, the more open are the inward eyes to the contemplation of truth.

paras.t: Hæc verba Alberti difficilia sunt, nec admodum resoluta. Nec asserendo, sed referendo ea commemoro: quorum discussio et explanatio multis indiget verbis, præsertim quum soleat dici, quod per somnum seu sensuum ligamentum, usus rationis ac liberi arbitrii impediatur. Propter quod quædam quæ fiunt in somno, excusantur a culpa, quæ alias essent prorsus illicita. Verba quoque Balaam ad litteram, aliam habent interpretationem convenientiorem; nec ipse Balaam sopore aut somno fuit oppressus, quando visiones illas duas accepit, propter quas allegata protulit verba, quemadmodum intuentibus textum libri Numerorum reor patere. Itaque propter prolixitatem vitandam pertranseo: non enim verba expositorum, sed textus, exponenda suscepi.
paras.en: These words of Albert are difficult, and not very clearly worked out. I record them by way of report, not of assertion; to discuss and explain them would need many words, especially since it is commonly said that through sleep, or the binding of the senses, the use of reason and of free will is hindered. For this reason certain things done in sleep are excused from fault which would otherwise be altogether unlawful. The words of Balaam, too, have another and more fitting literal interpretation; nor was Balaam himself overcome by deep sleep or by sleep when he received those two visions on account of which he uttered the words alleged, as I think is plain to those who look at the text of the book of Numbers. So, to avoid prolixity, I pass over it: for I have undertaken to expound not the words of the expositors, but the text.

paras.t: Circa hunc passum ait Gregorius: Horror nocturnæ visionis, est pavor internæ contemplationis. Humana etenim mens quo altius elevata, quæ sunt æterna considerat, eo de factis suis temporalibus gravius tremefacta formidat: quia tanto se ream verius cernit, quanto se ab illo lumine discrepasse, quod super se intermicat, conspicit. Sed quando ad infirmos mentis nostræ oculos illud incommutabile lumen, sicut est, non erumpit, adhuc Deum quasi in nocturna visione adspicimus: in cujus magnitudinis contemplatione mens horrescit, quoniam ipsis contemplationis ejus vestigiis se imparem sentit; atque ad se relapsa, eum arctius diligit, cujus miram dulcedinem ferre non valens, vix hanc sub incompleta visione gustavit. Denique, quisquis internam quærens quietem, mundi strepitum fugit, quasi obdormit. Somnus autem in Scripturis tripliciter sumitur. Primo, pro morte carnis, dicente Apostolo: Nolumus vos ignorare de dormientibus. Secundo, pro torpore negligentiæ, juxta illud: Tempus est nos de somno surgere. Tertio, pro quiete vitæ æternæ, ut voce Sponsæ in Canticis dicitur: Ego dormio, et cor meum vigilat.
paras.en: On this passage Gregory says: The [[4:13|horror of a vision by night|Horror nocturnæ visionis]] is the dread of inward contemplation. For the higher the human mind is raised to consider the things that are eternal, the more heavily is it shaken with fear over its own temporal deeds; for it sees itself the more truly guilty, the more it perceives how far it has departed from that light which gleams above it. But while that unchangeable light does not break forth upon the weak eyes of our mind as it is, we still behold God as it were in a vision by night: in the contemplation of whose greatness the mind shudders, since it feels itself unequal even to the traces of his contemplation; and falling back upon itself, it loves the more closely him whose wondrous sweetness it cannot bear, and which it has barely tasted in an incomplete vision. Then too, whoever seeks inward quiet and flees the din of the world, as it were falls asleep. Now sleep is taken in three ways in the Scriptures. First, for the death of the flesh, as the Apostle says: [[1 Thess 4:12|we will not have you ignorant brethren, concerning them that are asleep|Nolumus vos ignorare de dormientibus]]. Secondly, for the torpor of negligence, according to that saying: It is time [[Rom 13:11|for us to rise from sleep|nos de somno surgere]]. Thirdly, for the rest of eternal life, as is said in the voice of the Bride in the Canticles: [[Cant 5:2|I sleep, and my heart watcheth|Ego dormio, et cor meum vigilat]].

paras.t: Pavor tenuit me et tremor, id est, formido animæ et corporis trepidatio invaserunt et occupaverunt me. Ex hujuscemodi namque supernis atque insolitis auditis et visis, præsertim tempore noctis, naturale est homini, magno apprehendi timore. Unde quum homini fiunt revelationes insolitæ, in principio timore concutitur, patiturque tremorem. Porro, secundum Albertum, pavor motus est cordis secundum systolen; tremor est trepidatio corporis, estque magno aliquo apparente, fuga cordis intra se ipsum. Dum enim intra se fugiens, intra se claudit spiritum, calorem et sanguinem, exteriora membra his tribus destituta, mox tremunt. Virtus namque membro affixa et debilis, movet ad unum situm; destitutio autem caloris et spiritus, faciunt decidere ad situm oppositum: sicque causatur tremor inter duos situs oppositos.
paras.en: [[4:14|Fear seized upon me, and trembling|Pavor tenuit me et tremor]], that is, dread of soul and quaking of body came upon me and took hold of me. For at such heavenly and unwonted things heard and seen, especially in the night-time, it is natural for a man to be seized with great fear. Hence when unwonted revelations come to a man, at the beginning he is shaken with fear and suffers trembling. Further, according to Albert, fear is a movement of the heart by way of systole [that is, the heart's contraction]; trembling is a quaking of the body, and it is, when something great appears, a flight of the heart into itself. For while the heart, fleeing into itself, shuts up within itself the spirit, the heat and the blood, the outer members, deprived of these three, soon tremble. For the power fixed in the member, being weak, moves it toward one position, while the lack of heat and spirit makes it drop to the opposite position; and so a trembling is caused between two opposite positions.

paras.t: Et omnia ossa mea perterrita sunt, id est tremore concussa seu alterata, ita quod timor cordis tam ingens ac vehemens fuit, quod in totum corpus intime atque fortissime redundavit. Sic et Isaias de se ipso testatur: Corrui, quum audirem; conturbatus sum, quum viderem; emarcuit cor meum. Similiter Daniel ait in libro visionum suarum: Domine, in visione tua dissolutæ sunt compages meæ, et nihil in me remansit virium. Sed et halitus meus intercluditur. Spiritualiter, secundum Gregorium, ossa sunt opera virtuosa ac fortia: quæ qui agunt, alicujus aliquando momenti ea existimant, quia quam sit subtile judicium divinæ districtionis, ignorant. Sed quum per contemplationem rapti superna conspiciunt, a suæ securitatis præsumptione liquefiunt; et tanto magis in divino conspectu trepidant, quanto nec bona sua digna ejus examine quem conspiciunt, pensant.
paras.en: [[4:14|and all my bones were affrighted|Et omnia ossa mea perterrita sunt]], that is, shaken or altered with trembling, so that the fear of his heart was so huge and vehement that it overflowed into his whole body most inwardly and most strongly. So Isaias also testifies of himself: [[Is 21:3|I fell down at the hearing of it, I was troubled at the seeing of it|Corrui, quum audirem; conturbatus sum, quum viderem]]; [[Is 21:4|My heart failed|emarcuit cor meum]] [the margin, misread by the reading tool, gives Is. xxi, 3, 4]. Likewise Daniel says in the book of his visions: [[Dan 10:16|O my lord, at the sight of thee my joints are loosed, and no strength hath remained in me|Domine, in visione tua dissolutæ sunt compages meæ, et nihil in me remansit virium]]; [[Dan 10:17|moreover, my breath is stopped|Sed et halitus meus intercluditur]]. Spiritually, according to Gregory, the bones are virtuous and strong works: those who do them sometimes reckon them of some weight, because they do not know how fine is the judgment of the divine strictness. But when, rapt by contemplation, they behold the things above, they melt away from the presumption of their own security; and they tremble the more in the divine sight, the more they weigh that even their good works are not worthy of the scrutiny of him whom they behold.

paras.t: Et quum spiritus me præsente transiret, id est, me accederet, seque mihi adveniens præsentaret, intelligendo per spiritum, angelum in forma visibili apparentem, ut Thomas innuit, et Lyra apertius dicit. Albertus tamen, per spiritum, intelligit superiorem animæ portionem, in qua ponitur intellectus: qui transivit, id est, in transitu raptim intellectum visionis accepit. Coram me, inquit, id est ante meum conspectum. Sed expositio prior est aptior. Inhorruerunt, id est, horripilationem passi sunt, seu præ horrore in altum surrexerunt, pili carnis meæ. Calore namque et spiritu ad interiora retractis, frigus obrepit in pelle, qua contracta, eriguntur capilli: quod horripilatio nuncupatur. Nec mirum, si ad præsentiam angelicæ ac cœlestis præpotentis virtutis, virtus humana inferior fragilis, taliter alteretur ac varietur, præsertim in nocte, quando res apparens seu audita, visu discerni non valet: propter quod parva commotio tunc turbationem formidinemque inducit, opinantibus majus quid esse quam est.
paras.en: [[4:15|And when a spirit passed before me|Et quum spiritus me præsente transiret]], that is, came to me and, arriving, presented itself to me; understanding by the spirit an angel appearing in visible form, as Thomas hints and Lyra says more plainly. Albert, however, understands by the spirit the higher portion of the soul, in which the intellect is placed: which passed, that is, in passing received in a flash the understanding of the vision. He says [[4:15|before me|Coram me]], that is, in my sight [Albert's text reads coram me, ‘before me’, where the Vulgate has me præsente, ‘while I was present’]. But the first exposition is the more apt. [[4:15|stood up|Inhorruerunt]], that is, bristled, or rose on end for horror, [[4:15|the hair of my flesh|pili carnis meæ]]. For when the heat and the spirit are drawn back inward, cold creeps over the skin, and when it contracts, the hairs are raised: which is called horripilation. Nor is it any wonder if, at the presence of an angelic and heavenly power of great might, the lower and frail power of man is so altered and changed, especially at night, when a thing that appears or is heard cannot be made out by sight; for which reason a small stir then brings on disturbance and dread, as men think it something greater than it is.

paras.t: Mystice, juxta Gregorium, nobis præsentibus spiritus transit, quando invisibilia noscimus, et tamen hæc non solide, sed raptim videmus. Neque enim in dulcedine contemplationis intimæ diu mens figitur: quia ad semetipsam immensitate luminis reverberata, revocatur; et quum ire super se nititur, confestim ad infirmitatis suæ tenebras fracta relabitur. Pili vero carnis, designant vitæ veteris cogitationes, quæ transeunte spiritu pertimescunt, quoniam vi compunctionis et divinæ illustrationis gratia fugiunt.
paras.en: Mystically, according to Gregory, the spirit passes while we are present when we know invisible things, and yet see them not steadily but in a flash. For the mind is not long fixed in the sweetness of inmost contemplation: beaten back by the immensity of the light, it is recalled to itself; and when it strives to go above itself, it at once falls back, broken, into the darkness of its own weakness. The hairs of the flesh signify the thoughts of the old life, which take fright as the spirit passes, since they flee before the force of compunction and the grace of divine enlightenment.

paras.t: Stetit quiddam cujus non agnoscebam vultum, id est spiritus angelicus in specie vultus humani, cujus determinatam notitiam non habebam: sicut nec Gedeon, nec Manue, clara die angelos intuentes, primo noverunt qui essent. Et forte Eliphaz antea similem visionem non habuit, forsitanque in principio dubitavit an esset spiritus fallax. Dicendo autem, Stetit quidam, stabilitatem visionis ostendit, secundum Thomam, qui tamen paulo ante disseruit revelationem istam subitam transitoriamque fuisse: quod forte sic concordatur, quia comparatione visionum quas habuit Moyses, de quo ibi loquitur Thomas, subita et transitoria fuit, quamvis absolute loquendo satis fixa exstiterit. Imago coram oculis meis. Circa quod ait Albertus: Ne putetur fuisse sensualis visio, dicitur Imago, quasi dicat: Non veritas alicujus fuit, sed imaginaria visione imago repræsentata coram oculis meis imaginariæ visionis. Thomas vero aliter sentit, et dicit: Quia in somno spirituales revelationes minus discerni possunt a somniis consuetis ac frivolis: ideo ut ostendat hanc revelationem non dormienti, sed vigilanti factam, subjungit, Imago coram oculis meis: per quod significat se vidisse oculis per vigiliam apertis. Quem Lyra sequens, exponit: Imago, etc., quasi dicat, Angelus fuit in specie visibili mihi vigilanti apparens: quæ visio excellentior est, quam quæ in somniis habetur. Verumtamen Albertus non negat eam in vigilia factam, imo hoc innuit: siquidem aliqui vigilantes rapiuntur in mentis excessum, et alienantur a sensibus; res quoque quæ foris præsentari apparet, non nisi per similitudinem intus imaginarie demonstratam videtur. Denique, qui Thomam assequitur, quod ait, Imago, ita exponat, ut angelus vere apparuisse oculis exterioribus referatur: qui nihilo minus imago vocatur, quia in humana apparebat effigie. Sicque quod oculis objiciebatur, imago (id est similitudo) fuit hominis, non res seu veritas personæ humanæ.
paras.en: [[4:16|There stood one whose countenance I knew not|Stetit quiddam cujus non agnoscebam vultum]], that is, an angelic spirit in the likeness of a human face, of which I had no definite knowledge; just as neither Gedeon[[Judg 6:22||]] nor Manue[[Judg 13:16||]] [the margin gives Judg. xiii, 15; that Manue knew not who it was is said in v. 16], though they saw angels in broad daylight, knew at first who they were. And perhaps Eliphaz had not had a like vision before, and perhaps at the beginning he doubted whether it was a deceiving spirit. In saying [[4:16|There stood one|Stetit quidam]], he shows the steadiness of the vision, according to Thomas, who nevertheless had argued a little earlier that this revelation was sudden and passing. This may perhaps be reconciled thus: compared with the visions Moses had, of whom Thomas speaks there, it was sudden and passing, though, speaking absolutely, it was steady enough. [[4:16|an image before my eyes|Imago coram oculis meis]]. On this Albert says: Lest it be thought a vision of the senses, it says An image; as if to say: It was not the reality of anything, but an image shown in imaginary vision before the eyes of my imaginary vision [the sentence is obscure as printed; a note in the margin, of which only ‘visio, id’ can be read, seems to offer another reading]. Thomas, however, thinks otherwise, and says: Because in sleep spiritual revelations can less easily be told apart from ordinary, idle dreams, therefore, to show that this revelation was made to him not asleep but awake, he adds, An image before my eyes: by which he signifies that he saw with his eyes open in waking. Following him, Lyra expounds: An image, etc., as if to say, It was an angel appearing in visible form to me while awake: and this vision is more excellent than one had in dreams. Yet Albert does not deny that it was made in waking; indeed he hints as much, since some are rapt while awake into ecstasy of mind [excessus mentis: the mind carried out of itself] and are withdrawn from the senses; and a thing that seems to be presented outside is seen only through a likeness shown inwardly in the imagination. Finally, whoever follows Thomas should expound the word Image so as to say that the angel truly appeared to the outward eyes, and is nonetheless called an image because it appeared in human form. And so what was set before his eyes was the image (that is, the likeness) of a man, not the thing or reality of a human person.

paras.t: Et vocem quasi auræ lenis audivi, id est, gratiose, molliter atque suaviter locutus est mihi, quemadmodum lenis aura dulciter molliterque diffunditur. Aura enim lenis, sibilo tenui et murmure levi movet aures sine tumultu: sic spiritus bonus aures eorum, in quibus nec mundus tumultuat, nec caro inundat, nec dæmon inquietudinem parit. Hinc tertio Regum de apparitione facta Eliæ habetur: Post ignem sibilus auræ tenuis; ibi Dominus. Sibilus namque designat susurrium spiritus cum Deo, vel Dei seu angeli cum homine. Præterea, juxta Thomam, apparitiones aliquando fiunt a spiritu bono, aliquando a spiritu malo: et utrobique timorem patitur homo in principio propter visionem insolitam. Sed bono spiritu apparente, timor in consolationem finitur, ut patet in angelo confortante Danielem, et Gabriele confortante Zachariam Virginemque beatam. Spiritus autem malignus hominem perturbatum relinquit. Unde et nunc, per Vocem quasi auræ lenis, consolatio præcedentem sedans pavorem notatur, et visio a bono spiritu fuisse monstratur. Nihilo minus, in visionibus a spiritu bono exhibitis, aliquando voces horribiles et magnæ fiunt commotiones, quemadmodum in Exodo factum fertur in legis datione, in Ezechiele quoque et Apocalypsi. Quod fiebat ad incutiendam hominibus reverentiam majestatis divinæ, vel ad declarationem potentiæ ejus aut angeli, vel ob comminationes quæ præfigurabantur. Postremo, secundum Gregorium, per Vocem auræ lenis, cognitio Sancti Spiritus designatur, qui tenuiter nostræ menti infunditur.
paras.en: [[4:16|and I heard the voice, as it were, of a gentle wind|Et vocem quasi auræ lenis audivi]], that is, he spoke to me graciously, softly and sweetly, as a gentle breeze spreads sweetly and softly. For a gentle breeze, with a thin whistling and a light murmur, stirs the ears without tumult: so does the good spirit stir the ears of those in whom neither the world makes tumult, nor the flesh floods over, nor the devil breeds unrest. Hence in the third book of Kings it is said of the appearing made to Elias: [[3 Kings 19:12|after the fire, a whistling of a gentle air|Post ignem sibilus auræ tenuis]]; there was the Lord. For the whistling signifies the whispering of the spirit with God, or of God or an angel with man. Moreover, according to Thomas, apparitions are sometimes made by a good spirit, sometimes by an evil one; and in either case a man suffers fear at the beginning because of the unwonted vision. But when a good spirit appears, the fear ends in consolation, as is seen in the angel strengthening Daniel[[Dan 10:12||]][[Dan 10:18||]], and Gabriel strengthening Zachary[[Luke 1:13||]] and the blessed Virgin[[Luke 1:30||]]. The evil spirit, however, leaves a man troubled. So here too, by [[4:16|the voice, as it were, of a gentle wind|Vocem quasi auræ lenis]], a consolation calming the fear that went before is signified, and the vision is shown to have been from a good spirit. Nonetheless, in visions given by a good spirit there are sometimes fearful voices and great commotions, as is related to have happened in Exodus at the giving of the law[[Ex 19:16||]][[Ex 19:18||]], and in Ezechiel[[Ezech 1:24||]] [the margin's verse number is unreadable] too, and in the Apocalypse[[Apoc 1:10||]]. This was done to strike into men reverence for the divine majesty, or to declare his power or the angel's, or because of the threats that were foreshadowed. Lastly, according to Gregory, by [[4:16|the voice, as it were, of a gentle wind|Vocem auræ lenis]] is signified the knowledge of the Holy Ghost, who is poured gently into our mind.

paras.t: Deinde ponit Eliphaz quod sibi in visione prolatum est. Numquid homo Dei comparatione justificabitur? quasi dicat, Non utique: quia quantumlibet magna sit hominis justitia, a divinæ tamen perfectione justitiæ deficit infinite: ideo comparatione illius, est nullius momenti, et injustitia potius quam justitia, sicut comparatione Dei nemo bonus aut sapiens. Propter quod loquitur Isaias: Quasi pannus menstruatæ universæ justitiæ nostræ. Et Psalmista: Non justificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens. Ecclesiasticus quoque: Non te justifices ante Deum. Aut factore suo purior erit vir? id est, impossibile prorsus est, ut homo quicumque creatore suo sit mundior, sanctior sive præstantior: imo immense distat a puritate, simplicitate et sanctitate mentis divinæ; et quidquid puritatis aut bonitatis sortitur, a suo adeptus est creatore. Hinc Isaias asserit: Facti sumus ut immundi omnes nos. Et nunc, Domine, pater noster es, nos vero lutum.
paras.en: Next Eliphaz sets down what was spoken to him in the vision: [[4:17|Shall man be justified in comparison of God|Numquid homo Dei comparatione justificabitur]]? As if to say, Surely not: for however great a man's justice may be, it falls infinitely short of the perfection of the divine justice; and so, compared with that, it is of no weight, and rather injustice than justice, just as, compared with God, none is good[[Mark 10:18||]] or wise. Hence Isaias says: [[Is 64:6|all our justices as the rag of a menstruous woman|Quasi pannus menstruatæ universæ justitiæ nostræ]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 142:2|in thy sight no man living shall be justified|Non justificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens]]. And Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 7:5|Justify not thyself before God|Non te justifices ante Deum]]. [[4:17|or shall a man be more pure than his maker?|Aut factore suo purior erit vir?]] That is, it is altogether impossible that any man should be cleaner, holier or more excellent than his creator: rather, he is immeasurably far from the purity, simplicity and holiness of the divine mind; and whatever purity or goodness he has, he has obtained from his creator. Hence Isaias declares: [[Is 64:6|we are all become as one unclean|Facti sumus ut immundi omnes nos]]. And: [[Is 64:8|And now, O Lord, thou art our father, and we are clay|Et nunc, Domine, pater noster es, nos vero lutum]].

paras.t: Ex quibus Eliphaz probare intendit, quod Job non sine sua culpa a Deo punitus sit: alioqui Deus esset injustus, quum opus justitiæ sit reddere unicuique quod meretur. Pœnam autem nemo meretur sine prævia culpa. Aliqui quoque homines tantæ sunt æquitatis, quod nullum volunt plagare, nisi pro sua iniquitate. Si ergo Deus quem punit absque suo demerito, sequitur, virum aliquem Deo consistere puriorem seu æquiorem. Hæc autem argumentatio contra Job non concludit, quoniam apud Deum opus justitiæ non solum est, reddere pœnam pro culpa, seu præmium pro merito, sed etiam electos innocentes adversis exponere, ut gloriosius coronentur, amplius mereantur, tentamentis probentur, (qui enim non est tentatus, quid scit?) aliis quoque in exemplum proponantur, aut suis afflictionibus opem aliis præbeant, sicut et Christus sua passione mundum redemit. Alius demum est processus divinæ justitiæ, quam humanæ, ut patuit. Vel ideo dicit Eliphaz verba hæc, ut demonstret, quod licet Job secundum se humano modo justus fuisset, comparatus tamen ad Deum, defectu non caruit culpæ, quam Deus in eo poterat juste punire; et si se dicit sine culpa punitum, Deum affirmat injustum. Ac si Eliphaz dicat: Quisquis de percussione murmurat, quid aliud quam justitiam ferientis accusat? Puriorem ergo vir factore suo se æstimat, si contra flagellum querelam parat; eumque sibi postponit, cujus judicium de sua afflictione redarguit.
paras.en: From these words Eliphaz means to prove that Job was not punished by God without fault of his own; otherwise God would be unjust, since the work of justice is to render to each what he deserves. And no one deserves punishment without a fault going before. Some men, too, are of such equity that they will strike no one except for his own wickedness. If then God punishes anyone without his deserving it, it follows that some man stands purer or more equitable than God. But this argument does not conclude against Job, since with God the work of justice is not only to render punishment for fault, or reward for merit, but also to expose the innocent elect to adversity, that they may be more gloriously crowned, may merit more, may be proved by trials (for [[Ecclus 34:9|What doth he know, that hath not been tried?|non est tentatus, quid scit?]]), may be set before others as an example, or may bring help to others by their afflictions, as Christ too redeemed the world by his passion. In short, the procedure of divine justice is other than that of human justice, as has been shown. Or else Eliphaz says these words to show that, though Job had been just in himself after the human manner, yet, compared with God, he was not without the defect of fault, which God could justly punish in him; and that if he says he was punished without fault, he declares God unjust. As if Eliphaz were saying: Whoever murmurs at being struck, what else does he do but accuse the justice of him who strikes? So a man thinks himself purer than his maker if he makes complaint against the scourge; and he puts below himself him whose judgment on his affliction he gainsays.

paras.t: Consequenter ostendit hominem sine peccato non esse, comparatione naturæ angelicæ. Ecce qui serviunt ei, non sunt stabiles, id est, cives superni, qui incessabiliter Creatori laudibus puris deserviunt, non sunt penitus immutabiles et impeccabiles per naturam, sed vertibiles atque peccabiles, quando sibi ipsis relinquuntur, gratia destituti. Propter quod adstruit Damascenus, quod omne creatum sit vertibile. Et juxta divinum Dionysium, omnis creatura incessanter conservatur a Deo, a quo si penitus relinqueretur, in nihilum laberetur. Verumtamen angeli sancti per gratiam in Deo sunt confirmati, et ab omni culpa præservati. Idcirco ex his non sequitur error Origenis, dicentis in cœlo esse ruinam. Et in angelis suis quibusdam reperit pravitatem superbiæ, antequam confirmarentur in bono, fruerenturve Deo: quem qui semel in patria per speciem beatificæ viderit, nunquam ab eo averti aut ruere potest. De casu autem primi angeli scriptum est in Isaia, et Ezechiele, ubi Dominus ait: Tu Cherub extentus et protegens, et posui te in monte sancto Dei. Repleta sunt interiora tua iniquitate; et ejeci te de monte sancto Dei, et perdidi te. Elevatum est cor tuum in decore tuo. Christus insuper ait: Videbam Satanam sicut fulgur de cœlo cadentem. Et Petrus in secunda sua Canonica: Deus angelis peccantibus non pepercit.
paras.en: Next he shows that man is not without sin, by comparison with the angelic nature. [[4:18|Behold, they that serve him are not steadfast|Ecce qui serviunt ei, non sunt stabiles]], that is, the citizens on high, who serve the Creator unceasingly with pure praises, are not wholly unchangeable and incapable of sin by nature, but changeable and capable of sin when they are left to themselves, bereft of grace. For this reason Damascene affirms that every created thing is changeable. And according to the divine Dionysius, every creature is unceasingly kept in being by God, and if it were wholly forsaken by him, it would sink into nothing. Yet the holy angels are confirmed in God by grace, and kept from all fault. Therefore the error of Origen, who said that there is falling in heaven, does not follow from these words. [[4:18|and in his angels|Et in angelis suis]], in some of them, [[4:18|he found wickedness|reperit pravitatem]], the wickedness of pride, before they were confirmed in good or enjoyed God: for whoever has once seen him in the fatherland face to face, in the beatific vision, can never be turned away from him or fall. Of the fall of the first angel it is written in Isaias[[Is 14:12||]] [the margin gives Is. xiv, 11 and following], and in Ezechiel, where the Lord says: [[Ezech 28:14|Thou a cherub stretched out, and protecting, and I set thee in the holy mountain of God|Tu Cherub extentus et protegens, et posui te in monte sancto Dei]]. [[Ezech 28:16|thy inner parts were filled with iniquity|Repleta sunt interiora tua iniquitate]]; [[Ezech 28:16|and I cast thee out from the mountain of God, and destroyed thee|et ejeci te de monte sancto Dei, et perdidi te]]. [[Ezech 28:17|And thy heart was lifted up with thy beauty|Elevatum est cor tuum in decore tuo]]. Christ moreover says: [[Luke 10:18|I saw Satan like lightning falling from heaven|Videbam Satanam sicut fulgur de cœlo cadentem]]. And Peter in his second Canonical epistle: [[2 Pet 2:4|God spared not the angels that sinned|Deus angelis peccantibus non pepercit]].

paras.t: Quanto magis hi qui habitant domos luteas, id est homines, quorum terrena sunt corpora, juxta illud Genesis: Formavit Deus hominem de limo terræ. Et Isaias dicit Deo: Fictor noster es tu; nos vero lutum. Qui terrenum habent fundamentum, id est carnem mortalem animæ rationali substratam: quæ caro in generatione hominis prima est, quemadmodum fundamentum in constitutione domus. Anima autem, in quantum est forma corporis, habet se ad illud sicut fundatum ad fundamentum: in eo namque fundatur ad consistendum, et illud subjicitur ei. In quantum vero est corporis motor, habet se ad illud, ut habitator ad domum, et nauta ad navem, juxta quem modum ait Apostolus: Habemus thesaurum istum in vasis fictilibus. Et item: Scimus quia si terrestris domus nostra hujus habitationis dissolvatur, quod ædificationem ex Deo habemus, domum non manufactam, in cœlis. Dicitur quoque homo habitare in hujusmodi lutea domo, ratione partis suæ principalioris, videlicet animæ corpus inhabitantis. Consumentur velut a tinea. Quod licet de corporali morte accipi possit, qua homo consumitur sicut vestis a tinea, tamen intentio Eliphaz est de consumptione spirituali per culpam, ut constat ex dictis. Ideo sensus est: Consumentur, id est, spiritualem vitam caritatis et gratiæ peccando amittent, velut a tinea consumitur tunica.
