Nam sicut ex tunica oritur, eamque corrodit, ita ex carne est fomes peccati, et sensualitas ipsa infecta, ratio cæca, voluntas ad vitia prona: sicque homo ex his qui in ipso sunt, et oriuntur ex ipso, per culpam consumitur. Habet enim ex se inclinationem et pronitatem ad mala: quod angeli non habebant. Ideo scriptum est in libro Sapientiæ: Corpus quod corrumpitur, aggravat animam, et deprimit terrena inhabitatio sensum multa cogitantem. In Genesi quoque: Sensus et cogitatio cordis humani prona sunt in malum ab adolescentia sua.
paras.en: [[4:19|How much more shall they that dwell in houses of clay|Quanto magis hi qui habitant domos luteas]], that is, men, whose bodies are of earth, according to that word of Genesis: [[Gen 2:7|God formed man of the slime of the earth|Formavit Deus hominem de limo terræ]]. And Isaias says to God: [[Is 64:8|thou art our maker|Fictor noster es tu]]; [[Is 64:8|we are clay|nos vero lutum]]. [[4:19|who have an earthly foundation|Qui terrenum habent fundamentum]], that is, mortal flesh laid under the rational soul: for the flesh comes first in the begetting of man, as the foundation does in the building of a house. The soul, in so far as it is the form of the body, stands to it as what is founded stands to its foundation: for it is founded on it in order to subsist, and the body is set under it. But in so far as it is the mover of the body, it stands to it as a dweller to his house, and a sailor to his ship; in which manner the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 4:7|we have this treasure in earthen vessels|Habemus thesaurum istum in vasis fictilibus]]. And again: [[2 Cor 5:1|we know, if our earthly house of this habitation be dissolved, that we have a building of God, a house not made with hands|Scimus quia si terrestris domus nostra hujus habitationis dissolvatur, quod ædificationem ex Deo habemus, domum non manufactam]], in heaven. Man is said, too, to dwell in such a house of clay by reason of his more principal part, namely the soul that dwells in the body. [[4:19|be consumed as with the moth|Consumentur velut a tinea]]. Though this can be taken of bodily death, by which man is consumed as a garment by the moth, Eliphaz's meaning is of spiritual consumption through sin, as is clear from what has been said. So the sense is: they shall [[4:19|be consumed|Consumentur]], that is, they will lose by sinning the spiritual life of charity and grace, as a coat is consumed by the moth. For as the moth springs from the coat and gnaws it away, so from the flesh comes the tinder of sin [fomes peccati: the inclination to sin that remains in fallen nature], and sensuality itself infected, reason blinded, the will prone to vices; and so man is consumed through sin by the things that are in him and spring from him. For he has of himself an inclination and proneness to evil, which the angels did not have. Therefore it is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 9:15|the corruptible body is a load upon the soul, and the earthly habitation presseth down the mind that museth upon many things|Corpus quod corrumpitur, aggravat animam, et deprimit terrena inhabitatio sensum multa cogitantem]]. In Genesis too: [[Gen 8:21|the imagination and thought of man's heart are prone to evil from his youth|Sensus et cogitatio cordis humani prona sunt in malum ab adolescentia sua]].

paras.t: De mane usque ad vesperam succidentur, id est, per totum diei processum frequenter peccando, a spirituali vita virtutum tollentur. Quod item de continua consumptione seu abbreviatione naturalis vitæ accipi potest. Indeficienter enim quid deperit de vita nostra qualibet hora, secundum illud in Isaia: De mane usque ad vesperam finies me. Et quia nullus intelligit, nullus videlicet comparative, id est perpauci, quid sint et quam fragiles, et quot vitiis subditi, juxta quod scriptum est: Delicta quis intelligit? In Osee quoque: Populus non intelligens vapulabit. Et Apostolus ait: Qui ignorat, ignorabitur. In æternum peribunt, qui ista non pensant, quum sint mortaliter vitiosi, quibus pœna debetur æterna. Ex quo certum est, quod Eliphaz ex revelatione hac, novit animæ immortalitatem infernaliumque pœnarum perpetuitatem.
paras.en: [[4:20|From morning till evening they shall be cut down|De mane usque ad vesperam succidentur]], that is, by sinning often through the whole course of the day they will be taken away from the spiritual life of the virtues. This can also be taken of the continual wasting or shortening of natural life. For something of our life is unfailingly lost every hour, according to that in Isaias: [[Is 38:13|from morning even to night thou wilt make an end of me|De mane usque ad vesperam finies me]]. [[4:20|And because no one understandeth|Et quia nullus intelligit]], no one, that is, comparatively speaking, that is, very few understand what they are, how frail, and to how many vices subject; according to what is written: [[Ps 18:13|Who can understand sins?|Delicta quis intelligit?]] In Osee too: [[Osee 4:14|the people that doth not understand shall be beaten|Populus non intelligens vapulabit]]. And the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 14:38|if any man know not, he shall not be known|Qui ignorat, ignorabitur]]. [[4:20|they shall perish for ever|In æternum peribunt]], those who do not weigh these things, being mortally sinful, to whom eternal punishment is due. From this it is certain that Eliphaz knew by this revelation the immortality of the soul and the everlastingness of the pains of hell.

paras.t: Qui autem reliqui fuerint, id est, qui præter illos non intelligentes jam dictos exstiterint, scilicet boni atque electi, quæ Dei sunt intelligentes, auferentur ex eis, id est, de illorum reproborum consortio secernentur, nec peribunt cum eis. Morientur, morte naturali et corporali, quæ bonis et malis communis est, et non in sapientia, id est, quantum ad sapientiam quam habent a Deo, non morientur, ita quod sapientia per mortem non tolletur ab eis.
paras.en: [[4:21|And they that shall be left|Qui autem reliqui fuerint]], that is, those who shall be found besides those who do not understand, just spoken of, namely the good and elect, who understand the things of God, [[4:21|shall be taken away from them|auferentur ex eis]], that is, shall be separated from the company of those reprobate, and shall not perish with them. [[4:21|they shall die|Morientur]], by natural and bodily death, which is common to good and bad, [[4:21|and not in wisdom|et non in sapientia]], that is, as regards the wisdom they have from God they shall not die, so that wisdom will not be taken from them by death.

paras.t: Vel sic: Qui autem reliqui fuerint, id est posteri pereuntium vitia parentum sequentes, seu alii a Deo non statim damnati, sed propter pœnitentiam agendam dilati, nec tamen pœnitentiam operati, auferentur de vita hac post patrum discessum. Porro, quod additur, Ex eis, secundum Lyram non est in Hebræo neque de textu. Morientur, et non in sapientia vera ac spirituali, id est, sine ea decedent, quia nec eam habuerunt; sed in stultitia propria, seu carnali et sæculari prudentia perierunt, juxta illud Baruch: Quia non habuerunt sapientiam, interierunt propter suam insipientiam.
paras.en: Or thus: [[4:21|And they that shall be left|Qui autem reliqui fuerint]], that is, the descendants of those who perish, following their parents' vices, or others not condemned by God at once but given time to do penance, and yet not doing it, [[4:21|shall be taken away|auferentur]] from this life after their fathers' departure. Further, what is added, [[4:21|from them|Ex eis]], according to Lyra is not in the Hebrew nor part of the text. [[4:21|they shall die, and not in wisdom|Morientur, et non in sapientia]] true and spiritual, that is, they will depart without it, because they never had it; but they perished in their own folly, or in carnal and worldly prudence, according to that of Baruch: [[Bar 3:28|because they had not wisdom, they perished through their folly|Quia non habuerunt sapientiam, interierunt propter suam insipientiam]].

paras.t: Itaque Eliphaz per omnia ista intendit tam fragilem atque immundam esse naturam humanam, quod sine peccato esse non possit; et quod dicens se purum, quum puniatur a Deo, dicit Deum esse impurum sive injustum, et præfert se ei: sicque credendum sit, quod Job et filii ejus ob sua peccata percussi sint.
paras.en: So by all this Eliphaz means that human nature is so frail and unclean that it cannot be without sin; and that he who calls himself pure when he is punished by God calls God impure or unjust, and sets himself above him; and so it must be believed that Job and his sons were struck down for their sins.

paras.t: Quæritur, an Eliphaz habuit revelationem præscriptam a Deo, vel eam confinxerit. Hoc Thomas relinquit sub dubio. Lyræ autem videtur, quod finxit hæc, quia in fine libri Dominus ait ad Eliphaz: Non estis locuti rectum coram me. Rursus, quia inducit et applicat eam ad falsum intellectum. Potius tamen reor, quod eam non finxit: quod et Gregorius sentire videtur. Nec Job ita sensit de Eliphaz, ut apparet, quod finxerit ista: non enim aliquid imponit sibi de hoc. Nec argumenta concludunt. Non enim dubium est, quin Eliphaz in processu disputationis suæ multa vera protulerit: nihilo minus ipse et ejus amici dicuntur non recta locuti, quia ad falsam conclusionem seu finem perversum hæc retulerunt, videlicet ad probandum Job pro suis excessibus esse plagatum, atque ad confirmandum positiones suas erroneas circa modum providentiæ Dei, ut dictum est supra. Præterea revelatio jam præscripta, in se vera atque sublimis est, sicque a Deo manavit. Eliphaz tamen abusus est ea, male applicans eam ad Job, sicut frequenter ratio sub veris principiis male subsumit: quod passio maxime facit.
paras.en: It is asked whether Eliphaz had the revelation described above from God, or made it up. Thomas leaves this in doubt. Lyra, however, thinks he made it up, because at the end of the book the Lord says to Eliphaz: [[Job 42:7|you have not spoken the thing that is right before me|Non estis locuti rectum coram me]]; and again, because he brings it in and applies it to a false sense. Yet I rather think he did not make it up, and Gregory too seems to think so. Nor did Job, it appears, think of Eliphaz that he had made these things up: for he lays no charge against him on this score. Nor do those arguments conclude. For there is no doubt that Eliphaz, in the course of his disputation, uttered many true things; nonetheless he and his friends are said not to have spoken rightly, because they turned these things to a false conclusion or a perverse end, namely to prove that Job had been struck for his excesses, and to confirm their erroneous positions about the manner of God's providence, as was said above. Moreover, the revelation set down above is in itself true and sublime, and so came from God. But Eliphaz misused it, wrongly applying it to Job, just as reason often subsumes wrongly under true principles [that is, brings a particular case under a true general rule where it does not belong, and so draws a false conclusion]: which passion above all brings about.

5.title: Expositio litteralis capituli quinti: Voca ergo, si est qui tibi respondeat.
5.title_en: Literal exposition of the fifth chapter: Call now if there be any that will answer thee

paras.t: Recitata revelatione sibi desuper facta, Eliphaz irrisorie ac invective loquitur contra Job. Voca ergo: id est, quoniam mihi hæc revelata sunt, tu quoque qui te tam innocentem ac justum præsumis, invoca Deum, qui justos magis quam peccatores exaudit; si est qui tibi respondeat, id est, precibus tuis effectum impendat, et tibi quæ dixi revelet; et ad aliquem Sanctorum convertere, orando aliquem civem regni cælestis, ut oret pro te, si de tuis meritis non confidis. Istud fuit et est sanum consilium, si recta intentione et ex caritate fuisset propositum: quia et nos in dubiis et ignotis Deum pro illuminatione invocare debemus, juxta id Jacobi: Si quis vestrum indiget sapientia, postulet a Deo, et dabitur ei. Postulet autem in fide nihil hæsitans. Et Psalmista: Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini. Denique, considerantes imperfectum nostrum, peccata et scelera nostra, propter quæ indigni sumus per nos ipsos immediate accedere ad thronum gratiæ Dei, ad aliquem vel aliquos Sanctorum nos convertamus, ad quos specialem affectionem fiduciamque habemus, præsertim ad Virginem gloriosam, ut intercedat pro nobis.
paras.en: Having recounted the revelation made to him from above, Eliphaz speaks mockingly and reproachfully against Job. [[5:1|Call now|Voca ergo]]: that is, since these things have been revealed to me, do thou also, who presumest thyself so innocent and just, call upon God, who hears the just rather than sinners[[John 9:31||]]; [[5:1|if there be any that will answer thee|si est qui tibi respondeat]], that is, who will give effect to thy prayers and reveal to thee what I have told thee; [[5:1|and turn to some of the saints|et ad aliquem Sanctorum convertere]], by praying some citizen of the heavenly kingdom to pray for thee, if thou hast no confidence in thine own merits. This was and is sound counsel, had it been put forward with a right intention and out of charity: for we too, in things doubtful and unknown, ought to call upon God for light, according to that saying of James: [[Jas 1:5|if any of you want wisdom, let him ask of God|Si quis vestrum indiget sapientia, postulet a Deo]], [[Jas 1:5|And it shall be given him|et dabitur ei]]. [[Jas 1:6|But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering|Postulet autem in fide nihil hæsitans]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 33:6|Come ye to him and be enlightened|Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini]]. Lastly, considering our imperfection, our sins and crimes, on account of which we are unworthy of ourselves to approach directly to the throne of God's grace, let us turn to some one or more of the saints for whom we have a special affection and trust, above all to the glorious Virgin, that she may intercede for us.

paras.t: Consequenter insinuat sanctum Job iracundum invidumque fuisse, quamvis in generali loquatur. Cujus etiam verba in generali sunt exponenda: sic nempe profunda sunt, vera atque subtilia. Virum stultum, qui vera ac spirituali sapientia caret: stultitia quippe dono sapientiæ directe opponitur. Stultus quoque vocatur, qui discretionem non habet eligendorum ac vitandorum. Talem interficit iracundia, formaliter, quoniam ira quum sit peccatum mortale ex genere, animæ mors est: sicque spiritualiter interimit hominem. Interficit etiam eum, quoniam morte damnationis æternæ, et interdum etiam morte corporali, eum efficit dignum. Imo quicumque peccat mortaliter, meretur divina conservatione in esse privari, protinusque a Deo corporaliter quoque occidi. Nec mirum, quum mereatur et mortem gehennæ æternam. Quoniam vero sapientia facit hominem in omnibus ordinatum, et prudentia reddit discretum, qui sapientia atque prudentia caret, confestim superatur ab ira: ipsaque ira facit hominem stulto consimilem, rationis lumen vehementer obtenebrando, ita quod homo instar canis impetum sequitur passionis. Ideo dicit Jacobus: Ira viri justitiam Dei non operatur. Ecclesiastes quoque: Ne sis velox ad irascendum; ira enim in sinu stulti requiescit. Præterea, quum scriptum sit: Tu dominator, Domine, cum tranquillitate judicas, ira facit hominem in judicando specialiter Deo difformem, dum homo cum turbulentia judicat: quod maxime indecens est. Unde ad iram specialissime devitandam admonet Christus: Discite a me, quia mitis sum et humilis. Per iram etiam socialis vita confunditur, concordia dissipatur, societas aggravatur, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Spiritum ad irascendum facilem quis poterit sustinere? Et: Impetum spiritus concitati quis sustinebit? Itemque: Noli assiduus esse cum homine iracundo, ne discas semitas ejus, et sumas scandalum animæ tuæ.
paras.en: Next he hints that holy Job was given to anger and envy, though he speaks in general terms. His words too are to be expounded in general: so taken, they are deep, true and subtle. [[5:2|the foolish|Virum stultum]] [Denis reads *Virum stultum*, "the foolish man", where the Vulgate has *Vere stultum*, "indeed … the foolish"]: one who lacks true and spiritual wisdom; for folly is directly opposed to the gift of wisdom. He too is called a fool who has no discernment of what is to be chosen and what avoided. [[5:2|Anger indeed killeth|interficit iracundia]] such a one formally [that is, by its very nature, not merely by what follows from it], since anger, being a mortal sin by its kind [that is, of a kind that is mortal unless lessened by want of full consent or by slightness of matter], is the death of the soul: and so it slays a man spiritually. It kills him also because it makes him worthy of the death of eternal damnation, and sometimes even of bodily death. Indeed whoever sins mortally deserves to be deprived of God's keeping him in being, and forthwith to be slain by God in the body too. And no wonder, since he deserves even the eternal death of hell. But since wisdom makes a man ordered in all things, and prudence makes him discerning, he who lacks wisdom and prudence is at once overcome by anger: and anger itself makes a man like a fool, darkening the light of reason violently, so that the man follows the rush of passion like a dog. Therefore James says: [[Jas 1:20|the anger of man worketh not the justice of God|Ira viri justitiam Dei non operatur]]. Ecclesiastes also: [[Eccles 7:10|Be not quickly angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of a fool|Ne sis velox ad irascendum; ira enim in sinu stulti requiescit]]. Moreover, since it is written: [[Wis 12:18|thou being master of power, judgest with tranquillity|Tu dominator, Domine, cum tranquillitate judicas]] [Denis has *Tu dominator, Domine*, "Thou, O Lord, the ruler", for the Vulgate's *Tu autem dominator virtutis*], anger makes a man unlike God especially in judging, when a man judges in turmoil: which is most unbecoming. Hence Christ admonishes us most especially to shun anger: [[Matt 11:29|learn of me, because I am meek, and humble|Discite a me, quia mitis sum et humilis]]. By anger, too, the common life is thrown into confusion, concord is broken up, company is made a burden, according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 18:14|a spirit that is easily angered, who can bear?|Spiritum ad irascendum facilem quis poterit sustinere]] And: [[Prov 27:4|who can bear the violence of one provoked?|Impetum spiritus concitati quis sustinebit]] And again: [[Prov 22:24|Be not a friend to an angry man|Noli assiduus esse cum homine iracundo]] [Denis reads *Noli assiduus esse*, "Be not constantly with", for the Vulgate's *Noli esse amicus*], [[Prov 22:25|Lest perhaps thou learn his ways, and take scandal to thy soul|ne discas semitas ejus, et sumas scandalum animæ tuæ]].

paras.t: Denique, secundum Thomam, non est aliqua conditio hominum, cui non adsit aliqua pronitas ad peccatum. Sunt autem duæ hominum conditiones. Quidam sunt magni elatique animi, qui facile provocantur ad iram, quoniam ira est appetitus vindictæ ex præcedenti offensa proveniens: quanto autem quis fuerit animi magis elati, tanto ex leviori causa se putat offensum. Talem vero nominat stultum, quia per superbiam homo præcipue metas rationis excedit, et humilitas viam sapientiæ parat. Stultitia quoque iracundiæ competit, quoniam in ultione modum rationis transgreditur. Quidam autem sunt pusillanimes, et hi ad invidiam proni sunt: de quibus statim dicetur.
paras.en: Further, according to Thomas, there is no condition of men in which there is not some proneness to sin. Now there are two conditions of men. Some are of a great and lofty spirit, and are easily provoked to anger, since anger is a desire for revenge arising from an offence received before: and the loftier a man's spirit, the slighter the cause for which he thinks himself offended. Such a one he calls *foolish*, because it is above all through pride that a man oversteps the bounds of reason, while humility prepares the way of wisdom. Folly also befits wrath, since in taking revenge it goes beyond the measure of reason. Others are faint-hearted, and these are prone to envy: of them we shall speak presently.

paras.t: Postremo advertenda sunt, quæ hic scribit Gregorius de ira per zelum. Solerter, inquit, sciendum est, quod alia est ira quam impatientia excitat, alia quam zelus format: illa ex vitio, hæc virtute generatur. Si enim nulla ira ex virtute surgeret, divinæ animadversionis impetum Phinees per gladium non placasset. Hanc iram quia Heli non habuit, motum contra se implacabiliter supernæ ultionis excitavit. Sed quum per zelum animus movetur, curandum summopere est, ne ira quæ pro instrumento virtutis assumitur, menti dominetur, nec quasi domina præeat, sed velut ancilla ad obsequium parata, a rationis tergo nunquam recedat. Tunc enim robustius contra vitia erigitur, quum subdita rationi famulatur.
paras.en: Lastly, we must note what Gregory writes here about anger through zeal [that is, anger moved by zeal for what is right, as distinct from the vice of anger]. "We must carefully understand," he says, "that one anger is stirred up by impatience, another is formed by zeal: the one is born of vice, the other of virtue. For if no anger arose from virtue, Phinees would not have appeased the onset of God's vengeance by the sword[[Num 25:11||]] [the margin gives Num. xxv, 7, 8, 11–13]. Because Heli had not this anger, he stirred up against himself, beyond appeasing, the movement of vengeance from on high[[1 Kings 3:13||]]. But when the mind is moved by zeal, the greatest care must be taken that anger, which is taken up as an instrument of virtue, does not master the mind, nor go before it as a mistress, but, like a handmaid ready to serve, never withdraws from behind reason. For it rises up more strongly against vices when it serves in subjection to reason."

paras.t: Et parvulum, eum videlicet, qui se ex prosperitate et bonis aliorum reputat minorari, occidit invidia: quæ est tristitia de bono alterius, in quantum apprehenditur ut proprii boni minorativum. Sicque invidens, per suam sibi invidiam testis est quod parvulus sit, quia ex aliorum magnificatione se æstimat parvificari. Ideo dicit Gregorius: Invidere non possumus, nisi eis quos nobis in aliquo meliores putamus. Parvulus ergo est, qui livore occiditur: quoniam ipse sibi testimonium perhibet, quod eo minor sit cujus torquetur invidia. Porro, quum caritas sit directe spiritualis vita animæ, princeps et forma virtutum, invidia quæ ei directe opponitur, est pessimum vitium, occisio mentis, et corporali quoque vitæ multum nociva, Salomone dicente: Vita carnium, sanitas cordis; putredo ossium, invidia. Invidi insuper specialiter imitantur diabolum, juxta quod Sapiens asserit: Invidia diaboli mors introivit in orbem terrarum; imitantur autem illum, qui sunt ex parte ejus.
paras.en: [[5:2|the little one|Et parvulum]], namely him who reckons himself made less by the prosperity and the goods of others, [[5:2|envy slayeth|occidit invidia]]: envy, which is sorrow at another's good, inasmuch as it is apprehended as lessening one's own good. And so the envious man by his very envy is his own witness that he is little, since he reckons himself made small by the magnifying of others. Therefore Gregory says: "We cannot envy any but those whom we think better than ourselves in some respect. He then is little who is slain by envy: for he bears witness against himself that he is less than the one by envy of whom he is tormented." Further, since charity is directly the spiritual life of the soul, the prince and form of the virtues, envy, which is directly opposed to it, is the worst of vices, the slaying of the mind, and very harmful to the life of the body as well, as Solomon says: [[Prov 14:30|Soundness of heart is the life of the flesh: but envy is the rottenness of the bones|Vita carnium, sanitas cordis; putredo ossium, invidia]]. Moreover the envious imitate the devil in a special way, as the Wise Man declares: [[Wis 2:24|by the envy of the devil, death came into the world|Invidia diaboli mors introivit in orbem terrarum]]; [[Wis 2:25|And they follow him that are of his side|imitantur autem illum, qui sunt ex parte ejus]].

paras.t: Quum itaque unusquisque nostrum ex naturali dispositione seu assuefactione ad aliquod speciale vitium inclinetur et pronus sit, debet contra illud specialissimam pugnam assumere, Deum jugiter pro triumphandi gratia implorando, aptiora remedia inquirendo, seque ad virtutem oppositam cordialissime applicando. Unde qui singulariter ad superbiam seu iram proclivis est, contra vitia hæc specialissime prælietur, et ad humilitatem mansuetudinemque se disponat et det tanto exuberantius, quod oppositis vitiis magis tabescit.
paras.en: Since, then, each of us is inclined and prone, by natural disposition or by habit, to some particular vice, he ought to take up a most particular fight against it, continually imploring God for the grace to triumph, seeking out the fitter remedies, and applying himself most heartily to the opposite virtue. Hence he who is singularly inclined to pride or to anger should fight most particularly against these vices, and dispose and give himself to humility and meekness the more abundantly as he wastes away the more with the opposite vices.

paras.t: Ego vidi stultum, id est vitiosum, superbum, et temporalia spiritualibus præferentem: quod summæ insaniæ est; firma radice, id est in terrenis prosperitatibus firmiter radicatum, instar arboris firmam in terra radicem habentis, ita quod forti fundamento tanquam radici videbatur inniti ac stabiliri, in temporalibus abundando. Et maledixi, id est, mala prænuntiavi ventura, atque a Deo maledicendum prædixi, pulchritudini ejus, id est terrenæ prosperitati, floritioni, ornatuique ipsius. Sapientes enim perpendunt impiorum prosperitatem celeriter finiendam, et ad miseriam deducendam: imo, quod tanto sunt infeliciores, quanto plus prosperantur in sæculo isto. Ideo de viro justo ait Psalmista: Ad nihilum deductus est in conspectu ejus malignus. Et Sapiens: Adulterinæ plantationes non dabunt radices altas, nec stabile fundamentum collocabunt. Sic quoque in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Omnis potentatus brevis vita. Sic rex hodie est, et cras morietur. Taliter venerabilis Mathathias maledixit pulchritudini impii, præsertim Antiochi: A verbis peccatoris ne timueritis, quia gloria ejus stercus et vermis; hodie extollitur, et cras non invenietur. Hujusmodi autem maledictio oritur ex affectu justitiæ; vel est prænuntiatio futuri magis quam imprecatio mali. Adjecit autem Eliphaz, statim, ad insinuandum quod ex zelo æquitatis non distulit, vel quia impiorum prosperitas mox cessabit. Talem ergo pulchritudinem vanam ac prosperitatem fallacem despicit virtuosus, qui metuendum Dei pensat judicium, prævidetque infernale supplicium. Quod agens Psalmista edocuit: Noli æmulari in malignantibus, neque zelaveris facientes iniquitatem: quoniam tanquam fœnum velociter arescent, et quasi olera herbarum cito decident.
paras.en: [[5:3|I have seen a fool|Ego vidi stultum]], that is, a man given to vice, proud, and preferring temporal things to spiritual: which is the height of madness; [[5:3|with a strong root|firma radice]], that is, firmly rooted in earthly prosperity, like a tree that has a firm root in the earth, so that, abounding in temporal things, he seemed to rest and be made stable on a strong foundation as on a root. [[5:3|and I cursed|Et maledixi]], that is, I foretold evils to come, and predicted that it would be cursed by God, [[5:3|his beauty|pulchritudini ejus]], that is, his earthly prosperity, his flourishing and his adornment. For the wise weigh the fact that the prosperity of the wicked is soon to end and to be brought down to misery: nay, that they are the more unhappy the more they prosper in this world. Therefore the Psalmist says of the just man: [[Ps 14:4|In his sight the malignant is brought to nothing|Ad nihilum deductus est in conspectu ejus malignus]]. And the Wise Man: [[Wis 4:3|bastard slips shall not take deep root, nor any fast foundation|Adulterinæ plantationes non dabunt radices altas, nec stabile fundamentum collocabunt]] [Denis reads *Adulterinæ plantationes*, "adulterous plantings", where the Vulgate has *spuria vitulamina*, "bastard slips"]. So too it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:11|All power is of short life|Omnis potentatus brevis vita]]. [[Ecclus 10:12|so also a king is to day, and to morrow he shall die|Sic rex hodie est, et cras morietur]]. In this way the venerable Mathathias cursed the beauty of the wicked, above all of Antiochus: [[1 Mach 2:62|fear not the words of a sinful man, for his glory is dung and worms|A verbis peccatoris ne timueritis, quia gloria ejus stercus et vermis]]; [[1 Mach 2:63|Today he is lifted up, and tomorrow he shall not be found|hodie extollitur, et cras non invenietur]]. Such cursing springs from a love of justice; or it is a foretelling of what is to come rather than an imprecation of evil. Eliphaz added [[5:3|immediately|statim]] to suggest that out of zeal for equity he did not delay, or because the prosperity of the wicked will soon cease. Such vain beauty, then, and deceitful prosperity the virtuous man despises, who weighs the judgment of God that is to be feared and foresees the torment of hell. Doing this, the Psalmist taught: [[Ps 36:1|Be not emulous of evildoers; nor envy them that work iniquity|Noli æmulari in malignantibus, neque zelaveris facientes iniquitatem]]: [[Ps 36:2|For they shall shortly wither away as grass, and as the green herbs shall quickly fall|quoniam tanquam fœnum velociter arescent, et quasi olera herbarum cito decident]].

paras.t: Longe fient filii ejus a salute: id est, qui non solum secundum carnis propaginem, sed per impietatis quoque sequelam, filii ejus sunt, vera beatitudine privabuntur; et vicissim in sæculo isto pericula incidunt, puniuntur et pereunt. Juxta quem modum scriptum est: Ex iniquis omnes qui nascuntur filii, testes sunt nequitiæ adversus parentes suos in interrogatione sua. Et conterentur in porta, id est, per publicam justitiam in loco judicii morti adjicientur. Olim enim judices sedebant in urbium portis, ubi et impii accusati atque convicti, condemnabantur ad mortes. Unde in Deuteronomio scribitur: Judices et magistratus constitues in omnibus portis tuis. Et non erit qui eruat eos de morte. Propter enormitatem enim suorum excessuum, aliquando liberari non queunt. Vel, quia pravitatibus suis facti sunt omnibus odiosi seu detestandi, non est qui velit eos eruere. Nullus quoque de potestate divini judicii eos eripiet. Hinc et in Exodo habetur: Maleficos non patieris vivere.
paras.en: [[5:4|His children shall be far from safety|Longe fient filii ejus a salute]]: that is, those who are his children not only by fleshly descent but also by following his wickedness shall be deprived of true beatitude; and in their turn they fall into dangers in this world, are punished and perish. In which manner it is written: [[Wis 4:6|the children that are born of unlawful beds, are witnesses of wickedness against their parents in their trial|Ex iniquis omnes qui nascuntur filii, testes sunt nequitiæ adversus parentes suos in interrogatione sua]] [Denis reads *Ex iniquis omnes qui nascuntur filii*, "all the children born of the wicked", where the Vulgate has *Ex iniquis enim somnis filii qui nascuntur*, "the children born of unlawful beds"]. [[5:4|and shall be destroyed in the gate|Et conterentur in porta]], that is, by public justice they shall be put to death in the place of judgment. For of old the judges sat in the gates of the cities, where the wicked, when accused and convicted, were condemned to death. Hence it is written in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 16:18|Thou shalt appoint judges and magistrates in all thy gates|Judices et magistratus constitues in omnibus portis tuis]]. [[5:4|and there shall be none to deliver them|Et non erit qui eruat eos de morte]] from death [Denis's text adds *eos de morte*, "them from death"]: for because of the enormity of their excesses they sometimes cannot be set free. Or, because by their depravities they have become hateful or detestable to all, there is no one willing to rescue them. Nor will anyone snatch them from the power of God's judgment. Hence too it is said in Exodus: [[Ex 22:18|Wizards thou shalt not suffer to live|Maleficos non patieris vivere.]].

paras.t: Cujus messem, id est blada et opes, famelicus comedet, id est, prædo depopulator, seu depauperatus, vel pauper necessitate compulsus, avide devorabit; et ipsum rapiet armatus, id est, a viro bellicoso armato ducetur captivus, aut spoliationem sustinebit rerum suarum; et bibent sitientes divitias ejus, id est, potando consument.
paras.en: [[5:5|Whose harvest|Cujus messem]], that is, his corn and wealth, [[5:5|the hungry shall eat|famelicus comedet]], that is, a plundering robber, or one who has been made poor, or a poor man driven by need, shall greedily devour; [[5:5|and the armed man shall take him by violence|et ipsum rapiet armatus]], that is, he shall be led captive by a warlike, armed man, or shall suffer the plundering of his goods; [[5:5|and the thirsty shall drink up his riches|et bibent sitientes divitias ejus]], that is, they shall consume them in drinking.

paras.t: Ista frequenter ad litteram ita fiunt; sed quod non semper, certissimum est, quum cernamus impiissimos parentes ac filios usque decrepitam senectutem impune peccare, mirabiliter prosperari, a nemine molestari. Interdum vero vitiosi parentes eorumque filii pravi, hæc patiuntur in vita præsenti, sicut et filiis Israel multoties contigisse in libris Regum ac Judicum legitur. Unde, quoniam multa eorum quæ amici Job dicunt generaliter, non implentur eo modo quo dicunt verbaque sonant, B. Gregorius non immerito talia spiritualiter interpretatur. Sed quia amici Job erronearum opinionum fuerunt, et ea quæ dicunt, ad suorum confirmationem errorum inducunt, non mirum si aliquando universaliter vera non sint quæ proponunt. Ideo talia caute ac sapienter sunt exponenda et capienda. Nec enim verba eorum in omnibus verba sunt Spiritus Sancti, quemadmodum verba Job: imo multa dicunt non vera, ut in processu patebit.
paras.en: These things often happen so, to the letter; but that they do not always is most certain, since we see most wicked parents and children sinning with impunity even to decrepit old age, prospering wonderfully, troubled by no one. At times, though, vicious parents and their wicked children suffer these things in the present life, as we read in the books of Kings and of Judges happened many times to the children of Israel. Hence, since many of the things that Job's friends say in general are not fulfilled in the way they say and as the words sound, Blessed Gregory not without reason interprets such things spiritually. But since Job's friends held erroneous opinions, and bring forward what they say to confirm their errors, it is no wonder if what they put forward is sometimes not universally true. Such things, therefore, are to be expounded and taken cautiously and wisely. For their words are not in all things words of the Holy Ghost, as the words of Job are: indeed they say many things that are not true, as will appear as we go on.

paras.t: Nihil in terra sine causa fit. Hoc secundum unum intellectum clarissimum atque certissimum est. Si enim fit, sequitur quod sit effectus seu quid causatum: quo dato, sequitur quod habeat causam, eo quod causa et effectus correlative se habeant. Itaque ad minus habet causam efficientem determinatam vel indeterminatam, per se vel per accidens. Sic et Plato loquitur in Timæo: Nihil fit, cujus ortum causa legitima non præcessit. Nam et Philosophus ait: Causa est, ad cujus esse sequitur aliud, haud dubium quin effectus. Nec obstat quod sunt quidam effectus casuales atque fortuiti. Nam et hi habent causam per accidens: et quamvis sint tales per comparationem ad causas secundas et proximas, tamen respectu primæ causæ seu providentis Dei, nihil casuale fortuitumque consistit, sed certus est ordo causarum.
paras.en: [[5:6|Nothing upon earth is done without a cause|Nihil in terra sine causa fit]]. Taken in one sense this is most clear and most certain. For if a thing is done, it follows that it is an effect, something caused: and granted this, it follows that it has a cause, since cause and effect are correlatives. So at the least it has an efficient cause, determinate or indeterminate, per se or per accidens [that is, a cause that produces the effect of itself, by its own nature, or one that produces it only incidentally]. So too Plato says in the Timæus: "Nothing comes to be whose origin no lawful cause has gone before." And the Philosopher says: "A cause is that upon whose being something else follows", no doubt an effect. Nor does it stand in the way that there are some chance and fortuitous effects. For these too have a cause per accidens: and though they are such in relation to second and proximate causes, yet with respect to the first cause, that is, God who provides, nothing is by chance or fortuitous, but the order of causes is certain.

paras.t: Porro, si verbum inductum intelligatur de causa determinata et propria, et de causa per se, veritatem non habet, ut in casualibus patet effectibus. Rursus, si accipiatur secundum Eliphaz intentionem, veritate carebit. Nempe Eliphaz verbo hoc voluit dicta Job falsificare, quibus se dixit sine suo demerito ita plagatum. Quasi Eliphaz diceret: Sicut in naturalibus nihil fit sine determinata et legitima causa, ita in rebus humanis nil fit sine causa meritoria præcedenti. Tua ergo, o Job, adversitas, non nisi propter præcedentia tua demerita seu peccata, inflicta est tibi a Deo. Istud argumentum non valet, tam quia in naturalibus non semper effectum præcedit causa determinata per se, tum quoniam in humanis causa pœnæ inflictæ non solum est prævia culpa, sed et aliquæ causæ diversæ, ut dictum est et dicetur. Deus quippe ex sua sapientia, pietate et potestate flagellat aliquando et justum, non ob præviam culpam, sed ob ampliorem ejus profectum, aliorumque ædificationem, ac diaboli confusionem; vel ob divinæ omnipotentiæ declarationem, beatitudinisque futuræ augmentum. Deus etiam in hominibus nihil facit, nec fieri sinit, nisi ob causam quamdam finalem, ut vel sua justitia in reprobis manifestetur, vel sua clementia in electis reluceat.
paras.en: But if the saying brought forward is understood of a determinate and proper cause, and of a cause per se, it is not true, as is plain in chance effects. Again, if it is taken according to Eliphaz's intention, it will be without truth. For by this saying Eliphaz meant to prove false the words of Job in which he said he had been so stricken without any desert of his own. As if Eliphaz said: As in natural things nothing is done without a determinate and lawful cause, so in human affairs nothing is done without a preceding cause of desert. Thy adversity, then, O Job, has been inflicted on thee by God only because of thy preceding misdeeds, that is, sins. This argument does not hold, both because in natural things a determinate cause per se does not always go before the effect, and because in human affairs the cause of a punishment inflicted is not only a preceding fault but also certain other, different causes, as has been said and will be said. For God, out of his wisdom, goodness and power, sometimes scourges even the just man, not for a preceding fault, but for his greater progress, for the edification of others and the confusion of the devil; or for the showing forth of the divine omnipotence and the increase of future beatitude. God, too, does nothing among men, nor lets anything be done, except for some final cause: that either his justice may be shown forth in the reprobate or his mercy shine out in the elect.

paras.t: Et de humo non egredietur dolor. Hoc, secundum Thomam, metaphorica exstat locutio. Quædam etenim herbæ sine jacto in terram semine producuntur, quæ de terra sponte nasci dicuntur. Sicque metaphorice quidquid sine causa propria fit, diceretur de humo sine semine nasci. Itaque, De humo non orietur dolor, id est, adversitas sine propria causa, scilicet prævia culpa, nulli continget, desuperque præstabitur. Quæ argumentatio, ut tactum est, non est fortis. Non enim culpa est dumtaxat causa pœnæ inflictæ. At vero, secundum Albertum, de humo, id est terra humida et commixta in naturam corporis humani, puta de carne mortali, non egredietur dolor, id est causa doloris, videlicet secundum quod caro est, et quoad id quod habet a Creatore. Sic enim non est origo peccati, quod, secundum Eliphaz, est causa doloris seu pœnæ. Imo, secundum Dionysium et Augustinum, voluntas, ut ex nihilo facta atque ex se ipsa defectuosa ac labilis, est radix peccandi, et per eam infecta est caro. Unde Albertus allegat illud Fulgentii: Deus non est ultor cujus est actor.
paras.en: [[5:6|and sorrow doth not spring out of the ground|Et de humo non egredietur dolor]] [Denis reads *egredietur*, "shall come forth", where the Vulgate has *oritur*, "springeth"; a little below he gives *orietur*]. This, according to Thomas, is a metaphorical way of speaking. For some plants are brought forth without seed being cast into the earth, and these are said to spring up from the earth of themselves. And so, metaphorically, whatever is done without its proper cause would be said to spring out of the ground without seed. Thus [[5:6|sorrow doth not spring out of the ground|De humo non orietur dolor]], that is, adversity without its proper cause, namely a preceding fault, will befall no one and be sent from above. This argument, as was touched on, is not strong. For fault is not the only cause of a punishment inflicted. But according to Albert, [[5:6|out of the ground|de humo]], that is, out of moist earth mixed into the nature of the human body, namely out of mortal flesh, [[5:6|sorrow doth not spring|non egredietur dolor]], that is, the cause of sorrow: that is to say, inasmuch as it is flesh, and as regards what it has from the Creator. For in that way it is not the origin of sin, which according to Eliphaz is the cause of sorrow or punishment. Indeed, according to Dionysius and Augustine, the will, as made from nothing and of itself defective and liable to fall, is the root of sinning, and through it the flesh has been infected. Hence Albert cites that saying of Fulgentius: "God is not the avenger of that of which he is the author."

paras.t: Porro, quod nihil fiat sine causa in terra, quasi exemplificando in rationali irrationalique creatura, subjungit: Homo ad laborem nascitur, et avis ad volatum: id est, Deus creator nec hominem nec avem frustra, sed rationabili causa instituit, ut homo per laborem sibi de necessariis victui, habitationi, vestituique provideat; et avis per volatum, quæ suæ conveniunt naturæ exerceat, nidificando, victum quærendo, pericula fugiendo. Unde et avibus pro vestimentis et armis natura contulit plumas et rostra ac ungues; hominem vero nudum nasci instituit, ut laborando, vestimentum habitaculumque, si desint, conquirat. Vult itaque dicere, quod res nascatur ut actus suos exerceat, non ut Deus eam sine causa affligat. Nam et naturalia esse dicuntur propter suas operationes, propter quod in necessariis natura non deficit. Omnia namque habent dispositionem operationi propriæ congruam: quo constat, quod naturales rerum dispositiones non sunt sine causa, sed propter determinatum et congruum finem. Præterea verba hæc altius queunt exponi, sicut, præstante Deo, sequenti tangetur articulo.
paras.en: Further, that nothing upon earth is done without a cause, he adds, as if giving examples in the rational and the irrational creature: [[5:7|Man is born to labour, and the bird to fly|Homo ad laborem nascitur, et avis ad volatum]]: that is, God the Creator made neither man nor bird in vain, but for a reasonable cause: that man by labour might provide himself with what he needs for food, dwelling and clothing; and that the bird by flight might do what suits its nature, building nests, seeking food, fleeing dangers. Hence nature has given birds feathers, beaks and claws for clothing and arms; but man it has ordained to be born naked, so that by labouring he may get himself clothing and a dwelling, if he lacks them. He means, then, that a thing is born to exercise its own acts, not that God may afflict it without cause. For natural things too are said to exist for the sake of their operations, which is why nature does not fail in what is necessary. For all things have a disposition fitted to their own operation: from which it is plain that the natural dispositions of things are not without a cause, but are for a determinate and fitting end. Moreover, these words can be expounded at a deeper level, as, God granting, will be touched on in the following article.

paras.t: Omnia hæc Eliphaz ponit, ad concludendum, quod omnia providentiæ divinæ subjaceant, eo quod singula ad proprios actus ac fines sint ordinata. Quod (secundum Albertum) inducit ad confutandum errorem philosophorum quorumdam, dicentium, quod gubernatio hominis esset ex infaustis vel faustis scintillationibus periodi: quoniam quamvis creator Deus res faciat, factas tamen mutabiles gubernandas committit periodo, et casuali mutabilitati naturæ mortalis: quam opinionem dicit Rabbi Moyses Ægyptius, in tertia collatione Ducis neutrorum, fuisse Aristotelis et quorumdam Peripateticorum. Verumtamen ista non fuit omnium philosophorum opinio, quia nonnulli eorum ex prætacta Eliphaz consideratione testati sunt, providentiam Dei excelsi et gloriosi usque ad inferiora et ima pertingere, secundum quod decimo de Civitate Dei Augustinus ostendit, dicendo: Plotinus Platonicus de Providentia disputans, eam a summo Deo (cujus est intelligibilis atque ineffabilis pulchritudo) usque ad hæc terrena et ima pertingere, flosculorum ac foliorum pulchritudine comprobat: quæ omnia quasi abjecta et velocissime pereuntia, decentissimos formarum suarum numeros habere non posse confirmat, nisi inde formentur, ubi forma intelligibilis et incommutabilis simul exemplariter habens omnia, perseverat. Hoc et Dominus Jesus ostendit in Evangelio: Considerate, inquiens, lilia agri quomodo crescunt. Dico autem vobis, quod nec Salomon in omni gloria sua coopertus est sicut unum ex illis.
paras.en: All these things Eliphaz sets down in order to conclude that all things are subject to divine providence, since each is ordered to its own acts and ends. This (according to Albert) he brings in to refute the error of certain philosophers, who said that the governing of man came from the unlucky or lucky sparklings of the cycle [*periodus*: the revolution of the heavens and their stars]: for although God the Creator makes things, yet once made, being changeable, he commits them to be governed by the cycle and by the chance changeableness of mortal nature: which opinion, says Rabbi Moses the Egyptian [that is, Maimonides] in the third part of the *Guide of the Doubting* [*Dux neutrorum*, the medieval Latin title of his *Guide for the Perplexed*], was that of Aristotle and certain Peripatetics. Yet this was not the opinion of all the philosophers, for some of them, from the consideration of Eliphaz just mentioned, have testified that the providence of God most high and glorious reaches down to the lower and lowest things, as Augustine shows in the tenth book of the City of God, saying: "Plotinus the Platonist, discussing Providence, proves from the beauty of little flowers and leaves that it reaches from the highest God (whose beauty is intelligible and ineffable) down to these earthly and lowest things: all of which, cast aside as it were and perishing most swiftly, he affirms could not have the most fitting proportions [Latin *numeros*, "numbers", that is, measured harmonies] of their forms unless they were formed from that place where the intelligible and unchangeable form, holding all things together within itself as their exemplar, abides." This the Lord Jesus too showed in the Gospel: [[Matt 6:28|Consider|Considerate]], he says, [[Matt 6:28|the lilies of the field, how they grow|lilia agri quomodo crescunt]]. [[Matt 6:29|But I say to you, that not even Solomon in all his glory was arrayed as one of these|Dico autem vobis, quod nec Salomon in omni gloria sua coopertus est sicut unum ex illis]] [the margin's reading looks like Matth. v, 28, 39; the words are Matt 6:28–29].

paras.t: Quum ergo divinæ providentiæ omnia subsunt, Eliphaz subdit: Quamobrem ego deprecabor Dominum, ut te convertat et me dirigat: quem orare esset inane, nisi rerum cognitionem providentiamque haberet: quam quia habet, exorandus est semper; et ad Deum ponam, id est dirigam, eloquium meum, ipsum orando atque laudando, et secundum voluntatem ipsius loquendo. Scriptum est enim in libro Sapientiæ: Auris zeli audit omnia. Propter hoc, qui loquitur iniqua, non potest latere.
paras.en: Since, then, all things are subject to divine providence, Eliphaz adds: [[5:8|Wherefore I will pray to the Lord|Quamobrem ego deprecabor Dominum]], that he may convert thee and direct me: and to pray to him would be idle unless he had knowledge and providence of things: and because he has, he is always to be entreated; [[5:8|and address|et ad Deum ponam]], that is, direct, [[5:8|my speech to God|eloquium meum]], praying to him and praising him, and speaking according to his will. For it is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 1:10|the ear of jealousy heareth all things|Auris zeli audit omnia]]. [[Wis 1:8|Therefore he that speaketh unjust things, cannot be hid|Propter hoc, qui loquitur iniqua, non potest latere]].

paras.t: Qui facit magna, in operibus naturæ, et inscrutabilia, in mysteriis gratiæ, et mirabilia, in supernaturalibus donis gloriæ, absque numero nobis noto, quamvis non absque numero absolute, quum scriptum sit: Omnia in mensura, et numero, et pondere constituisti. Denique, quod ait, Absque numero, referendum est ad tria prædicta. Quamvis etiam tria præfata per quamdam coaptationem ad opera naturæ et gratiæ ac gloriæ sint relata, nihilominus, tam in operibus naturæ quam gratiæ et gloriæ, efficit Deus magna, quantitate et virtute; et inscrutabilia, quantum ad omnia quæ in rebus creatis consistunt, quorum omnes ac singulas rationes, proprietates, vires et actus, nemo nostrum potest discutere, scrutari et invenire; et mirabilia, quæ considerantium mentes in admirationem convertunt ob eminentiam suam, qualia maxime sunt supernaturalia opera Dei, et quæ proprie miracula appellantur. De quibus fert Psalmista: Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, qui facit mirabilia solus. Hinc rursus cantat Psalmista: Non est similis tui in diis, Domine, et non est secundum opera tua. Quemadmodum enim incomparabilis sapientiæ atque potentiæ actor est Deus, sic decet opera ejus præclarissima esse. Cujus incomparabile opus est totus hic mundus, de quo in libro de Civitate Dei asserit Augustinus: Omni miraculo quod exhiberi potest in mundo, majus miraculum est ipse mundus. Prædicta igitur facit Omnipotens absque numero, secundum modum expositum. Item, quum sit potestatis penitus infinitæ, non potest in tot et tanta per effectum procedere, quin possit in plura atque majora infinities utique.
paras.en: [[5:9|Who doth great things|Qui facit magna]], in the works of nature, [[5:9|and unsearchable|et inscrutabilia]], in the mysteries of grace, [[5:9|and wonderful things|et mirabilia]], in the supernatural gifts of glory, [[5:9|without number|absque numero]] known to us, though not without number absolutely, since it is written: [[Wis 11:21|thou hast ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight|Omnia in mensura, et numero, et pondere constituisti]]. Further, his saying [[5:9|without number|Absque numero]] is to be referred to all three things named before it. And although these three have been referred, by a certain fitting, to the works of nature, of grace and of glory, nevertheless in the works of nature as well as of grace and glory God brings about great things, in quantity and in power; and unsearchable things, as regards all that exists in created things, all and each of whose reasons, properties, powers and acts none of us can examine, search out and find; and wonderful things, which turn the minds of those who consider them to wonder by their excellence, such as above all are the supernatural works of God, those that are properly called miracles. Of these the Psalmist says: [[Ps 71:18|Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone doth wonderful things|Benedictus Dominus Deus Israël, qui facit mirabilia solus.]]. Hence again the Psalmist sings: [[Ps 85:8|There is none among the gods like unto thee, O Lord: and there is none according to thy works|Non est similis tui in diis, Domine, et non est secundum opera tua.]]. For as God is the author of incomparable wisdom and power, so it befits his works to be most excellent. His incomparable work is this whole world, of which Augustine declares in the book of the City of God: "Greater than every miracle that can be shown in the world is the world itself." These things, then, the Almighty does without number, in the way explained. Again, since he is of power wholly infinite, he cannot go forth in effect into so many and such great things but that he could go into more and greater, indeed infinitely so.

paras.t: Præterea, in minimis rebus, sicut in arboris folio atque similibus, excellentiam Dei satis mirari non possumus, neque in particulari assignare omnes rationes formationis, dispositionis ac virtutis hujusmodi rerum. Hinc quinto de Civitate, loquitur Augustinus: Deus nec exigui et contemptibilis animantis viscera, nec avis pennulam, nec herbæ flosculum, nec arboris folium sine suarum convenientia partium et quadam veluti pace reliquit. Unde et Hugo in libro de Tribus diebus, ait: Est verum et evidens divinæ sapientiæ argumentum, quod omne genus sibi simile procreat, et in tam multis similitudo una propagata, primæ originis formam non variat. Unumquodque suam speciem habet, et unumquodque generis sui similitudinem servat. Vide folium quomodo serratis dentibus per gyrum distinguitur; quomodo intrinsecus productis costulis huc illucque intexitur. Numera unum, numera aliud: omne quod unius est generis, unius invenies similitudinis.
paras.en: Moreover, in the least things, as in the leaf of a tree and the like, we cannot wonder enough at the excellence of God, nor assign in particular all the reasons for the forming, the arrangement and the power of such things. Hence Augustine says in the fifth book of the City: "God has not left the inward parts of even a small and contemptible animal, nor the feather of a bird, nor the little flower of a plant, nor the leaf of a tree, without a harmony of their parts and a kind of peace." And so Hugh too says in the book On the Three Days: "It is a true and evident proof of the divine wisdom that every kind brings forth its like, and that one likeness, spread through so many, does not vary the form of its first origin. Each thing has its own species, and each keeps the likeness of its kind. See how the leaf is marked off all round by its toothed edge; how within it is woven this way and that by the little ribs drawn out through it. Count one, count another: everything that is of one kind you will find of one likeness."

paras.t: Qui dat pluviam super faciem, id est superficiem, terræ. Divina etenim ordinatione per solis calorem vapores elevantur in aere, et condensantur ibi in nubes, ac resolvuntur in aquas pluviales, guttatim seu rivulatim in terram ruentes, ut eam fecundent, atque concepta in ea germina nutriant, juxta illud Isaiæ: Descendit imber de cælo, inebriat terram, et germinare eam facit. Quod quia Deo est proprium, loquitur Jeremias: Numquid sunt in diis gentium qui pluant? Et Psalmista: Qui operit cælum nubibus, et parat terræ pluviam. Quod et Christus docet in Evangelio, loquens de Patre, dicensque: Qui pluit super bonos et malos. Hinc legitur in Amos: Qui vocat aquas, et effundit eas super faciem terræ; Dominus nomen ejus. Et irrigat aquis universa terræ nascentia, seu loca terrarum quibus aqua est necessaria: quod facit tempore sibi placente atque præfixo; sæpe autem ob hominum vitia subtrahit beneficium istud. Ait autem Thomas hoc loco: Res naturales contemperatæ esse videntur ad vitam hominum aliorumque animalium conservandam. Unde licet naturalis ordo elementorum aliud requirere videatur (si quis enim in elementis gravitatem et levitatem consideret, manifestum est naturaliter terram in elementis aquæ subjacere, et aeri aquam, aerem vero igni), invenitur tamen aliqua pars terræ discooperta ab aquis, immediate aeri subjacere. Aliter namque animalia respirantia vivere in terra non possent.
paras.en: [[5:10|Who giveth rain upon the face|Qui dat pluviam super faciem]], that is, the surface, [[5:10|of the earth|terræ]]. For by God's ordinance vapours are raised into the air by the heat of the sun, and there they are condensed into clouds, and resolved into rain-waters, falling upon the earth drop by drop or in streams, to make it fruitful and to nourish the seeds conceived in it; according to that word of Isaias: [[Is 55:10|the rain and the snow come down from heaven|Descendit imber de cælo]], [[Is 55:10|soak the earth|inebriat terram]], [[Is 55:10|and make it to spring|et germinare eam facit]]. And because this belongs to God alone, Jeremias says: [[Jer 14:22|Are there any among the graven things of the Gentiles that can send rain?|Numquid sunt in diis gentium qui pluant?]] [Denis reads *in diis*, "among the gods", where the Vulgate has *in sculptilibus*, "among the graven things"] And the Psalmist: [[Ps 146:8|Who covereth the heaven with clouds, and prepareth rain for the earth|Qui operit cælum nubibus, et parat terræ pluviam]]. Christ too teaches this in the Gospel, speaking of the Father and saying: [[Matt 5:45|raineth upon the just and the unjust|Qui pluit super bonos et malos]] [Denis runs together the two clauses of the verse: the Father "maketh his sun to rise upon the good, and bad, and raineth upon the just and the unjust"]. Hence we read in Amos: [[Amos 5:8|that calleth the waters|Qui vocat aquas]], [[Amos 5:8|and poureth them out upon the face of the earth: The Lord is his name|et effundit eas super faciem terræ; Dominus nomen ejus]]. [[5:10|And watereth all things with waters|Et irrigat aquis universa]] that grow from the earth, or the places of the earth that have need of water: which he does at the time that pleases him and that he has fixed; but often, because of men's vices, he withdraws this benefit. Now Thomas says on this place: Natural things seem to be so tempered as to preserve the life of men and of the other animals. Hence, although the natural order of the elements might seem to require otherwise (for if one considers heaviness and lightness in the elements, it is plain that by nature earth lies beneath water among the elements, water beneath air, and air beneath fire), yet some part of the earth is found uncovered by the waters, lying immediately beneath the air. For otherwise animals that breathe could not live upon the earth.

paras.t: Consequenter Eliphaz actum divinæ providentiæ monstrat in dispositionibus hominum. Qui ponit humiles in sublime: quod Deus multipliciter facit, et aliquo modo non facit. Contingit quippe interdum, ut dejectos, humiliatos, contemptos a suis eripiat adversitatibus in præsenti, et ad dignitates, potestates vel prosperitates promoveat, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Sedes ducum superborum destruxit Deus, et sedere fecit mites pro eis. Et Virgo beata: Deposuit, inquit, potentes de sede, et exaltavit humiles. Frequenter quoque contingit oppositum, ita quod quidam electi vel etiam reprobi usque ad ultimum vitæ opprimantur ab impiis, ut patet in multis martyribus. Unde Jacobus ait in sua epistola primitivæ Ecclesiæ filiis: Nonne divites per potentiam opprimunt vos? Porro veraciter humiles, Deo in sancta humilitate subjectos, erigit Deus semper in vita præsenti ad altitudinem gratiæ, in futuro quoque ad sublimitatem gloriæ, dummodo in virtutibus perseverent. Interdumque ponit tales in sublimitate præsidentiæ spiritualis aut sæcularis, dando fidelibus principes aut prælatos idoneos et condignos.
paras.en: Next Eliphaz shows the working of divine providence in the ordering of men's affairs. [[5:11|Who setteth up the humble on high|Qui ponit humiles in sublime]]: which God does in many ways, and in some way does not do. For it happens at times that he delivers the cast down, the humbled and the despised from their adversities in this present life, and promotes them to dignities, powers or prosperity, according to that word of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:17|God hath overturned the thrones of proud princes, and hath set up the meek in their stead.|Sedes ducum superborum destruxit Deus, et sedere fecit mites pro eis.]] And the Blessed Virgin: [[Luke 1:52|He hath put down|Deposuit]], she says, [[Luke 1:52|the mighty from their seat and hath exalted the humble|potentes de sede, et exaltavit humiles]]. Often, too, the opposite happens, so that some of the elect, or even of the reprobate, are oppressed by the wicked to the very end of their life, as is plain in many martyrs. Hence James says in his epistle to the sons of the primitive Church: [[Jas 2:6|Do not the rich oppress you by might?|Nonne divites per potentiam opprimunt vos?]] But the truly humble, those subject to God in holy humility, God always raises up in the present life to the height of grace, and in the life to come to the sublimity of glory, provided they persevere in the virtues. And at times he sets such men on the height of spiritual or secular rule, giving the faithful princes or prelates who are fit and worthy.

paras.t: Et mœrentes erigit sospitate, id est, eos qui bono ac virtuoso afficiuntur dolore, sua vel proximorum peccata deflendo, Christi passionibus condolendo, Dei injuriam, Ecclesiæ ruinam, cælestis beatitudinis dilationem ex caritatis fervore plangendo: tales Deus a sua mœstitia transfert ad consolationem, ad animi sanitatem, ad mentis vigorem, sicut et Christus promittit: Beati qui lugent, quoniam ipsi consolabuntur. Ideo ad Corinthios ait Apostolus: Benedictus Deus qui consolatur nos in omni tribulatione nostra. Et rursus: Sicut abundant passiones Christi in nobis, ita per Christum abundat consolatio nostra. Itemque Psalmista: Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo, consolationes tuæ lætificaverunt animam meam. Itaque, tempore adversitatis et afflictionis simus constantes, Dei misericordiam fiducialiter implorantes, ac longanimiter præstolantes, illud Tobiæ intuentes: Non delectaris, Domine, in perditionibus nostris, quia post tempestatem tranquillum facis, et post fletum exsultationem infundis.
paras.en: [[5:11|and comforteth with health those that mourn|Et mœrentes erigit sospitate]]: that is, those who are moved by a good and virtuous sorrow, bewailing their own sins or their neighbours', suffering with the sufferings of Christ, lamenting from the fervour of charity the wrong done to God, the ruin of the Church, the delay of heavenly beatitude: such men God brings from their sadness to consolation, to health of soul, to vigour of mind, as Christ also promises: [[Matt 5:5|Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.|Beati qui lugent: quoniam ipsi consolabuntur.]] Therefore the Apostle says to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 1:3|Blessed be the God|Benedictus Deus]] [[2 Cor 1:4|Who comforteth us in all our tribulation|qui consolatur nos in omni tribulatione nostra]]. And again: [[2 Cor 1:5|as the sufferings of Christ abound in us: so also by Christ doth our comfort abound|Sicut abundant passiones Christi in nobis, ita per Christum abundat consolatio nostra]]. And likewise the Psalmist: [[Ps 93:19|According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, thy comforts have given joy to my soul.|Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo, consolationes tuæ lætificaverunt animam meam.]] So in time of adversity and affliction let us be constant, imploring God's mercy with confidence and waiting for it with long patience, keeping before our eyes that word of Tobias: [[Tob 3:22|thou art not delighted in our being lost, because after a storm thou makest a calm, and after tears and weeping thou pourest in joyfulness|Non delectaris, Domine, in perditionibus nostris, quia post tempestatem tranquillum facis, et post fletum exsultationem infundis]].

paras.t: Qui dissipat, id est, ab opere ac fine intento multoties impedit, cogitationes malignorum, quibus contra justos insidiose cogitaverunt, ne possint implere manus eorum, id est potentiæ operativæ, vel etiam corporales manus, quæ sunt instrumenta intellectus practici, sicut lingua instrumentum est intellectus speculativi, quod cœperant, vel per cordis affectum, vel per operis inchoationem. Deus quippe suorum defensor est, et insidias impiorum frequenter convertit in caput eorum, quemadmodum in libris Regum, Paralipomenon ac Judicum, per multa exempla describitur, pugnante Deo pro Israel. Prout etiam in Esdra habetur: Dissipavit Deus consilia eorum, videlicet Samaritanorum. Ideo cantat Psalmista: Dominus dissipat consilia gentium, reprobat autem cogitationes populorum. Et in Isaia impiis dicitur: Inite consilium, et dissipabitur; accingite vos, et vincimini.
paras.en: [[5:12|Who bringeth to nought|Qui dissipat]], that is, very often hinders from the work and the end they intended, [[5:12|the designs of the malignant|cogitationes malignorum]], which they have craftily devised against the just, [[5:12|so that their hands cannot accomplish|ne possint implere manus eorum]] (that is, their working powers, or even their bodily hands, which are the instruments of the practical intellect, as the tongue is the instrument of the speculative intellect) [[5:12|what they had begun|quod cœperant]], whether by the heart's desire or by beginning the work. For God is the defender of his own, and often turns the snares of the wicked upon their own heads, as is described by many examples in the books of Kings, of Paralipomenon and of Judges, God fighting for Israel. So too we have in Esdras: [[2 Esd 4:15|God defeated their counsel|Dissipavit Deus consilia eorum]], that is, the counsel of the Samaritans. Therefore the Psalmist sings: [[Ps 32:10|The Lord bringeth to nought the counsels of nations; and he rejecteth the devices of people|Dominus dissipat consilia gentium, reprobat autem cogitationes populorum]]. And in Isaias it is said to the wicked: [[Is 8:10|Take counsel together, and it shall be defeated|Inite consilium, et dissipabitur]]; [[Is 8:9|gird yourselves, and be overcome|accingite vos, et vincimini]].

paras.t: Qui apprehendit, id est, concludit, capit, vincit et impedit, sapientes, secundum carnem et sæculum, id est astutos et callidos, in astutia eorum, convertendo fraudulentam eorum versutiam in nocumentum et damnationem ipsorum; innocentes quoque, justos et simplices eruendo ab illis, quemadmodum in Absalone, Achitophel, et Aman legitur factum. Ideo dicit Psalmista de fraudulento: Lacum aperuit et effodit; et incidit in foveam quam fecit. In Isaia quoque legitur: Sapientia tua et scientia decepit te. Veniet super te malum, et nescies ortum ejus. Hinc in Proverbiis ait Scriptura: Abominatio est Domino omnis illusor, et illusores ipse deludet. Cum simplicibus autem sermocinatio ejus. Sincero ergo, vero ac simplici corde coram Domino ambulemus, omnem simulationem, duplicitatem, dolositatem vitantes. Quum enim similitudo sit causa amoris, ipseque Deus gloriosus ac adorandus, sit supersincerissima, simplicissima atque rectissima mens, constat quod astutos et fraudulentos vehementer abhorreat, sinceros vero, rectos et simplices præcipue amet.
paras.en: [[5:13|Who catcheth|Qui apprehendit]], that is, shuts in, takes, overcomes and hinders, [[5:13|the wise|sapientes]] according to the flesh and the world, that is, the cunning and the crafty, [[5:13|in their craftiness|in astutia eorum]], turning their deceitful wiles to their own harm and damnation, and delivering from them the innocent too, the just and the simple, as we read was done in the case of Absalom, Achitophel[[2 Kings 17:23||]] and Aman[[Esth 7:10||]]. Therefore the Psalmist says of the deceitful man: [[Ps 7:16|He hath opened a pit and dug it: and he is fallen into the hole he made.|Lacum aperuit et effodit; et incidit in foveam quam fecit]] And in Isaias too we read: [[Is 47:10|Thy wisdom, and, thy knowledge, this hath deceived thee|Sapientia tua et scientia decepit te]]. [[Is 47:11|Evil shall come upon thee, and thou shalt not know the rising thereof|Veniet super te malum, et nescies ortum ejus]]. Hence Scripture says in Proverbs: [[Prov 3:32|every mocker is an abomination to the Lord|Abominatio est Domino omnis illusor]], and [[Prov 3:34|He shall scorn the scorners|illusores ipse deludet]]; [[Prov 3:32|and his communication is with the simple|Cum simplicibus autem sermocinatio ejus]]. Let us walk, then, before the Lord with a sincere, true and simple heart, shunning all pretence, doubleness and guile. For since likeness is the cause of love, and God himself, glorious and adorable, is a mind supremely sincere, most simple and most upright, it is certain that he vehemently abhors the cunning and the deceitful, and loves above all the sincere, the upright and the simple.

paras.t: Denique, ut in Proverbiis habetur: Non est sapientia, non est scientia, non est consilium contra Dominum. Hinc frequenter contingit, quod quanto quidam astuti atque dolosi acutius contra justitiam cogitant, et quæ recta sunt Deoque placita, callidius impedire conantur, eo plus oppositum accidit: quemadmodum tyranni quo graviora martyribus intulerunt supplicia, ut christianam fidem penitus abolerent, eo amplius per beatissimorum martyrum constantiam, merita atque miracula, crevit Religio christiana. Propter quod fertur in Psalmo: Narraverunt ut absconderent laqueos. Dixerunt: Quis videbit eos? Scrutati sunt iniquitates, defecerunt scrutantes scrutinia. Unde mox subditur, et consilia pravorum dissipat: contraria consiliatis inducendo, vel saltem vana consilia ab effectu impediendo, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Facienti nequissimum consilium, super ipsum devolvetur, et non cognoscet unde illi adveniat illusio. Sic legitur Deus dissipasse consilia Achitophel, sicut et David oravit: Infatua, quæso, Domine, consilium Achitophel. Hinc in Isaia fertur de Deo: Dat scrutatores secretorum quasi non sint. Præterea contemplandum, quod Deus sublimis et benedictus frequenter justo atque occulto judicio permittit filios hujus sæculi, reprobos, dolosos et ambitiosos, cogitationes suas astutas et iniqua consilia ad effectum perducere concupitum, et mirabiliter prosperari in adinventionibus suis, ad graviorem eorum damnationem. Finaliter tamen apprehendet eos in suis astutiis, quando revelabit abscondita tenebrarum, et manifestabit consilia cordium. Tunc enim juxta exigentiam impietatis ac fraudulentiæ suæ, confusiones sortientur et pœnas, juxta quod in Proverbiis prædicitur: Comedent igitur fructus viæ suæ, suisque consiliis saturabuntur.
paras.en: Finally, as we have it in Proverbs: [[Prov 21:30|There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord|Non est sapientia, non est scientia, non est consilium contra Dominum]] [Denis reads *scientia*, "knowledge", where the Vulgate has *prudentia*]. Hence it often happens that the more sharply certain cunning and deceitful men devise against justice, and the more craftily they try to hinder what is right and pleasing to God, the more the opposite comes about: as the heavier the torments the tyrants inflicted on the martyrs in order to abolish the Christian faith altogether, the more the Christian religion grew through the constancy, the merits and the miracles of the most blessed martyrs. For this reason it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 63:6|They have talked of hiding snares; they have said: Who shall see them?|Narraverunt ut absconderent laqueos. Dixerunt: Quis videbit eos?]] [[Ps 63:7|They have searched after iniquities: they have failed in their search|Scrutati sunt iniquitates, defecerunt scrutantes scrutinia]]. And so there follows at once: [[5:13|and disappointeth the counsel of the wicked|et consilia pravorum dissipat]], bringing about the contrary of what they counselled, or at least keeping their vain counsels from taking effect; according to that word of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 27:30|A mischievous counsel shall be rolled back upon the author, and he shall not know from whence it cometh to him|Facienti nequissimum consilium, super ipsum devolvetur, et non cognoscet unde illi adveniat illusio]] [Denis adds *illusio*, "mockery": "he shall not know whence the mockery cometh to him"]. So we read that God brought to nought the counsels of Achitophel[[2 Kings 17:14||]], as David also prayed: [[2 Kings 15:31|Infatuate, O Lord, I beseech thee, the counsel of Achitophel|Infatua, quæso, Domine, consilium Achitophel]] [the margin here is partly illegible; the defeat of Achitophel's counsel is told at 2 Kings 17:14, David's prayer at 2 Kings 15:31]. Hence it is said of God in Isaias: [[Is 40:23|He that bringeth the searchers of secrets to nothing|Dat scrutatores secretorum quasi non sint]]. Moreover we should consider that God, exalted and blessed, often by a just and hidden judgment allows the children of this world, the reprobate, deceitful and ambitious, to bring their cunning thoughts and wicked counsels to the effect they desired, and to prosper wonderfully in their inventions, to their heavier damnation. Yet in the end he will catch them in their craftiness, when he [[1 Cor 4:5|will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts|revelabit abscondita tenebrarum, et manifestabit consilia cordium]]. For then, as the measure of their impiety and deceit requires, they will receive confusion and punishment, as is foretold in Proverbs: [[Prov 1:31|Therefore they shall eat the fruit of their own way, and shall be filled with their own devices.|Comedent igitur fructus viæ suæ, suisque consiliis saturabuntur.]]

paras.t: Per diem, id est, dum prosperari et luce sapientiæ suæ non vere uti videntur, incurrent tenebras adversitatis et ignorantiæ, ita quod in consiliando circumspecti non erunt, et quasi in nocte sic palpabunt in meridie, id est, eatenus excæcabuntur in mente, quod in his quæ tam clare vera ac justa sunt sicut meridies, nutabunt, dubitabunt, errabunt, sicut in his quæ magnæ sunt difficultatis et obscuritatis. Rursus, dum in maxima videntur suæ prosperitatis ac sæcularis prudentiæ claritate consistere, gravius obtenebrantur in corde. Quibus consonat illud Isaiæ: Palpavimus sicut cæci parietem, et quasi absque oculis contrectavimus; impegimus meridie quasi in tenebris. Ad quod spiritualiter pertinet illud: Occidit ei sol quum adhuc esset meridies. Denique in omnibus his videtur Eliphaz sanctum Job tangere, quasi ipse occulte vitiosus astutusque fuerit, atque per plagam sibi inflictam impeditus sit implere quæ male concepit; et quando maxime florere apparuit, subito est dejectus. Est enim consuetudo quibusdam, ut quum aliquem pungere velint, disputent in generali contra peccata, quibus eum implicatum sciri insinuareque cupiunt.
paras.en: [[5:14|in the day|Per diem]], that is, while they seem to prosper and to use the light of their wisdom (not truly so), [[5:14|They shall meet with darkness|incurrent tenebras]] of adversity and of ignorance, so that they will not be circumspect in taking counsel; [[5:14|and grope at noonday as in the night|et quasi in nocte sic palpabunt in meridie]]: that is, they will be blinded in mind to such a degree that in things as clearly true and just as the noonday they will waver, doubt and go astray, as in things of great difficulty and obscurity. Again, while they seem to stand in the fullest brightness of their prosperity and worldly prudence, they are the more grievously darkened in heart. With this agrees that word of Isaias: [[Is 59:10|We have groped for the wall, and like the blind we have groped as if we had no eyes: we have stumbled at noonday as in darkness|Palpavimus sicut cæci parietem, et quasi absque oculis contrectavimus; impegimus meridie quasi in tenebris]]. And to this belongs, in the spiritual sense, that word: [[Jer 15:9|her sun is gone down, while it was yet day|Occidit ei sol quum adhuc esset meridies]] [Denis reads *meridies*, "noonday", where the Vulgate has *dies*, "day"]. Lastly, in all these things Eliphaz seems to be touching holy Job, as though he had been secretly vicious and cunning, and had been hindered by the stroke laid upon him from carrying out what he had wickedly conceived; and, just when he seemed most to flourish, had suddenly been cast down. For it is the custom of some, when they wish to sting someone, to argue in general against the sins in which they want him to be known to be entangled, and to hint as much.

paras.t: Porro salvum faciet egenum de gladio oris eorum, id est de verbis eorum detractoriis, maledictoriis, pungitivis: quæ gladio comparantur, quoniam penetrant viscera mentis. Unde in Psalmo: Gladius in labiis eorum; et: Lingua eorum gladius acutus. In Proverbiis quoque: Est generatio quæ pro dentibus habet gladios, et commandit molaribus suis, ut comedat inopes de terra, et pauperes ex hominibus. Et de manu violenti, pauperem. Quandoque hæc Deus facit in vita hac; interdum vero permittit innocentes, justos et inopes usque ad mortem ab impiis molestari. Hinc ait Psalmista ad Dominum: Tibi derelictus est pauper, orphano tu eris adjutor. Et in Jeremia scriptum est: Laudate Dominum, quia liberavit animam pauperis de manu malorum.
paras.en: [[5:15|But he shall save the needy from the sword of their mouth|Porro salvum faciet egenum de gladio oris eorum]], that is, from their words of detraction, cursing and stinging: which are likened to a sword because they pierce the inmost parts of the mind. Hence in the Psalm: [[Ps 58:8|a sword is in their lips|Gladius in labiis eorum]]; and: [[Ps 56:5|their tongue a sharp sword|Lingua eorum gladius acutus]]. In Proverbs too: [[Prov 30:14|A generation that for teeth hath swords, and grindeth with their jaw teeth, to devour the needy from off the earth, and the poor from among men.|Est generatio quæ pro dentibus habet gladios, et commandit molaribus suis, ut comedat inopes de terra, et pauperes ex hominibus]] [[5:15|and the poor from the hand of the violent|Et de manu violenti, pauperem]]. Sometimes God does this in this life; but at times he allows the innocent, the just and the needy to be harried by the wicked even to death. Hence the Psalmist says to the Lord: [[Ps 9:35|To thee is the poor man left: thou wilt be a helper to the orphan|Tibi derelictus est pauper, orphano tu eris adjutor]] [the margin gives Ps. ix, 14, the Hebrew numbering; in the Vulgate the words are at Ps 9:35]. And in Jeremias it is written: [[Jer 20:13|praise the Lord: because he hath delivered the soul of the poor out of the hand of the wicked|Laudate Dominum, quia liberavit animam pauperis de manu malorum]].

paras.t: Et erit egeno spes evadendi. Ex hoc enim quod experitur auxilium Dei et providentiam ejus circa regimen hominum, spem suam ponit in Deo. Ipseque Deus est spes ejus, id est objectum suæ fiduciæ, tanto amplius, quanto minus ab hominibus videt se adjuvandum. Sic et nos semper in Domino confidamus, obtemperando ejus mandatis, juxta illud: Spera in Deo tuo semper. Iniquitas autem contrahet os suum, id est, iniqui divina potestate repressi, a solitis pravitatis suæ sermonibus refrenabuntur. Hoc et Psalmista fatetur: Adjuvit, inquit, pauperem de inopia; et omnis iniquitas oppilabit os suum. Et iterum: Obstructum est os loquentium iniqua.
