Per Isaiam quoque impio loquitur Deus: Ponam circulum in naribus tuis, et frenum maxillis tuis.
paras.en: [[5:16|And to the needy there shall be hope|Et erit egeno spes]] of escape. For from his experience of God's help and of his providence in the governing of men, he puts his hope in God. And God himself is his hope, that is, the object of his trust, and the more so the less he sees that he is to be helped by men. So let us too always trust in the Lord, obeying his commandments, according to that word: [[Osee 12:6|hope in thy God always|Spera in Deo tuo semper]]. [[5:16|but iniquity shall draw in her mouth|Iniquitas autem contrahet os suum]], that is, the wicked, held down by the power of God, will be curbed from the words of wickedness that they are used to. The Psalmist too declares this: [[Ps 106:41|he helped|Adjuvit]], he says, [[Ps 106:41|the poor out of poverty|pauperem de inopia]]; [[Ps 106:42|and all iniquity shall stop her mouth|et omnis iniquitas oppilabit os suum]]. And again: [[Ps 62:12|the mouth is stopped of them that speak wicked things|Obstructum est os loquentium iniqua]]. Through Isaias too God says to the wicked man: [[Is 37:29|I will put a ring in thy nose, and a bit between thy lips|Ponam circulum in naribus tuis, et frenum maxillis tuis]] [Denis reads *maxillis*, "jaws", where the Vulgate has *in labiis*, "lips"].

paras.t: Beatus homo qui corripitur a Domino, id est, qui in præsenti castigatur et emendatur a Deo per suæ paternæ pietatis flagella aut increpatoria verba. Hoc enim est signum paternæ dilectionis, curæ atque clementiæ Dei ad hominem, quum peccata sint animæ vulnera, quæ per adversa tanquam emplastra optimaque remedia jam curantur. Propter quod Dominus protestatur: Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo. Et alibi inducitur: Etenim multo tempore non sinere peccatoribus ex sententia agere, sed statim ultiones adhibere, magni beneficii est indicium. Hinc Jeremias sapienter rogavit: Corripe me, Domine; verumtamen in judicio, et non in furore tuo. Porro non castigari ita a Deo, sed in propriis voluntatibus derelinqui, et cum securitate peccare atque ad libitum prosperari, horribilissimum est, indiciumque maximæ iræ ac odii Dei, et metuendissima ultio ejus, secundum quod ipse de reprobis fatetur in Psalmo: Dimisi eos secundum desideria cordis eorum; ibunt in adinventionibus suis. Et per Ezechielem indurato populo ait: Zelus meus recessit a te: non irascar tibi amplius. Cupiamus ergo nunc visitari a Deo; patientiamque postulemus ab eo, qua omnem vitæ hujus adversitatem æquanimiter toleremus, tanquam purgamentum vitiorum nostrorum, et tanquam præparamentum gratiæ amplioris, pensantes illud Apostoli: Quum judicamur autem, a Domino corripimur, ut non cum hoc mundo damnemur. Et illud: Quis filius quem non corripit pater? Quod si extra disciplinam estis, ergo adulteri, et non filii estis.
paras.en: [[5:17|Blessed is the man whom God correcteth|Beatus homo qui corripitur a Domino]], that is, who in this present life is chastised and amended by God through the scourges or the rebuking words of his fatherly love. For this is a sign of God's fatherly love, care and clemency towards man, since sins are wounds of the soul, which are healed even now by adversities as by plasters and the best of remedies. For this reason the Lord declares: [[Apoc 3:19|Such as I love, I rebuke and chastise|Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo]]. And elsewhere it is set down: [[2 Mach 6:13|it is a token of great goodness, when sinners are not suffered to go on in their ways for a long time, but are presently punished|Etenim multo tempore non sinere peccatoribus ex sententia agere, sed statim ultiones adhibere, magni beneficii est indicium]]. Hence Jeremias wisely prayed: [[Jer 10:24|Correct me, O Lord, but yet with judgment: and not in thy fury|Corripe me, Domine; verumtamen in judicio, et non in furore tuo]]. But not to be chastised thus by God, and instead to be left to one's own will, to sin without fear and to prosper at one's pleasure, is most horrible: a sign of God's greatest wrath and hatred, and his most fearful vengeance; as he himself declares of the reprobate in the Psalm: [[Ps 80:13|I let them go according to the desires of their heart: they shall walk in their own inventions|Dimisi eos secundum desideria cordis eorum; ibunt in adinventionibus suis]]. And through Ezechiel he says to the hardened people: [[Ezech 16:42|my jealousy shall depart from thee|Zelus meus recessit a te]]: I will [[Ezech 16:42|be angry no more|non irascar tibi amplius]]. Let us desire, then, to be visited by God now; and let us ask him for patience, by which we may bear every adversity of this life with an even mind, as a purging of our vices and a preparing for fuller grace, weighing that word of the Apostle: [[1 Cor 11:32|But whilst we are judged, we are chastised by the Lord, that we be not condemned with this world|Quum judicamur autem, a Domino corripimur, ut non cum hoc mundo damnemur]]. And that one: [[Heb 12:7|what son is there whom the father doth not correct?|Quis filius quem non corripit pater?]] [[Heb 12:8|But if you be without chastisement|Quod si extra disciplinam estis]], [[Heb 12:8|then are you bastards and not sons|ergo adulteri, et non filii estis]].

paras.t: Ex his Eliphaz convertit se ad exhortationem ipsius Job, quem putavit ex impatientia, desperatione et tædio vitæ, verba capituli tertii protulisse etiam secundum rationem passione devictam, videlicet, Pereat dies in qua natus sum. Increpationem ergo Domini, id est hanc tuam tribulationem et quamcumque adversitatem tibi ex judicio divinæ providentiæ accidentem, ne reprobes, murmurando et maledicendo; quia ipse vulnerat, peccatorem in corpore plagando, et medetur, inflictam plagam tollendo, et consolationem præstando, a vitiisque purgando: imo vulnerando medetur, ita quod ejus vulneratio est peccati medela. Pœnæ etenim vitæ præsentis sunt remedia vitiorum. Sic et medicus vulnerando medetur, dum incidendo expellit materiam morbum causantem. Percutit pœna, et manus ejus sanabunt a culpa, itemque crebro a pœna inflicta, quemadmodum in Deuteronomio testatur: Ego occidam, et ego vivere faciam; percutiam, et ego sanabo. Salomon quoque huic alludit doctrinæ, dicens: Disciplinam Domini, fili mi, ne abjicias, et ne deficias quum ab eo corriperis. Quem enim diligit Dominus, corripit; et quasi pater in filio complacet sibi. Et Apostolus ad Hebræos: Omnis disciplina in præsenti quidem non videtur esse gaudii, sed mœroris; postea autem fructum pacatissimum exercitatis per eam reddet justitiæ. Postremo, ad patientem ac humilem disciplinæ, sive in verbis, sive in pœnis susceptionem, potissime monent nos libri Sapientiales; laudantque eos, qui eam gratanter recipiunt, eam vero spernentes dire vituperant. Hinc nempe scriptum est: Egestas et ignominia ei qui deserit disciplinam; qui autem acquiescit arguenti, glorificabitur. Alibi quoque: Qui projicit disciplinam, despicit animam suam; qui autem acquiescit increpationibus, possessor est cordis. Similiter in Ecclesiastico legitur: Quam bonum est correptum manifestare pœnitentiam! Sic enim effugies peccatum.
paras.en: From this Eliphaz turns to exhorting Job himself, whom he thought had spoken the words of the third chapter out of impatience, despair and weariness of life, and even with his reason overcome by passion: namely, [[Job 3:3|Let the day perish wherein I was born|Pereat dies in qua natus sum]]. Therefore [[5:17|the chastising of the Lord|Increpationem ergo Domini]], that is, this tribulation of yours and whatever adversity befalls you by the judgment of divine providence, [[5:17|refuse not|ne reprobes]] it by murmuring and cursing; [[5:18|For he woundeth|quia ipse vulnerat]], striking the sinner in his body, [[5:18|and cureth|et medetur]], taking away the stroke he has dealt, giving consolation and purging from vices: nay, he heals by wounding, so that his wounding is the remedy of sin. For the pains of the present life are remedies for vices. So too the physician heals by wounding, when by cutting he drives out the matter that causes the disease. [[5:18|he striketh|Percutit]] with punishment, [[5:18|and his hands shall heal|et manus ejus sanabunt]] from guilt, and often also from the punishment inflicted; as he testifies in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 32:39|I will kill and I will make to live: I will strike, and I will heal|Ego occidam, et ego vivere faciam; percutiam, et ego sanabo]]. Solomon too alludes to this teaching, saying: [[Prov 3:11|My son, reject not the correction of the Lord: and do not faint when thou art chastised by him:|Disciplinam Domini, fili mi, ne abjicias, et ne deficias quum ab eo corriperis]] [[Prov 3:12|For whom the Lord loveth, he chastiseth: and as a father in the son he pleaseth himself.|Quem enim diligit Dominus, corripit; et quasi pater in filio complacet sibi]] And the Apostle to the Hebrews: [[Heb 12:11|all chastisement for the present indeed seemeth not to bring with it joy, but sorrow: but afterwards it will yield to them that are exercised by it the most peaceable fruit of justice|Omnis disciplina in præsenti quidem non videtur esse gaudii, sed mœroris; postea autem fructum pacatissimum exercitatis per eam reddet justitiæ]]. Lastly, the Sapiential books above all urge us to receive correction patiently and humbly, whether in words or in punishments; and they praise those who receive it gladly, but sharply rebuke those who spurn it. For thus it is written: [[Prov 13:18|Poverty and shame to him that refuseth instruction: but he that yieldeth to reproof shall be glorified.|Egestas et ignominia ei qui deserit disciplinam; qui autem acquiescit arguenti, glorificabitur]] And elsewhere: [[Prov 15:32|He that rejecteth instruction, despiseth his own soul: but he that yieldeth to reproof, possesseth understanding.|Qui projicit disciplinam, despicit animam suam; qui autem acquiescit increpationibus, possessor est cordis]] [Denis reads *projicit*, "casteth away", where the Vulgate has *abjicit*] Likewise we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 20:4|How good is it, when thou art reproved, to shew repentance!|Quam bonum est correptum manifestare pœnitentiam!]] [[Ecclus 20:4|for so thou shalt escape|Sic enim effugies]] sin.

paras.t: Consequenter Eliphaz specificat, a quibus adversitatibus eruendus fuerit Job, si pœnitentiam veram egisset, atque illata flagella de manu Dei æquanimiter suscepisset. In sex tribulationibus liberabit te, et in septima non tanget te malum. Hæc autem liberatio dupliciter potest intelligi. Primo, per anticipationem, ita quod nulla earum eveniet justo, seu peccatori per pœnitentiam et flagella sufficienter purgato et emendato. Secundo, per sublationem, ita quod quum aliqua earum cuique evenerit, auferetur, si ille pœnitentiam fecerit. Quumque per sex fuerit emendatus, in septima adversum nil patietur.
paras.en: Next Eliphaz specifies from what adversities Job would have been delivered if he had done true penance and had borne with an even mind the scourges laid on him by the hand of God. [[5:19|In six troubles he shall deliver thee, and in the seventh, evil shall not touch thee.|In sex tribulationibus liberabit te, et in septima non tanget te malum.]] Now this deliverance can be understood in two ways. First, by prevention: so that none of them shall befall the just man, or the sinner sufficiently purged and amended by penance and scourges. Secondly, by removal: so that when any of them befalls someone, it will be taken away if he does penance. And when he has been amended through six, in the seventh he will suffer nothing adverse.

paras.t: Deinde nominat tribulationes. In fame eruet te de morte, id est, tempore caristiæ aliis fame labentibus, necessaria vitæ habebis. Vel, In fame, id est, si famem ex naturalium defectu pertuleris, providebitur tibi a Deo ne pereas fame. Et in bello de manu gladii, id est, si in bellum descenderis, non permittet te Deus occidi. Hæc est tribulatio secunda. De tertia subditur: A flagello linguæ absconderis, id est, persecutionem verborum ab aliis non patieris, videlicet detractionem, convitia, diffamiam. Justus enim, vereque pœnitens, digni sunt laudibus, exemplaresque aliis. Ideo eis non debent verborum inferre molestiam. Unde Ecclesiasticus dicit: A laqueo linguæ iniquæ liberasti me. Hæc tria Eliphaz commemoravit, quoniam fames causata est sancto Job ex ablatione substantiæ; bellum, quia Chaldæi contra eum tres turmas fecerunt; flagellum linguæ ex improperio conjugis. Et non timebis calamitatem, id est cladem pestilentialem sive hostilem, quum venerit aliis, certus de protectione divina. Hæc est tribulatio quarta. Alias duas tangens, subjungit: In vastitate, id est fructuum devastatione vel hominum oppressione, et fame inde procedente, ridebis, id est, lætus eris, quia nullum istorum tunc patieris. Sed quum superius posuerit famem pro prima tribulatione, cur nunc eam resumit et ponit pro sexta? Et respondendum, quod ibi sumitur fames pro ea, quæ generatur ex terræ sterilitate; hic pro ea, quæ concomitatur vastitatem terræ ab hostibus. Hæc tria Eliphaz dixit, quoniam filii et filiæ Job erant sibi repente ablati, sicut in pestilentia; et quoniam bona ejus erant a Chaldæis et Sabæis vastata, ex qua re etiam penuria sibi exorta est. Et bestias terræ non formidabis, quia securus eris, quod nec tibi, nec soboli aut familiæ, seu gregibus tuis nocebunt.
paras.en: Then he names the tribulations. [[5:20|In famine he shall deliver thee from death|In fame eruet te de morte]]: that is, in a time of dearth, when others are failing from hunger, thou shalt have the necessities of life. Or, [[5:20|In famine|In fame]]: that is, if thou suffer hunger through a failure of the fruits of nature, God will provide for thee so that thou perish not of hunger. [[5:20|and in battle, from the hand of the sword|Et in bello de manu gladii]]: that is, if thou go down to war, God will not let thee be slain. This is the second tribulation. Of the third he adds: [[5:21|Thou shalt be hidden from the scourge of the tongue|A flagello linguæ absconderis]]: that is, thou shalt not suffer persecution of words from others, namely detraction, abuse, defamation. For the just and the truly penitent are worthy of praise and an example to others; therefore men ought not to trouble them with words. Hence Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 51:3|from the snare of an unjust tongue|A laqueo linguæ iniquæ]] thou hast delivered me. Eliphaz mentioned these three because hunger was brought upon holy Job by the taking away of his substance; war, because the Chaldeans made three troops against him; and the scourge of the tongue by the reproaches of his wife. [[5:21|and thou shalt not fear calamity|Et non timebis calamitatem]], that is, slaughter by pestilence or by the enemy, [[5:21|when it cometh|quum venerit]] upon others, being sure of God's protection. This is the fourth tribulation. Touching on the other two, he adds: [[5:22|In destruction|In vastitate]], that is, in the laying waste of the fruits or the oppression of men, [[5:22|and famine|et fame]] that comes of it, [[5:22|thou shalt laugh|ridebis]], that is, thou shalt be glad, because thou shalt then suffer none of these things. But since he set down famine above as the first tribulation, why does he now take it up again and set it down as the sixth? The answer is that there famine is taken for that which is produced by the barrenness of the earth; here, for that which goes with the laying waste of the land by enemies. Eliphaz said these three things because Job's sons and daughters had been suddenly taken from him, as in a pestilence; and because his goods had been laid waste by the Chaldeans and the Sabeans, from which want also arose for him. [[5:22|and thou shalt not be afraid of the beasts of the earth|Et bestias terræ non formidabis]], because thou shalt be sure that they will do no harm to thee, nor to thy offspring or household, nor to thy flocks.

paras.t: Denique, verba hæc Eliphaz ad litteram generaliter stare non possunt. Quamvis interdum contingat justos, seu per pœnitentiam emendatos, ab his erui malis, non autem semper sic fit: imo sæpe virtuosi hæc patiuntur, vitiosi vero ab eis immunes sunt. Nam et Apostolus ait: Esurimus et sitimus. Multique martyrum ac justorum afflicti aut etiam perempti sunt fame. In præliis quoque interdum cadunt qui justam causam habebant, et sceleratissimi prævalent, sicut et filii Benjamin bis prævaluerunt contra filios Israel. Sed et justi detractionibus invidorum quotidie corroduntur, et ceteris adversitatibus jam præfatis electi a reprobis exercentur, juxta quod scriptum est in eorum persona: Quoniam propter te mortificamur tota die.
paras.en: However, these words of Eliphaz cannot stand as a general rule in the literal sense. Although it sometimes happens that the just, or those amended by penance, are delivered from these evils, it is not always so: on the contrary, the virtuous often suffer them, while the vicious are free of them. For the Apostle too says: [[1 Cor 4:11|we both hunger and thirst|Esurimus et sitimus]]. And many of the martyrs and of the just have been afflicted or even killed by hunger. In battles too those who had a just cause sometimes fall, and the most wicked prevail, as the children of Benjamin twice prevailed against the children of Israel[[Judg 20:21||]] [the margin gives Judg. xx, 16–25; the two victories of Benjamin are at vv. 21 and 25]. And the just are daily gnawed by the detractions of the envious, and the elect are tried by the reprobate with the other adversities already mentioned, according to what is written in their person: [[Ps 43:22|Because for thy sake we are killed all the day long|Quoniam propter te mortificamur tota die]].

paras.t: Deinde Eliphaz spondet beato Job abundantiam bonorum post sublationem malorum. Sed cum lapidibus regionum pactum tuum, id est, terræ saxosæ erunt tibi fructiferæ, quasi fœdus amicitiæ tecum inierint. Ita exponit Thomas. Quodque subjungitur, et bestiæ terræ pacificæ erunt tibi, exponit de brutis, quod ei nocumentum non inferent. Albertus vero, per lapides terræ, intelligit viros constantes, ob animi soliditatem sic dictos, cum quibus erit ei pactum socialis atque pacificæ conversationis; per bestias autem, intelligit crudeles sive tyrannos. Et scies, per experientiam, quod pacem habeat tabernaculum tuum, id est, domus tua erit quieta, et bene disposita in personis, rebus et fabricis; et visitans speciem tuam, id est proximum tuum seu conjugem ejusdem tecum speciei exsistentem, non peccabis, inordinate te ad eos habendo, sed moderate. Vel, Visitans speciem tuam, id est divitiarum et rerum decorem, non peccabis per superfluum affectum ad talia. Et scies quoniam multiplex erit semen tuum, id est, filii tui multi erunt et plurimos generabunt, et progenies tua erit virens, fecunda et pulchra, sicut herba terræ.
paras.en: Next Eliphaz promises blessed Job an abundance of good things after his evils are taken away. [[5:23|But thou shalt have a covenant with the stones of the lands|Sed cum lapidibus regionum pactum tuum]]: that is, stony lands will bear fruit for thee, as though they had made a covenant of friendship with thee. So Thomas explains it. And what is added, [[5:23|and the beasts of the earth shall be at peace with thee|et bestiæ terræ pacificæ erunt tibi]], he explains of the brute beasts, that they will do him no harm. But Albert understands by the stones of the land men of constancy, so called for the solidity of their minds, with whom he will have a covenant of friendly and peaceable dealing; and by the beasts he understands the cruel, or tyrants. [[5:24|And thou shalt know|Et scies]] by experience [[5:24|that thy tabernacle is in peace|quod pacem habeat tabernaculum tuum]], that is, thy house will be quiet and well ordered in persons, goods and buildings; [[5:24|and visiting thy beauty|et visitans speciem tuam]] [*species*, "beauty", also means "kind" or "species": Denis's first reading turns on this], that is, thy neighbour or thy wife, who are of the same species as thou, [[5:24|thou shalt not sin|non peccabis]], by behaving towards them inordinately, but with moderation. Or, [[5:24|visiting thy beauty|Visitans speciem tuam]], that is, the comeliness of riches and of things, [[5:24|thou shalt not sin|non peccabis]] by an excessive affection for such things. [[5:25|Thou shalt know also that thy seed shall be multiplied|Et scies quoniam multiplex erit semen tuum]], that is, thy sons will be many and will beget very many, [[5:25|and thy offspring|et progenies tua]] will be green, fruitful and fair, [[5:25|like the grass of the earth|sicut herba terræ]].

paras.t: Ingredieris in abundantia sepulcrum, id est, plenus divitiis morieris ac sepelieris, sicut infertur acervus tritici in tempore suo, id est tempore maturitatis seu messis, ita quod ante decrepitam senectutem non morieris. Circa quod scribit Albertus: Acervus ex multis colligitur, et triticum pretiosius granum est. Et vult dicere, quod merita cumulabit, et in æterna erit refectione pretiosissimorum bonorum. Unde Albertus, quantum ad hoc, subtilius considerasse censetur mentem amicorum Job, quod asserit eos posuisse vitam post hanc vitam, seu animam immortalem, quam alii quidam asserentes oppositum.
paras.en: [[5:26|Thou shalt enter into the grave in abundance|Ingredieris in abundantia sepulcrum]], that is, thou shalt die and be buried full of riches, [[5:26|as a heap of wheat is brought in its season|sicut infertur acervus tritici in tempore suo]], that is, at the time of ripeness or of harvest, so that thou shalt not die before decrepit old age. On which Albert writes: A heap is gathered from many grains, and wheat is the more precious grain. And he means that he will heap up merits, and will be in the eternal refreshment of the most precious goods. Hence Albert is judged on this point to have considered the mind of Job's friends more subtly, in holding that they set down a life after this life, or an immortal soul, than certain others who hold the opposite.

paras.t: Postremo, quoniam Eliphaz rhetorice disputavit, in fine sermonem suum de duobus commendat, videlicet, quod probatus exsistat et verus. Ecce hoc, totum quod nunc introduxi in istis duobus capitulis contra te, ut investigavimus, per diligentem considerationem et orationem ad Deum pro sua illuminatione fusam, ita est, id est, verum est. Quod auditum a me, mente pertracta, id est, mentaliter pensa, ut revertaris ad cor et corrigaris. Et in hoc, secundum Gregorium, Eliphaz animositatem suam ostendit. Sed (ut ante tactum est, et Thomas fatetur), quædam verborum Eliphaz secundum ejus intentionem universaliter vera non sunt, quamvis aliquando impleantur: imo promissio ista prosperitatis jam tacta, in ipso Job postea effectum sortita est.
paras.en: Lastly, since Eliphaz has argued as an orator, at the end he commends his speech on two counts, namely that it is well tested and true. [[5:27|Behold, this|Ecce hoc]], all that I have now brought forward against thee in these two chapters, [[5:27|as we have searched out|ut investigavimus]] by careful consideration and by prayer poured out to God for his light, [[5:27|is even so|ita est]], that is, it is true. [[5:27|which thou having heard|Quod auditum]] from me, [[5:27|consider it thoroughly in thy mind|mente pertracta]], that is, weigh it in thy mind, so that thou mayest return to thy heart and be corrected. And in this, according to Gregory, Eliphaz shows his self-assurance. But (as was touched on before, and as Thomas acknowledges) some of Eliphaz's words, in the sense he meant them, are not true universally, though they are sometimes fulfilled: indeed, this promise of prosperity just mentioned did afterwards come to pass in Job himself.
